->[Emblematic Engraving]<-
<note>The engraving is a complex <term>Hermetic</term> (related to the mystical teachings of Hermes Trismegistus) emblem. It illustrates the "Macrocosm" (the universe) and the "Microcosm" (the human or the laboratory scale). At the top, the Sun and Moon represent the primary polarities of alchemy, while the three figures on the hill represent the <term>Tria Prima</term>—Sulfur (Fire), Mercury (the Hexagram), and Salt (Water). The cave below, with seven seated figures, represents the seven planetary metals or the "Seven Sages" of the Rosicrucian tradition, seeking wisdom in the depths of the earth.</note>

*What exists in the realms above, is also found in the things below:* <note>original: "Quæ ſunt in ſuperis, hæc inferioribus inſunt"</note>
*What the heavens reveal, the earth often holds.* <note>original: "Quod monſtrat cœlum, id terra frequenter habet."</note>
*Fire and Water are two flowing contraries: happy are you,* <note>original: "Ignis, Aqua et fluitans duo ſunt contraria: felix,". The "flowing" likely refers to the spirit or Air that mediates between the heat of fire and the moisture of water.</note>
*If you unite such things: let it be enough for you to know!* <note>original: "Talia ſi jungis: ſit tibi ſcire ſatis!"</note>

->D.M. from C.B., Imperial Poet Laureate<-
<note>The initials "D.M. à C.B. P.L.C." refer to the author Daniel Mögling (who often wrote under the name Theophilus Schweighardt), a physician and mathematician from Constance. P.L.C. stands for *Poeta Laureatus Caesareus*, a prestigious title indicating he was a poet recognized by the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>

<summary>This page presents the core Hermetic philosophy of the text through an intricate engraving and a poem summarizing the "As Above, So Below" principle. It establishes the author's credentials as an Imperial Poet and a student of alchemical mysteries.</summary>

## Contained in this Book

I. *The Golden Treatise on the Philosopher’s Stone, written by an Anonymous Author, who was nevertheless a true possessor of the Stone.* page 1.
II. *The Golden Age Restored, by Henricus Madathanus.* 53. <note>Henricus Madathanus was a pseudonym for Adrian von Mynsicht, a German physician and alchemist.</note>
III. *The Sophic Water-Stone, or the Sages' Aquarium.* 73. <note>original: "Hydrolithus Sophicus, seu Aquarium sapientum." A famous work often attributed to Johann Ambrosius Siebmacher.</note>
IV. *The Demonstration of Nature, by Jean de Meung.* 145. <note>Jean de Meung was a 13th-century French poet best known for the Romance of the Rose.</note>
V. *The Philosophical Summary of Nicolas Flamel.* 172. <note>Flamel is perhaps the most legendary figure in Western alchemy, rumored to have achieved the Great Work.</note>
VI. *The Way of the Unique Truth.* 181.
VII. *The Glory of the World, or the Tablet of Paradise.* 203.
VIII. *A Treatise on the Generation of Metals.* 305.
IX. *The Author of the Book whose name is Alze.* 323.
X. *The Figures and Emblems of the Noble German Lambspring concerning the Philosopher’s Stone.* 337.
XI. *The Golden Tripod of Michael Maier; <note>Maier was a celebrated physician to Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II and a prolific writer on Hermeticism.</note> that is, Three Most Choice Chemical Treatises: namely, the Practice of Basil Valentine, <note>Valentine was a legendary Benedictine monk-alchemist, though many of his works are likely later creations.</note> a German Monk of the Benedictine Order, together with the Twelve Keys and an appendix, translated from the German.* 373.
XII. *The "Believe Me" or "Ordinal" of Thomas Norton, an English Philosopher, translated into Latin from an English Manuscript.* 433.
XIII. *The TESTAMENT of a certain Cremer, Abbot of Westminster, an Englishman; published for the benefit of various nations and adorned with figures skillfully engraved in copper.* 533.
XIV. *The New Chemical Light of Michael Sendivogius, <note>Sendivogius was a Polish alchemist and diplomat, famous for his work on nitre or "central salt."</note> drawn from the Fountain of Nature and manual experience.* 545.
XV. *The Second Treatise of the New Chemical Light, concerning <term>Sulfur|In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</term>.* 601.
XVI. *The Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King, by <term>Philalethes|Eirenaeus Philalethes, a pseudonym meaning "peaceful lover of truth," attributed to the American alchemist George Starkey.</term>; now indeed published in a more correct version from a manuscript.* 647.

# TO THE KIND READER.

**A**lchemy (most kind Reader), no one could call into doubt without doing an injustice, that it excels in variety, nobility, and dignity among all those arts which human reason has invented for the use of life. All Philosophers cry out as if with one voice (though in different tongues), proclaiming that this art is not only true, but indeed that after the divine law—in which lies the salvation of the soul—nothing more magnificent nor more sublime has been granted by the highest God to the human race in this world. Therefore, they preach that it must be investigated with the highest zeal and sought with all labor. 

But just as a noble wine has no need of hanging ivy <note>A reference to the Latin proverb *Vino vendibili suspensa hedera non opus est* ("Saleable wine needs no ivy hung up"), similar to the English "Good wine needs no bush." In historical times, an ivy branch or "bush" was hung outside a tavern to signal that wine was available for sale.</note>, so this art needs no herald's praise. Its truth is beyond doubt, and its utility—which is most particularly sought after in this art—is of the highest order and spread far and wide through the lives of all men. It is so clear and evident in Medicine, as well as the <term>pharmaceutical art</term> <note>original: *arte pharmaceutica*. In this context, it refers specifically to "iatrochemistry," the early modern practice of using chemical and mineral preparations for medicine, as championed by Paracelsus.</note> and many other sciences—especially in the transmutation of metals—that it seems to require neither the ornaments of speech nor the light of oratory in any way, Lest <note>The text ends mid-sentence. The catchword "quid" suggests the next page begins with "Lest anything..." (Ne quid).</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Museum Hermeticum" by praising alchemy as the most noble and useful of human arts, second only to divine law. It argues that alchemy's benefits in medicine and metallurgy are so obvious that the art requires no grand rhetorical defense.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, medicine, transmutation, iatrochemistry, Hermetic philosophy, philosophy of science</keywords>

# PREFACE.

...what shall I say now about the most necessary processing of minerals and metallic veins for the various uses of life, and the countless other benefits of this art, which I pass over for the sake of brevity? For it will be enough to mention them, since it would be too much to elaborate on them. Different people approach this art with different goals. The *Philosopher* is driven by the love and zeal for attaining wisdom, rejoicing in the knowledge itself, and in the elegant and abundant discourse concerning the divine miracles in nature to the glory of the almighty Creator. This fruit is noble enough and fruitful for a man who is a *Philosopher*, for whom there are also the most ready means for attaining wealth, if he wished to use them, and if he had not rather proposed to devote himself to this—inflamed by the love of Philosophy—while voluntarily neglecting the other <note>literally "trifles" or "toys"</note> mockeries of fortune. 

We see that the sages of the *Saracens*, *Egyptians*, *Arabs*, and *Persians* <note>In the early modern period, these groups were often credited with preserving and perfecting the "Hermetic" secrets of alchemy during the Middle Ages.</note> were of this mind; when they were oppressed by the cruelty of tyrants and driven as exiles from their homes in every direction, they provided for themselves by the remedy and protection of their art. By the discovery of <term>metallic transmutation</term> <note>original: *transmutatione metallica*. The process of changing "base" metals like lead into "noble" metals like gold or silver.</note>, they obtained for themselves not only a sufficient livelihood, but an honorable and even royal one. For they demonstrated by the deed itself that wherever one could reach with gold and silver, the way lay open to them also. 

Our discourse here is primarily concerning this true transmutation of metals, which is perfected by the <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: *Elixire*. Derived from the Arabic *al-iksir*, referring to the medicinal or transformative powder used in the Great Work.</note> or <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: *lapide philosophorum*. The legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and granting longevity.</note> alone. Even though books by many authors on this subject exist—just as this very book, the *Hermetic Museum*... 

<meta>catchword: is named (original: nuncupa-)</meta>

<summary>This page describes the motivations for practicing alchemy, contrasting the philosopher's quest for divine knowledge with the practical use of transmutation by ancient sages to survive exile and tyranny. It introduces the Elixir and the Philosopher's Stone as the primary focus of the following collection.</summary>

<keywords>metallic transmutation, Philosopher's Stone, Elixir, Museum Hermeticum, Saracens, Egyptians, history of alchemy, philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface" from the 1678 edition of the *Musæum Hermeticum*. The previous text was describing the origins of the collection and the motivations of its authors. This page explains why a new, expanded edition was necessary—specifically to counter the many fraudulent and "counterfeit" alchemical books circulating at the time.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...named <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to the title of the work.</note>, which already some years ago came to light <note>i.e., was published</note>. However, since there is no small abundance of chemical authors, and a great diversity and variety of writings—such that one writes more clearly and openly than another, and one explains the other—certain of my friends, most skilled in this art, suggested to me that I should add to this very book, the <term>Hermetic Museum</term> <note>original: *Musæo hermetico*; a famous anthology of alchemical texts first published in 1625 and expanded in 1678.</note>, several things relevant to the subject and most necessary to this art. Although, as said above, the book had been composed some years ago from the writings of select and most expert men in this art, it was not yet found to be so complete in all its parts or so perfect in every detail <note>literally "absolute in all its numbers," a Latin idiom for perfection</note> that it could bring enough of the hoped-for fruit to the studies of its readers.

Therefore, we have gladly yielded to this most honorable wish of our friends, which was primarily directed toward the common benefit of students of this art. We have seen to it that this entire book, enlarged by various most select authors and adorned with many copper-plate figures <note>original: *figuris æneis*; these high-quality engravings are a famous feature of the 1678 edition</note>, be printed. We did this especially because we reflected that many counterfeit books and false "recipes" <note>original: *recepta*</note> (as they call them) of <term>alchemists</term>—composed through the fraud and greed of impostors, and in which not even a spark of truth shines—are circulating among the investigators of natural and occult arts. By these books, very many people have been deceived and are still being deceived. In contrast, those who read this book, in which the <term>Mastery of the Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapidis magisterium*; the secret process for creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is expressed most clearly and plainly, will find no error placed there, and no...

## THE AUTHOR TO THE LOVER OF ART
### To the Reader

# PREFACE.

*<margin>D</margin>o not wonder, kind Reader and true seeker of nature’s secrets, why in this old age of the world—when it already has one foot in Charon’s boat <note>original: "in cymba habet Charontis". In Greek mythology, Charon is the ferryman who carries souls across the river Styx to the underworld. I have written this, whatever its worth may be, not for my own sake but for your benefit, so that by demonstrating the foundation of truth, I may lead you back from wandering paths into the true track; a matter in which you certainly have no small interest. As for what concerns me, I have long since known whatever I ought to know in this business, nor do I have need for a great number of books, since within twenty-two years I have read, read through, and re-read as many books as came into my hands; among their number, which was indeed great, there were many manuscripts as well as printed works.*

# THE GOLDEN TREATISE,

->ON THE<-

## PHILOSOPHERS' STONE.

**B**oth the ancient and modern philosophers, most beloved Reader and dearest seeker of true wisdom, have always made it their custom—once they attained the goal of their desire by God's will—to reveal themselves through their writings to their colleagues who are hidden here and there throughout the whole world. They did so not only for the purpose of wishing to make them certain that God, the Thrice-Greatest and Best, had enlightened their intellect, blessed the labors of their hands, and demonstrated to them the most secret and greatest <term>arcanum<note>A Latin term meaning "secret" or "mystery." In alchemy, it refers to the hidden, powerful essence of a substance or the ultimate secret of the Work.</note></term> of this earthly wisdom, for which benefit indeed deserved praise, honor, and glory are owed to Him; but also that they might provide an opportunity to their neighbor and the <term>art-loving<note>original: "technophilo." A Greek-derived term for someone who loves the craft or "art" of alchemy.</note></term> disciple to arrive, God willing, at this most holy art and the knowledge of it.

Men of this kind have existed in all nations: Egyptians—among whom Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure considered the founding father of alchemy; the name means "Thrice-Greatest Hermes."</note> stands out uniquely—Chaldeans, Greeks, Arabs, Italians, French, English, Dutch, Spanish, Germans, Poles, Hungarians, Hebrews, and many others. Yet it is a marvel that the aforementioned sages, writing in different languages at different times, agree with such harmony in their books that it is easy for any true philosopher to recognize that God has cheered their minds with this blessed stone, and that they themselves have completed this work with their own hands. Just as truth shines forth from such agreement, so from the disagreement of the pseudo-philosophasters and

<meta>catchword: sophists</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>

# ON THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE.

The sophists <note>In an alchemical context, "sophists" refers to "false alchemists" or "puffers" who lack true philosophical understanding and experiment blindly with the wrong materials.</note> are exposed here. For they, being ignorant of the foundation of this noble art and fashioning whatever they please from their own imaginations, reveal their errors to everyone.

However, the "harmony" mentioned before consists primarily in the knowledge of the matter, and in its dissolution, weight, the regulation of the fire, and its increase.

As for the matter, it is unique, containing within itself everything it requires. From this matter, the craftsman prepares whatever he wishes. It is the <term>effort<note>original: "Nisus."</note></term> in the <term>sand<note>original: "Arena."</note></term>, as the philosopher Anastratus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba." Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various sages.</note>: 
> *Nothing is more precious than the red sea-sand, and it is the spit of the Moon, which is joined to the light of the Sun and is congealed.*

That only this single matter is required is testified by Agadmon in the same book, where he says: 
> *Know that unless you take this body of mine which lacks a spirit, you will by no means achieve what you desire; for nothing foreign enters the work, nor anything but what is pure. Therefore, abandon all multiplicity. For Nature is content with one thing, and he who is ignorant of it will perish.*

In the same way, Arnold of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> writes in his *Flower of Flowers*: 
> *Our stone is made from one thing and with one thing.* 
Similarly, he says to the King of Naples: 
> *Everything that is in our stone is necessary to it, nor does it need anything foreign: for our stone is of one nature and is one single thing.* 
And Rosinus says: 
> *Know that there is a single thing from which all the things you desire are made.* 
And *The Lily* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical text.</note>: 
> *You have no need of anything but one thing, which in every stage of our work is changed into another nature.* 
So too Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of Islamic and Western alchemy.</note> says in his *Summa*: 
> *Our stone is one, one medicine, to which we add nothing, nor do we take anything away; we only remove the superfluities.* 
And Scites says in the *Assembly*: 
> *The foundation of this art is indeed one thing, which is stronger and more sublime than all other things; it is called the "sharpest vinegar," which makes pure gold to be spirit—without which neither the whiteness, nor the blackness, nor the redness exists. And when it is mixed with the body, it is contained and becomes one with it, and it turns the body into spirit, tingeing it with a spiritual and unchanging tincture; in turn, it receives from the tinged body a physical tincture that cannot be erased. And if you place the body on the fire without this vinegar, it will be burned and destroyed.*

But from these words of Scites, someone might conclude and infer that there are not one, but two things—namely, the body...

<summary>This page argues for the "Unity of Matter," citing various historical authorities like Geber and Arnold of Villanova to prove that the Philosophers' Stone is made from a single, self-sufficient substance often metaphorically called "sharpest vinegar" or "sea-sand."</summary>
<keywords>Unity of Matter, Turba Philosophorum, Arnold of Villanova, Geber, sharpest vinegar, albedo, nigredo, rubedo, sputum lunae, sophists</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument for the "Unity of Matter" from page 9. It addresses the technical requirements for combining the "moist" and "dry" principles and provides a list of various names used by famous alchemical authorities to describe the one secret substance. It concludes with the preparation of the spirits from this single matter.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>

### Golden Treatise,

...and vinegar <note>original: "acetum." In alchemy, "Philosophical Vinegar" is not common household vinegar, but a specialized acidic solvent used to dissolve metals.</note> (as he calls it) is required, and that necessarily the moist must be joined with the dry, lest the dry be burned up by the fire, but rather be preserved from such combustion by the moist. I willingly subscribe to this conclusion when it is rightly understood, while meanwhile preserving the previously cited philosophical opinions in their full value and truth. 

For it is more certain than certain that there is but one single matter of our blessed stone, though it is called by the many names of the sages. Nature prepared this matter for the craftsman long ago; she willed that it alone, and no other in all the world, should be the matter of our stone. This matter is set before the eyes of everyone; the whole world looks at it, touches it, loves it, and yet does not know it. It is noble and base, precious and of little value, and is found everywhere. 

Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine.</note>, in his book *On the Tincture of the Physicists*, calls it the **RED LION**, a name known by many but understood by few. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy.</note>, in the first chapter of his treatise, calls it *quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note> congealed in its innermost chambers*. In the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> it is called *brass* here and there. In the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosario." The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a seminal 16th-century alchemical text focusing on the "chemical wedding" or union of opposites.</note> it is designated by the name of *Salt*. 

But, to be brief, this matter of ours has as many names as there are things in the world; this is why it is so little recognized by the foolish. I call those people "foolish" who approach this art without a prior knowledge of Nature and her properties, just like a donkey coming to a manger, not knowing why it stretches out its snout, as Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says. Whence Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in Arabic alchemy; the "Summa Perfectionis" was the most influential alchemical textbook in medieval Europe.</note> beautifully writes in his *Summit of Perfection*: 
> *He who is ignorant of the natural principles within himself is already far removed from this art.* 

And the *Rosary* says: 
> *I advise that no one should involve themselves in this art of discovery unless they know the principle of true Nature and its governance; once this is known, one needs nothing more than this one thing. Nor does it require great expense, for there is but one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one governance, and one disposition.* 

Nevertheless, this unique matter is so separated by the work of Nature and the experience of the craftsman—as Theophrastus speaks—that it is transmuted into that <term>white eagle<note>original: "aquilam." In alchemy, the "Eagle" often refers to the volatile spirit or sal ammoniac that "flies" up during sublimation.</note></term>, so that the splendor of the sun no longer illuminates the <term>alchemist<note>original: "spagirum." A follower of spagyrics, the Paracelsian method of separating and recombining the components of plants and minerals.</note></term> with its rays. Or, as Basil Valentine <note>A legendary 15th-century Benedictine monk and alchemist, likely a pseudonym for Johann Thölde.</note> says: 
> *From it is made a white spirit like snow, and likewise another red spirit like blood; these two spirits contain a third hidden within themselves.* 

Whence King Aros <note>A figure often appearing in the "Turba Philosophorum" and other early Latin alchemical texts.</note> says not incorrectly: 
> *Our medicine is made from two of one essence, namely from the union...*

## On the Stone of the Philosophers.

...mercurial union of fixed and non-fixed nature, spiritual and corporal, cold and moist, hot and dry, and it can by no means be made from anything else. And Richard the Englishman <note>A 13th-century alchemist often associated with the "Correctorium Alchymiae."</note> says: *The Stone is one, a single medicine, which according to the philosophers is called* **REBIS** <note>original: "REBIS." A famous alchemical term meaning "two-fold thing," representing the union of opposites like male and female or spirit and body.</note>, *that is, made of two things: namely, of the body and the spirit, white or red. In this, many fools have erred, interpreting it in various ways:*

*REBIS is the most correct form figured in the sayings.* That is, two things: and these two things are one thing, namely, water joined to the body, by which the body is dissolved into spirit, that is, into mineral water, from which it was made from the beginning. And thus from body and spirit one mineral water is made, which is called **Elixir**, that is, a ferment <note>original: "fermentum." In alchemy, the Elixir acts like leaven in bread, "fermenting" base metals to turn them into gold.</note>: because then water and spirit are one thing, from which the tincture is made, and the medicine for purging all bodies. Therefore, from one thing, which is the water of the body and spirit, the medicine is perfected. And thus, according to the philosophers, we have the nature of sulfur and mercury <note>Sulfur and Mercury are the two primary "parents" of all metals in alchemical theory.</note> above the earth, from which gold and silver were made under the earth. And Bernard, Count of Treviso and the March <note>A 15th-century Italian alchemist famous for his lifelong quest for the Stone.</note> says: *Our work is made from one root and two raw mercurial substances, taken and drawn from the mine, pure and clean, joined by fire in friendship, as the matter itself requires, continuously cooked until from the two, one is made, etc.*

And Basil Valentine <note>A legendary 15th-century monk and alchemist; the name is likely a pseudonym for several authors.</note> in the book of *Natural and Supernatural Things*, chapter 4, says: *In all truth, through the love of God, I will reveal this to you besides: that the root of the philosophical sulfur—which is a celestial spirit—along with the root of the spiritual and metaphysical <note>original: "hyperphysici," meaning beyond the physical or supernatural.</note> mercury, and the principle of the spiritual salt, exist in one and are found in a single matter from which the Stone (which was before me) is made, and not from many things. Although mercury by itself, sulfur by itself, and salt by itself are specifically cited by all philosophers, as if mercury were found in one, sulfur in another, and salt in a third. I tell you, however, that they have brought these things forth from their abundance to show in which things they are found copiously, and how they can be conveniently applied and prepared in many particular ways, as much for healing human bodies as for transmuting metals. But that universal thing—surely the highest treasure of this earthly wisdom—and the principles of all three things, is a certain single thing, and they are found and extracted together in one thing, which is able to convert all metals into one. And these are the true spirit of mercury and the soul of sulfur, united together with the spiritual salt, and enclosed under one sky, as well as dwelling in one body; and they are the dragon and the eagle, the king and the lion, the spirit and the body, tinging the body of gold into a true medicine, etc.*

### The Golden Treatise

In this same way, our prepared matter is called male and female, active and passive; as Zimon says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various sages.</note>: *Know that the secret of the work consists of male and female, that is, the active and the passive. In lead is the male, in orpiment <note>original: "auripigmento." A bright yellow mineral, chemically arsenic trisulfide, used as a pigment and in alchemical experiments.</note> is the female. The male rejoices once the female is received and is helped by her, and the female receives the tinting seed from the male, and is colored by it.* And Diomedes says: *Join the male, the son of the red servant, to his fragrant wife, and joined they will give birth to the Art; to these do not introduce anything foreign, neither powder nor any other thing, and the conception will suffice for you, and a true son shall be born.* Oh, how very precious is the nature of that red servant, without which the regimen <note>original: "regimen." The controlled process, sequence of operations, or stages of heat in the alchemical work.</note> cannot be established. Others call it quicksilver, or mercury, and sulfur or fire, just as Roger Bacon <note>A 13th-century English friar and philosopher associated with the beginnings of experimental science and alchemy.</note> says in the third chapter of the *Mirror*: *From sulfur and mercury all metals are made, and nothing adheres to them, nor is joined to them, nor transforms them, except that which is of them.* And so, by right, we must take mercury and sulfur as the material for the stone. And Menabadus says: *He who joins quicksilver to the body of magnesia <note>original: "magnesiæ." In alchemy, this does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but rather a "mother" material or a primary substance from which the stone is extracted.</note>, and the female to the male, extracts the hidden nature by which bodies are colored.* Lully <note>Raymond Lully, a Majorcan polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> says in the *Codicil*: *The property of our mercury is that it is coagulated by its own sulfur.* And in the practice of his *Testament* he says: *Quicksilver is a floating and flowing moisture that preserves against burning.*

Others call it body, spirit, and soul. So says Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> in the *Flower of Flowers*: *The Philosophers said that our stone is composed of body, soul, and spirit, and they spoke truly. For they compared the imperfect body to the "body" because it is weak. They called the water "spirit," and truly so, because it is a spirit. They called the ferment <note>original: "fermentum." In alchemy, the substance that transforms or "leavens" the base matter into gold.</note> "soul," because it grants life to the imperfect body, which it did not have before, and produces a better form.*

And a little earlier he says: *The spirit is not joined to the body except by the mediation of the soul. For the soul is the medium between the body and the spirit, joining them together.* And Morienus <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have been the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: *The soul quickly enters its own body; but if you strive to join it to a foreign body, you will labor in vain.* And the *Lily* <note>Likely referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae* (Lily of Alchemy), a popular medieval treatise.</note>: *Soul, body, and spirit are together, and are one thing, which has all things within itself, and to which nothing is added.*

It emphasizes that the Great Work requires only internal components and the proper union of these opposites to succeed.</summary>

-> # On the Philosopher's Stone <-

But to what end shall we bring forth and explain all the names by which this matter of ours is designated? We shall rest content with these common names, as they are more frequent and closer to our intention. After the investigation of our matter—where it may truly lie hidden and from where it ought to be brought forth—we shall see something regarding the "solution" <note>In alchemy, "solution" refers to the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid state, often considered the first major step of the "Great Work."</note>, as it is the head of the matter, and by the treatment of it we shall sharpen our intellect.

Regarding the consideration of our matter—what it is and where it ought to be sought—it must be marked, as they say, with a white stone <note>original: "albo calculo." A Latin idiom meaning to mark something as special, lucky, or highly important.</note>, that the almighty Creator, whose wisdom is as infinite as He is Himself, created two things in the beginning of the world when there was nothing but Himself: namely, the celestial things and those things contained beneath the heavens. The celestial are the heavens themselves and the heavenly inhabitants, about whom we shall refrain from speaking or philosophizing too subtly or abundantly in this place. 

But beneath the heavens, three types of created things are found, made from the <term>four Elements</term> <note>The classic elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth, which were believed to compose all physical matter.</note>, and they are commonly divided into three genera. Among these, those that live and feel hold the first place and are called <term>animals</term>. The second genus holds whatever things are produced from the earth and do not feel, and these are called <term>vegetables</term>. Finally, whatever things come forth from beneath the earth are numbered in the third genus and are called <term>minerals</term>. 

These three genera of created things encompass everything produced from the elements beneath the globe of the Moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, which in ancient cosmology was the realm of all things subject to change, growth, and decay.</note>; no more and no fewer than these are found. In such a way has the highest God confirmed each thing in its own genus and species that it is impossible for them to leap from one genus to another. For example, if someone were to attempt to fashion a human or a tree out of a stone; or to make some monkey or lead out of a herb; or to make some animal or herb out of lead. This, I say, is impossible by the ordinance of the Highest King. Indeed, if this were permitted in the nature of things, some of these—nay, all genera—could be turned into one. But because everything would then collapse into ruin, the Lord of Lords did not wish to grant such a <term>transmutation</term> <note>original: "transmutationem." The fundamental change of one kingdom of nature into another.</note>. 

Nay, what is more, He not only willed that each thing be preserved in its own genus, but He also placed within each creature its own proper seed, by which it might be increased in its own species and persist in its own genus, so that the species of one cannot be changed into another. For instance, if one tried to change the species of a human into that of a horse, or an apple into a lettuce, or a diamond into...

...of another stone into gold, he would be wide of the mark <note>original: "toto ille cælo erraret." And as it was from the beginning, so it shall be also in the end, when the Almighty—who in the beginning said **LET IT BE**—shall say, **PERISH**. But among those things which share one common matter, seed, and composition of the Elements, improvement and exaltation can easily be achieved and perfected, according to the purity and perfection of their matter. For example, we see a man endowed with a subtle and sharp intellect raised to a higher degree of dignity than others who do not possess such a mind; this takes its origin from the purity and subtlety of the spirits which are born from a rectified and well-constituted body. Likewise, we see that one horse far excels another in its nobility, which is also clearly visible in all species of living creatures. 

Just as we see these things in animals, so we may observe them much more in herbs and trees: in trees, through transplanting, grafting, and other means known to gardeners; in herbs, however, we are taught by daily experience how the herbs and flowers of a single species differ from one another in their nobility, beauty, scent, and flavor. Let the carnations <note>original: "caryophylli," also known as clove-pinks.</note> and the tulips serve as examples for us, to say nothing of others. Good God, into how many species have these been extended? Into countless varieties, I say! Through diligent care, they become more noble and rare from day to day, so much so that it is widely admitted that such fragrant and elegant flowers did not exist before this time. 

But what shall I say of metals, which share one common matter—namely, <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note> digested and coagulated by the power of <term>sulfur</term>? # On the Philosophers' Stone.

The conclusion according to Saratanta <note>likely a reference to an alchemical authority or specific manuscript source</note>: *The matter of all metals is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, digested and imperfect in the belly of the earth, cooked by a sulfurous heat; and according to the variety of sulfur, different metals are generated in the earth, even though their primordial matter is one and the same, depending only on whether the action of the heat is greater or lesser, and whether it is tempered or not.* For this reason, we see daily how Nature herself is continually concerned with the mortification and perfection of these metals, until they are perfected into gold, which is the final intention of Nature. For all metals show that Nature, in working upon them, has achieved a somewhat less than perfect result <note>original: "adulteriorem perfectionem," suggesting an impure or "bastardized" state compared to the ideal</note>; indeed, no metal is found so diminished from perfection that it does not contain at least a grain of gold or silver. And indeed, it is so arranged with metals that Nature, from quicksilver containing its own sulfur within itself, strives to produce gold as soon as possible, and is indeed capable of it, unless some <term>external</term> impediment intervenes, <term>namely</term> an <term>unclean</term>, foul, and burning sulfur—just as we see in many places pure, clear, and refined <note>original: "obrizum," referring to gold of the highest purity</note> gold is dug out without the admixture of other <term>metals</term>. However, because in the mines an external sulfur is most often mixed with the quicksilver, it infects the quicksilver and prevents it from reaching perfection. According to the variety of this sulfur, various species of metals are generated, just as <term>Aristotle</term> says in the 4th book of Meteorology <note>original: "4. meteor." Aristotle’s work on natural phenomena, which was a cornerstone of medieval and early modern science</note>: *If the quicksilver is of good substance, and the sulfur is not pure and burning, it converts that quicksilver into copper. Also, if the quicksilver is stony, unclean, and earthy, and the sulfur is not pure, iron will be made from it. Tin, however, is seen to have good and pure quicksilver, but bad and poorly mixed sulfur. Lead, moreover, has coarse and bad quicksilver, of a bad and foul flavor, which is why it does not coagulate well.*

However, that hindering, burning, and foul sulfur is not the true fire that digests metals; rather, quicksilver contains its own proper sulfur within itself, which is sufficient for its own digestion, just as <term>Bernard, Count of Trevisan</term> <note>a famous 15th-century alchemist known for his search for the Philosophers' Stone</note> says: *Some mistakenly believe that some sulfurous matter intervenes in the procreation of metals; but on the contrary, it is clearly evident that sulfur is included within the mercury when Nature operates.*

## The Golden Treatise,

Truth <note>original: "Verum," referring here to the essential or pure nature of the matter</note> does not dominate in it, except through a warm motion, by which the said sulfur is altered, along with two other qualities of mercury. In this way, nature—through this sulfur in the veins of the earth—generates various forms of metals, according to the different degrees of alteration. For in metals, according to *Arnold* <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist</note> in part one, chapter three, there is a double superfluity: one is enclosed deep within the quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver," the standard term for mercury</note> and occurs at the start of its mixing; the other is outside its own nature and is corruptible. This second kind is removed with great effort; the first, however, can be removed by no skill of the craftsman.

Therefore, the combustible sulfurousness is removed by the <term>calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to remove volatile impurities or change its chemical state</note> of fire, or is deleted from the bodies; and because quicksilver holds and preserves from burning that which belongs to its own nature, it rejects the other, exposing it to the fire, which corrupts it. But that internal sulfur, which digests its own quicksilver and matures it toward perfection, is likewise either pure or impure, and combustible or incombustible. Impure sulfur hinders the "digestion" <note>in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation of matter through gentle heat</note> of the quicksilver, so that it is less able to transform into gold, until it is finally separated from it on all sides, and that other pure, incombustible, and fixed sulfur remains with it. Only then is gold or silver made from it, depending on whether that sulfur was white or red <note>Alchemists associated white sulfur with the creation of silver and red sulfur with gold</note>.

This internal sulfur is nothing other than mature mercury, or a more advanced and digested part of quicksilver; because of this, the quicksilver receives it so naturally <note>original: "amicè," literally "friendly"</note>, while rejecting what is foreign. As *Richard the Englishman* <note>Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century author often cited in alchemical compendiums</note> says in chapter nine: *Insofar as sulfur becomes more simple, to that same degree it rejoices in and clings to simple and clean mercury, so that they are more strongly joined together, and thus more perfect metals are then generated from them.* Such sulfur, according to the opinion of *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works on "The Soul in the Art of Alchemy" were widely read in Latin translation</note>, is not found upon the earth, except for what exists in those bodies of the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical code, the "Sun" (Sol) refers to gold and the "Moon" (Luna) refers to silver</note>. In the Sun it is more perfect, because it is more digested and "cooked." Indeed, according to *Richard* in chapter twelve: *The red sulfur of the Philosophers exists in the Sun through greater digestion, and white sulfur in the Moon through lesser digestion.*

Since all these things are so—namely, that there exists one unique and common matter of metals, which by the power of its innate sulfur either immediately...

...or after it has set aside the external and evil <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, combustible, and often "impure" principle that must be purged to reach the perfection of gold</note> of the remaining metals through <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of maturing or ripening matter through gentle, continuous heat, mimicking the Earth’s natural processes</note> over the course of time, it may pass into gold, which is the end of metals and the true intention of nature: we are certainly compelled to admit and say that nature, in this category as well as in the vegetable and animal kingdoms, seeks and demands the improvement and perfection of its nature according to the purity and subtlety of the subject.

I wished to pursue these things a little more at length, friend and seeker of nature, so that you might be able to know the material of our stone and put it to use all the more easily. For if you wished to produce this stone of ours from animal matter, the obstacle is that these two are founded in different kinds. For the stone is mineral, but you would be seeking animal matter. *But nothing can be drawn out from any thing, as our author **Richard** <note>likely referring to Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century alchemist</note> says in his first chapter, which is not already in it. Therefore every species in its own species, and every genus in its own genus, and every nature in its own nature naturally strives for the increase of its virtue, and brings forth fruit according to its own nature, and not in another nature contrary to itself: since everything sown corresponds to its own seed.* And **Basilius Valentinus** <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary 15th-century alchemist/monk whose works emphasized the three principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> says: *Consider and understand, my friend, that the animal soul is not to be chosen by you for this intention of yours. For just as flesh and blood were granted to animals by the Creator, so also they are proper to animals, from which animals were formed and born.* 

I cannot, therefore, sufficiently wonder at those who wish to seem great craftsmen, and yet do not fear to seek the material of the stone in menstrual blood, sperm, eggs, hair, urine, and other things of that sort <note>original: "ejus farinæ," literally "of that flour," an idiom for "of that kind"</note>, and to fill so many books with their vain and empty recipes, so that they may deceive and lead astray others less prudent with these foolish, futile, and useless things. **Roger** <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), a medieval friar and philosopher associated with early experimental science and alchemy</note> in the third chapter of his *Mirror* <note>original: "speculi," referring to the *Speculum Alchemiae* (The Mirror of Alchemy)</note> cannot sufficiently wonder at the vanities of such men, when he says: *Wherefore it is to be wondered at that any prudent man should base his intention upon animals or vegetables, which are very remote; since minerals are found to be close enough. Nor is it to be believed at all that any of the philosophers placed*

<header>The Golden Treatise.</header>

*...the art [cannot be found] in the aforementioned remote things, except by way of similarity. For our Stone (says **Basil**) <note>original: Basilius; referring to Basil Valentine, a legendary 15th-century alchemist</note> does not grow from combustible things. For indeed this Stone and its matter are safe enough from all violence <note>In this context, "violence" refers to the destructive power of fire</note>. Therefore, stop searching for it in animals; since it is not granted to nature to find it there.*

If anyone, however, convinces himself that our Stone can be found in vegetables—such as trees, herbs, or flowers—he will err no less, for the reasons mentioned above, than he who wishes to set his mind on making a rock from an animal. For indeed all herbs and trees, along with everything produced from them, are burned up and leave nothing behind but their own **salt** with their earth—the salt which they received from nature at the first composition of their species. Nor should anyone allow himself to be seduced by the fact that some boast that the **Philosopher's Stone** can be produced from wheat. Nor should those be listened to any more who convince themselves they can make our Stone from wine or its parts. For when they fail to grasp the mind of **Raymond Lully** <note>original: Raymundus Lullius; a 13th-century philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> as declared in his writings, they clearly demonstrate that by being "too wise" they actually know nothing at all, deceiving both themselves and others. I will not deny, of course, that most excellent <term>menstrua</term> <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a powerful solvent or liquid medium used to dissolve solids, named after the "menstrual" cycle due to its perceived role in the "conception" of new substances</note> are prepared and fashioned from such things—without which nothing solid can be done in either medicine or <term>chemistry</term> <note>original: chymia; at this time, chemistry and alchemy were often used interchangeably</note>. But that the Philosopher's Stone can be prepared from them, or its seed drawn out from them, I entirely deny; since, by the command of the Creator of all things, it is right for everything to persist in its own kind, as has been said, and it can in no way leap across to another. 

From this, anyone dedicated to true wisdom can gather that our Stone cannot be drawn from vegetables or animals—seeing as they are combustible. Reason therefore commands the conclusion that it must be sought and prepared only among incombustible things: namely, in the **mineral kingdom**. Since, therefore, the Stone of the Wise is something mineral, and there are many species of minerals—such as stones (among which clay and various earths are counted), salts, "middle" minerals, and metals—it is not unfitting to ask: from which of these should it be obtained? I answer that it is impossible for it to be made from common stones. The reason is that there is no fusible and liquefiable <term>mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury is the principle of liquidity and volatility, the "spirit" of metals, rather than just the element on the periodic table</note> in them; nor can they be melted, dissolved, or reduced back to their **first matter** <note>The "materia prima," the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things were thought to be created</note> because of the abundance of external <term>sulfur</term> <note>The principle of combustion and "staining" or impurity</note> and the adhering earthy properties.

<summary>The author rejects plants and wine as sources for the Philosopher's Stone, arguing that because the Stone is incombustible, it must be sought exclusively in the mineral kingdom, though not in common stones or clay.</summary>

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

A wise seeker of nature’s secrets will also cease searching for the material of the blessed stone in salts, alums, and things of that sort. For in these he will find a sharp, corrosive, and corrupting spirit, but he will never obtain **mercury** and **sulfur** from these, according to the opinion of the philosophers. Furthermore, the <term>middle minerals</term> <note>original: media mineralia; substances like ores and semi-metals that were thought to be "half-way" between stones and true metals</note>, such as magnesia, marcasite, antimony, etc., can much less ever become any metal; how then could the matter of the Stone—which is the end and perfection of all metals and minerals—be extracted from there? I add that they have nothing in common or familiar with metals, but instead burn, corrode, and corrupt them; how then can they serve their improvement?

Hear **Richard the Englishman** <note>original: Richardum Anglicum; a 13th-century physician and alchemist, likely Richard of Wendover</note> speaking on this matter in the tenth chapter:

> *Minor minerals cannot become metals, first because they were not generated from the first matter of metals, which is **quicksilver** <note>original: argentum vivum</note>. Since their generation differs from the generation of mercury in form, matter, and composition, they cannot become metals because for one species there is one first matter and the seed from which it is generated. But the first part of the premise is evident, because minor minerals are not generated from mercury, as is clear from **Aristotle** and **Avicenna** <note>the 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher whose works on geology influenced Western alchemy</note>. Therefore, if they were to become metals, it would be necessary for them to change into the first matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, they will by no means be metals, and consequently, they cannot be the matter of the Stone. Second, because minor minerals cannot artificially become the "principle of the art"—which is mercury—they also do not reach the middle and the end, which are metals and the **tincture** <note>the "tincture" is the Stone’s power to permeate and transform base metals into gold</note>. But because minor minerals are foreign to metals by nature, although they share in some mineral force, they are nevertheless of a weaker power and are combustible. Therefore, the metallic nature does not rejoice in them but rejects them, while it preserves those things that are of its own nature. Wherefore they are fools who bring forth so many and such diverse works and deceptions to mislead men—namely, disproportionate things that neither give nature [to metals] nor receive it. Thus says he.*

But truly, let no student of our wisdom [be misled] by the aforementioned and similar sayings of the philosophers when they speak at times of salts...

This is clear in the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosario philosophorum"; a foundational 14th-century alchemical text</note>, where it is said: *The salt of metals is the Philosopher's Stone: for our stone is water congealed in gold and silver, and it resists fire, and is dissolved in its own water, from which it is composed according to its kind.*

Moreover, **Geber** <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy</note> teaches in the 19th chapter of the *Book of Furnaces* that the "congealed water" of the philosophers is not mineral water, saying: *Strive to resolve the sun <note>gold</note> and the moon <note>silver</note> into their own dry water, which the common people call mercury.* The philosophers even designated their "earth" by the name of salt, as appears in the *Blare of the Trumpet* <note>original: "clangore buccinæ"; an influential alchemical treatise</note>, where it is said: *That which remains as a residue in the bottom of the gourd <note>the cucurbit, or the lower part of a still</note> is our salt; that is, our earth.* And in the *Allegories of the Sages*, they break forth into these words: *Note that these bodies are the alums and salts which flow forth from our bodies.*

Sometimes they even call the medicine itself "salt," as is said in the *Ladder* <note>original: "Scala philosophorum"</note>: *The work of the second water is to exalt the earth into its own mineral salt, only through its attractive power.* And **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says in the third book of *On the Preservation of Youth*: *But that to which nothing is equal (in the preservation of youth) is the salt of the mine.* The sages compared this prepared substance to the natural heat of healthy youth. Because of this similarity, the sages used and called the stone itself by the name of a living creature; others called it the <term>mineral chifir</term> <note>original: "chifir minerale"; likely a Latinization of an Arabic term for a hidden or protected substance</note>, and by some it is called the "perennial medicine" or the "water of life." The whole *art of the preparation is that it be reduced into a most pure and potable water with things that possess the same property as itself.*

From the preceding points, it is clearly evident that the Stone cannot be made from minor minerals, neither according to the doctrine of the philosophers nor the property of Nature itself.

Now, order requires that we look around a little to see whether the material of our Great Stone can be drawn from the <term>middle minerals</term> <note>original: "mediis mineralibus"; substances categorized between stones and true metals</note>—namely from marcasite, antimony, magnesia, and others—especially since the philosophers make frequent mention of them. when he says: *Unless there were in orpiment <note>original: "auripigmento"; a golden-yellow arsenic mineral whose name literally means "gold pigment"</note> a power for coagulating mercury, our Great Work <note>original: "magisterium"</note> would never be led to its conclusion.* And **Thomas Aquinas** <note>a famous medieval theologian to whom several alchemical works were [likely falsely] attributed</note> says: *Take our antimony, or the black-eyed earth <note>original: "terram nigram oculatam"; likely referring to the glistening, eye-like appearance of mineral crystals during the purification stage</note>, etc.* And **Parmenides** in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba Philofophorum"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among Greek philosophers</note> says: *Take quicksilver, and coagulate it in the body of magnesia, or in combustible sulfur.* However, it must be noted that the philosophers do not put forward such speeches to show that the Great Stone can be made from these common things, but rather they speak **parabolically and figuratively**.

And they certainly call it "orpiment" because it has the faculty of granting to gold a superfluous and exuberant color and tincture; but it is called "magnesia" by reason of its innate virtue and excellence, which derives and flows from it. Furthermore, that Thomas Aquinas wished to call it "antimony" was done on account of its shining blackness, to which it is led once the solution is completed. But someone will object to me, suggesting that some of these intermediate minerals <note>original: "mediorum mineralium"; substances that fall between "true" metals and "earthy" minerals</note> are not only born from mercury and sulfur, but can even be reduced into metals—just as we see magnesia join with lead and tin in a state of flux, and antimony not only mixes with metals, but even a lead not foreign to the natural kind is made from it. Moreover, they may argue that many people of both noble and common status have seen gold produced from these minerals more than once. They argue that because these things are generated from sulfur and mercury (into which they can be reduced by the benefit of the art), they are of the same origin as the metals; therefore, the matter of our Stone can be drawn from them. 

But I wish to answer this person as follows: first, a certain distinction must be made among these minerals—namely, between those that have mercury within them, and those that mostly lack it. <page-num>22</page-num>
# The Golden Treatise

...[Mercury] can be transformed into gold and silver through our medicine, and for this reason, in my opinion, it is not undeservedly held in high regard among the metals that are surely inclined toward a metallic nature. However, the rest, in which no mercury is present, are of no use for this Mastery. But because of the "evil" and burning sulfur within them, it is not permitted for them to reach such an end; they cannot be recognized as the material for our Stone, which must be pure and perfect mercury, and pure, subtle, and incombustible sulfur.

That these substances are quite impure and completely infected by their own sulfur is easily placed before our eyes during their examination, when their potential is tested. For we see in **Zinc** <note>original: "Zineto"; an early term for metallic zinc or its ore</note>, which will be judged by the imprudent to be pure mercury based on its face—judging by its luster and weight—that as soon as the fire takes hold of it, it quickly flies away in the manner of sulfurous smoke. **Marcasites**, however, cannot be melted by the power of fire on account of their earthy and coarse impurity.

But **Antimony**, which can be purged of its excessive filth in a certain way by a learned <term>encheiresis</term> <note>original: "encheirefi"; a Latinization of the Greek word for a manual operation or chemical procedure</note> and brought into a most white and beautiful <term>regulus</term> <note>original: "regulum"; literally "little king," referring to the metallic bead or heart of a mineral produced through smelting</note>, will easily persuade us that something remarkable can be produced from it. Indeed, many people, who attribute a great deal to themselves, claim that the philosophical Stone can be prepared from it. Nevertheless, however it may be, even if this antimony is purged of its blackness by whatever method or skill, it retains its "malice" and the hard quality of sulfur. This is clear from the fact that it cannot be drawn out under the hammer or made malleable, which is indeed a property of any true metal—by which, according to other properties, it is judged to be a metal. I will say nothing of the fact that it contains a coarse and unclean mercury, and likewise that it always retains a "fleeing" sulfur within itself.

Therefore, you who wish to be great Philosophers, and who seduce so many with your books and copious writings by thinking this very thing is the foundation of your "Universal," I wish for you to be asked again and again to take it in good part that I cannot subscribe to your opinion. For **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: *It is foolish to seek in a thing that which is not in it.* And in the *Exercise on the Assembly* <note>original: "exercitatione in Turbam"; refers to a commentary on the "Turba Philosophorum," a core alchemical text</note> it is said: *The Stone of the philosophers is pure matter.* And **Lully** <note>Raymond Lully, a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> in his *Last Testament* says:

# On the Stone of the Philosophers.

It is cited: *Our tincture is nothing but pure fire.* And in the *Vade Mecum* <note>Latin: "Go with me"; a title for a portable manual or reference book, often attributed to alchemical authors like Arnold of Villanova</note> he says: *It is only the subtle spirit which tints and cleanses bodies of their leprous states.* <note>Alchemists used "leprosy" as a metaphor for the impurities and corrosion found in common metals.</note> But this mineral, like all the others without exception, is so coarse and impure that in no way can that impurity be sequestered from it except through the mediation of our tincture; therefore, the material for our great Stone cannot be elicited from it, since nothing can be drawn out of something which is not already in it, according to Richard <note>likely Richard the Englishman, a 13th-century alchemist</note> in chapter 1.

But what shall we say of <term>vitriol</term> <note>a term for metallic sulfates, such as copper sulfate (blue vitriol) or iron sulfate (green vitriol)</note>, which by its wonderful qualities leads many into error, especially because some small part of it turns into copper, and it even turns iron itself into copper. Briefly, it should be known about this that it is nothing other than the principle and material of copper, where in the mines and veins of the earth a mineral vapor—a "vaporous mercury," so to speak—finds a certain place in which a bitter, acidic, sharp, and Venereal sulfur <note>"Venereal" refers to Venus, the alchemical and astrological name for copper.</note> lay hidden in abundance; this it immediately receives, and in it, it is coagulated so that it might become a metal. 

But because nature satisfied its duty by separating the pure from the impure and the combustible from the incombustible—yet the abundance of the said sulfur far exceeded the quantity of mercury—the mercury, necessarily separated in such a sequestration, was forced to turn into that Venereal greenness. Common sulfur demonstrates this very thing as the cause of this corruption: when it is joined to copper and moved to the fire (for art performs in a short space of time with a strong fire what nature could not accomplish with gentle heat over a long interval), it thoroughly burns the copper in a short time, and by a common <term>encheiresis</term> <note>original: "encheireſi"; a Greek term for a manual operation or chemical procedure</note> reduces it to the nature of <term>vitriol</term>. And according to the abundance of sulfur, the <term>vitriol</term> becomes richer or poorer in color; hence it happens that one vitriol contains more copper, and another less. And because coarse sulfur is also contained in iron, the <term>vitriol</term> corrodes it with its sharp acidity and seeks out its mercury, which is not much different from its own; and by conjunction with that sulfur which overcomes the mercury, it is reduced into pure, unadulterated copper.

But this must be noted with a "white stone," as they say <note>original: "albo... calculo"; an ancient idiom for marking something as favorable or particularly noteworthy</note>, that the acidic spirit of <term>vitriol</term> draws its origin from sulfur, just as spirits of this kind...

For it should be known that sulfur arises from the fatness of the earth, thickened in the mine by temperate decoction, until it hardens and becomes thick: and finally, when it has hardened, it is called sulfur.

However, sulfur is twofold: living <note>Latin: *vivum*</note> and burning <note>Latin: *adurens*</note>. Living sulfur is the active part in metals, which, when purified from all filth by nature, is the material of our Stone. But burning and common sulfur is not the material of metals or the Stone, but exists as an enemy to them. # On the Philosopher's Stone.

...when that is burned, it retreats into an earthy substance, like dead dust. How then could it grant life to others? For it has two causes of corruption: an inflammable substance and earthy dregs. With these things thus established, consider common sulfur—and not that of the philosophers—which is a simple, living fire, giving life to other dead bodies and maturing them, and so forth. By this name, common sulfur cannot be the material of the Stone.

But what shall we conclude regarding common mercury, since all philosophers say that the matter of our Stone is a certain mercurial substance, and it possesses many qualities which are also attributed to our mercury? For it is the element of all meltable things, as Arnold says in the first part of the *Rosary*, chapter two: <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a legendary physician and alchemist. The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers) is a famous 14th-century alchemical florilegium or collection of authoritative quotes.</note> *Since all liquefiable things, when they are melted, are converted into it, and it is mixed with them because it is of their substance: although those bodies differ in their composition from quicksilver in the way that it was pure or impure from the foul sulfur foreign to it.* <note>original Latin: "Argentum vivum" (living silver), the standard name for mercury/quicksilver.</note> And in chapter 4 he says: *Living mercury in all its operations is clearly the most perfect and most proven; since it is a preservative against burning, and an effector of fusion when it is fixed. And it is a tincture of redness, most abundant in perfection, of glowing brightness, and it does not withdraw from the mixture as long as it exists; and it is friendly, and mild in its harmony, and a medium for joining tinctures, since it is mixed through the smallest parts with them, and also naturally adheres in the depths; because it is of their nature. It alone is that which overcomes fire, and is not overcome by it, but rests in it, rejoicing in a friendly manner.* And Bernard says: <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist whose writings emphasized that the "Stone" is made from one thing alone—mercury.</note> *We imitate nature most exactly, which in its mines has no other material upon which to work except the pure mercurial form. In this mercury there is a fixed and incombustible sulfur, which perfects our work without any other substance than the pure mercurial substance.* When such excellent qualities are in mercury, it necessarily follows that it is the material of our Stone. I respond: Just as sulfur is twofold, so also mercury is twofold: namely, common and philosophical. That common mercury is a still raw, immature, and "open" body, not persisting in the fire like that of the philosophers, but under the pressure of a light fire it turns into smoke...

...a form that flees and departs. From this, a general rule of the philosophers has been established: *Our quicksilver is not the quicksilver of the common people.* <note>original Latin: "argentum vivum vulgi," referring to the ordinary liquid metal mercury used by miners and smiths as opposed to the "philosophical mercury" sought by alchemists.</note> And Lully <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan polymath; the *Clavicula* or "Little Key" is a famous alchemical text attributed to him.</note> in the first chapter of the *Little Key* says: *We say that common quicksilver cannot be the quicksilver of the philosophers, by whatever artifice it may be prepared; for the common sort cannot be held in the fire, except by another corporeal quicksilver, which is hot and dry, and more thoroughly digested.* 

But the greater part of those who practice philosophy have spoken of the sublimation of common mercury and its other preparations out of their own abundance of ideas, from which so many varied and wonderful ways of working have been devised. Through these, the properties of this subject have been more fully explained; however, the goal itself which they sought so greatly—namely, the treasure of this earthly wisdom—they have been unable to reach in this subject until now, since nature did not place it there. 

Nevertheless, in its operation, mercury is so marvelous that it sometimes seduces even those who consider themselves the wisest. Let us take as an example a certain close acquaintance of mine, once very well known to me, who treated gold amalgamated with mercury (as they say) so subtly and accurately that, passing through all the colors, it finally turned to a lemon-yellow color <term>citrinitas: the "yellowing" stage of the alchemical work, traditionally following the black and white stages</term>; yet it would not rise above that color by any means. Thereupon, that good chemist, moved by hope, supplied a higher degree of fire, fully persuading himself that the matter would now be most fixed and that, according to the philosophers, one could no longer err in the governance of the fire. 

But frustrated in his hope and persuasion, the glass shattered into many pieces, and the work was reduced to nothing, as the still-volatile mercury carried the gold with it up into the furnace <note>The mercury evaporated (volatilized) and took the gold with it as a vapor or fine dust, a common and dangerous laboratory accident in early chemistry.</note> (which should be carefully noted), almost gilding the chimney; as a result, a great deal of the gold was later scraped together and reduced back to its original form, or "body," as they call it. In this it appeared that the mercury, which was his "body," was able to dissolve the gold into the smallest parts so that it turned into a tincture <note>A liquid extract or "stain" that alchemists hoped would transform base metals into gold.</note>, even though many colors appeared as the heat acted upon the moisture. If, indeed, that good man, and many others with him, had heeded the words of Arnold in the *Flower of Flowers*, he certainly would have proceeded by a different method.

For thus Arnold, speaking of those laboring in this way, says:
> *Those who, looking more closely, have considered that mercury is the*
> ->*beginning*<-
> *of metals...*

<summary>The author argues that common mercury is not the true "Philosophical Mercury" and recounts a cautionary tale of a chemist whose experiment ended in a laboratory explosion and loss of materials.</summary>

# On the Philosopher's Stone.
D 2

...principle and their origin. By cooking with sulfuric heat, they sublimated mercury by itself; afterward they fixed, dissolved, and coagulated it. However, when they came to the **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone is cast onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term>, they found nothing, etc. For this reason, we cannot convince ourselves that common quicksilver <note>original Latin: "argentum vivum vulgare," referring to the liquid metal mercury found in nature</note> is the material of the Stone. Nevertheless, we do not deny that without its assistance, nothing solid can be achieved in either philosophical or medical chemistry.

Hitherto we have anxiously sought the material of our Stone in animals, in vegetables, in stones, and in lesser, middle, and greater minerals; but we have not yet been able to find it in those. Therefore, we must look further around us to see if it lies hidden in metals; and if it should be in them, whether it is in all of them at once, or indeed in only some, and in which ones it ought finally to be tracked down. Indeed, it is known, and Roger <note>likely Roger Bacon (c. 1220–1292), an English friar and philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> testifies in the *Mirror* <note>original: "spec. [Speculum] cap. 3," referring to the *Speculum Alchemiae* or Mirror of Alchemy</note>, chapter 3, that all metals are generated from sulfur and quicksilver, and that nothing adheres to them, nor can be applied to them or change them, except that which took its origin from them: since the improvement of any thing improves the nature of that thing to which it belongs, as Richard <note>likely Richard the Englishman (Ricardus Anglicus), a 13th-century alchemical author</note> says in chapter 1.

I will not say that the Supreme Architect <note>original: "Sumus opifex," a common alchemical way of referring to God as the master craftsman of the universe</note> willed it to be so arranged in all of nature that every thing should generate and produce its own like, lest a horse should come forth from a man. *And just as brute animals cannot multiply their own kind through the means of generation except by the benefit of a similar nature: so you should not presume to seek the blessed stone (says Basil Valentine) <note>a legendary 15th-century alchemist and monk, though the name was likely a pseudonym for several authors</note> from anywhere else than from its own seed, from which our stone was made from the beginning. However, so that you may find the seed, you will safely and rightly consider within yourself for what purpose you intend to seek our stone, and you yourself will be able to gather that it can have no other origin than from the metallic root, from which the metals themselves were ordained by God to be made.* I add that there is also a great conformity between the generation of metals and of the stone. *For in both, sulfur and quicksilver—which contain salt within themselves as a noble soul—are necessarily required; nor is it possible to perceive a likeness of utility in the metallic form until these three, taken from the metallic substance, meet as one; since nothing ought to be added to metals which did not take its origin from them. And it is left clearly enough to us, says Draco <note>likely a reference to an author or text titled "The Dragon," a common alchemical symbol</note>, that no foreign thing, which is not from these two, sulfur and mercury...*

<summary>The author concludes that common mercury is not the primary matter of the Philosopher's Stone and argues that the Stone must instead be sought within the "metallic root," as like must produce like.</summary>

# Golden Tract
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

...took its origin, is powerful and sufficient to perfect them, or to make a new transmutation of them. Therefore, of necessity, **metallic matter** must be chosen for the generation of the stone. Whether that matter lies hidden in imperfect <note>In alchemy, "imperfect" metals are base metals like lead or copper, as opposed to "perfect" metals like gold and silver.</note> metals will be for us to investigate briefly. Many are found who imagine that the material of the stone can be elicited from **tin** or **lead** for the white [work]; and for the red [work] from **copper** or **iron**, or from both; seduced, no doubt, by a sinister <note>original: "sinistrè," meaning wrongly or perversely interpreted</note> understanding of the philosophers themselves. For thus Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> says in the *Book of Furnaces*, chapter 9: *We extract the paste to be fermented for the most part from imperfect bodies. And therefore we give you a general rule, that the white paste is extracted from **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iove," the planetary name for Tin</note> & **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, but the red from **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, **Saturn**, & **Mars** <note>Iron</note>.* And Basil Valentine <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, often associated with the study of antimony.</note> in his book on *Physical and Hyperphysical Matters* teaches that the tincture is prepared from the conjunction of Mars and Venus. The same author in the *Triumph of Antimony* bursts forth in these words: *Following this tincture of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, there follows further the tincture of vitriol, or Venus, as well as the tincture of Mars; these two also comprehend the tincture of the Sun within themselves, when they are first perfected beyond fixation. These are followed by the tincture of Jupiter and Saturn for the coagulation of mercury, and finally the tincture of mercury itself.* 

But the investigator of nature ought to know that this was never the mind of either Geber or Basil; otherwise they would contradict themselves, which cannot be, since the philosophers never lie in their writings, even if they wrap the truth in parabolic words. For no perfection can arise from imperfect metals—whether alone or mixed together—from which they might be improved even in the slightest. This cannot be from themselves alone, since the purest substance of mercury is required for the material of our stone, as *The Sound of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangor buccinae," a famous 14th-century alchemical text</note>, Avicenna, Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>, and almost all philosophers testify, saying: *In our work, the purest substance of mercury must be chosen by us.* But that purest substance of mercury is not found in imperfect metals, since they are so defiled by their unclean and alien sulfur that, like **leprous bodies** <note>Alchemists frequently used medical metaphors, describing base metals as "diseased" or "leprous" and the Stone as the "medicine" that heals them into gold.</note>, they cannot reach intimate and perfect depuration <term>depuration: the process of freeing a substance from impurities</term>, no matter what artistry is applied. I add, moreover, that they persist less in the fire, which property is required above all others in our material. Let us hear Geber...
