## On the Stone of the Philosophers

<margin>D 3</margin>

*...in Chapter 63 of his Summa* <note>original: "Summæ suæ," referring to the *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (The Sum of Perfection), the most influential medieval Latin alchemical work, attributed to Geber.</note> *speaking of this impurity of imperfect metals and the properties of perfect mercury: "Through this, by true investigation, we have discovered a wonderful kind of two secrets. One indeed is that there is a double cause* <note>The text says "double cause" but proceeds to list three points; this discrepancy is common in period transcriptions.</note> *of the corruption of any (imperfect) metal by fire; the first of which is that the combustible sulfur enclosed within its internal substance is ignited by strong fire, annihilates the entire substance of the bodies, turns it into smoke, and finally consumes it, despite the goodness of their quicksilver* <note>original: "argenti vivi." Quicksilver (mercury) was considered the "soul" or "life" of metals.</note>. *The second cause is that the external flame is increased through them, penetrates them, and dissolves them into smoke, however fixed* <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that resists the heat of fire and does not evaporate or change.</note> *they may be. The third is that their bodies are opened through calcination* <note>term: calcination <gloss>The process of heating a metal or mineral in air to reduce it to a powder or oxide.</gloss></note>. *For then the fire’s flame can penetrate them and turn them into smoke, even if they had been fixed. When, however, all the causes of corruption come together, the bodies are necessarily corrupted and annihilated; but when they do not concur, the speed of the bodies' corruption is somewhat diminished. The second kind of this secret is the goodness which is considered by reason of the quicksilver within the bodies. For quicksilver, since there is no other cause of corruption or propulsion within it, does not allow itself to be divided into the parts of its composition, but remains in its entire substance in the fire; from which the cause of its perfection can be known. Praise be therefore to God, blessed and most high, who created that, and gave it substance, and to that substance a property which can be found in no other natural thing, so that this [perfection] could be thrust into it by any art, which is found in this [mercury] as a near potential. For this is that which overcomes fire and is not overcome by fire, but rests in it amicably and rejoices in it."*

In these words **Geber** clearly demonstrates that the matter of our Stone cannot be in the imperfect metals: because, being impure of themselves, they flee from the fire when we wish to purify them; but our mercury, by reason of its purity, can persist in the fire without any harm. Just as, therefore, the imperfect metals alone are not the matter of our Stone, so also when mixed together they can produce it even less, since by their mixing they become no purer than they were before—not to mention that a new confusion would occur here, plainly contrary to our intention, which requires a **single matter**, as was said above.

## The Golden Treatise

This is clearly testified by the sixth chapter of the books of secrets by <term>Haly</term> <note>original: "Haly," likely referring to the Persian physician Haly Abbas or the legendary Khalid ibn Yazid, frequently cited in medieval alchemy.</note>, saying: *The Stone is one, to which you shall mix no other thing; the wise work with this, and from this remains that which heals us. Nothing else is mixed with it, neither in its whole, nor in its parts.*

*And <term>Morienus</term> <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have initiated the first Arab prince into alchemy.</note> says: This mastery* <note>original: "magisterium," referring to the entire process of the Great Work.</note> *originates in the beginning from one root; which is afterwards dispersed into many parts, and is converted into one thing.*

If, therefore, imperfect metals cannot be the matter of the Stone, why did the philosophers command us to work upon them? I answer: When the philosophers commanded us to take "unclean bodies," they did not mean copper, iron, lead, tin, etc., but rather their own body, or their own earth; just as <term>Arnold</term> <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in the <term>Flower of Flowers</term> <note>original: "Flore florum," an alchemical treatise attributed to Arnold.</note>: *Mercury is joined to the earth; that is, to the imperfect body.* For even if their earth is in itself of such perfection and purity as nature was able to complete; nevertheless, in respect to the physical Stone, it is still imperfect and unclean. And in this, Art surpasses Nature, because it completes what Nature could not. Moreover, that the earth is imperfect before its full purification and regeneration is evident from the fact that at that time it is not yet able to tinge and "more than complete" <note>The author uses a phrase implying the Stone's power to perfect other substances beyond their natural state.</note> [others], nor does it have more than what nature bestowed upon it: but after regeneration, it can do much. Indeed, its impurity is perceived most clearly in our work; namely when it is black, and is likened to lead or antimony; afterwards grey, and is called <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note>, or tin, or magnesia, and this indeed before the whiteness; but after the whiteness it is called <term>Mars</term> <note>The alchemical name for Iron.</note> and <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note>, before it is led to the perfect redness. That <term>Basil Valentine</term> <note>A 15th-century Benedictine monk and famous alchemical author.</note> is of the same opinion as I, and thinks quite differently than what he left written in said book, he testifies in his treatise on the Great Stone, where, investigating the matter of the Stone, he said that in the <term>Sun</term> <note>The alchemical name for Gold.</note> the gift of all three perfections meets, and from that it has the power to persist in fire, and that the <term>Moon</term> <note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note> by reason of its fixed mercury does not easily retreat from fire, and bears its testing; finally he breaks out into these words: *That noble harlot <term>Venus</term> is clothed and covered with an overabundant color, and the greatest part of her body is filled with a most rich tincture* <note>term: tincture <gloss>A spiritualized substance or "soul" capable of transmuting and coloring base metals into gold.</gloss></note>, *and such is the color which also dwells in the best metal, and because of*

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

*...its abundance turns toward redness. But because its body is leprous* <note>original: "leprosum"; in alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities or "disease" of base metals that prevent them from being gold.</note>*, that fixed tincture cannot remain in it, but vanishes along with its body. For when the body is corrupted through mortification, the soul also cannot remain, but is forced to yield and flee. The fixed salt has attributed and left a hard, vigorous, and coarse body to strong <term>Mars</term>* <note>The alchemical name for iron.</note>*, from which the strength of its soul is recognized; this leader is not easily conquered. Indeed, its body is hard, so that it is wounded only with difficulty.*

*But if anyone should suggest that the fixed <term>sulphur of Venus</term>* <note>The "soul" or active combustible principle of copper.</note> *from the doctrine of <term>Basilius</term>* <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary 15th-century alchemist often credited with discovering antimony.</note>*, when joined with the spirit of perfect mercury, could pass into a tincture: let him know and gather what has been repeated more often before—namely, that our matter does not depend on many things. This Basilius also affirms, teaching that the universal is a single thing, and is found and drawn out from a single thing; and that it is the spirit of mercury and the soul of sulphur, together with the spiritual salt, united and enclosed together under one heaven, and dwelling in one body. And undoubtedly, having been led back from his errors into the true path, leaving the imperfect metals behind, he turned his mind to the more perfect ones, considering that saying of <term>Plato</term> in the second quarter: "Why do you calcine and dissolve other bodies with great labor, when in these (the perfect ones) you find what you seek?" If indeed you wish to use those [imperfect metals], it is necessary that you first convert them into the nature of perfect bodies. Therefore, most friendly seeker of natural secrets, leave behind all animals and vegetables, all salts, alums, vitriols, marcasites, magnesias, antimony, and all imperfect and impure metals. If you therefore study to make gold and silver by the philosophical art, take for that purpose neither eggs nor blood, but gold and silver, which, being naturally and prudently (and not manually) calcined, produce a new...*

*...you should leave behind all minerals likewise, and metals alone. And in the Exercise on the Turba it is said: Just as mercury is the beginning of all metals, so also the Sun is the end and the ultimate of metals, and...*

# The Golden Tractate

In all metals, whether pure or impure, there are internally the <term>Sun</term> <note>gold</note>, the <term>Moon</term> <note>silver</note>, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>. But there is only one true Sun, which is drawn out from them. In this way, you will perceive that the <term>Gold of the Philosophers</term> <note>the vital essence used in alchemy</note> is quite different from common gold, even if it takes its origin from it. For it is said in chapter 16 of the <term>Rising Dawn</term> <note>original: "Aurora Consurgens"; a famous medieval alchemical treatise</note>: "From this it is clear that philosophical gold is not the gold of the common people, neither in its color nor in its substance. Rather, that which is extracted from them is the white and red tincture." Furthermore, the gold of the philosophers is that which is bought at a small price, as <term>Alphidius</term> <note>an early alchemical authority, likely of Arabic origin</note> says, and as <term>Morienus</term> <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> remarks:

> *Every thing which is bought at a high price is a lie. For with a very little of this gum, and a tiny bit of gold, we buy much.*

Moreover, our gold is a living gold, and our silver is a living silver, which can bring nothing but life and growth. Common gold and silver are dead; they can no longer achieve more than nature has granted them, until they are awakened from the dead by a wise craftsman and regain their life. Then, indeed, they live, and in the propagation and multiplication of their own kind, they can accomplish much. Regarding the life of common and "our" metals, our most excellent <term>Michael Sendivogius</term> <note>a renowned Polish alchemist (1566–1636)</note>—a most preeminent Philosopher who still draws breath—speaks thus in the second tractate of his little book on the <term>Philosophical Stone</term>:

> *Be warned not to take the gold and silver of the common people, for these are dead. Take ours, which are living. Afterward, place them in our fire, and from them will be made a <term>dry liquor</term> <note>a paradoxical alchemical term for a substance that flows like water but does not wet the hands</note>. First, the earth will be resolved into water, which is called the Mercury of the Philosophers, and that water dissolves those bodies of the Sun and Moon, and consumes them, so that nothing remains except a tenth part with one part. And this shall be the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid</note> of the metals.*

But to treat the gold of the philosophers more fully, it must be noted that philosophers sometimes call their "water" gold, and sometimes even their "earth." Regarding the first way, we have already heard from <term>Nicarum</term>—whom the author of the <term>Rosary of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Rosarium Philosophorum"; a cornerstone 16th-century alchemical text</note> cites—saying:

> *But what do you say about this, that the philosophers say: "Our gold is not the gold of the common people, and our silver is not the silver of the common people"? I say that they call the water "gold"—that which ascends to the higher regions by the power of fire. And truly that gold is not the gold of the common people; for the common people would not believe it could ascend to the higher regions because of its <term>fixity</term> <note>original: "fixionem"; the property of a substance that resists the fire and does not evaporate</note>.*

<summary>This page distinguishes between common "dead" metals and the "living" philosophical gold and silver used in alchemy, explaining that the true matter is a refined essence or "water" extracted from them. It cites authorities like Sendivogius and the Rosarium to explain how metallic bodies must be dissolved into their "radical moisture" to become transformative.</summary>

# On the Philosophers' Stone.

The same author testifies that the philosophers also wished to call their earth their gold: *Know that the bronze <note>original: "æs"; used here as a technical term for the base matter of the work</note>, which is the gold of the philosophers, is their gold: This earth is called bronze, leaven <note>original: "fermentum"; a substance added to trigger a transformation</note>, and tincture <note>a concentrated essence capable of changing the color and quality of metals</note>, just as their white and foliated water is called earth.* Whence the author of the *Sound of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangoris buccinæ"; a famous medieval alchemical treatise</note> in the chapter on solution speaks thus: *Wherefore Hermes says: Sow your gold in the white foliated earth, which through calcination <note>the process of heating a solid to high temperatures to purify it</note> has become fiery, subtle, and airy—namely, to such a degree: to sow gold is to sow the soul and the dyeing power into the white earth, which by preparation has been made white and clean, in which there are no impurities.* From these things it is clear that it is gold by nature, not by the matter of the leaven; indeed, the gold of the philosophers is the dyeing leaven itself. And in the *Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scala philosophorum"</note>, step 7, it is said: *Their earth is white, in which their gold is sown, and their soul is gold; and that body is the place of knowledge, gathering it together, and the dwelling of the tinctures.* And a little after, the same author says: *For this reason Hercules says: melt it again—that is, dissolve the body of magnesia <note>in alchemy, "magnesia" refers to the crude, dark "first matter" of the stone, not the modern chemical element</note>, which has been made white and like the leaves of a bramble. For it is that which flees toward the best, and the gold which is extracted from it is called the gold of the philosophers, and it is the tincture, which is the soul.* For when the water of the spirit ascends into the upper air, and this white body—when the gold has been made white—they called that "our gold" after the blackness. Whence <term>Senior</term> <note>refers to Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist</note> says: *Mix gold with gold, that is, water and ash.* And <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>: *Sow gold in the white foliated earth.* Wherefore the philosophers have set down in writing that our gold is not the gold of the common people.

To this stated opinion, however, someone might interject and ask why the philosophers understand their gold to be water at one time and earth at another; it might seem that they either contradict themselves and are in disagreement, or that they intended to confuse everything and deliberately mislead their students. I reply that all and every philosopher, when they reveal the truth itself, wrap it in veiled and allegorical words; yet they do not contradict themselves, but agree in a marvelous way, so much so that they seem to have spoken as if from a single mouth. Moreover, they confuse nothing, nor do they intend to mislead a worthy follower, but clearly and openly—though through mystical expressions—they expose the truth before their eyes, which they nevertheless hide from the unworthy and the impious, and conceal from them.

<summary>This page explains that "Philosophical Gold" is a symbolic term for the transformative "leaven" or "soul" extracted from matter, appearing as "white earth" or "foliated water" during the process. The author defends the confusing terminology of ancient alchemists, arguing it is a deliberate veil to protect sacred truths from the unworthy.</summary>

<header>Golden Tractate.</header>

[they hide] as much as is permitted by the grace of God, lest pearls be cast before swine—those who strive only to indulge their own desires and pleasures—and the sanctuary be trampled underfoot, just as the reality of this matter testifies in this very question. Indeed, it has been demonstrated more than once, but repeatedly, to the kind seeker of our art, not only from where our matter should be taken, but also that it must be a single substance, which through the prudence of the craftsman is to be dissolved into two things: namely, earth and fire, or mercury and sulfur <note>In alchemical theory, mercury and sulfur are the two primary principles—the "parents"—of all metals.</note>.

Therefore, when the philosophers call their water or their earth "gold," they do not do so wrongly, and it is within their power to name them by whatever name they wish; for they have not feared to identify their stone as "their gold," "gold more than perfect," "regenerated gold," and by many other such names. But the fact that their meaning is not understood at first glance should be attributed to one's own ignorance rather than to the secrecy <note>original: "invidiæ"; literally "envy," but in alchemical Latin, it refers to the philosophers' intentional withholding of secrets from the unworthy.</note> of the philosophers.

And so the art-loving seeker of this renowned secret will be abundantly and copiously instructed regarding the matter of our stone: namely, that it should be extracted from no plant, from no animal, nor from anything that proceeds from them; nor from any minerals, nor from any imperfect metals, but from gold and silver. Furthermore, our gold and our silver are not common and "dead" gold and silver, but the "living" gold and silver of the wise. It remains now for us to bring forward certain things regarding **solution**, as it is the hinge of the matter and the greatest secret.

Now, **solution** occurs when we make a moist thing from a dry one, a soft thing from a hard one, and a manifest thing from a hidden one; that is, when a hard thing is turned into water. This is not common water, however (as Parmenides and Agadmon teach in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; an influential early alchemical text depicting a gathering of ancient philosophers.</note>, saying: *Certain people, when they hear of the "solution of bodies," think it is the water of the clouds; but if they had read and understood our books, they would know also that our water is permanent*), but the water of the philosophers—that is, the **first matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the primordial, undifferentiated substance required to begin the alchemical transformation.</note>. As Arnold says in the *Rosary*, Book 1, Chapter 9: *The work of the philosophers is to dissolve the stone into its own mercury, so that it may be reduced to its first matter.* And Avicenna <note>A Latinized reference to Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose works were central to medieval alchemy.</note> says: *You who wish to work, you must first labor in the solution and sublimation of the two luminaries <note>The "two luminaries" are the Sun (gold) and the Moon (silver).</note>, which is the first step...*

[of the] work is that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; also known as Mercury.</note> be made from them. Wherefore Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> also in the *Rosary*, Book 2, chapters 1 and 2, describes **Solution**, stating it is the division of bodies and the preparation of the first matter or nature; And Richard the Englishman <note>A 13th-century alchemist often identified with Richard of Wendover.</note> in chapter 18 writes thus: *The first beginning is to dissolve the stone into its first matter, and it is the conjunction of body and spirit, so that from them one mercurial water may be made.* Just as solution is the first and most highly necessary labor in our operation, so it also stands as the most difficult, as Eobald Vogelius testifies, saying: *How difficult a thing solution is can be testified by those who have devoted effort to it.* And Bernard, Count of Trevisan, in his booklet to Thomas of Bologna, writes: *He who knows the art and the secret of dissolution has indeed reached the secret of the art, which is to mix the species and to effectively extract natures from natures that lie hidden within them.* 

Solution, indeed, must not be done with **sharp and strong waters** <note>original: "aquis acutis & fortibus"; this refers to mineral acids like nitric acid, which alchemists warned would "corrupt" the soul of the metal rather than truly dissolving it philosophically.</note>, since all sharp and strong waters corrode and corrupt the body that is to be led to solution and improvement. Next, as has been said, no solution occurs into water that wets the hands, but into a **dry water**, which is called not only mercury but also sulfur, as Zeumone testifies in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: *Unless you grind the body, destroy it, soak it, and diligently govern it until you extract its fatness and make it an impalpable spirit, you labor in vain.*

And Richard the Englishman, showing the way of Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath.</note> in chapter 11, says: *The philosophers have subtly imagined how those sulfurs could be elicited from these more perfect bodies, and how their qualities could be better purged through art, so that this might happen in art by means of nature—something which did not appear in them before, although they possessed it fully in secret.* And they by no means allow this to happen without the **solution of the body** and its reduction into the **first matter**, which is quicksilver, from which they were made from the beginning; and this without any admixture of foreign things: since foreign natures do not improve our stone. For no water dissolves our bodies except that which is of its own kind, and which can be thickened by the bodies, says Bernard in his letter to Thomas of Bologna; And a little before in the same letter he writes: *Solution requires simultaneous permanence, namely of the solvent and the dissolved, so that from both—namely the masculine and feminine seed—a new species may result. Truly I say to you, that no water by natural reduction [can change] the species...*

[no water] dissolves the metallic nature, unless it is that which remains with them in matter and form, and which the dissolved metals themselves can recongeal. And **Morfoleus in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*** <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> says:
> *Every body is dissolved with the spirit with which it is mixed, and without doubt it likewise becomes spiritual. And every spirit is altered and colored by the bodies, to which spirit a tinting color, constant against the fire, is mixed.*

Since these things are so, the **art-loving disciple** <note>original: "technophilus discipulus"</note> must most diligently inquire what that water might be. For the knowledge of the **solvent** <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstruum"; in alchemy, this refers to a solvent or "mother water" capable of dissolving a solid without destroying its essential nature, analogous to how the womb nourishes an embryo.</note>, says Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy.</note> in the *first part of the Compendium of the Soul*, is one of those things without which nothing can be done in the mastery of this art. For there is nothing that joins the dissolutions of metals except our solvent, because it is the water with which the dissolution of metals is performed while preserving their species, as he says in the *Codicil*. Because, therefore, this is the greatest **secret** <term>arcanum</term>, which the philosophers have not only hidden again and again in their writings, but have even forbidden to reveal: nevertheless, as far as is permitted to me, I shall lead you back to the true path by the sayings of two philosophers. The first saying is found in the *Abridged Rosary* in almost these words:
> *The first preparation and the foundation of this art is solution—that is, the reduction of the body into water, which is into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the metal Mercury.</note>. And they called this "solution" when they said: Let the gold hidden in the body of **magnesia** <note>original: "magnesiæ"; here referring to a symbolic crude material or "mineral mass" used as a starting point, not modern magnesium.</note> be dissolved, so that it may be reduced into its first matter, so that from there **sulphur** and quicksilver may be made, and not so that it should be reduced into [common] water again. For our solution is nothing other than making the body moist, and resolving it into the nature of quicksilver; and the falseness of its sulphur is diminished, which divine sulphur is abstracted from two sulphurs when the spirit meets the body.*

The second saying is brought forth by **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and canon of Bridlington.</note> in his *preface to the Twelve Gates*:
> *I shall certainly teach you, so that you may understand there are three mercuries, which are the keys of the science, which Raymond calls his solvents <note>original: "menstrua"</note>, without which nothing is done correctly for me. But two of these are superficial; the third is the essential mercury of the **sun and moon** <note>original: "solis & lunæ"; in alchemy, "Sun" represents Gold and "Moon" represents Silver.</note>, whose properties I will show you sincerely. For the essential mercury of other metals is the chief material of our Stone. In our sun and moon, our solvents are not visible to the sight, nor do they appear except by their effect. This is that stone which we mean, if anyone understands our writings correctly. It is the soul and the splendid substance of the sun and*

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

...of the moon, and their subtle influence through which the earth receives its splendor. For what else is gold and silver (says **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicenna"; the Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to European alchemy.</note>) than clean earth, white and red? Take away from it the aforementioned splendor, and then the earth will be of little importance. The whole composite we call **our lead** <note>original: "noſtrum plumbum"; alchemists often used the names of common metals like lead to refer to their secret starting material or a specific stage of the process.</note>. The quality of splendor proceeds from the sun and moon. And these, in short, are our **solvents** <term>menstrua</term>. First, we naturally calcine the perfect bodies, but no unclean body enters except for one, which is commonly called by the philosophers the **Green Lion** <term>leo viridis</term> <note>original: "leo viridis"; a famous alchemical symbol representing a raw, acidic mineral (often vitriol or antimony) capable of "devouring" or dissolving gold.</note>, which is the means of joining the tinctures between the sun and the moon with perfection. With the second, which is a **vegetable humidity** <note>original: "humiditas vegetabilis"; likely referring to a life-giving or organic solvent derived from wine or other organic matter.</note> reviving that which was previously dead, both the material and formal principles must be dissolved, otherwise they would be of little account. With the third, which is a most permanent humidity, incombustible, and oily in its nature, **Hermes' tree** <note>original: "Hermetis arbor"; a symbol for the alchemical process or the growing "Stone" itself, named after Hermes Trismegistus.</note> will be burned into ashes. This is our most certain natural fire, our mercury sulphur, our clean tincture, our soul, our stone lifted by the wind, generated in the earth. Hide these things in your mind. This stone, I dare to tell you, is the **potential vapor of metal**; you must be cautious in how you acquire it. For this solvent is indeed invisible, although with the **second philosophical water** it can appear to the sight in the form of clear water through the separation of the elements. From this solvent, labored over until it overflows, the **sulphur of nature** can be made, if it be naturally sharpened and circulated into a pure spirit: then with it you will be able to dissolve your base or mass.

These are the words of those philosophers, in which the whole mystery of **solution** <note>original: "ſolutionis"; the process of turning a solid into a liquid state, the first step of the Great Work.</note> is revealed. If, therefore, you have rightly and thoroughly considered the faculties and powers of nature, and compared them with these words, and have **annihilated** <note>original: "annihilaveris"; here used in the sense of breaking a substance down into its basic components or "nothingness."</note>—that is, reduced—all the operations of nature, and have unwound the threads like a ball of yarn, you will find all truth plainly and fundamentally in them. But if you cannot gather it from these things, then the gates are barred against you; you know neither the matter nor the powers of nature. To the knowledge of this, neither **spectacles** <note>original: "perſpicilla"; an early reference to eyeglasses or magnifying lenses, implying that physical tools alone cannot reveal spiritual truths.</note> nor trifles will lead, but rather the most ardent prayers with untiring study and consideration of the impossibility of nature.

Indeed, according to the revelation of the highest and greatest God, solely and only by assiduous studies, vigils, and frequent and repeated reading...

<page-num>40</page-num>

# ->The Golden Treatise<-
<meta>catchword: Res</meta>

...from authentic books I have attained this art: not indeed as to the matter, which I began to know from the revelation of **GOD** alone, but that which I learned, I thereafter confirmed and shaped [by those books]. I also learned the solution (which among all philosophers is one and only, and without which neither the ancient nor more recent philosophers could accomplish anything; hence it is called both the secret of the art and the mystery of the philosophers, which no one but **GOD** ought to reveal) and all the labors involved. For this benefit, I give immortal thanks with mouth and heart to the Creator of things, from now and forevermore. **AMEN.**

But so that every cause for complaining against me may be cut off from you, friend reader, I will reveal one more mystery to you through the love of **GOD**. Know that even if there is but one solution <note>original: "solutio"; in alchemy, "solution" refers to the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid state, often seen as a return to its "first matter."</note>, it is nevertheless distinguished according to the "before" and "after," as they are accustomed to say in the schools. The first solution is that of which **Arnoldus** <note>original: "Arnoldus"; likely referring to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note> speaks, as was said above: namely, the reduction into **first matter** <term>prima materia</term> <note>The primitive, formless base of all substance that alchemists sought to recover from metals.</note>. The other is that perfect solution of the body and spirit together, where the solvent and the thing to be dissolved always remain together; and with this solution of the body, the coagulation <note>The thickening or solidifying of the liquid back into a stone.</note> of the spirit is likewise perfected.

Here you will be able to see clearly and plainly with your eyes whatever you have long desired to know and see; and it is nonetheless **women's work** <term>opus mulierum</term> and **child's play** <term>puerorum ludus</term> <note>These are traditional alchemical phrases used to suggest that once the secret is known, the work is easy, or that it requires only gentle heat and patience, similar to common household tasks.</note>, of which we will refrain from speaking further. For once the beginning is rightly known, the end will also follow by the assistance of the divine power. There, we shall attain all glory—this fleeting kind, I mean, and that eternal one, where with our bodies made clear we shall see **GOD** face to face. Despising all worldly pleasures and uniquely desiring this eternal, infinite, and ineffable glory, we shall obtain it with our very own eyes.

With these words I will put an end to this little treatise of mine, relegating whatever remains for you to know to the following parable, where you will find the entire operation and practice clearly demonstrated. If you follow it rightly, I do not doubt that you yourself will arrive at the perfect end and true wisdom, which **GOD the Father**, **GOD the SON**, and **GOD the Holy Spirit**, blessed forever, may wish to show to you and all good men.

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

## M. S.

*The **MATTER** is one in number, the thing is one in essence,*
*Which nature strives to transform, but with the aid of art,*
*Into two, and twice two, and three, as the writings shall teach us;*
*Mercury and sulfur <note>original: "Mercurius, sulphur"; the two primary principles of alchemy representing fluidity/spirit and stability/soul.</note> provide nourishment to one another.*
*Spirit, and soul, and body, and the four elements,*
*That which they provide as a fifth <note>A reference to the "Quintessence" or "Aether," the purest fifth element that transcends the earthly four.</note> is the stone of the philosophers.*
*Take your matter without deception: and let it be twofold,*
*Let it shine forth at once as pure mercurial essence.*
*Choose it pure from all foreign sulfur,*
*And destroy it utterly in the fire of the furnace.*
*Recompose it again with balanced weight. Thus I deem you*
*To have entered the path of the art and of the mystery.*
*After you have dissolved it, you shall soon sublime it; and by this means*
*Grind it; let the love of distilling never cease.*
*Afterward let it insist on congealing, and proceed by cooking,*
*Thereafter you may begin to <term>tinge</term> <note>original: "tingere"; in alchemy, "tinging" is the final act of transmutation where the Stone changes the color and nature of base metals into gold.</note> most generously:*
*Then you have a medicine for men, and the highest for metals;*
*To heal at will whomever you wish, in whatever way.*

### THERE FOLLOWS A PARABLE IN WHICH
->*the mystery of the whole work is declared.*<-

**W**hile I was once walking in a thicket and a most elegant little wood, I was considering the misery of this life, and at the same time I was deploring that we had been led into this lamentable and most wretched state through the pitiable fall of our first parents <note>A reference to the biblical Fall of Adam and Eve, which alchemists often linked to the "corruption" of nature and metals.</note>: proceeding thus, I fell into a bypass, and came upon a certain rough path, unusual and trackless, and overgrown with many briars, so that it could easily be guessed that it was rarely frequented. When I had noticed this, struck with horror, I would have gladly withdrawn my step if it had been in my power; but a more violent wind so followed me, that it was easier [to go forward]...

<sig>F</sig>

**"He must also be brought back to life, if he wishes to be our colleague."**

Therefore, casting aside all ambiguities, I left the pit and arrived in a large courtyard—how I got there, I still do not know...

# On the Philosophers' Stone

Therefore, spending many days in these anxieties, and reflecting on how I might look after my affairs, it finally occurred to me how **Medea** had restored the dead body of **Aeson** to life <note>In Greek mythology, the sorceress Medea rejuvenated Jason's father, Aeson, by cutting his throat, draining his old blood, and refilling his veins with a magical potion of herbs and minerals.</note>; and I reasoned with myself thus: if this Medea could accomplish such things, it will not be impossible for you either. I began, therefore, to consider how I might bring that effect to pass. But I found no better method than if I were to maintain a **continuous heat** until the waters vanished and the dead bodies of our lovers appeared again; for then I did not doubt that all dangers would be escaped, to my great profit and honor.

Therefore, with the heat continued, I proceeded for up to **forty days** <note>The number forty is symbolic in alchemy, representing a period of testing or "quarantine" necessary for the first stage of transformation.</note>. There I observed the waters being consumed from day to day, and the corpses appearing again **black as coal**. This indeed would have happened sooner had the chamber not been too tightly hidden and sealed (which, however, was in no way to be opened by me). For I noticed that the waters, ascending and approaching the clouds in the top of the chamber, gathered together and fell down like rain, and nothing at all could escape until our **bridegroom** <term>Sponsus: representing the masculine principle or gold/sulfur</term> with his most beloved **bride** <term>Sponsa: representing the feminine principle or silver/mercury</term> had rotted in death, and from that place it smelled excessively foul.

Meanwhile, in the chamber, from the solar rays acting upon the humidity, a most beautiful **rainbow** <note>In alchemy, this stage is known as the *Cauda Pavonis* or "Peacock's Tail," where many colors appear on the surface of the matter, signaling that the "blackness" of death is ending.</note> was seen, decorated with the loveliest colors. This affected me with no small joy after so many exhausted sorrows; I especially rejoiced because I saw my lovers lying before me. But as no joy is so solid that it is not disturbed by some adversity, so I also was saddened in this joy of mine, because I realized those entrusted to me were still dead and without any life. But this one thing consoled me: that their chamber was most firmly closed and did not let out their souls and spirits, but still held them well-preserved. For this reason, I continued to warm them with my said heat and to perform my assigned duty abundantly, fully persuading myself that they would not return to their bodies as long as those humidities lasted (since they delight in moist natures); which I also found to be exactly the case. For toward evening, I noticed many vapors exhaling from the earth by the power of the sun...

matter <note>original: "res"</note>, and in that manner was raised up just as waters are drawn up by the sun. Having thickened <note>original: "coagulati"</note> during the night, at the first break of dawn these vapors watered the earth like a most fertile dew; they washed our "corpses," which from day to day, as this washing was performed more frequently, were rendered more beautiful and whiter. I was overwhelmed with the greatest joy, as you might easily imagine, especially when I saw her rise clothed in a most elegant and sumptuous robe—the likes of which have been seen by very few mortals—and adorned with a supreme crown crafted from pure diamonds. She then broke out into these words:

> Listen, mortals, and pay close attention: the Most High God alone has the power to appoint and depose kings. He makes men rich or poor according to His will; He kills and restores life. I myself am a sufficient example of this. I was great, and was made humble; but now, having been humbled, I have been appointed Queen of many kingdoms. Life has been restored to me after death; the treasures of the wise and powerful have been entrusted and handed over to me, though I was poor. Therefore, the power has been granted to me to make the rich out of the poor, to grant grace to the lowly, and to restore health to the sick. Yet, I am not yet equal to the task of raising my most beloved brother, the most powerful King, from the dead; but when he arrives, he will prove by his very presence that my words are true.

When she had said these things, the sun illuminated everything with its clearest splendor, the heat of the day intensified, and the dog days <term>Canicular days: The "Dog Days" of summer, associated with the star Sirius and the period of intense heat required for the final alchemical stages.</term> approached. I wondered how this could be, especially when I saw a new stole or robe prepared, for I knew that no one had entered the bedchamber except the groom with his bride. But this struck me with even greater wonder: as soon as any robe was ready, the previous ones vanished, so that I did not even know what had become of them or who had put them away. 

Therefore, when that most precious scarlet <note>original: "coccynea"</note> garment was finished, that great and powerful king appeared in such splendor and magnificence that none can equal. Because he felt himself shut in, he pleaded with me with the sweetest and most eloquent words to open the door for him and allow him to come out of the chamber by my hand, promising that this would result in my own great benefit. Although I had been repeatedly forbidden from opening the chamber, the magnificence and sweet eloquence of the king so awed me that I did not refuse to open it. When he came out, he showed himself to be so humane, so kind, and so humble, that he truly proved that nothing becomes or adorns great men as much as these virtues.

Because he had lived through the dog days <note>original: "caniculares"; the hottest days of summer, representing the intense heat required in the alchemical furnace</note> in great heat, he was burning with a great thirst and was exceedingly tired and weary. For this reason, he gave me orders that I should not disdain to draw water for him from the flowing stream or torrent beneath the drums <term>tympanis: likely referring to the drum-shaped components of an alchemical distillation apparatus</term>. When I had done this willingly, he drank a great draft with the greatest appetite and then returned to his chamber, commanding me to shut the door tightly so that no one might disturb him or wake him from his sleep. 

He rested here for a few days and then called for me to open the door again. He seemed to me far more beautiful, more blood-red <note>original: "sanguinolentior"; this indicates the "Rubedo" or Red Work, the final stage of the alchemical process</note>, and more magnificent. He himself noticed this and judged this water to be precious and healthy; immediately he asked for more water and drank a greater quantity than before, so much so that I felt compelled to enlarge the chamber. Therefore, when our king had drunk his fill of this precious potion—which the ignorant nonetheless think nothing of—he grew into such beauty and magnificence...

# PREFACE
## TO THE WORTHY CHRISTIAN-
### and Reader.

**M**ost friendly and pious Reader, and especially you, the sons of wisdom and learning; after several years ago, Almighty God—in response to my daily and most fervent prayers—opened my eyes so widely through the illumination of His Holy Spirit (through whom we receive all wisdom, and who was sent to us from the Father through Christ) that I might recognize the true Center in the Triangle of the center <note>original: "verum Centrum in Trigono centri"; a geometric-mystical reference to the divine or elemental core of matter</note>, and identify the one and true matter of the noble **Philosophical Stone** <note>original: "Philosophici lapidis"; the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting longevity</note>, and essentially have it in my hands. Nevertheless, for almost five years I remained ignorant of how, namely, I should proceed with it profitably, rightly, and fittingly to separate from it the **blood of the red lion** and the **glue of the white eagle** <note>original: "rubri leonis sanguinem, & albæ aquilæ gluten"; these are alchemical metaphors for the fixed (sulfuric) and volatile (mercurial) principles of the work</note>; much less how to mix them very closely and optimally, according to the proportionate weight of nature, to enclose them, seal them, and commit them to the **secret fire** <note>original: "arcanoque igni"; a specialized, often low-temperature heat source required for alchemical maturation</note>—a thing which ought not to be done without singular reason and practiced prudence. And although I have searched with singular industry in the writings, parables, and various figures of the Philosophers, and toward manifold, wondrous, and partly...

**A**fter I had recalled to my memory the miracles of the Most High, the mysteries of hidden Nature, and the ignited and burning love for my neighbor: then I remembered the wheat harvest, in which **Reuben**, the son of **Leah**, found mandrakes <note>original: "Dudaim"; these are plants mentioned in Genesis 30:14, traditionally associated with fertility and used here as a symbol for natural secrets</note> in the field, which **Leah** gave to **Rachel** in exchange for a night with the Patriarch **Jacob**. And as soon as he spoke, the whole Harem politely bared themselves. But intent upon my thoughts, I could find or judge nothing, and my eyes were closed so that I did not recognize her.

Alchemists often used this to describe the sudden "illumination" of their own work.</note>

I proceeded in this manner in silence and hope, just as that old motherly woman had revealed to me, until at last, after a long stretch of time, my **intellect became silver** and my **memory became gold**, according to the promise of Solomon.

And behold: By the help of the Planets and the fixed stars, the Sun at last overcame the Eclipse, and a very serene day began to dawn upon all the mountains and valleys. Then all fear and terror ceased; and all who had seen that day rejoiced in the Lord, and said: *The winter has passed, the rain has ceased: Flowers have appeared on the earth: Spring has arrived, and the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in the land. Quickly, therefore, let us catch the foxes, the little foxes, I say, that ruin the vineyard, so that we may gather mature grapes, and being made into wine, we may drink; and in due time be fed with milk and the honeycomb, and become full and intoxicated.* <note>These biblical metaphors describe the successful growth and "ripening" of the alchemical Stone.</note> 

After the day had declined and evening approached, the whole sky changed its color, and the **Pleiades** <note>original: "Vergiliæ", an old name for the Pleiades star cluster, often associated with the timing of spring and rebirth.</note> arose with tawny rays, completing their natural course through the night, until in the morning they were overshadowed, overcome by the **Redness of the Sun** <note>The "Rubedo" or red stage is the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. And behold, the wise men dwelling on the earth were awakened from sleep, gazed at the sky, and said: *Who is she that breaks forth like the dawn, elegant as the moon, choice as the Sun, and no spot is found in her: her fervor is ignited, even a flame of the Lord, so that even much water cannot extinguish her love, nor the rivers overflow it.*

<summary>The narrator describes a symbolic eclipse representing the alchemical "Nigredo" (blackness) and its eventual transformation into a glorious "Rubedo" (redness). Using extensive metaphors from the Song of Solomon, the text celebrates the "rebirth" of the matter into a perfected, radiant state.</summary>

## A BRIEF EXPLANATION OF THE ADMIRABLE
### and most excellent Water-Stone of the Wise, which is otherwise called the *Philosopher’s Stone*.

From the very beginning of the world, in all times, there have existed and been found many unique men, highly illuminated by God, most experienced Philosophers, and wise Gentiles <note>The author refers to ancient pre-Christian thinkers like Hermes Trismegistus, Plato, or Aristotle who were believed to possess secret knowledge.</note>, who most diligently considered the nature and powers of lower creatures and attempted to learn them exactly. From all of these things, they investigated with great desire and labor whether anything might be found in the nature of things that could protect the earthly body of man from destruction and mortality, and preserve it in perpetual vigor and an intact state. For by a singular divine influence and the light of nature, they saw and knew that there must be a singular secret and a certain wonderful thing in this world which Almighty GOD had established for the benefit of the human race; namely, so that everything in the whole circle of the earth that was imperfect, defective, and corrupt might be renewed again through that singular and secret thing, and be perfectly restored to an intact state.

However, through that most diligent and exact investigation of theirs, they finally discovered and learned this: namely, how nothing at all was to be found in this world that could free the earthly and corruptible body from death—inasmuch as it <note>Death</note> had been established and imposed as a punishment upon the First-Created <note>original: "Protoplastis"; referring to the first-formed humans.</note>, Adam and Eve, and from their <margin>poste-</margin> <note>Catchword for the next page, likely "posterity" or "descendants."</note>

->Tell me, where will you find such men now?<-
*Why then are they so dear? They have not fallen fairly during this year.*
*They excel others in weight, in essence, and in their labor.*

Since, therefore, there are still to be found in many places faithful and diligent workers and students of this secret <term>philosophical art</term> <note>original: "artis philosophicæ"; a common term for alchemy, emphasizing its status as a branch of natural philosophy rather than just manual labor.</note>, who desire to set out toward it by a straight and certain path without many other winding detours, but who are nonetheless so disturbed by the aforementioned wicked men and <term>sophistic</term> <note>In this context, "sophistic" refers to fraudulent alchemists who used deceptive arguments or "tricks" to appear successful while lacking true knowledge.</note> impostors—and by their worthless clamor and pretensions—and are so entangled in error that many almost do not know whether they should proceed further in this art or retreat. Therefore, I have resolved to bring to light and explain a few things about this art which are brief, yet true and supported by their own foundation. Even if I judge myself unworthy to treat or write about so great a mystery, nevertheless, since by the grace of **GOD, THRICE GOOD AND GREATEST**, (to speak here without desire for glory) I have progressed so far—where few, indeed, hardly any out of so many thousands, reach—I do not wish the talent <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14–30), suggesting that God-given knowledge must be shared or put to use rather than "buried" or kept secret.</note> most mercifully granted to me, an unworthy servant, by the Almighty Lord and Liege, to remain hidden and buried within me. For that reason, I will show to all <term>lovers of chemistry</term> <note>original: "philo chemicis"; those who pursue the chemical art out of a love for wisdom.</note> from a faithful heart (as far as is fitting) an **Epitome** <note>A brief summary or abstract.</note> and **Declaration** of this entire art. At the same time, I shall point out the straight, infallible, and most certain way by which they may reach it, if perhaps by divine grace the eyes of some might be opened, and they might be led from their preconceived false opinions back to the right path, and thus the <term>mighty works of God</term> <note>original: "magnalia Dei"; the wonders of creation revealed through nature.</note> might be made more manifest. For the sake of memory and easier understanding, I will distribute this treatise into four parts.

In the **First**, I will indicate the beginning and entrance of this art, and how one should prepare oneself for it.

In the **Second**, through a philosophical description and instruction on the quality, condition, and knowledge of the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materiæ"; the "First Matter" or starting substance required for the Great Work.</note>, the entire method of preparation and the <term>regimen</term> <note>The specific "rule" or sequence of heat and timing required for the alchemical process.</note> will be indicated therein.

In the **Third**, the most abundant utility of the art, and the ineffable efficacy and power granted to it, will be discussed.

### Psalm 25.

> *Who is the man who fears the Lord? He will instruct him in the best way.*

**F**irst, every pious and God-fearing alchemist, and every philosopher of this art, should consider above all else that such a secret is to be held and judged not merely as the highest and greatest, but even as a **holy art** (since the highest and heavenly good, and the most holy image of the Almighty, is impressed and depicted within it). Therefore, if anyone intends to reach that supreme and ineffable mystery, let him know that such an art does not stand in the power of man, but consists in the most merciful will of God; and that it is not one’s WILLING <note>original: "VELLE"; a reference to Romans 9:16: "It is not of him that willeth... but of God that showeth mercy."</note> or desire, but the MERCY of the Almighty that carries one forward to it. For this reason, it is necessary above all else that you be pious, that you lift up your heart to Him alone, and that with true, most ardent, and unwavering prayer, you ask for that gift from Him alone. For from Him alone is it given and obtained.

If, therefore, Almighty God (who is the most certain searcher of all hearts) perceives and finds in you a right, faithful, and guileless soul—namely, that you endeavor to investigate and learn this for no other end than for His praise and glory alone—then, beyond all doubt and according to His promise, He will hear you. He will lead you through His Holy Spirit in such a way that you may conveniently reach some beginning through these means, of which you surely never could have thought; so much does He Himself [kindle] in your heart...

At this point, you must again implore the grace and direction of the **Almighty** in all your purposes, and your work will not only succeed easily, but will also obtain a happy, fortunate, and desired outcome.

# The Water-Stone of the Wise.

...is known <note>original: "scitur." This word completes the final sentence of the riddle on the previous page: "He who dissolves... is known."</note> (which knowledge even the philosophers at all times held to be the principal part of this work), then all the requirements, and what further preparation the work seems to demand, must be performed with the greatest zeal. Before, however, a single manual labor is undertaken with it, it is necessary that every pious artist diligently recall to mind the teaching already given. At the same time, he should be faithfully warned not to involve himself with this secret work and the **inscrutable spirit** <note>In alchemy, the "spirit" often refers to the volatile essence of a substance, but here it also suggests a dangerous supernatural or vital force within the matter.</note> that lies hidden within it, unless he has first explored it in its deep qualities and properties, and according to the requirements of nature’s conformity. 

As one of the Philosophers warns about this matter, saying: "Let there be no dealings between you and this spirit, unless you have first exactly learned the knowledge and science of it." For God is wonderful in His works, and His wisdom is beyond measure; and He is one who, as said above, does not allow Himself to be mocked. 

Truly, several examples of this matter could be brought forward here: namely, how many have involved themselves in this work quite lightly, but once the die was cast, things turned out so badly for them that some were partly killed in the laboratory or seriously injured by some other unfortunate accident. For it is not a work of light importance, as some imagine for themselves; they value it so little because philosophers compare it to **"child’s play and women’s work."** <note>original: "lusui puerili & labori mulierum." This famous alchemical phrase implies that once the "Stone" or "Medicine" is found, the remaining work is as simple and repetitive as laundry or a child's game.</note> 

The opinion of the philosophers was different; they understood the secondary labor of this work to be easy enough in itself and of almost no consequence, and they pointed it out so simply and lightly only to those whom God has deigned to grace and enrich with its knowledge. 

Beware therefore—beware, I say—and look out for yourself, lest you involve yourself in danger here too prematurely. Rather, begin your whole undertaking with prayers poured out to God and with divine help, as we faithfully advised from the start; then you will fear nothing at all, nor will you perhaps be subject to any danger.

If, therefore, you have now exercised yourself in your **oratory** <term>oratorio</term> <note>A private room for prayer and meditation.</note> with the greatest zeal, and you have the known matter at hand, then you can conveniently apply your diligence and zeal in the **laboratory** <term>laboratorio</term> <note>The physical workspace for chemical experimentation.</note>, take the appropriate labor in hand, and thus make a beginning.

# The Water-Stone of the Wise.

First, however, you must before all things dissolve that first matter, often mentioned before, or First Being <note>original: "primum Ens," a philosophical term for the fundamental substance of reality</note>, which the Philosophers also called the highest Good of Nature <note>original: "summum Naturæ Bonum"</note>. Then it must be purified from its wateriness and earthiness—for at first a heavy, thick, phlegmatic <note>original: "pituitosum," referring to one of the four humors, here meaning thick or mucus-like</note> earthly body, watery like a certain cloud, appears to those looking at it. Its dark, thickly misty shadow, by which it is overshadowed, must be taken away by you, so that in this way, through further sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here as a metaphor for purification.</note>, its heart and inner soul, which lie hidden and concealed within it, may then be separated and reduced into a sweet essence.

All these things can be accomplished by our Pontic <note>original: "Pontica." In alchemy, "Pontic water" usually refers to a sharp, universal solvent or a specific "bitter" quality of the primordial sea.</note> and universal water, which by its reciprocal course waters and fertilizes the entire world, and which is sweet, beautiful, clear, limpid, and splendid, wonderfully surpassing all the splendor of gold and silver, of carbuncle and diamond. Our aforementioned matter also keeps and contains this blessed water shut up within itself.

That extracted Heart, Soul, and Spirit must afterwards be distilled and congealed again with its own Salt—which is inserted into the aforementioned matter in its own kind and is blood-red in color in its interior, but after preparation becomes white, snowy, clear, and transparent, called the Salt of Wisdom <note>original: "Sal sapientiæ"</note> by the Philosophers—so that it may be reduced back into a single thing. And thus, through your process employed up to this point (which is called the preliminary work <note>original: "labor anterior"</note>), you have at least first separated the pure from the impure, and made the visible invisible, and then the invisible visible or tangible again. This substance is now no longer so heavy, coarse, and unrefined as it was from the beginning, but most bright, of a most sweet scent, and of a piercing taste. Moreover, it is of such a subtle and airy nature that if it were permitted to the air, it would fly away and vanish of its own accord (even though it is fixed within itself). For this reason, the Wise have named it Mercurial Water, or Mercury of the Sun <note>original: "Mercurium Solis"</note>, and also their own Mercury. But this "subject," as long as it remains in the aforementioned form, if you wish to use it in medicine without further preparation, will be of little use; it will rather be a poison to you.

Therefore, if you wish to enjoy its most abundant gift and manifold use, it is necessary for you to proceed further, and to attempt more through other singular means and labors.

Meanwhile, however, you will necessarily and diligently be forewarned that you should properly observe the operations of Nature, which she carries out in the course of time, and emulate them in all your labor. If you know this, then take two parts of the aforementioned prepared watery matter, and again three different parts; keep those first two parts. To the three parts, however, add another matter, namely the most noble **Body of Gold**, most highly endowed by the Creator, which is most closely related by affinity to the first matter and is friendly to it. Add one part of this by weight to the twelfth part for the first <term>Fermentation</term> <note>In alchemy, fermentation is the process where the "Stone" is given a specific direction—in this case, turning it toward gold—by adding a small amount of the pure metal.</note>; for both of these—namely the spiritual and celestial prepared watery matter, and this earthly **Body of the Sun** <note>original: "Solis corpus." The Sun is the alchemical symbol for gold.</note>—must be joined and coagulated into one body.

It must be noted here, however, that common gold does not serve this matter, but must be regarded as less suitable and as if dead. For although it was declared by Almighty God to be the most beautiful and precious of all metals, nonetheless, while it still lay hidden in the mines, it was hindered in its perfection of growing. Furthermore, through daily use, its inner powers—that is, the <term>Sulphur</term> or <term>Soul</term>—are indeed weakened, and it is still daily mixed, joined, and defiled with other illicit things that do not suit it at all. And so it is rendered more and more unsuitable for this work. Therefore, with the greatest care, provide for yourself pure gold that has a **living spirit**, which in its sulphur (as we said before) is not yet weakened nor sophisticated <note>sophisticated: in this context, it means adulterated, "tricked," or chemically corrupted.</note>, but is found to be entirely pure (if it has passed through **Antimony** or through the heaven and **Sphere of Saturn** <note>original: "Sphæram Saturni." Saturn is the alchemical name for lead. This refers to the process of refining gold by melting it with lead or antimony to remove impurities.</note> and there purified itself from its dross); otherwise, the other matter with its spirit and virtue cannot enter into this. For this work requires an entirely pure body, nor can it ever tolerate anything impure near, with, or around itself.

They differ in this way: the first substance, after preparation, is easy to work, thin, subtle, and soft; the other, however, is very heavy, firm, and hard. Once they are joined in a dissolving dish and reduced into a dry liquor or <term>amalgam</term> <note>A soft or liquid-like mixture of metals; here, the blend of the "watery matter" and the gold.</note>, you should leave them for six or seven days in a gentle heat that is at least lukewarm. Then, take one part from the three parts of water mentioned before and pour it into a round glass vessel—shaped like a phial or an egg. Place the tempered liquor in the middle of it and leave it again for six or seven days; the **Body of the Sun** <note>original: "Corpus Solis." The Sun is the alchemical symbol for gold.</note> will be gradually dissolved by the water. When this is done, the union of these two begins, and one is mixed into the other as smoothly and elegantly as ice in hot water. The Philosophers have described this in various ways, comparing it to a Bridegroom and a Bride (just as Solomon says in his *Song of Songs* <note>original: "Cantico Canticorum."</note>). When this is accomplished, add the remaining third part that was set aside to the others. However, do not add it all at once or in a single day, but in seven separate stages; otherwise, the body within would become too moist and eventually be destroyed by being completely submerged.

For just as a seed sown in the earth produces no fruit if it receives too much water, rain, or moisture at the start—instead, the farmer's crop is choked and dies—so it is with our work. When this is finished, seal the glass very carefully with wax or glue so that the compound does not lose its scent or fly away <note>A warning against "volatilization," where the vital chemical vapors might escape if the vessel is not airtight.</note>. Then place it in your furnace and provide it with a light, continuous, airy, and vaporous heat of a single degree, which is similar to the warmth of a hen sitting on her eggs.

...[mate]rial, but essential or preternatural fire, which is also called the **Divine Fire**. This is the <term>Water of Mercury</term> <note>original: "aqua Mercurii"; the specialized solvent used by alchemists to dissolve gold without harsh acids.</note>, which is incited by the aid and art of common fire. From the beginning, digest and cook it gently; take care that none of it sublimes <note>Changes from solid/liquid to vapor too quickly</note>, or—as the Philosophers speak in parables—lest the wife rule the husband, or the husband abuse his authority over his rib, etc. <note>This gendered metaphor refers to the balance between the "volatile" (female) and "fixed" (male) components of the mixture; if one overpowers the other, the experiment fails.</note> Then, the process completes itself in a continuous order without any other labor (except for the care and management of the fire). 

First, the earthy adjunct, the <term>Body of the Sun</term> <note>original: "Corpus Solis"; a common name for Gold.</note>, is totally dissolved, ground down, destroyed, and putrefied. Thus, it is despoiled of all its powers. At the beginning, this produces a dark color, and afterwards a completely black color; the Philosophers have called this the <term>Raven’s Head</term> <note>original: "caput corvi"; the 'Nigredo' or black stage, signifying the death and purification of the matter.</note>, and it usually occurs within the space of forty days. Eventually, the <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "Anima"</note> is also stripped from it, led on high, and utterly separated. For a while, the matter will stick to the bottom of the glass like ash, lacking any strength, like a dead thing. 

Afterward, however, if the fire is increased and directed unceasingly, the matter gradually and drop by drop descends again; it imbibes, moistens, feeds, and preserves its **Body**, lest it waste away and be burned entirely. It then ascends and descends again, and this happens nearly seven times. At this stage, the fire must again be intensified by one degree, yet not so much that you feel you must hurry; for the "governance of the fire" <note>The precise control of temperature over time.</note>, in which so much of the work consists, must be administered with the greatest care and diligence. Meanwhile, various signs and colors (which must be observed and well noted) will appear in the glass or vessel. When these are seen in their proper order, it is a good sign that a most happy outcome will follow.

First, grains like "fish eyes" show themselves; then a circle appears around the matter, which becomes now reddish, now whitish, and finally green and yellow like a <term>Peacock's Tail</term> <note>original: "cauda pavonis"; a famous alchemical stage where the matter displays iridescent colors before turning white.</note>. Afterward, it becomes a brilliant white, and finally a deep red, until—with the last degree of fire applied—the **Soul** and **Spirit** [are united].

All these are the most certain signs of a **sinister Disposition, Management**, or **Negligence**.

## THIRD PART.

->Sirach 43:27-33<-

> *Who can praise Him as highly as He is? We see but the smallest of His works. For things much greater than these are hidden from us. For the Lord made all things, and gives wisdom to those who fear God.* <note>original Latin: "Quis illum tam alte prædicare potest..." This citation from the Book of Sirach (often called Ecclesiasticus) serves as a reminder that the wonders of alchemy are reflections of the greater mysteries of God's creation.</note>

**R**egarding this highest art, so often mentioned now, or the ingenious **Philosopher’s Stone** brought to its desired end, and regarding its praise, virtue, and efficacy—and its ineffable utility—writers have not been able to write sufficiently or praise it worthily enough. For the Philosophers first esteemed and celebrated it as the highest and greatest happiness on this earth, without which no one in this world can reach perfection. For **Morienes** <note>Morienes was a legendary 7th-century hermit of Jerusalem, famous in alchemical lore for being the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: *He who possesses this stone possesses everything, and stands in need of no outside help. For in it is all temporal happiness, bodily health, and every good fortune.*

They further commended that same stone because its spirit and efficacy, which lie hidden within it, become the spirit of the **Fifth Essence** <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>Also known as the "Quintessence," this was believed to be a fifth, celestial element beyond earth, air, fire, and water—a pure, incorruptible substance that could heal the body and perfect matter.</note>, which exists beneath the circle of the **Lunar splendor** <note>This refers to the "sublunary" realm—the world under the moon where things are subject to change, decay, and death.</note>; indeed, it is the supporter of the heavens and the mover of the sea. It is, moreover, an elect spirit, more subtle, noble, and pure than all other celestial spirits, to which all others obey as if to a King. It confers all health and prosperity upon men, heals all diseases, and grants temporal honor and long life to the pious; but it subjects the wicked, who abuse it, to eternal punishment. In all these things, it has been found to be a proven, perfect, and infallible discovery. Wherefore **Hermes** and **Aristotle** <note>Hermes Trismegistus is the mythical founder of alchemy; Aristotle's name was often invoked by medieval alchemists to lend scientific authority to their work, though his actual views on transmutation were more complex.</note> call it the *truth without lies*, the *certainty of all most certain things*, the *secret of all secrets*, and the *Divine Virtue hidden from fools*. In short, it is the final and highest thing that can be seen under heaven, and a marvelous conclusion...

It frames the alchemical achievement as a gift from God, citing both biblical and legendary philosophical authorities.</summary>

...or they have called the same thing the epilogue <note>original: "epilogum" — implying the final summary or the ultimate perfection of all study.</note> of all philosophical works. For this reason, some pious Philosophers have firmly established that it was revealed to ***Adam***, the first man, from the heavens above, and was thereafter sought with singular desire by all the Holy Patriarchs.

For ***Noah***, the builder of the ark, and ***Moses***—who made the tabernacle and the golden vessels within it—just as ***Solomon*** built the temple in honor of God and completed many other famous works, ornaments of every kind, and other great deeds, are said to have obtained their long lives and vast riches from this very thing <note>Alchemists often claimed that the long lives of biblical figures were due to the "Universal Medicine" or Elixir of Life derived from the Stone.</note>.

Just as the ***Philosophers*** also confess, they discovered the **seven liberal arts** <term>seven liberal arts</term> <note>The traditional core of medieval education: grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> through it, and from it they both sought and obtained their sustenance. And God bestowed this upon them for their benefit, so that they might not be hindered in their studies and the search for wisdom by the cause of poverty. Nor would they be held in contempt and mockery by the wealthy and wicked of this world because of their beggary, or be forced to flatter the powerful or reveal those secrets for the sake of money, bringing their wisdom into disrepute.

Moreover, they recognized and learned the great and hidden mysteries of divine miracles, as well as the immense riches of divine Glory, from this source. And by this very means, certain hearts were stirred and set on fire by **GOD**, so that they were led further toward the knowledge of Him. For through that treasure, they did not seek great riches, worldly or temporal pleasure, and pride, nor did they desire to attain them; but rather, they derived all their pleasure and joy from the contemplation of the miracles hidden within created things. They certainly considered and looked upon these famous works and creatures of the **Almighty** in a far different way than—alas!—is customary for men of the modern age. When Almighty God, through His divine voice, wished to reveal to the human race something difficult and singular concerning His wonderful, high, and heavenly mysteries, He usually did so by means of parables. These parables are known to us in this earthly life; they are observed daily by our eyes, and are set before us and depicted for us. For example, when God, in Genesis chapter 3, wished to indicate to Adam in Paradise—after the Fall—his punishment, namely bodily mortality and physical death, He wished to hint and signify it to him in the following manner: that since the earth has no life in itself, and he [Adam] was taken and formed from the earth, for that reason he ought to become like the earth again. Likewise, in Genesis chapters 15 and 23, when God wished to point out to Abraham the increase of his seed and family, He commanded him to look upon the stars in the heaven, the sand in the sea, and the dust of the earth as a type <term>Type</term><note>In theology, a 'type' is a person, event, or object in the Old Testament that foreshadows a reality in the New Testament or a spiritual truth.</note>. God also commanded that various, very pleasant, and sweet typical prefigurations of this kind be proposed and shown to His Israelite people through the Prophets whenever He wished to announce something singular to them. And afterward, Christ Himself—the mouth and foundation of truth—did this in His Testament, and indeed set forth all things through parables so that His doctrine might be better understood: such as when He hints to us the highest blessedness, His divine word, and the Gospel, He then uses as a prototype <note>original: "protypo"</note> the good and bad seed, or
