### XLII. LAMECH
**The Stone of the Philosophers**: in it are the first elements and the final colors of mineral things; the lime, the soul, the spirit, the body, and at the same time the fixed. This Stone, in which all things are present, is called **Zibeth** <note>original: Zibeth; likely referring to the civet-like, pungent, or oily quality of the matter in a certain stage</note>, and natural operation has left it imperfect.

### XLIII. SOCRATES
The mystery of any thing is its life, which is to say: the water. For the water dissolves the body into spirit, and raises up some living spirit from the dead. My son, do not despise my **Practice**: for I have briefly revealed to you everything that is necessary for you, and you lack nothing else.

### XLIV. ALEXANDER
It is by no means necessary that the good must remain hidden for the sake of the evil. For **GOD** reigns over all things according to His divine will. Note, therefore, that **Salt** takes its origin from the stone, from **Mercury**, and is more excellent than all others: and this is that which we seek; for it embraces all our secrets within itself. But enough of these things. We have revealed enough in our writing to those skilled in these matters, and to the unskilled nothing at all: for **Mercury** is our stone, which is tempered by the dry and the moist together, and is so joined through tempered heat that they can never be torn apart from one another. These things suffice, for even a little wisdom is enough.

### XLV. SENIOR
**Senior** <note>Referring to Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist</note> commands that **Salt** must be made from ash, and through various labors, and then converted into the **Mercury of the Philosophers**: for our mastery is made from our water, and requires nothing else.

### XLVI. ROSARIUS
The **Stone** is, and is not a stone; it is the **Eagle Stone** <term>Lapis Aquilae (Eagle Stone): A stone (aetites) believed to have another stone rattling inside it, used here as a metaphor for the spirit contained within matter</term>, of which one speaks, and of which **Arrius** <note>Possibly a reference to a specific alchemical author or a corruption of another name</note> speaks; the well-known stone in whose belly there is a stone, and if it is moved or dissolved, then its water breaks out, which had been coagulated within it: thus the extracted stone is the spirit from our indestructible body, holding the **Mercury**—that is, the fluid water—within the body, which is the firm earth, with the retention of its nature. And that has been spoken plainly enough.

XLVII. **PAMPHILUS**: Note this, for it is **Rock Salt** <term>Sal Gemmæ: Literally "salt-gem," referring to pure, crystalline rock salt, often used by alchemists to represent the "salt of the earth" or a purified mineral base</term> which is in its very belly; it rises together with the water above the **alembic** <term>alembic: A classic alchemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling liquids</term>, and they are separated from one another, and then joined again through natural heat and reduced into one. Thus it truly becomes spirit and body, just as **King Alexander** <note>Refers to Alexander the Great, who was frequently claimed as an alchemical initiate in medieval lore</note> testifies.

XLVIII. **DEMOCRITUS**: Our Art is joined from a dry and a moist thing, and coupled again through heat; this, divided through vapor or heat, is changed into moisture as if into water, and in this water our stone is found. For the vapor carries away with it even the most subtle air into the most subtle earth, and for this reason it is tempered to be like the most subtle elements. It is called the **First Matter** <term>prima materia: The original, formless substance from which all things were created, sought by alchemists as the starting point of the Great Work</term>, and the matter is separated—namely into earth and water—and the earth is found there visible to the eye. You understand, therefore, that the vapor will become tempered like the four elements; the subtle and fleeting earth ascends at the same time and is found fixed in the separation, but in the coupling, **Mercury** <note>original: Mercurius; here representing the transformative, volatile principle that must be "fixed" or made solid</note> is then made fixed. We Philosophers indeed highly celebrate the almighty Creator, because we have recognized Him and His miracles, and have received His fruit until the end of our lives.

XLIX. **SIROS**: The **calcined** <term>calcinatum: A substance reduced to a dry powder or "lime" through the application of high heat</term> body of the Philosophers is called eternal water, which coagulates our Mercury with a perpetual coagulation; and if the body is purified and dissolved, then such a great mixture or union exists that no fire will ever be able to separate it.

L. **NOAH**, that man of God, writes thus in his tablet: My children and brothers, know that no other stone is found in the world that has more virtue in itself than this stone: no mortal in the world can find the true art without this stone. Blessed be God of heaven, who created nature in Salt, indeed in **Rock Salt**.

LI. **MENALDES**: From all natural things, the fire of Philosophy can be extracted, which is named the **fifth essence** <term>quinta essentia: The "quintessence" or a fifth element above the earthly four, believed to be the pure, incorruptible essence of a substance</term>; and that is its nature and species, as it occurs in earth, and in water, and in air, and in fire. Furthermore, it has no cause of corruption nor any contrary quality.

LII. **HERMES**, in his second tablet, writes thus: Dissolve the ash in the second element and coagulate it into a stone, and do this seven times.

will be done: For just as **Naaman from Syria** <note>original: "Naeman ex Syria"; Refers to the biblical story in 2 Kings 5, where the commander Naaman is cured of leprosy by bathing seven times in the Jordan River. In alchemy, "leprosy" represents the impurities or "corruptions" of base metals</note> washed himself seven times in the Jordan, and was thereafter cleansed of his leprosy as thoroughly as a pure new man, so too must the same be done in this art of ours: namely, by **calcining** <term>calcionando: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or cause oxidation, reducing it to a powder</term> and **dissolving** <term>solvendo: The process of liquefying a solid or "opening" a metal so its inner spirit can be accessed</term>, and then the materials attain their colors, higher and higher. Therefore fire is so holy and venerable that God's eternal wisdom lived with it in the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "SS. Trinitatem"</note> of eternal glory, for which God we pay eternal thanks.

LV. **BONIDUS** <note>Likely referring to Petrus Bonus, the 14th-century author of "The Precious Pearl"</note>: In the fountain of nature our art is found, and nowhere else on earth; and our stone, which we know, is fire, and it grew in fire, yet it was not consumed in the fire.

LVI. **ROSINUS** <note>A name often attributed to Zosimos of Panopolis in medieval Latin translations</note>: Two things are hidden in two, and they denote our stone alone: in the earth is fire, and in the water is air; and there are only two extremes, namely the extreme of earth and the extreme of water. ...more is required than **Mercurial substances**, which are well purified by art, penetrating, tinting, persevering in the fire, and standing firm at the **very edge of the fire** <note>original: "acie ignis"; refers to the most intense point of heat where substances usually fail or evaporate</note>, not abandoning themselves in their **kingdoms** <note>original: "Monarchiis"; likely referring to the different states or "regimes" of the elemental process</note>, but preserving themselves in their own Mercurial essence. LVIII. **AROS** <note>An authority often cited in alchemical florilegia, sometimes associated with the legendary Mary the Prophetess</note>: Our Medicine is made from two things and one essence. Concerning the unity of the Mercurial matter—fixed and not fixed, spiritual and corporal, cold and moist, hot and dry—it is not possible to fashion it from any other things.

LIX. **ARNOLDUS** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>: All your intention shall be directed toward cooking and guiding the **Mercurial substance**; according to its worthiness, it will deign to transform the bodies, etc.

LX. **ALPHIDIUS** <note>An Arab alchemist often quoted in Western medieval texts</note>: Transmute the nature, and you will find what you seek; this is true: For in our **Mastery** <term>Magisterio: The 'Great Work' or the specialized process of alchemical transformation</term>, we first extract the tender from the coarse—that is, the **spirit from the body** <note>The process of "spiritualizing" a metal involves making a solid substance volatile or liquid</note>: then the dry from the moist—that is, the earth from the water: and so we transmute and perfect the true nature, from corporal to spiritual, and from spiritual to corporal, as it is said: let the lowest be converted into the highest, and the highest into the lowest; that is, the spirit becomes body, and the body becomes spirit.

LXI. **BERNHARDUS** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a celebrated alchemist who spent his life searching for the Philosopher's Stone</note>: The mediums are nothing other than **coagulated Mercury**: and the **First Matter** <term>prima materia: The original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</term> is nothing other than doubled Mercury. For our Medicine is made from two things: the fixed and the less fixed, the spiritual and the corporal, the cold and moist, and the hot and dry. Likewise, Mercury must be cooked in a certain **triple vessel** <note>May refer to a specialized furnace or a nesting of glass vessels to maintain precise heat</note>, so that the dryness of the acting fire converts it into a vaporous moisture of the oil surrounding the matter; the fire does not "digest" our matter directly, but rather its heat is altered into dryness, and that is the true fire.

LXII. **STEPHANUS** <note>Stephanus of Alexandria (7th century), a philosopher and alchemist</note>: Concerning metals: Metals are earthly bodies, and they are generated in water. Water extracts vapor from the stone, and from the moisture of the earth, through the operation of the Sun, God allows gold to grow and be gathered: thus earth and water are united into a metallic body, etc.

LXIII. **GUIDO BONATUS** <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), a famous Italian astrologer and mathematician</note> writes briefly about the **Quintessence** <term>Quintessence: From the Latin 'quinta essentia' (fifth essence); the purest part of a substance, superior to the four physical elements</term> in this way: that it is the purest of the four elements, that is, the Quintessence which contains within itself all four elements; this is the **First Matter** <term>First Matter: 'Prima Materia'; the primitive, formless base of all matter required for the alchemical Great Work</term>, where God created all things, and still creates them. And this **Mass** (page 34) <note>likely a reference to a specific folio in a manuscript source</note> is the confused nature of each and every thing; whatever it may become, nonetheless that nature exists in all things and is called **Hyle** <term>Hyle: A Greek term for 'matter', specifically the raw, primordial substance of the universe</term>, of which mention was made above.

LXIV. **ALRIDOS** <note>An authority frequently cited in alchemical anthologies</note>: The virtue, efficacy, and excellent operation of each and every thing, whatever it may become on earth, lies hidden in its Quintessence, whether it be of a hot, cold, moist, or dry Nature and **Complexion** <term>Complexion: In medieval science, the specific balance of the four humors or qualities in a body</term>. And in the Quintessence of each thing, it requires again the most excellent and most noble smell that is, or ever could be, devised; for this reason, the highest perfection is necessary.

LXV. **LONGINUS** <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-alchemical author rather than the Roman soldier</note> describes the labor to us in this way: Take care that your vessel is continually closed and has an even heat. And further: This **water** is prepared in **dry ash** <note>original: "aqua conficitur in sicco cinere"; a 'sand bath' or 'ash bath' used to provide steady, indirect heat</note>, in a closed vessel, and is cooked for so long until the two become one. ## NOW FOLLOWS THE TRUE EXPLANATION
### *of certain previously mentioned philosophical sayings, word for word, regarding all points and articles of these opinions.*

**I**n order that you, kind Reader, may better understand what the Philosophers were looking toward in their obscure and allegorical statements—all of whom mentioned above were true Philosophers and both knew and practiced this art—although many more have existed since the time of **Adam** <note>Alchemists often traced their lineage back to Adam, believing God granted him divine knowledge of nature</note>, nevertheless, not all of them have come into my hands. Furthermore, it is impossible for me to touch upon every individual here; it suffices that the truth and foundation of the art be taught and explained in these sayings, the least of which would be sufficient. 

That I have produced so many in order, however, was done for your benefit, so that you might be more learnedly informed, work more securely, and diligently guard yourself against the loss of money and useless expenses. Wherefore, out of Christian charity, I have declared and explained this true **Philosophy** <term>Philosophy: Here referring to 'Hermetic Philosophy' or Alchemy, the study of the hidden laws of nature</term> according to my understanding and as much as **GOD** has granted me. I ask anyone skilled in the art, who has labored in it as I have, not to despise me if I have perhaps erred in words while writing, but to be willing to correct the errors from a faithful heart—just as I have done—and let no one rashly seduce or deceive others, so that the name of God may be glorified and the benefit of one's neighbor promoted. You shall not, however, change my sense or opinion, for I know what I have written, and that it was divine truth.

### EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING OF ABEL.

**T**his saying almost explains itself, and it is also sufficiently declared in the words of GOD, and in the sentence of Adam. Yet according to my judgment and knowledge I respond to it thus: that man has within himself all the powers of those things, just as that sentence is a witness of this matter, while man is esteemed as a **little world** <note>original: "parvo mundo"—referring to the Microcosm, a central idea in alchemy and Renaissance philosophy suggesting that the human body contains a miniature version of the entire universe's structure and elements.</note>, and also is entirely compared with the world; for his bones hidden beneath the skin are compared with stony mountains: for with them the body is strengthened, not otherwise than the earth with stones, and the flesh is esteemed as the earth, and the great veins as great streams, and the small indeed as tiny rivers, which discharge themselves into the great ones. The bladder is the sea, in which both the great and also the tiny rivers are equally gathered: Hair is as growing herbs: Nails on the hands and feet, and whatever is detected both within and without in man, all things according to their species, are compared with the world. The interior of man also—such as the Heart, lung, liver, and other things of that kind—are similar to the metals of the mountains: But these hairs are roots, which have their roots in the air, and the head in the earth, as if in the flesh, in which they receive their powers and growth: just as the <term>Philosophers</term> <gloss>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists or natural scientists of the past.</gloss> also say, that the root of their minerals will be in the air, and the head of the same in the earth. For that which ascends through <term>distillation</term> <gloss>The process of heating a substance to create vapor and then cooling it back into a liquid to purify it.</gloss> is fleeting: in that it has its feet in the air, and that which remains fixed below at the bottom, its head is in the earth; for the feet carry the head, and the head rules the feet. Wherefore one cannot be without the other, if otherwise [the work] its operation...

...ought to have its own. * Thus man is compared to an **inverted tree**: for he has his roots, namely the hair, in the air, while other trees have their hair—that is, their roots—in the earth.

In a similar way, a comparison is made with **our stone** <note>original: "lapide noſtro"—the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical work.</note>: for that reason the Philosophers can rightly affirm that they have their head in the earth and their root in the air. For that is the **First Matter** <note>original: "prima materia"—the formless, original substance from which all things are made.</note>, or the origin of all things, from which each new thing is prepared. Know that it becomes the First Matter when something is buried everywhere in the dug-up earth; it putrefies, just as food is cooked within a man, and in <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of decomposition (nigredo) where the matter breaks down to release its essence.</note> the coarse separates itself from the subtle, like the stench from the pure; and the pure is the First Matter, which has been separated through putrefaction. If you understand these things, then you possess the true art. However, keep these things constantly to yourself, and **do not cast pearls before swine**: for that art is held in mockery by those ignorant of things; but those skilled in it deservedly value and venerate it.

The spirit, just like distilled water, is called the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol." In alchemy, the Sun usually represents gold or the active, masculine principle of the work.</note>; for the element of air is indeed hidden within it. However, the body must be broken down in its own water, so as to be dissolved into itself. This occurs in the water of the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna." This represents silver or the receptive, feminine principle.</note> etc., which becomes well-tempered—that is, a certain natural heat works within itself and is changed into water. Then you have dissolved the body, and you have two waters: namely, the distilled spirit and the dissolved body. These two waters are joined and united by gentle and slow cooking: so that the distilled spirit becomes a body during coagulation, and the body becomes spirit during dissolution. What was <term>fixed</term> <note>A substance that remains solid and stable when exposed to fire.</note> becomes <term>volatile</term> <note>original: "fugax" (fleeting). A substance that evaporates or escapes when heated.</note>, and the volatile becomes fixed, through dissolution and coagulation; it is then converted into a most brilliant white color, which is followed by red. 

By this the Philosopher wishes to signify: The White and the Red are worked in one water. Once the white is prepared, it is then changed into the red; for the red is hidden under the white, and the red follows the white, just as the white follows the black—in which the whole art consists. With these things the Philosopher finally concludes and says: This art is accomplished solely with the **supreme vinegar** <note>original: "summo aceto." This is not household vinegar, but a powerful alchemical solvent, often called the "Acetum Philosophorum."</note>, by divine power, and the perfection of the work. He implies that the art is worked from only one thing, which is compared to the sharpest vinegar and is collected and prepared through the **dew of philosophy** <note>original: "rorem Philosophiæ." A poetic term for the subtle substance or "heavenly" influence captured at the start of the work.</note>. This vinegar, through divine grace and the perfection of the work, is established so that through preparation it is changed from vinegar into the **Highest Good** of heaven and earth—a Good which could never be paid for by the whole world, nor by all its Kings and Princes.

That air then becomes thick when it is transmuted into a body along with fire, and thus the air corrects the matter in its thickness. It both brings forth and brings in our Stone, correcting it as much in its ascent as in its descent. In the same way, the air corrects all growing or vegetable things of this world; from this, it offers them their food. It bestows upon them water and fire, by which they are sustained, just as you yourself are an eyewitness to the fact that the air carries the clouds and brings them back as dew and rain. In this dew or rain, a fire is hidden, which the air conceived from the earth and the splendor of the **Sun** during its ascent, and it bestows this upon all things in place of food.

...live, and nourish creatures: through boiling they receive their splendor, from which they obtain their life. For this reason, the air is exceedingly great, for through the grace of Almighty God, it performs great works.

Furthermore, when the Philosopher says: "If the air be thick—namely, if the Sun wanders or is changed—and there is thickness while it raises itself up," he signifies this: If distilled water, which is taken as the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) often represents Gold or the active, masculine principle of Fire.</note> or for fire, is applied to the body placed in a glass, and is transmuted into a single body, then the Sun falls and lowers itself into the earth. When this happens, the air becomes thick, for it is joined with the earth. And if the Sun is exalted again, then the air becomes thin; that is, while water is extracted from the earth through an **alembic** <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used to purify substances by heating them into vapor and condensing them</term>, then fire simultaneously tends upward—that is, the Sun is exalted—and then the air is thin. 

And when he further says: "That also is heat and cold, and thickness and thinness (or softness)," the Philosopher implies by this: The Sun is hot, the **Moon** <note>The "Moon" (Luna) often represents Silver or the passive, feminine principle of Water.</note> is cold. For the Earth is considered the Moon if it is dissolved; and the water in which fire is contained stands for the Sun. These two must be united and joined so that they can no longer be separated. And if they are united in this way, the elements are then immediately united in all metals into which they are cast, bringing both metallic and fleshly <note>The author suggests the alchemical medicine heals both "sick" metals (turning them to gold) and human bodies.</note> bodies to perfect purity and health. 

When finally the Philosopher concludes and says that thickness and thinness denote summer and winter, he means that our art consists in thickness and thinness. These two must be joined by a certain temperate heat—not too hot, nor yet too cold, lest nature be burned—that is, winter and summer. And when these two come together, a temperate heat arises from them, as if in a certain natural bath <note>original: "balneo." Referring to a gentle, consistent heat source like a water bath, often called a *balneum Mariae*.</note>. These temperate heats bring together the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, our Issindrus proposed this parable, which, through divine grace, has been correctly explained by me—provided you have prudently observed my meaning.

# EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING OF ANAXAGORAS. #

<note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that "Mind" (Nous) was the initiating force of the cosmos. Alchemists often claimed him as one of their own to lend ancient authority to their texts.</note>

**G**od is from the beginning of all things. That is true, for God is light, just like fire: Therefore, God in His Essence is compared with fire: For fire is the beginning of all living <note>original: "vegetabilium," referring to things that grow or possess a vegetative soul.</note> and visible things. The same holds true for our art: For the beginning is fire: heat drives nature so that it may begin to work, and in that operation, the **Body**, **Spirit**, and **Soul** manifest themselves; that is, like earth and water: as the earth is the body, the oil is the soul, and the water is the spirit. This happens through divine gentleness and goodness, since without that, Nature can accomplish nothing at all, just as the Philosopher <note>In alchemical texts, "The Philosopher" usually refers to Aristotle, but here it likely refers back to Anaxagoras.</note> himself says: "The gentleness of God rules all things." 

And under the thickness of the earth, after creation, gentleness and integrity reveal themselves—under the thickness of the earth: Where the Philosopher implies: If the earth is separated from the water (at the commencement, which is called creation) and is dissolved into oil and water within itself, then the oil is integrity and the water is gentleness. For the water bestows the soul upon the oil and the body, and it assumes nothing more than what is granted to it from heaven—that is, from the water—and the water is manifested under the oil, and the oil under the earth. 

For subtle fire, along with subtle waters, ascends upward from the earth and is hidden in the earth; but the oil is not raised from the earth under labor. Instead, only the fire, water, and air, together with the oil and the earth, are purified through their own spirit. Therefore, the oil in the body is integrity, and the Spirit is gentleness, and the body is constricted <note>original: "coangustatur," suggesting the body is compressed or tightened during the chemical process.</note>. And although the spirit descends from the body in the first operation (for it restores life to the body, even though the oil becomes pure and always remains with the body), nevertheless, it cannot be of help to the body without the spirit. Rather, the body, as was said, suffers force and distresses; for by force it is dissolved and purified. 

And when the Philosopher says, "under the thickness of the earth," although gentleness is not perceived except in the body, he implies: The thickness of the earth is transmuted into thin matter, such as water and oil, and then gentleness is perceived in the body. For the body is so gentle or soft that it is even converted into water or oil, although it was previously entirely dry. Therefore, in the earth the oil con-

# EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING
## of Pythagoras.
<note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher. While best known today for mathematics, alchemists revered him as a master of the "Music of the Spheres" and the hidden harmonies of nature.</note>

**T**he Philosopher asks, what shall that be which is touched, and yet not seen? By this, the Philosopher means to signify: There is one thing of our art, which is prepared by our art: and it is one thing which is touched, and not seen. This is to be understood thus: it is felt, but not beheld, nor is its operation known: But he who knows it, and yet remains ignorant of its operation, he never attains the art. For in the whole world there is no more than one thing from which the art is composed and worked out. And this thing proceeds from a certain dark place, where it is never seen, nor are its operations and virtues recognized by anyone, except by the wise of this art alone. Similarly, a great mystery is hidden within the matter itself, namely air and fire—that is, the **Sun**, **Moon**, and **Stallae** <note>Sun, Moon, and Stars represent the celestial influences or the metallic principles of Gold, Silver, and the fixed salts.</note>: it is hidden within it, and yet it is invisible, just as the Philosopher says: "That which is not seen, nor known, is heaven alone. By which the Philosopher hints: The earth is the thickness <note>original: "crassities," meaning the dense, physical residue.</note>, or the body, which is found at the bottom of the matter, and that which has accumulated itself in the matter can be felt and known. ## EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING OF PARMENIDES.

**K**now this, you hateful and spiteful ones: the Philosophers have spoken of many waters, and likewise of many metals, stones, etc. And they did this for the purpose of trying to deceive you. By this, the Philosopher <note>Parmenides, an ancient Greek philosopher often cited in alchemical florilegia.</note> intends that they have hidden those things from us so that they might not be revealed to all men. For those who wish to work in this way—and according to the literal letter of the text—will deceive themselves (even though the Philosophers have written rightly and truly), because they wish to work and yet are devoid of the foundation or the knowledge of the art. And the fault is not with the Philosophers, but with the worker’s own ignorance. For the Philosophers wrote of stones, and they are indeed Stones, but they are dug from our mountains. They write of metals, and then the metals are waters, but liquefied from our air. They write of waters, and then they are waters, but drawn from our spring and sea. They write of sulfur,

## EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING OF LUCAS <note>Lucas is a recurring figure in the "Turba Philosophorum," one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, where various sages debate the secrets of the art.</note>

**T**ake the living water from the Moon: by which the Philosopher signifies the <term>living water<note>original: "aquam vivam"; also known as "aqua vitae" or "mercurial water," the solvent capable of dissolving gold.</note></term>. This is distributed into two parts. For first, the distilled water is considered as the Moon. For the Sun, like fire, is hidden within it, and he is the father of all things. Therefore, it is compared to a man, and this is because the Sun is in the water. Thus, it is called "living water," for the life of the dead body is hidden in the water. Secondly, the Philosopher calls that "water from the Moon." Observe therefore the name of the Moon: for the Sun is the father, and the Moon is the mother. From this, you can understand both as male and female. For the "Body" is taken for the Moon, and she is the mother in this art; and the distilled water, which we regard as the male, ascends upward from the earth. Therefore, it is also named for the Moon, for it is the water of the Moon, just like the water of the body which is held to be the Moon. Indeed, it has gone out from the body, and therefore it must enter it again if the art is to be perfected in any other way. For this reason, you must understand that clearly regarding the man, or regarding the Moon: for the Sun is the husband, and the Moon is the wife. The Earth is the Moon, and the water is the Sun, just as is sufficiently [evident]...

In this book you have been guided: for everywhere it is blessed.

Furthermore, the Philosopher says: **Coagulate it according to our manner or custom**, as if you might not notice that I am speaking of our own human habits. He is hinting that we should offer the spirit to the body for it to drink, and do this uniquely or gradually, so that it may drink of the spirit as if from water, until it recovers its life and acquires health and strength. This is done through a <term>tempered heat<note>A gentle, steady warmth often compared to the heat of a brooding hen or the natural warmth of the human body.</note></term>, just as food is <term>concocted<note>original: "concoquitur"; in alchemy, "concoction" refers to the process of ripening or "digesting" a substance through heat to bring it to perfection.</note></term> in the stomach, and just as fruit grows in its natural place.

For it already possesses what it ought to have; nothing is to be added to it, and nothing is to be taken away. Rather, it is separated within its own nature and joined together again, just as you are taught in this preparation.

And when the Philosopher says further: **I command you to take the water of life, which descends from the Moon, and bring it to our earth until it becomes white**, he means this: If the water and earth are separated from one another, then the dry body is our **earth**, and the water drawn away is the **water of the Moon**. This must be done frequently and repeatedly—by pouring on, drying, grinding, and coagulating—until the body becomes white during the boiling. Then we have achieved our "conglutination," which is constant (as the Philosopher says), and then we have our <term>Magnesia<note>A traditional name for the crude or transforming matter of the Stone, specifically when it reaches the white, shimmering stage.</note></term>, and it rejoices...

## EXPOSITION OF THE SAYING OF ETHELIUS

**H**e says: Cook our <term>stone<note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemical work.</note></term> for so long until it shines like some flashing marble; then let it be the great and <term>secret stone<note>original: "lapis arcanus"; a stone containing hidden or "arcane" powers.</note></term>. For <term>sulfur<note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter, not merely the chemical element.</note></term> added to sulfur, preserving its own property within itself—by which he implies: If our stone is now made separate, as the moist is from the dry, then the dry is taken as the foundation for our stone, and it is black, like a raven <note>The "blackness" or "raven's head" (nigredo) is the first stage of the alchemical process, representing putrefaction and the stripping away of impurities.</note>. That dry foundation must be cooked with its own water, which was separated from it, until its <term>blackness<note>original: "nigredo."</note></term> passes away and it grows white, like some white, shining marble. And then it is the <term>secret stone</term>, which, by the grace of God, has been transmuted during the cooking into <term>fixed mercury<note>original: "Mercurium fixatum"; mercury that has been made stable and no longer evaporates when exposed to heat.</note></term>.

Furthermore, that stone is called secret for the following two reasons. One is that it is found in a certain secret place which no one pays attention to, so that in such a vile thing <note>Alchemists often claimed the "materia prima" was found in "filth" or common places like dunghills, making it "vile" to the uninitiated.</note> so great a power, <term>mystery</term>, and the highest treasure should be hidden. Thus, no one can find it by their own reason without a teacher and the instruction of a master, or by a singular gift of God. Therefore, the <term>Philosopher<note>Often used to refer to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, but here referring to the collective wisdom of alchemical masters.</note></term> can rightly affirm: IT IS THE SECRET STONE.

And while he further says: <term>Sulfur</term> is joined to sulfur, preserving its own property within itself, there the <term>Philosopher</term> understands: When the matter is separated—namely, the <term>spirit<note>The volatile or gaseous part of the substance.</note></term> apart and the <term>body<note>The solid or fixed residue of the substance.</note></term> also apart—they are indeed separated for a time. And although two matters are present there, it is nevertheless at least one matter, and it is transmuted back into one body. For the lowest part, acting as the body, is <term>sulfur</term>, and the highest part, the spirit, is also <term>sulfur</term>. And when the spirit approaches the body, then one <term>sulfur</term> comes to the other—that is, sulfur joined to sulfur—and that is its property. For the spirit belongs to the body, and the body belongs to the spirit; for one cannot do without the other. Therefore, those two sulfurs are hidden in nature, both the white and the red, and the white sulfur is in the body...

No foreign thing intervenes there, and this is its unique property. Therefore it takes in nothing but its own spirit. For the body has preserved the <term>soul<note>original: "animam"; the mediating principle that connects the volatile spirit to the solid body.</note></term> of the body within itself, and that which was extracted from the body must always be restored to that same body alone. Therefore nothing is more pleasing or acceptable to it than its own soul and its own body—that is, its own nature—to which end the Philosopher says: "If it is thus accumulated—namely, the spirit to the body, sulfur to sulfur, earth to water—and it is made entirely white, then the body will hold the spirit within itself, and it will not fly away, so that they can never be separated from one another again." And in this way, you have the "earth of the Philosophers," purified to a brilliant whiteness, into which we sow our grain so that it may bring forth infinite fruit.

# EXPOSITION OF THE SAYING
## of Pythagoras.

**N**ot without reason might you marvel at the wondrous sayings of the Philosophers regarding the earth: for however manifoldly they have described this thing, they nevertheless agree entirely in this one matter, since all their sayings look toward a single goal. If only you observe rightly, you will surely discover the truth. For where the Philosopher says: "We give you the <term>regimen<note>The specific set of instructions or the "rule" for managing the alchemical fire and process.</note></term> of these things: that it shall become a <term>dry water<note>original: "aqua sicca"; a classic alchemical paradox usually referring to Mercury, which wets nothing it touches.</note></term>, like the <term>water of the Moon<note>original: "aqua Lunae"; often a reference to silver-based solutions or the "white" stage of mercury.</note></term> which you have prepared," the Philosopher means: When we wish to labor at this art, we must conform ourselves properly according to our understanding. If we err in this and do not aim at the mark, then we might deservedly blame them as impostors. For they hand down the regimen publicly; but if you do not hit the mark, it must be ascribed to your own cleverness or your folly, for you interpret the scripture according to your own insane and restless heads, differently than it actually sounds. Furthermore, when the Philosopher says that [one's] own...

## EXPOSITION OF THE EMERALD TABLET
### *of Hermes.*

**W**hen Hermes says: "The Art is true and most true," he signifies by this: The Art is correctly handed down by the Philosophers, but the foolish interpret the writing differently than it sounds, and they take up something other than what they ought to take. Since they are in error, they then say that the Art is not true, and that they have been deceived by the Philosophers who wrote lies. They say the Art itself is not true, but false; thus, those who labor even with the Art itself are considered worthless <note>original: "nauci aestumantur"; literally "valued at a nutshell," meaning of no value.</note> and are despised. But the blame is to be attributed to no one but the ignorant fools who do not understand the Scripture. For if they had truly looked into the Art, read with understanding, and conformed themselves according to it—and had not followed their own stupid heads and their own personal understanding—then...

Furthermore, you are able to drive away all diseases from both metals and the human body. You will no longer dare to suffer poverty; instead, by the benefit of this art and through divine grace, you will possess and recognize all good temperaments <note>term: "complexiones" – the balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in the body or soul.</note> in all intelligence and wisdom. For this matter changes **Mercury** into pure gold and silver, and it penetrates all hard and solid bodies, such as precious stones and metals. Therefore, Hermes may rightly affirm and boast of himself:

# ANOTHER WORK CORRESPONDING WITH THE PREVIOUS ONE, and very useful to read.

## PREFACE.

**N**ot without merit might all wonder why the Philosophers, in honor of this most precious and divine art which is called the <term>SECRET OF THE PHILOSOPHERS</term><note>Latin: *Secretum Philosophorum*. This refers to the Great Work of alchemy, specifically the creation of the Philosophers' Stone.</note>, have devised so many occult and allegorical sayings. They did this so that the art would by no means be revealed to the unworthy; yet, this creates no fruit for the disciples of these secrets, since the authors were intent on hiding the truth by that very means. And while the foolish read and hear their writings—specifically regarding what great riches, virtues, and powers our art can produce—they then perceive a pleasant and most sweet sound in their ears, so much so that they imagine themselves sitting upon golden leaves, and that pure strings are fixed to heaven. From this, a great art and desire arises, so that they soon persuade themselves they will be future Teachers; they attempt to perform great miracles, yet they do not perceive themselves to be wandering in error. Nor do they realize that the Philosophers are deceiving them—much less do they know that the wise have hidden the foundations of this art from the very beginning, and have explained the truth only to their "children" <note>In alchemical literature, "children" or "sons of the art" refers to initiated students or those deemed spiritually worthy of the secret.</note> through parables and similarities. 

Furthermore, it is hardly possible for a person, as long as they live in this troubled and unclean world, to explore the sense and opinion of all the Philosophers, much less to read through their books and writings with proper judgment. Indeed, it is much more impossible for anyone to draw a sufficient foundation and full desire from those books and writings, unless Almighty God, out of singular grace and compassion, opens their understanding. This is so that they may recognize the property of Nature, by which they may be able to judge the writings and sayings of the Philosophers. For it is Nature alone which performs all things through art in our <term>Mastery</term><note>Latin: *Magisterium*. This refers to the entire process of the alchemical work, the mastery of matter.</note>, and she alone, I say, [provides] the correct knowledge of the matter...

Therefore, anyone unskilled in these matters and in this most noble art must imitate nature; just as it is equally necessary that he understand the nature of the substance, for art must follow nature. However, many craftsmen are found who wish neither to understand nor even to pay attention, laboring without reason; they are confused in their own thoughts, ignorant of whether or not their art will be an imitator of nature, which they nevertheless attempt to correct and improve. Concerning these men, that most celebrated philosopher <term>Arnoldus</term> <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famed physician and alchemist whose works emphasize the natural origins of the Stone.</note> says that they approach the art much like an ass approaching a manger, not knowing where to stick its snout. In the same way, they are ignorant of what they are busy with, knowing even less of the principle of nature, nor do they know how they ought to imitate it through their art.

They indeed attempt to perfect the works of nature, but once the work is finished, they see clearly what they have actually found. Therefore the proverb is true: "He who is sluggish in turning the pages of books cannot be worthy to prepare the materials of the art," since there is no doubt that this divine art possesses the true principle of nature. For the nature of the <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemical authors often used "Art" to refer to the "Great Work" (alchemy) which mimics and accelerates the natural processes occurring within the earth.</note> produces true bodies in the earth—some perfect, such as gold and silver, and some imperfect, namely Venus <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note>, Mars <note>The alchemical name for Iron.</note>, Saturn <note>The alchemical name for Lead</note>, and Jupiter <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note>, according to how the course of the planets labors and exerts its influence.

Therefore, whoever wishes to complete our <term>magisterium</term> <note>Latin: "mastery." In alchemy, this refers to the complete process of creating the Philosophers' Stone or the "Great Work."</note> or desires to participate in that most noble art, must know from what seed these metallic bodies are generated by nature in the earth. We take that seed from nature and purify and prepare it through art, so that we may receive from it something far more noble and excellent, enabling us in a short time to make the impure and imperfect bodies of both men and metals pure and perfect. Indeed, we must extract that seed from perfect, pure, and mature bodies if we wish and intend to reach the desired end.

This denotes nothing other than this: if our Matter is still coarse and whole, it can bring forth no fruit for so long as it is not divided, and the coarse is separated from the subtle, or the water from the earth. For water is esteemed as *Eve*, or the spirit, and earth as *Adam*, or the body. And just as the male is as if dead in procreation until he lies with the female, so also the earth is dead until water is added to it, if it wishes to attain life, by which the earth—or the body—receives its life again. And this is the same thing of which *Hermes*, <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> that most ancient *Philosopher*, speaks: namely, that the dead must be made to live again, and the sick must be made healthy.

<meta>This page continues the alchemical allegory from page 299, where the author links the creation of humanity to the chemical process of the "Great Work." The previous page ended with the description of God creating the world and the necessity of Adam and Eve. Here, the author explains the union of opposites—body and soul, earth and water—using the biblical figures of Adam and Eve as metaphors for chemical substances.</meta>

# The Glory of the World.

It is therefore necessary that you join the body and the soul together, and thus the lower is turned upward; that is, the Body becomes spirit, and the spirit becomes body. This is not to be understood as if the spirit transforms into the body or the body into the spirit by its own accord, but rather it is necessary for both to be joined so that the spirit, like water, may dissolve the body (which is like the earth)—that is, to revive it. In turn, the body must draw in the spirit, as if it were water, and the two must unite themselves for so long until they become one Mass. This means the earth is softened by the water, and the water is hardened by the dryness of the earth, just as little boys playing in the streets bear witness: taking dry dust, they sprinkle it with water and make a paste or an amalgam <note>original: "amalga"; a soft, pliable mixture, usually of metal and mercury, but here used more generally for a paste.</note> out of it. Hence the Philosophers also say that our labor is **the play of children**, in which the death of one is the life of the other; or, the hardening of one softens the other. This is nothing else than the body and the spirit, which are two things of one and the same nature, born from one mother. Toward this end, the philosopher <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "father of alchemy" to whom many foundational texts were attributed.</note> speaks, or rather exclaims: "O strong nature, conquering, transcending, and gladdening nature!" For water is the strongest Nature, which transcends and excites the fixed nature in the body—that is, it brings it joy. You will hear more on this matter later (do not be vexed by the delay).

Therefore, just as it was said that Adam (that is, the body) would be dead in childbirth without Eve (that is, without the spirit), it must be noted from this that when the water is distilled away from our matter, the body at the bottom of the <term>alembic</term> <note>A vessel used in distillation, consisting of a gourd-like base and a cap with a downward tube.</note> becomes dead and weak in its "birth." This is because the spirit, or soul, has been withdrawn and has departed from it. The body is then entirely black, poisonous, and lethal, just as it is described by the Philosophers.

If anyone, therefore, wishes to revive the body again and purify it from its blackness and stench so that it becomes fit and suitable for generation, then the extracted "sweat" (the soul) must be restored to it. This is the spirit of his Eve, so that the body may embrace the soul and work within her so that she may conceive. <term>Senior</term> <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a famous 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note> says that the "highest smoke" must be led back to the "lowest smoke," and the divine water is the king descending from heaven; it is the restorer of the soul to its body, which it finally brings to life from its death. Note well, however, that the **fixed salt** (or constant salt) becomes hidden in the body, enclosed within it...

# The Glory of the World.

[...neces]sary <note>The text likely completes the phrase "necessum est" from the previous page.</note> it is, not otherwise than the masculine seed was hidden in Adam, which the spirit—acting as Eve—attracts and becomes pregnant with. It is said that the seed of the body, which is called the **fixed salt** <term>fixed salt</term> <note>original: "sal fixum"; the stable, non-volatile residue that remains after a substance has been burned or calcined, considered the "body" of the material.</note>, is extracted from the body by its own water (which had been separated from it), so that it may also become subtle and fleeting, and ascend with the spirit into the heavens. In this way, that which was fixed is made fleeting, or the dead is resurrected; and, as has been said, nature is gladdened by this union and receives life from its spirit. For this reason, the **living water** is also called "from the man" by the Philosophers, for it is extracted from the body as if from a man. To this end, **Lucas the Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to a traditional alchemical authority or a pseudonym used in medieval texts.</note> commands that it be taken and cooked according to the custom of nature.

Other Philosophers call the body "black soil" alone, and for the following reasons: because the fixed salt, like a fruit, is invisibly hidden within the body. Others call it the **black raven** <note>original: "nigrum coruum"; a symbol for the "nigredo" or blackening stage, the first step of the Great Work signifying decomposition.</note> in which the **white dove** <note>original: "alba columba"; a symbol for the "albedo" or whitening stage, signifying purification.</note> lies hidden, and they call the water distilled from the body **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lac virginis"; a common alchemical term for a restorative solvent or the white mercurial water used to "wash" the matter.</note>, by which that white dove is to be enticed out of the black raven. This substance is called by many other names by the Philosophers, as their writings testify more than enough; therefore, it is not at all necessary to say more on that matter.

And in the manner mentioned, the water is embraced by the body, and the seed of the body—that is, the **Fixed Salt**—works upon the water so that it may conceive and become pregnant. For the water dissolves the body, and during distillation, it carries a small portion of the fixed salt with it through the **alembic** <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "alembicum"; the upper part of a distilling apparatus, used to catch and condense vapors.</note>. Through the repetition of this distillation, the water begins to grow thicker and thicker, time and again.

Because of this, much depends upon repetition or **reiteration**; it is highly praised by the Philosophers, who say that this labor should not cause anyone distress. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> speaks on this matter thus: "When I saw that the water began gradually to grow thicker and harder, I rejoiced, for I knew for certain that I would find what I sought and obtain what I desired." Therefore, water is to be poured over the body and digested with it so that the body may be dissolved, and then drawn off again so that the body may be coagulated. In this way, the body is well ground and purified by washing. This must be done quite often, indeed by pouring on and drawing off for as long as it takes until all its salt, or its power and efficacy...

# The Glory of the World.

...will be extracted from the body: and this is recognized from the fact that if the water becomes white and thick, and—coagulated in the cold like ice—it becomes hard, but in heat, it melts like butter and dissolves nothing further from the body. At that point, the remaining body is to be removed, for it is the superfluous part of the matter. Whence the Philosophers also say: "In preparation we remove what is found to be superfluous in it, and we perform our mastery with a single thing," wherein otherwise we add or take away nothing, except, as has been said, the superfluous. For it has in abundance what it ought to have, and the water—which is called the **white foliated earth** <note>original: "alba foliataque terra"; a technical term for the purified, crystalline state of the matter during the whitening stage.</note> by the Philosophers—can be taken and cast upon **living mercury** <term>living mercury</term> <note>original: "mercurio vivo"; the volatile, "spiritual" principle of the work, not to be confused with common quicksilver.</note>, and it is then transmuted into good and constant silver.

But something much higher and nobler is hidden in this water, which can be extracted without any care or trouble. For if the matter reaches that point, then let no one doubt any longer that they will achieve their desire: for the water grows and increases, like an infant in the mother’s womb. For just as an infant first grows in the vessel of the womb—growing for a time in the form of seed, and then being transmuted into flesh and blood, that is, into a thicker substance, after which the limbs are first formed—so also does this water grow. First, it grows in its white color; then it is moved by natural heat so that it grows further day by day, and changes itself from one heat to another, not unlike an infant being transmuted into flesh and blood by the natural heat of its mother. 

Then, if the matter begins to turn red, a great joy is seen—understand that when the infant receives its limbs and life, then it must be seen what ought to happen. Thus this mystery is hidden in nature, and has its progress through nature.

And in the manner mentioned, concerning the conjunction of the man and woman (that is, of the body and the spirit), I have now taught concerning the impregnation of the water. This is the end of the first combination, and the **whiteness** <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedo"; the second major stage of the Great Work, symbolizing purification and the achievement of the "Silver" stone.</note> of the matter extracted from the **blackness** <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "nigredine"; the first stage of the work, "nigredo," representing the death or putrefaction of the initial material.</note>, which is to say, from the body. Nothing more is required here but delay and patience, just as **Morienus** <note>An influential, likely legendary, 7th-century alchemist famous for his dialogue with King Khalid.</note> speaks on the matter. This coagulated water is the true white foliated earth, in which the **Philosopher** <note>Generally refers to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle in alchemical contexts.</note> commands us to sow our gold and silver, so that [they may bring forth] a hundred thousand fruits...

# CHAPTER I.

Since all temporal things derive their origin, state, and essence from the earth according to the order of time—which the influences of the heavens, the stars, and the planets (such as the Sun, Moon, and others) as well as the four qualities of the elements <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, whose balance was thought to determine the properties of all matter.</note>, both internally and externally, set in motion without any pause—by that very process, the individual and peculiar species of all things that grow, endure, and generate are produced in their own proper substance, just as it was created and established from the beginning of creation by the Most High, that is, by God.

Therefore, no one can deny that metals certainly derive their origin from the earth. They have flowed together and collected into one singular and proper matter from the four qualities or properties of the four elements, through the impression of metallic forces or spirits, and in their universality, by the influences of the stars and planets serving that purpose. This is excellently described by the doctors of nature, especially by Aristotle in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*, <note>original: "lib. 4. Meteor."; a foundational text for medieval and early modern science where Aristotle discusses the formation of minerals and metals.</note> when he says that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for the element mercury.</note> becomes the common matter of all metals.

Indeed, it must certainly be understood that in nature, the first thing is the **Matter** (of which we have already spoken), accumulated into one from the four elements. This is understood solely according to the knowledge and properties of nature; this matter is called by the Philosophers **Mercury**, or quicksilver. However, it is still imperfect because of a sulfurous and superfluous earthiness, which is excessively drossy, muddy, and combustible, and likewise because of a superfluous wateriness, through which all things were collected into one from the four elements by the operation of the higher planets. And Matter of this kind, [mixed] <note>The word "mixed" is the translation of the catchword "mixta" found at the bottom of the page, intended to lead into the first word of the next page.</note> from a sulfurous, scorching earth and a watery substance...

## CHAPTER III.

**I**n the aforementioned chapter, mention was made of a certain form or Medicine by which imperfect metals could separate their impurity from perfected Mercury and be reduced into perfect metals with that form of gold or silver; now time advises that we also bring forth something into the open concerning the form and Medicine to be made by art.

I find all the books of the philosophers filled with this topic when they say that the Alchemical art, or their own art, consists solely in gold, silver, and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento vivo"</note>, provided those have been reduced to their origin, perhaps as they were thousands of years ago, and before the metals were fully formed. For natural labor always proceeds forward and does not go backward. For this reason, various methods are also attempted, such as: dissolution in <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; this refers to nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids used to dissolve metals.</note>, and the <term>amalgamation</term> <note>The process of mixing a metal (like gold or silver) with mercury to form a paste.</note> of gold and quicksilver, or of silver and quicksilver, and they think those have been reduced to their first principle. But in the actual truth of the matter, they have wandered far from the mark. For if the metal is immersed in water, or if one distills the water from them, or if the quicksilver is <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note> from them, or if one applies smoke to it, then the whole metal is found again exactly as it was first put in. Therefore, it is not possible for that unique form to be introduced into it, since the first form does not destroy the nature and species of the metal's own properties, as **Aristotle** well demonstrates, saying: that metals are not changed unless they have been reduced into their <term>prior matter</term> <note>original: "priorem suam materiam"; in Aristotelian physics, this is the undifferentiated "prime matter" that must be reached before a substance can be fundamentally changed into something else.</note>.

Here you should also observe whether two, three, or four metals are mixed and allowed to flow together in a melt: nevertheless, one cannot bring help to the other that would serve that origin and its perfection, insofar as each individual part lacks the help of another. And even if some imperfect metal is added to gold, the gold nevertheless does not in the least abandon its own constant perfection: for it lacks nothing, nor does it possess anything superfluous, such that it might communicate something to an imperfect metal. And even if it were possible for imperfect metals to assume the gold’s virtue, they would nonetheless become inconsistent and blameworthy. In vain, therefore, is that <term>form</term> and **Medicine** sought in metals, which would lend its assistance to the perfected Mercury enclosed within those metals.

## CHAPTER VII.

**S**ince, therefore, that final uniting of metals, or their perfection, is not to be sought in that [simple] mixing—for everywhere their origin and <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "prima Materia"; the primordial substance from which all things were thought to be created.</note> is closed off through natural <term>congelation</term> <note>original: "congelationem"; the process by which a liquid or fluid substance becomes solid.</note> and its own specific form—and since one metal cannot dissolve another except as much as the matter allows (whether it be pure or impure), it then desires to remain in its own species, just as nature has shaped it. Yet, all metals are of one and common origin, born as if from one father and mother, and are separated only by the accident of some other form or species, but not in their underlying First Matter. 

And for that very reason, the First Matter or Origin of all of them is one single thing which, through the operation of nature, coalesced from a fluid state. It always desires the purest form, which it ought to have according to its own natural condition. And this is the **form of gold**, the highest and best state regarding the nature of metals. If, therefore, a pure form of this kind—which can be prepared through <term>Art</term> <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy, the human skill used to assist or perfect natural processes.</note> acting as the intermediary for nature—is added to imperfect metals, then the impurity of those imperfect metals is overcome. For the impure is not similar to that pure form, but the pure matter is: since it is the original form for which that Matter was first made. Therefore, like is joined with like in a time beyond our understanding; they separate the impurity, as if the metal were saying: "Have you come, you who are mine and who belongs to me?"

Although the proper "body" of metals is made from common metallic materials, the form of gold, once united through nature, cannot extend its influence to transform the metals of other substances. This white stage must be produced from the quicksilver without any intermediary, and the <term>whiteness</term> must necessarily precede the <term>redness</term>, since reaching the redness before the whiteness would result in the destruction of the entire work.

## CHAPTER X.

The aforementioned <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> of the Philosophers is not, by itself, the form of the imperfect metals that we have been discussing. For unless gold and silver are added to it, it remains initially only in its own essence and primary origin. It lacks the metallic powers, the spirit, the color, and the ability to grant "induration" <note>The process of hardening or solidifying into a permanent metallic state</note>—properties usually attributed to gold and silver—even though it is made of that same natural substance. It does not yet possess these powers operatively, unless it is strengthened and matured in the <term>coction</term> <note>original: "coctione"; a process of slow, transformative heating</note> itself by the addition of gold and silver.

For example: The first origin of metals, in Nature as well as in Art, is similar to water. If you mix <term>crocus</term> <note>original: "crocum"; while literally saffron, in alchemy this usually refers to a fine metallic powder, often an oxide</note> with water, the two mix together, and the water takes on the color of the saffron. If that colored water is then mixed with some other water, it passes on that same color which it first received from the saffron.

In the same way, if the "first origin" (or quicksilver) is not "tinged" <note>dyed or transformed at a fundamental level</note> with gold and silver and made <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixum"; rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by fire</note> by their constant efficacy, then it can communicate no color, nor can it mix itself with the water or "origin" of the imperfect metals. For by its own nature it is a spirit and <term>volatile</term> <note>original: "fugax"; literally "fleeing," referring to a substance that evaporates when heated</note>; if it is applied to imperfect metals, it cannot take on their origin or water—which is, in one respect, permanent and constant because of its own <term>sulfur</term> <note>The active, "combustible" principle that gives metals their body and structure</note> which has coagulated it.

If, however, the origin is made "fixed" by the addition of gold and silver, then it becomes a permanent and eternal water. When this is mixed with imperfect metals, it takes on their origin and water, and thus they are mixed together. Then, by the benefit of the fire, the combustible and impure parts are necessarily forced to withdraw from them. 

And just as this origin (or "water," or the <term>Philosophers'</term> quicksilver) cannot gain constant and permanent power without the addition of gold and silver, so too gold and silver cannot be dissolved and brought back to their "first origin" (as was stated above in Chapter 4) without the mixing of quicksilver or Mercurial water, which was also mentioned above. And in this, the saying of the philosopher <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arabic astrologer and alchemical authority often cited in Western medieval texts.</note> Haly is true:

The Spirit, he says—understand this to mean <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>—is not coagulated <note>solidified or "fixed" so it no longer evaporates</note> unless the body is first dissolved, namely gold and silver; and in this matter, time is not a matter of indifference. For then the gold and silver are made spiritual and flowing, and can be extended to the common matter of all metals, insofar as the metallic powers and the spirit of the quicksilver are coagulated and united with it more deeply and thoroughly. One cannot achieve this without the other, just as we hinted above in chapter 5. And although it may flow in a strong fire, nevertheless (Note) if that primary body should cool down again, it has neither been changed into a consistent and spiritual essence, nor is it united with that medium any more than saffron is with water, if it is expected to impart its color to other water. Therefore, there is no true art in <term>Alchemy</term> except in quicksilver alone. Truly, the power of every form mentioned above consists in quicksilver. If anyone lacks it, he must also lack the feminine virtue of gold and silver, by which they grow in the earth.

## EPILOGUE.

Enough and more than enough has been said regarding what <term>quicksilver</term>—or the origin of all metals—truly is, without which no metal can be made perfect, whether in nature or by art. However, it is not yet known where it must be sought and found. The Philosophers hide and conceal this with the greatest zeal, so much so that out of many thousands, not even one is chosen by God to know the method of seeking that <term>Philosophical</term> quicksilver. And although many people write many things about it, I nevertheless find one particular Philosopher who says this about it: That God from the beginning created the earth flat, simple, rich, and extremely fruitful, without flint, sand, stones, valleys, or mountains. But, through the influence of the Planets and the operation of Nature, the earth has now been changed into various forms: outwardly indeed into hard stones, high mountains, and deep valleys; but inwardly into rare things and colors, such as the ores of the seven metals or their origins. He claims that because of these things, the earth has entirely departed from its first form, and that this happened for the following reasons.

## Treatise on the Philosophers' Stone.

First, it is understood that the earth was created thick, great, deep, wide, and ample. Therefore, through the daily operation of the heat of the Sun, a bubbling, boiling, and vaporous heat was produced within it, which penetrated the entire earth, even to the <term>abyss</term> <note>original: "abyssum"; referring to the deep, primordial depths of the earth</note>. Since the earth is cold in its own nature, and not without the internal moisture of water, the penetrating heat of the Sun stirred up a powerful smoke, or a cloudy and airy vapor, all of which were enclosed within the earth. In the course of time, many of these vapors were produced, and they eventually became so strong that the earth could no longer contain them within itself as they naturally sought to penetrate upwards. Finally, in those places of the earth where many of them had gathered, they piled up a part of the soil—one part here, another part in another place—and by this means they raised up many small mountains, hills, and deep valleys. In those regions especially, where such mountains and hills were made, the earth was cooked, boiled, mixed, and tempered by heat, cold, and moisture; it is there that the best <term>copper</term> <note>original: "æs"; can refer to copper, bronze, or base metal in general</note> or metal is found.

Where the earth became flat, however, such smokes and vapors did not raise up mounds of that kind, especially in places that were muddy, fatty, and viscous. In such places, moisture from above penetrated the earth, whereby it was made soft again and, like a thick mass, clung firmly together. This mass—through the <term>expression</term> <note>original: "expressionem"; the act of pressing or squeezing out moisture</note> of the Sun’s heat a long time later—was strengthened more and more, hardened, cooked, and finally changed into very hard stony rocks.

However, where the earth remained frugal, soft, and thin—or where small sand, gravel, or little stones remained, clinging together like clusters of grapes—that earth was too lean because of an excess of "fatness" <note>Early scientists believed "fatness" or "sulfur" was a sticky principle that bound matter together; if the balance was wrong, the earth became brittle rather than solid stone</note> and had too little moisture. For this reason, it could not be sufficiently cooked together, and in this way, it remained like a poorly ground pulse <note>a legume or bean</note> or a mealy mass that was not sufficiently moistened. For no earth is converted into stone unless it is made from some fatty and viscous earth well-mixed with moisture. After the squeezing out of the water and the solar heating, this fatness must hold the earth together; otherwise, it remains soft and fragile and would be torn apart again. And what has not been made perfectly hard, that still...

These vapors push up mountains and valleys, while the "cooking" of the earth's "fatness" and moisture leads to the formation of metals and various types of stone.</summary>

### Treatise on the Philosophers' Stone

even in our own day, through the constant operation of nature and the heat of the sun, it can be converted into hard and firm stones. Moreover, within the earth, the aforementioned smokes and vapors—which first gave themselves up—are tightly enclosed by the qualities of the four elements, and are cooked through the nature and influences of the Sun and the other planets, or by their operations. If, furthermore, the earth captures watery humors along with some pure, subtle, and earthy substance, then it produces the <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the alchemical principle of fluidity, transformation, and the "spirit" of metals</note> of the Philosophers. But if, on the other hand, it is reduced to a fiery and earthy hardness, then it produces the <term>sulphur</term> <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemy, this represents the principle of combustion, soul, and structure</note> of the Philosophers.

And indeed, the discourse just provided shows us the way of seeking and finding mercury, or the origin of our art. And although that mercury is found in abundance in copper mines, it is nevertheless recognized by very few men. It is not silver, or gold, or common mercury, nor any of the other metals or sulphur, nor <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "atramentum sutorium"; literally "shoemaker's ink," a historical term for ferrous sulfate used in making inks and in alchemical experiments</note>, etc. But the Philosopher says: It is a vaporous substance from the four elements, watery and pure. And although it may be found in all metals, it is nonetheless immature in the imperfect ones. Therefore, it must most certainly be sought in that <term>air</term> <note>original: "aere"; here referring to the vaporous or gaseous state within the earth</note> where gold and silver can be found. 

And since he further says: If this mercury is reduced to its hardness, then it is that sulphur of the Philosophers, and this can happen in no other way than through gold and silver, which it captures and, at the same time, is sublimated and coagulated; and this occurs through its own constant natural cooking by the heat of the Sun and within its own <term>mineral vein</term> <note>original: "minera"; the source or ore-body from which minerals and metals are extracted</note>.

**S**i <note>The original text begins with a large, ornate decorative initial 'S' depicting floral vines.</note> anyone wishes to ask about the order touched upon here—namely, why the most reverend <term>Alze Medicine</term> <note>original: "ALZE Medicinae"; "Alze" likely refers to a specific alchemical preparation or the "Elixir" itself, which is the goal of the work</note> should not be placed first, but rather first the Moon, then the Sun, and the other Planets, with certain others as follows, and in the third place the Law of Medicine—let doubt be satisfied in this way: because the true end becomes more worthy than the beginning. Concerning this, the Philosophers of this art say that the red lies hidden within the white, and they dare not extract it until it becomes entirely red. Thus, in the second turn, one can work with the Sun, and by the Sun the Medicine is perfected without the aid of other Planets. From which you can gather why the Medicine is placed last, just as the Son proceeds from the Father, and from those two the Holy Spirit.

He therefore who now has "ears to hear," let him hear and perceive the remarkable philosophy in the book called the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the earliest and most famous Latin translations of Arabic alchemical texts</note>, where it is read: "Know that no true <term>Tincture</term> <note>the substance that imparts color and quality during transmutation</note> is made except from our copper."
