-># THE BOOK OF ALZE ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.<-

*Lucas* <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-Lucidarius or an alchemical authority cited in the Turba Philosophorum</note> calls it white brass, and it is distinguished by various names by other Philosophers, and this is because of the various colors which it takes on during the work itself: and also because the envious and the impious hide this brass from men, and by it they might deceive men, just as *Hermogenes* <note>A legendary figure often associated with Hermes Trismegistus in alchemical lore</note> says: And *Pythagoras* says: Although many names are attributed to it, yet it is nothing else than the true and unique thing, and that is through the transformation of its own nature. Furthermore, the envious call it by the names of all bodies, such as a coin, lead, copper, etc., since it possesses colors and becomes an <term>Elixir</term> <note>a preparation capable of transmuting metals or healing the body</note>. Similarly, *Lucas* also says: You have no need for many things, but only for a single thing. *Diomedes* and *Basan* say: Beware, lest you bring anything foreign to the single thing: for the nature of Metals is a single thing, which excels and surpasses all other things. Thus the whole work and its management may be nothing else than water, that is, one with this thing which corrects the water: otherwise, that which you seek does not happen. *Synon* <note>possibly a corruption of "Zosimos" or another authority from the Turba</note> says: Understand, descendants, that <term>sulfur</term> and brass shall be made from one thing, and it is changed into four. *Lucas* says: Cook the white brass so long until it generates itself. Thus joined, it becomes perfect in all four elements: Likewise, let it show, with its generation, life and soul. Thus at all times it is one and a single thing, and not many or several: and the thing is made from three, namely: from soul, body, and spirit; however, I name the infusion <term>Vegetability</term> <note>original: "Vegetabilitatem"; refers to the vital, growing power of the stone, likening its development to that of a plant</note>. Man is from it, and this is his life after God. Thus the brass receives spirit from humidity, from which it receives its powers, and, like other things, it is increased. To these things the Philosophers speak: If the brass is frequently <term>blinded</term> <note>original: "occæcatur"; likely referring to the "nigredo" or blackening stage where the matter loses its "sight" or luster</note> in its cooking, then it becomes better than before: and if the brass has a body and a soul, it is like a man. Therefore, one body does not penetrate another, but the nature of the soul, which is agile, penetrates and tints the body. The soul, hidden within it, is called <term>sulfur</term>, and it is hidden in four bodies. The four bodies are named "male" and "masculine," and they denote liquefaction without water, and water is made from our brass. *Arisleus* says: Observe the water which went out from it, that is, the <term>permanent water</term> <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a central alchemical concept referring to a solvent that does not wet the hands and is the key to the transformation</note>: Receive the humidity which it rejects from itself: Thus other Philosophers say: Take the water with its companions, and let it be dried with that vapor which is similar to it, and let it be coagulated in its own water.

It describes the stone as having a body, soul, and spirit, emphasizing that the "permanent water" extracted from the material is the key to its perfection.</summary>

## *The Book of Alze on the Philosopher’s Stone.*

This water is also called "poison," and it is similar to a kind of birth and life, for the reason that it becomes the soul, and is extracted from many things. Indeed, its Tincture <note>original: *Tinctura*; a substance or "dye" capable of infusing a new, permanent color and quality into a base metal</note> is the life of those things into which it enters, and it brings a loss to the bodies from which it is drawn. Its power is a spiritual blood; if this is rubbed together with the bodies, it then transmutes them into spirit, and they are transformed and mixed together into one. That body draws the spirit to itself, and in turn, the spirit retains the body in some staining spirit, just like blood. For everything that has a spirit also has blood, as the Philosophers say. Therefore, if the poison penetrates the body, it provides it with an unchangeable color, and then the body never allows the soul to be torn away from itself. For if, fleeing, it turns its back, and becomes an obstacle to the one chasing it, then its flight has vanished. From this follows the truth: that nature has taken hold of its own likeness as a friend, and they grow together into one another. From the mixture of Saturn <note>original: *Saturno*; in alchemy, Saturn represents lead and the "black" stage of the work</note> there emerges a most noble color, which is not changed nor does it flee from the fire, just as the soul passes into the inner parts of the body, and retains and colors the body. Since that same water is of a cold nature, one must then beware of excessive fire: fire is the enemy of cold, if its primary moisture has been produced, as the *Fictitious Philosopher* <note>original: *Fictus Philosophus*; a reference to an anonymous or pseudo-epigraphical alchemical authority</note> says.

And the spirit is called the male and the Agent, which cannot be obtained except from a flowing body. And let this be understood regarding the moisture in the following way: namely, that which is produced as long as the two "married" partners are joined in a lawful manner, until the white <note>The *Albedo* or "white" stage of the process, signifying purity and the first success</note> is reached. Do you wish to know further when the body "flows" in that cooking process? Hear what *Bonellus* <note>An alchemical authority often cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: "If you see blackness swimming in the water, then the body has been made quite fluid."

Before these two aforementioned things—namely, the body and the spirit—they also have a third, which is their substance, and it is called "body." It is also called a certain "round cloud," likewise "death," "blackness," as well as "darkness and shadow," "ashy lead," or "brass," "airy and subtle," because of that which is born from it and perfected; and it is called <term>gold</term> <note>referring to the philosophical gold or the perfected state of the matter</note>, which had been hidden in the body of <term>Magnesia</term> <note>original: *Magnesiæ*; not modern magnesium, but a symbolic term for the "mother" or crude mineral body containing the secret essence</note>. Concerning this, it is said: "Extract the shadow from its brightness." And that is the same thing of which many have spoken. There are three things which...

...which join the true copper <note>original: *æs*; while usually "brass," in alchemy it often refers to the "primary material" or an impure metallic body to be transformed</note>, namely: Body, Soul, and Spirit. Therefore, it is not without reason compared to an egg, and indeed is even called by that name: for just as a chick is born from the three parts which make up an egg, so too Alchemy <note>referring here to the alchemical result or the Stone itself</note> is born from these three aforementioned parts, as many Philosophers testify in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>. The Male, or the water, is also called "nature": for water is the nature which overcomes the elements in bodies through their own governance, yet it joins them together again and brings them back into one. Regarding this water, Fictes <note>an alchemical authority cited in early texts</note> says: "O, the nature of this thing! How it transmutes the body into a spirit! O, most wondrous nature! How it comes and appears alone, conquering all things; it is a superior, bitter, and sharp vinegar <note>original: *acetum*; in alchemy, a specialized acidic solvent or "philosophical vinegar"</note> which reduces gold to a pure spirit." Without this vinegar, nothing can be achieved—neither the red, nor the black, nor the white <note>referring to the three major stages of the Great Work: *rubedo*, *nigredo*, and *albedo*</note>. And know that when it is mixed with bodies, it then changes the body into a spirit, and does so by a certain celestial fire and an unchangeable Tincture <note>original: *Tinctura*; a substance capable of infusing a permanent quality or color into a metal</note> which cannot be destroyed, and so forth.

Know that at the start of the mixing, the pure and "justified" <note>refined or balanced</note> elements are gathered in a gentle fire; however, a strong fire should be avoided until the elements are brought back into one, while in the meantime they follow and embrace one another in that gentle heat. Know also that one burns and consumes the other, and conversely, one strengthens the other and teaches it to endure the fire. The elements, having been diligently "cooked" <note>original: *cocta*; referring to *coctio*, the process of maturation through heat</note>, rejoice and are transmuted into a foreign nature; this is because the moisture is flowing and influential, like a head, while the thick and dry body is the spirit. But the staining spirit is a strong champion <note>original: *athleta*; a common metaphor for a substance that can endure the trials of the furnace</note> against the fire. Therefore the Philosophers say: "Invert the elements, and then you will find what you seek." Now, the "inversion of the elements" means making the moist dry and the fleeting <note>volatile</note> fixed. And the man forces the union so that it may give birth to itself. Many search for these separations <note>original: *dissectiones*; the breaking down of the substance into its components</note>, and some indeed find separations that nevertheless cannot endure the necessity of the fire. Indeed, in that fire, they become diminished. But our separations, which are made from the venerable stone, endure a greater burden of fire and are never reduced by it to a small amount. For they are sustained by the fire, since no mother would kill her own child...

...should kill him, whom it nevertheless nourished. Likewise, there are singular things which, both from within and from without, produce the red and the white. First, this is done by some slow and gentle fire, and that is the beginning of its excellence, as the Philosophers say. If you now see it "born," then observe that the **whiteness** <note>original: *albedo*; the second major stage of the Great Work, representing purification</note> is preserved hidden within the body of **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*; the first stage, symbolizing decay and the "death" of the old form</note>. And it is then necessary for you to extract the whiteness from the blackness. But if it then appears white, remember then that the **red** <note>original: *rubrum* or *rubedo*; the final stage of the work, indicating the completion of the Philosopher's Stone</note> lies hidden, concealed within the white.

Having noticed this, you should pause its extraction and begin the "cooking" <note>original: *coctionem*; a prolonged heating process</note>, until it becomes entirely red. And do not wonder that our "copper" <note>original: *æs*; here referring to the primary alchemical material</note> is designated by the Philosophers with various kinds of names, such as Soul, Spirit, and Body. For they are often called "brothers," and, since they are compared to those joined in marriage, they are called "wedded partners," says Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of chemistry</note>; sometimes it is called only spirit, or at least only body. 

Therefore, it must be observed that unless each of these is changed into water, the work is by no means completed. For this reason, the flame of the fire must endure and weaken the body near itself, until everything is converted into water. This, however, is not water from the clouds <note>meaning common rain water</note>, as the foolish say, but, according to the Philosophers (whom they ought to have read), it must be a "permanent water," which nevertheless cannot be permanent without its own body. Thus says Hermogenes <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the Hermetic tradition</note>: "Take the hidden spirit, and do not despise it for that reason, because it exerts great power with its brother." And that brings the correct Tincture <note>the essence capable of transforming metals</note>, if it becomes united in all things with its partner. 

It is also called the most bitter vinegar, by which it must be washed until it becomes thick: and that is nothing other than "women's work and children's play," as Socrates <note>In alchemical texts, "Socrates" often appears as a symbolic authority figure rather than the historical philosopher</note> says. For the secret of this work proceeds from a male and a female, and the husband receives his <term>tingiblem</term> <note>original Latin: *tingibilem*; meaning "capable of coloring" or "staining," referring to the power to transmute the color and nature of a substance</note> spirit from the wife. But if the man and wife now come together, then the woman does not flee <note>an alchemical metaphor for "fixation," where a volatile substance becomes stable and no longer evaporates when heated</note>. And if the conjunction is transmuted into the red, then from it is made the treasure of the world, as Synon says; if the water passes into the body, then it changes that body first into earth, then indeed into dust and ash.

Then the labor has vanished, and the stone by its own nature has the Tincture within itself in the body of Magnesia <note>not modern magnesium, but a term for the "crude" matter or the transformative mineral of the alchemists</note>. To which end the Philosophers say: "Son, extract..."

There are also other explanations of Alchemy before we arrive at the labor of our stone. **Observe:** Let him who seeks this art beware, lest he fall into great errors, for this reason: that the Philosophers have given many names to our stone, and this because it represents various colors—as many as anyone could even think of—just as was written before; and also for this cause, because it is prepared from the four elements. The stone should be ground with its own water <note>original: *sua aqua*; likely referring to the "mercurial" solvent produced during the work</note>, so that it might drink in the whole moisture and take its power in the contest of fire; and it should remain in it so well until it becomes a powder, like burnt blood <note>original: *instar combusti sanguinis*; a technical term for the deep red state of the matter after intense heating (calcination)</note>, and overcomes the nature of fire. Kings seek this stone, yet they do not find it, except for those to whom it is given by God. It is even sold publicly for money <note>The author suggests that the raw material of the Stone is common and cheap, but its value is unrecognized by the ignorant.</note>; if this were known to men, they would call it a lie. And if they knew its power, they would not despise it. Therefore God has hidden it from the world. And he who strives to labor in it, let him first consider upon what foundation he wishes to rely, lest he labor in vain and waste both time and expense. Let us at least speak of our stone, which desires a gentle fire; and if it should die for an interval of some days, just as a man in his tomb, then its spirit is restored to it by God; He takes away its sickness and purifies it.

# The Book of Alze on the Philosopher’s Stone.

He says: Oh, what a nature is heavenly truth! Oh, how strong a nature, which conquers another nature, and rejoices with it. And it is a spiritual thing which is granted by God, which nature itself cannot bestow upon it: wherefore let us honor it; for nothing in nature is so noble as the true <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: *Tinctura*; in alchemy, a potent substance capable of infusing its qualities into other bodies, often synonymous with the Elixir</note>, to which nothing is similar: and if it becomes fluid with its bodies, then it brings forth the highest work. For that Tincture overcomes the things that are mixed with it, and colors them with its own labor: and those things which it makes white on the outside, those are also entirely white within—first by a certain gentle fire, if one wishes to work with our stone. For by one work, and one way, with one substance, and one "sending," the whole work is completed, and all purity is unique. Understand this according to the opinions of the Philosophers: namely, how the work may be divided into grinding, cooking, and so forth: yet let this not bring you any trouble or weariness.

Next, when the work is thus divided, then mix, cook, roast, heat, and whiten it: and their names are very many, yet they all submit to one <term>regimen</term> <note>original: *regimen*; the systematic method of governing the heat and the chemical environment during the alchemical process</note>. And if the Philosophers had known that only a single cooking sufficed, then they would not have employed so many varied sayings. Afterward, there is but a single labor, and no one can reach the enjoyment of its usefulness except through the most diligent management of the labor, nor is it grasped without divine permission. Therefore, do not be impatient with the labor, and repeat the regimen now a second, now a third time, until the **King is crowned** <note>A symbolic phrase referring to the completion of the "Great Work," when the base matter is successfully transformed into gold</note>, and then you shall carry back a vast reward. Ask then, how precious our stone shall become, if the poor man may possess it just as the rich man does.

Wherefore many have been reduced to poverty, because they despise what the Philosophers honor: and I adjure you: if Kings and Princes knew of it, none of us would ever obtain it. Only one vessel is required for the entire work and labor, which should be made of stone and must not dread the fire.

Thus the weight of our <term>bronze</term> <note>original: *aes*; here referring not to common bronze, but to the specific metallic starting material of the work</note> is to be grasped by the body, which should be only pure, raw, cheerful, and upright, like a "man of heaven," as the Philosophers say. The vessel is to be placed upon the <term>alembic</term> <note>original: *alembico*; a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>, where the flames reverberate from one vessel to another. Let the fire be present at the vessel, and let it be well observed, so that in this manner he might be able to keep his companion with him, and allow him to kindle his own whiteness, just as Lucas <note>Likely referring to Lucas, an authority often cited in alchemical compendiums like the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says.

For once our vessel has been placed, fire should be added to the air, since from the elements—without mixing and <term>governance</term> <note>original: *regimine*; the management of the heat and timing in the alchemical process</note>—nothing happens, because it is born of blood. If therefore a man and a woman come together within the span of forty nights, then the seed is released with moisture and heat, and God himself has granted much blood for the warming. If that seed is born into a fetus, then it is first sustained with a little milk by a small fire; and as it becomes more mature, it is strengthened even more. Thus the work must be followed, and without fire nothing happens; but through the excessive heat of the fire, it is burned. Therefore the fire shall be moderate, like the heat of the sun.

And this should be done under some empty vessel with a few coals: then more and more, until the <term>alembic</term> <note>original: *alembicus*; a distillation apparatus used for refining substances</note> is well dried out and wateriness appears in the work. Yet water alone suffices, which coagulates and fixes all things, just as Democritus <note>Pseudo-Democritus, an early alchemical authority often cited for the principle of natures conquering natures</note> says. It is also called spirit from spirit, sulfur from sulfur, <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; mercury, considered a fundamental principle in the creation of the Stone</note> from quicksilver. It is also called vapor, for that vapor keeps its companion near itself. Thus our work is nothing other than earth and vapor: and if I speak of two, then I am thinking of four, all of which need one thing, by which Nature—overcoming all nature—is extracted. For nature, because of its own nature, rejoices in itself, and Nature overcomes nature, and retains nature within itself, and yet one is not opposed to the other, but one embraces the other within itself, by which it excels the other; and the Philosophers call this water the "purifying water."

The first part of the ice-water purifies the universal from corruption, and the liquefaction in the fire must be renewed quite often until the first <term>blackness</term> <note>original: *nigredo*; the initial stage of the alchemical process, representing putrefaction and the dissolution of the matter</note> occurs. Then a second blackness comes upon it, and then consider that the <term>redness</term> <note>original: *rubedo*; the final stage of the work, representing the perfection and power of the Stone</note> is extracted after the <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: *albedo*; the stage of purification and spiritualization following the blackness</note> from the blackness. For blackness is the middle point between the fleeting and the non-fleeting, and it restores these two to peace. Therefore the key of the work cannot be revealed without the blackness: and as long as the blackness lasts, the woman rules, until the whiteness arrives. That is called the first power of our stone, and it is called the "best vinegar" of which they speak: Vinegar is the water which introduces colors into any metal and into infusible stones. But beware lest you change the vinegar into dung <note>original: *fimum*; a warning against overheating or spoiling the chemical mixture</note>, concerning which Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath and highly influential figure in Latin alchemy</note> says: "Natural heat [acting] on moist bodies..."

The smoke, better coagulated with its own dregs <note>the solid sediment or residue</note>, becomes living and white; roast the white bronze <note>original: *æs*; here referring to an intermediate metallic state of the Stone</note> so that it may bring itself forth. It must be further noted: That the body which lives without earth <note>a purified or spiritualized state where the "gross" matter has been removed</note> and takes the Tincture, that body has greater strength than its brother. For indeed, everything that is mixed with it, it overcomes and brings back to its own color, as the Sages are fond of saying. Dry fire tints, air confirms, white water washes away the blackness from the bodies, the earth remains stable and receives the Tincture. ...having been perfected <note>original: *verisato*, likely a corruption of *verificato* (verified/made true) or *vitrificato* (turned to glass)</note>, it is then already at the stage of redness. The aforementioned water transforms all bodies into spirit, even thick bodies that do not naturally possess such a nature; it bites <note>corrodes or dissolves</note> them until they are grasped by nature. Know that unless you place the bodies in this state until they die and their soul is extracted, you will never be able to tinge any body with them; for nothing tinges unless it has first been tinged itself. If the body is made to flow and is burned, it then turns back to its generator, and the subtle <term>Magnesia</term> <note>in alchemy, this refers not to the modern element magnesium, but to the "materia prima" or the "mother" of the stone</note> becomes airy and is turned to earth, which makes it spiritual and gives it life. This all occurs before the true whiteness arrives. Do not care much for the colors before the whiteness, for they are not at all stable.

From these things you can now gather that our work originates from gold, which is hidden in <term>Magnesia</term>, and is made from one <term>sulfur</term> by <term>sulfur</term>, and from <term>mercury</term> by <term>mercury</term>, and it becomes one thing. This is our <term>stone</term>, and it is made in one way and with one labor. Therefore, let all false chemists stop deceiving the foolish, especially with their multiple sublimations and distillations, for they speak what is false. Let those also be silent who say that our work comes from the powder of the Basilisk <note>a mythical reptile; its "powder" was often cited in fraudulent or highly allegorical recipes</note>. Know the time of the labor: when the year is divided into four parts, this work must be begun in winter, which is moist. Then let us extract the moisture until Spring, which turns green, so that then the colors may appear to us under a gentle fire during the labor. Then we proceed to Summer, and then the work must be pulverized with a strong fire. Finally, we reach Autumn, and then, as the fruits ripen, we arrive at the noble redness of the work. Nor should the movements of the stars and planets be cared for, as I have often read in certain books. For our truth is a physical thing in which the spirit we seek lies hidden; with this we tinge, and we make glass so that it can withstand the hammer <note>referring to "malleable glass," a legendary material that would not shatter</note>, and we make carbuncles <note>deep red gemstones, often associated with the finished Stone</note> from crystals. This particle of our <term>Elixir</term>, like a raindrop, tinges a thousand parts, so that all things succeed prosperously.

### The Book of Alze on the Philosopher’s Stone.

And finally, we shall say something regarding the supreme medicine. Since man is the Noblest Creature, for whose sake and benefit all other things were created by God—so much so that no earthly thing can be compared to him—it follows that he should look to this medicine with the greatest zeal, above all the riches of the world, so that he may be able to preserve his flowering youth, drive away all diseases from himself, and guard against those yet to come. For our **Elixir** excels all the medicinal preparations of **Hippocrates**, **Avicenna**, and others <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC) and Avicenna (980–1037 AD) were the foundational authorities of ancient Greek and medieval Islamic medicine respectively.</note>, and it even cures leprosy publicly. Indeed, a drinkable Antidote <note>original: *potabile Antidotum*, often referring to "potable gold," a legendary liquid medicine</note> is to be prepared from our spirit. And just as the bodies of metals are restored to order, purified, and healed by fire, so much more is the natural heat of a man restored and renewed by this spirit; all diseases are driven away by it, and future ones are prevented. Nor are certain men ignorant of the fact that the Pagans <note>original: *Gentiles*</note> take care to have gold filed and prepared with diamonds so that they may preserve their health and not lose their youthful form.

O, how much more powerfully however could this gold—which lies hidden in <term>Magnesia</term> <note>In this context, Magnesia refers to the "Mother of the Stone" or the raw alchemical material, not the modern mineral magnesium.</note>, and has been well purified and made spiritual—possess even greater powers! For the more subtle a Medicine is, the greater its operation and strength, as all Physicians are by no means ignorant. What more then shall I say? For all these things which I have faithfully recounted here, I have seen, heard, learned, and finally perfected through labor.

And while I was acting in this way, and began to recognize and grasp this truth, horrible things happened to me because of my companions in whose midst I lived. I almost despaired of the work because of certain thoughts that caused delay. Therefore, I entrusted the care of completing this work to another who was a friend to me, and I instructed him faithfully so that the work might finally be brought to a fruitful end.
> For which may God be blessed for ever and ever. AMEN.

# PREFACE OF BROTHER BA-
# SIL VALENTINE OF THE
## BENEDICTINE ORDER CONCERNING
### THE GREAT STONE OF THE
### ANCIENT SAGES.
<note>original: "Magno Lapide Antiquorum Sapientum." This refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy, believed to possess the power of transmutation and healing.</note>

*After I had experienced something of human fear, I began to consider the miseries of this world from the simplicity of nature, and I deeply mourned within myself the sins committed by our first parents,* <note>A reference to the Fall of Adam and Eve, which in the worldview of the time, corrupted both humanity and the natural world.</note> *and that there was no place for penance on earth, but that men were becoming worse every day, and that eternal punishments, lasting for an inscrutable end, hung over those not performing penance; Therefore, I hurried as much as I could to withdraw myself from evil, to bid farewell to the world, and to dedicate myself to God as a servant:*

# PREFACE.

*...restored to his former health: For this <term>spirit<gloss>original: "spiritus." In alchemy, a spirit refers to a highly refined, volatile substance or essence extracted from a material, believed to carry its medicinal or life-giving power.</gloss></term> was so strong that it could strengthen the spirit of my brother, who daily prayed his <term>hours<gloss>The "Canonical Hours," the set sequence of prayers and psalms recited at specific times by members of religious orders.</gloss></term> for me until he died; yet he survived a long time after he had recovered. **I** N my preface, best friend and seeker of the <term>Art<gloss>original: "artis." In this context, "the Art" specifically refers to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or the "Hermetic Art."</gloss></term>, I gave hope that I would point out to you and others burning with the desire to learn the properties of nature and inquiring more deeply into the sciences, the <term>cornerstone and the rock<gloss>original: "lapidem angularem & petram." This is a dual reference: it alludes to biblical descriptions of Christ as the "cornerstone" while simultaneously referring to the "First Matter," the essential starting substance required to create the Philosopher's Stone.</gloss></term>—so far as it has been granted to me from above—from which our predecessors and the ancients made their stone. This stone they received from the Most High to be used for the health and comfort of this earthly life. 

Therefore, so that I may fulfill my promises and not lead you astray for long into the labyrinths of <note>original: "sophisticis erroribus." In the 17th century, "sophisticated" meant deceptive or fraudulent. He is warning against "puffers"—false alchemists who used trickery instead of true natural philosophy.</note> sophisticated errors, but instead open from the foundation the fountain of all benefits, hold fast to my following words and weigh them well, if indeed you are moved by a desire to know the arts. Indeed, I cannot make a great display of words, nor is that my intention, since very little can be learned from such talk; rather, I delight in brief words that contain the foundation of the matter.

Know therefore, that few arrive at the possession of this mastery, even though very many are occupied in building our stone. For the Creator willed that true knowledge and its attainment not be common, but granted only to certain individuals who turn away from lies and embrace the truth, and who, being devoted to the art with <note>original: "gemitibus cordis" (sighs of the heart). A phrase suggesting deep, sincere, and humble prayer or longing.</note> sighs of the heart, seek it most diligently; and especially to those who love God without hypocrisy and therefore pray to Him.

# The Practice, concerning the <term>Stone of the Wise<gloss>original: "Lapide Sapient." Commonly known as the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life.</gloss></term>.

Therefore I tell you in truth, if you attempt to make our great and ancient stone, you must be devoted to my teaching, and before all other things pray to the Creator of every creature, that He may grant you His grace and blessing for this purpose; and if you have sinned, confess and do good, and resolve in your purpose that you will no longer be wicked, but upright; so that your heart may be enlightened toward every good thing. And remember, when you are raised to honor, to succor the poor and the needy, to free them from their miseries, and to refresh them with your generous hand, so that you may obtain a greater blessing from the Lord, and secure a seat in heaven through the confirmation of your faith.

Do not despise, my friend, nor look down upon the truthful writings of those who possessed the stone before us: For after God’s own revelation, I have my knowledge from them; and let that reading be multiplied and very often repeated, lest the foundation be lost, and the truth be extinguished like a lamp.

After this, do not forget your most diligent labor in always investigating the writings of the authors; but do not keep a fickle mind. Instead, plant yourself upon that <term>fixed rock<gloss>original: "petram præfixam." In alchemy, this refers to a stable, unchanging principle or "First Matter" that remains constant while other substances change.</gloss></term> in which all the wise unanimously agree: For a man of a wandering mind often fails to walk the true path and plunges himself into errors; nor are long-lasting houses built by men of a changeable spirit.

Since our most ancient stone also does not arise from <term>combustible things<gloss>original: "combustibilibus rebus." Materials that can be destroyed or consumed by fire.</gloss></term>—because it is itself safe from every danger of fire—cease therefore to seek it in those things in which it is not granted by nature to exist or be found; as if it were said to be a <term>vegetable work<gloss>original: "opus vegetabile." An alchemical process using plants or herbs.</gloss></term>, which cannot be; although a certain growth is present in it.

For note, if it were so with our stone as it is with any other herb, it would be most easily burned, so that nothing would remain but a certain salt; and although those who were before me wrote many things about the <note>original: "lapide vegetabili." Alchemists often used "vegetable" to mean something that has the power to grow or "vegetate," rather than meaning it was a biological plant.</note> vegetable stone, yet know, my friend, that this will be "easily difficult" for you to conceive; for since our stone grows and increases itself, they therefore called it a vegetable thing.

Furthermore know, that brute animals produce no increase of themselves unless it happens within a nature similar to their own: and therefore you have no need [of] the true stone...

<summary>Valentine outlines the moral requirements for an alchemist—piety, repentance, and charity—before explaining that the Philosopher's Stone is not made of plants (vegetables), though it is called "vegetable" because of its unique ability to grow and increase.</summary>

Stone, or presume to make it for yourself, except from its own proper seed, from which our stone was made from the beginning: From this you should perceive and understand, my friend, that you should not choose the soul of a living creature <note>original: "animalis animam." In this context, Valentine is warning against using organic matter from animals to create the Stone.</note> for this inquiry. For flesh and blood, just as they were given and granted to living beings by the Creator, belong to the living creatures from which God composed them, so that a living animal might be made therefrom. Truly, our stone, handed down to me by the most ancient of men as an inheritance, comes and is born from two things and one thing, which hold a third hidden: This is the purest truth and rightly spoken. For male and female were accepted by the ancients as one body—not considering them outwardly as they appear to the sight, but for the sake of the love implanted within them and the grace infused from the beginning in the operation of nature—to be known as one; and just as these two can propagate and increase their seeds, so also can the seed of the matter from which our stone is made be supplanted and increased.

But if you are now a true lover of our art, you will prize this speech and consider it wisely, lest you fall and slip with other blind <term>Sophists<gloss>False practitioners of alchemy who used deceptive methods or lacked true understanding of natural philosophy.</gloss></term> into the pit prepared by the enemy.

However, so that you may know, my friend, from where a seed of this kind proceeds, you should ask yourself toward what end you strive to lead our stone; then it will become manifest to you that it flows from nothing except a certain metallic root, from which the metals themselves were ordained by the Creator to be generated; note well how this happens.

In the beginning, when the <term>Spirit moved over the waters<gloss>A reference to the Book of Genesis; Valentine ties the "First Matter" of alchemy to the original creation of the world.</gloss></term>, and all things were still covered in darkness, then God almighty and eternal—whose beginning is without end, and whose wisdom has been from eternity—out of His inscrutable counsel, created heaven and earth, and all things contained in them, visible and invisible, by whatever name they are called, out of nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note>; for God made all things out of nothing. But how this most precious creation occurred, I shall not philosophize upon now; let the sacred scriptures and faith judge that.

In such a creation, the Creator implanted a peculiar seed in every nature, lest it tend toward destruction and ruin, so that by it an increase might occur, and that men, living creatures, plants, and metals might be preserved; nor...

...to obtain in metallic form, unless you have joined the three aforementioned principles into one without defect. Then, furthermore, you must understand that the animals of the earth are composed of flesh and blood, just like man, and they have an indwelling life-giving spirit and breath, which they possess just like man; but they are destitute of a <term>rational soul<gloss>original: "rationali anima"; in alchemy and medieval philosophy, this is the highest part of the soul, unique to humans, allowing for reason and eternal life.</gloss></term>, with which man is endowed above all other living things. Therefore, when beasts exchange life for death, it is utterly finished with them, nor does any hope remain for them to endure into eternity.

Man, however, if he yields his life through temporal death to his Creator, lives on as a surviving soul; and when he has been <note>original: "clarificatus"; in an alchemical context, this means "refined" or "made bright," like a metal purified by fire.</note> glorified, the soul, having returned into his glorified body, will dwell there, so that body, soul, and spirit are gathered as one and are able to demonstrate their celestial glorification, which can never be separated for all eternity, etc.

Wherefore man, by reason of his soul, is known as a <term>fixed<gloss>original: "fixa"; an alchemical term for a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when heated.</gloss></term> creature, since (although he dies if considered externally) he is to live forever. For the death of man is only a glorification, so that through certain degrees ordained by God, he may be freed from the liability of sin and transposed into a better place, which does not happen to beasts. Therefore, they are held as non-fixed creatures. For after their destruction, they can enjoy no resurrection, since they lack a rational soul, for which the one and true Mediator, the Son of God, suffered and shed his blood.

A spirit indeed can dwell in a certain body, but it does not follow from this that it will be <term>fixed</term>, even if the body agrees with the spirit and the spirit in no way quarrels with the body. For both are destitute of that strong thing which binds and confirms the body and spirit, and guards and defends them against all dangers—namely, the most precious, noble, and **fixed soul**. For where the soul is entirely lacking, there no hope of redemption remains. For a thing without a soul is imperfect, and that is one of the greatest <term>secrets<gloss>original: "arcanis"; hidden or specialized knowledge intended for initiates.</gloss></term> which it is fitting for the wise man and the one devoted to inquiry to know.

...and their soul and bodies are unequal, and whichever metal has all three gifts of fixity <note>original: "fixitatis"; the ability of a substance to withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating.</note> joined in itself, to it falls that strength by which it can endure fire and overcome all its enemies; and this is found in the **Sun** <note>original: "sole"; the alchemical symbol for Gold, the most perfect and fixed metal.</note> alone: The **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> has a fixed mercury within itself, therefore it does not fly away so quickly in the fire like the other imperfect metals, but awaits its examination in the fire and proves it most clearly through its victory, since most voracious **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus"; the alchemical symbol for Lead, often described as "voracious" because it was used in the process of cupellation to "consume" base metals, leaving only silver or gold.</note> can obtain no prey from it.

A fixed Salt added and left a hard, constant, and thick body to warlike **Mars** <note>The alchemical symbol for Iron.</note>, whence the nobility of its mind is demonstrated, and hardly anything can be taken from this warlike leader: For its body is so hard that it can hardly be wounded: But if its strenuous virtue were spiritually joined through mixing and concordance with the fixity of the Moon and the beauty of Venus, a sufficiently sweet Music could yet be composed, through which some keys might be deemed worthy of their honor, so that one in need of bread might particularly enjoy it, if he ascends to a higher step of the ladder: For the <term>phlegmatic<gloss>original: "phlegmatica"; referring to the "humoral" quality of being cold and moist.</gloss></term> quality or moist nature of the Moon must be dried out with the burning blood of Venus, and its great blackness must be corrected by the **Salt of Mars**.

Then Saturn, the first in order, began to speak with a rather sharp oration in this manner:

> I, Saturn, the highest of the planets in the firmament, testify before all you Lords, that among you I am the most useless and cheapest, of a weak and corruptible body, of a black color <note>In alchemy, Saturn represents Lead and the "Nigredo" or blackening stage, which is the beginning of the Great Work.</note>, subject to the injuries of many afflictions in this valley of miseries; yet I am the prover of you all. For I have no permanent dwelling, and I carry away with me those like myself. Therefore I pray you Lords likewise to take vengeance on him for this, and since he has already been handed over to custody, to kill him utterly and keep him there even unto <term>putrefaction<gloss>original: "putrefactionem"; the stage where the alchemical matter is broken down and decomposed by heat.</gloss></term>, until not a drop of his blood <note>the liquid state of the metal</note> may be recognized any longer.

When Saturn had thus finished his speech, behold, dusky Jupiter comes forward and begins his discourse with a bending of the knees and a singular reverence of the scepter, praising the demands of his colleague Saturn, and commands that he himself will pursue all those who do not assist in the execution of these matters: and thus he made an end.

After him came Mars with a drawn sword, marvelously distinguished with colors <note>This likely refers to the "peacock's tail," an alchemical stage where the material in the vessel displays many iridescent colors.</note>, like a fiery mirror, flashing with diverse and unusual rays; and he offered the sword to Vulcan the executioner, so that he might carry out all those things commanded by the Lords, and when he had killed Mercury, he should utterly burn his bones with fire. ...a shining woman in a long silver-colored garment, interwoven with many waters, arrived. She fell prostrate on her face and with many tears and groans prayed for her husband, the Sun, to be released from the prison into which he had been treacherously thrust by the trickery and power of Mercury, where he was still being held by the command of the other planets. 

But Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and blacksmithing; in alchemy, he represents the literal and metaphorical fire of the furnace.</note> utterly refused; for it had been forbidden to him. But [the woman], persevering in her purpose, diligently oversaw the execution of the sentence passed, until at last Lady Venus arrived in a garment of deep red, interwoven with green, with a most beautiful face, most eloquent and pleasant speech, and the most charming gesture, carrying very fragrant flowers in her hand, which by the variety of their colors wonderfully refreshed and delighted human eyes. She interceded with the Judge Vulcan in the Chaldean language <note>original: "Chaldæo idiomate"; refers to an ancient, occult tongue associated with the Babylonian magi, often used in alchemy to represent secret knowledge.</note> for the liberation [of Sol], and reminded him that redemption would come through the female sex. Meanwhile, while these two were talking, heaven opened, and from there a powerful animal came out with many thousands of chicks, driving away and pushing back the executioner <term>lictorem<gloss>Previously identified as Vulcan or the alchemical fire that "punishes" or restricts the metals.</gloss></term>. It opened its jaws wide and devoured the most precious Venus, its helper, exclaiming at the same time in a clear voice: "I am born from women, and women have abundantly propagated my seed, and with it they have enriched the earth. Her soul is devoted to mine, and therefore I will feed and nourish myself on her blood."

And when the animal had said these things clearly, it withdrew into a certain chamber and bolted the door behind it. All the chicks followed after in order, and they needed much more food than before; and they drank of the former incombustible oil <note>original: "oleo incombustibili"; a legendary alchemical substance that can withstand heat without vaporizing, often associated with the finished Stone or "Potable Gold."</note>; and they digested the food and drink very easily, and the chicks became many more than before, and this happened so many times until they filled the whole world.

When all these things had so happened, many men of that region assembled, who were learned and skilled in letters; they contended among themselves with all zeal to acquire an explanation of all these deeds and speeches, so that they might for the most part enjoy a better understanding of them. # Practice of the Philosophers' Stone

...mercy, until there appeared a man of great age, with hair and beard white as snow, clothed in purple from head to foot. On his head he wore a crown, in which a most precious carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, likely a garnet or ruby; in alchemy, it represents the final "Red Stage" or the glowing perfection of the Stone.</note> radiated light. About his waist he was girded with the belt of life. This man ascended a platform and exhorted the gathered people to keep silence and listen to him most diligently; for he said he had been sent from above to open the aforementioned writings to them and to reveal them through philosophical discourse.

And when they all stood quiet, he began in this manner:

> "Awake, O man, and gaze upon the light, lest the darkness seduce you. The gods of fortune and the gods of the greater nations <note>original: "dii majorum gentium"; a reference to the primary Roman deities, used here to suggest celestial or planetary powers.</note> have revealed to me in a deep sleep: O how blessed is the man who recognizes the gods, and what wondrous <term>magnalia: great or miraculous works of nature</term> they perform! And happy is he whose eyes are opened, so that he may see the light which before was dark.
>

>

Give wings to the beast of the east, just as the one from the south has, so that they may become equal. For the animal of the east must be stripped of its lion skin, and its wings must vanish, and then together they must enter the great salt-sea of the Ocean, and emerge again in beauty. Submerge your unstable spirits into the deep fountain, whose water never fails, so that they may become like their mother, who lies hidden therein and was brought forth into the world from three.

Therefore, Hungary is my fatherland, and my mother encompasses the whole world."

<header>Brother Basil Valentine</header>

## Brother Basil Valentine

That which is above, make below; and that which is visible, make invisible and palpable, impalpable; and likewise, make the lower rise above, that the invisible may become visible and the impalpable, palpable. <note>This is a variation of the famous Hermetic axiom "As above, so below," describing the transformation of matter from solid to spirit and back again.</note> This is the entire part, completely perfected without any defect or diminution. But that in which death and life, destruction and resurrection dwell, is a round sphere, with which the Goddess of Fortune drives her chariot and imparts the gift of wisdom to the men of God. In its own name, according to temporal understanding, it is called **all in all**; <note>original: "omnia in omnibus"; a phrase used to describe the "Universal Essence" or the prima materia that contains the potential for everything.</note> yet over eternal things, that highest Arbiter and Judge exists.

Whoever now desires to know what this **all in all** is, let him make for the earth most ample wings and urge her strongly, so that she may raise herself up and, flying through the air, elevate herself into the highest region of the supreme heaven. Then, burn her wings with a most powerful fire, so that the earth falls headlong into the **Red Sea** <note>In alchemy, the "Red Sea" often symbolizes a stage of the process where the matter is submerged in a corrosive or transformative "solvent" that has turned red, or the "blood" of the philosophical lion.</note> and is there suffocated. Then, with fire and air, dry up the water so that it becomes earth again. Then, I say, you have **all in all**.

But if you are unable to find this, you should look into yourself and search all around in all things which are found throughout the world. Then you will find the **all in all**, which is the attractive force of all metallic and mineral things arising from salt and sulfur, and twice-born from Mercury. More than this, I say, it would not be proper for me to say regarding that which is **all in all**, since **all in all** is comprised of all things.

After these words, he spoke further: "O friends, if by hearing you have perceived wisdom from my voice, you have learned from what and in what manner you ought to find the Great Stone of the ancient philosophers. It cures <term>leprous and imperfect metals: base metals like lead or tin, which alchemists believed were "sick" versions of gold</term>, and opens to them a new generation; it also preserves men in health and leads them to a long age. It has strengthened me until now by its heavenly power and operation, so that of my own will I desire to die, being weary of this life."

> God is to be praised through all ages for His grace and wisdom, which He has mercifully imparted to me over a long time. Amen.

And so, he vanished before their eyes.

When this speech was finished, each person returned to the place from whence they had come, thinking and laboring upon these matters day and night, according to the measure of talent each had been granted, etc.

## Now follow the twelve Keys

# OF BROTHER BASIL VALENTINE
# of the Benedictine order, by which the doors to the most ancient stone of our ancestors are opened and the most secret fountain of all health is unlocked.

## THE FIRST KEY.

![Alchemical Emblem: The First Key. A King and Queen stand before a castle; a wolf leaps over a crucible on the left, while on the right, an old man with a wooden leg representing Saturn tends a furnace with a scythe nearby.](image-placeholder)

**L**et my friend know that all things impure and spotted are unworthy of our work. For their leprosy <note>In alchemical texts, "leprosy" (Latin: *leprositas*) refers to the impurities, oxides, or "base" qualities of a metal that must be purged to reach its pure, "noble" essence.</note> can provide no assistance to our work; rather, the good is hindered by the impure.

All tradable goods from the mines are worth their own price; but when adulteration is added to them, they become unfit. For they are corrupted by deceit <note>original: "fuco"; literally "dye" or "paint," used here to mean a deceptive appearance or counterfeit quality.</note>, nor are they of the same efficacy as they were before.

And just as a physician cleanses and purifies the interior of the body by means of his medicines, expelling all filth from it; so too must our bodies <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" often refers to the metals themselves, particularly gold and silver.</note> be purified and cleansed of all their impurity, so that perfection may operate in our generation. Our masters require a pure, immaculate body, which is corrupted by no spot or foreign mixture. For the addition of something alien is the <term>leprosy of our metals</term> <note>Alchemists used the term "leprosy" to describe the oxidation, impurities, or base qualities that "infected" noble metals like gold and silver.</note>.

->Let the King's crown be of pure gold, and let a chaste bride be joined to him in marriage.<-

Therefore, if you wish to work by means of our bodies, take the **grey, most ravenous wolf**, who by reason of his name is subject to warlike Mars, but by the origin of his birth is the son of old Saturn <note>The "grey wolf" is a code for the mineral stibnite (antimony). It is called "son of Saturn" because it looks like lead, but "subject to Mars" because iron is used to refine it.</note>, who is found in the valleys and mountains of the world, seized by the sharpest hunger. Throw to him the body of the King <note>Gold</note>, so that he may have nourishment therefrom; and when he has devoured the King, make a great fire, into which throw the wolf to burn him entirely; then the King will again be set free. When this has been done three times, then the **Lion** has overcome the wolf, and will find nothing more in it to consume. And thus our body is suitable for the beginning of our work.

And know that this alone is the right and legitimate way to purge our bodies. For the **Lion** purifies himself with the blood of the wolf, and the tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is the essential soul or coloring power of a substance that can transform other things.</note> of his blood wonderfully rejoices in the tincture of the Lion; indeed, the blood of both of these is joined together by a certain closeness of affinity. When the Lion is satisfied, his spirit is made stronger than before, and his eyes shine with great splendor, like the **Sun**. His interior essence is of great value and is useful for all things for which it is required. And when he has been so prepared, the sons of men—vexed by the gravest falling sickness <note>original: "morbis caducis"; a historical term for epilepsy.</note> and other ailments—give thanks to him. Those ten lepers follow him and desire to drink of the blood of his soul, and all who are afflicted by evil rejoice deeply in his spirit.

For whoever drinks from this **golden fountain** feels a certain renovation of his nature, the removal of evil, the balancing of the blood, the strengthening of the heart, and perfect health of all the limbs.

But let my friend observe most diligently that the **fountain of life** <note>original: "fons vitæ." In alchemy, this refers to the specialized solvent, often called "Philosophical Mercury," used to dissolve the purified metals.</note> be found pure and clear. When a certain tree bears unhealthy and unpleasant fruits, it is cut around the trunk and another species of fruit is grafted into it; then the bud joins itself with the trunk, so that from the trunk and the root, together with its new sprout, a good tree comes forth, which bears healthy and pleasing fruit at the will of its gardener.

The **King** <note>The King represents Gold or the Sun. If you now understand what I am saying, then with this key you have opened the first lock and removed the obstacle of the bolt. Therefore, I shall say no more about this key, just as Lucius Papirius <note>Likely a reference to Lucius Papirius Cursor, a Roman figure known for his severity and silence; here, the author uses the name to signal that he is bound to silence and will not explain the secret more plainly.</note> taught me.

# II. THE SECOND KEY.

**I**n the courts of the great and powerful, various kinds of drinks are found, of which hardly any one is like another in smell, heat, or taste. For their preparation is manifold; nevertheless, all are drunk, since each is ordained for its own use and is necessary for the household management <note>original: "œconomiam." In an alchemical context, this refers to the organized "economy" or systematic arrangement of the laboratory processes.</note>.

When the sun sends out its rays and scatters them through the clouds, it is commonly said that the sun is "attracting the waters" <note>The visual phenomenon of sunbeams appearing to pull moisture up from the earth. Valentine uses this as a metaphor for the Sun (Gold/Sulfur) drawing up its "water" (Mercury) during distillation.</note> and that rain is near; and if this happens frequently, it makes the year fruitful.

To build a most precious palace, various and diverse craftsmen and mechanics apply their hands and labor before it can be called a most ornate and perfect palace: for that which requires stone cannot be made of wood.

Through the daily ebbs and flows <note>original: "cursus ac recursus." Literally the "running and returning" of the tides.</note> of the raging sea—which are caused by a certain sympathy <note>In the Hermetic tradition, "sympathy" is the invisible, magnetic-like connection between the stars/planets and earthly materials.</note> from above through the influence of the heavens—many and great riches come to the lands. For as often as they flow back, they bring something good with them to mankind.

<note>The emblem for the Second Key shows Mercury as a winged man holding two caducei (staffs with entwined serpents). They stand above the wings of the "Spirit," signifying the volatile nature of the matter being prepared.</note>

**A** virgin to be given in marriage is first splendidly adorned with a variety of the most precious garments, so that she may please her bridegroom, and by the sight of her, enkindle the fire of love deep within him. But when the bride is to be joined to her spouse in the carnal rite <note>original: "carnalia ritu copulanda." Refers to the physical consummation of the marriage, used here as a metaphor for the chemical union of substances.</note>, all diversity of clothing is removed, and the bride retains nothing except that which was granted to her by the Creator at her birth.

In the same way, when our bridegroom **Apollo** <note>Apollo represents the Sun, or Gold/Sulfur in the alchemical work.</note> is to celebrate his nuptials with his bride **Diana** <note>Diana represents the Moon, or Silver/Mercury.</note>, various garments are first prepared for them, and their heads and bodies are washed thoroughly with waters. You must learn to prepare these waters through different methods of distillation, since they are very unequal—some large, some small, as their necessity requires, just as I spoke regarding the various types of drinks. 

And you should know, when the moisture of the earth ascends and the mist is raised, it is congealed in the upper part, and falls back down by its own weight, by which means the moisture taken from the earth is restored. This refreshes, nourishes, and sustains the earth, so that leaves and grasses can spring up from it. Therefore, some preparations of your waters must be repeated frequently by distilling, so that you may very often return to the earth that which was abstracted from it and abstract it again, just as the *Euripus* <note>original: "Maris Eurypus." The Euripus Strait is famous for its strong, reversing currents; Valentine uses it to describe "reflux distillation," where liquid is evaporated and then flows back down into the vessel.</note> of the sea often leaves the land and covers it again, until it reaches a certain goal.

When the **King’s Palace** has been prepared and adorned in this way by various handicrafts, and the *glassy sea* <note>original: "mare vitreum." A reference to the clear liquid or solvent within the glass vessel.</note> has finished its course and filled the palace with good things, then the King may safely enter and place his seat therein.

But, my friend, note this especially: that the bridegroom must be joined with his bride *naked with naked*. Therefore, all things prepared for the decoration of garments and the beauty of the face must be removed again, so that they may possess the tomb <note>In alchemy, the "tomb" or "sepulcher" is the sealed vessel where the substances "die" (decompose) to be reborn.</note> naked, just as they were born naked, lest their seed be corrupted by the admixture of a stranger.

To conclude this discourse, I tell you in all truth that the most precious water, from which the bridegroom's bath must be made, is to be prudently prepared with great care from **two pugilists** <note>original: "duobus pugilibus." These "fighters" represent two contrary or reactive substances (often an acid and a base, or "the eagle" and "the lion") whose violent reaction produces the necessary chemical solvent.</note> (understand: from two contrary materials), so that one adversary may propel the other, and [ready] for the fight...

ought to triumph and gain victory again: However, no triumph can happen in this pursuit unless the **King** <note>The "King" typically represents Gold or the perfected solar principle in the alchemical process.</note> adds the strong force and power of his water, and grants it the key of his own proper color: so that through it, he may be destroyed and become invisible; yet this time his visible form must return, albeit with a lessening of his simple essence and an improvement of his state.

A painter can paint yellow upon white, and red upon yellow, and eventually a purple color: and although all those colors are still present, nevertheless the last one, being the highest in its grade, prevails. The same must happen in our **magistery** <note>original: "magisterio." The "Great Work" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>: and when that is done, then you have before your eyes the light of all wisdom, which shines in the darkness, although it does not burn: For our **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur." In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle, though here Valentine describes a "philosophical sulfur" that is incombustible.</note> does not burn, and yet it gleams far and wide: nor does it color anything unless it has been prepared and colored with its own color, with which it may afterward be able to color weak and imperfect metals. However, it is not granted to that sulfur to color anything unless that color has been surrendered to it with great perseverance: For the weaker cannot overcome, but the stronger obtains dominion over the weaker, and the feeble is compelled to yield to the robust. Therefore, for this discourse, remember the following conclusion and opinion: a small thing cannot help another small thing, nor provide aid in the working; and a combustible thing cannot defend another combustible thing from being burned: if, therefore, a defender is to be present who may provide help to the combustible thing and defend it, then the defender himself shall have more power than the one whose defense he takes up, and above all, he himself must necessarily exist as incombustible in his own substance.

In this way, whoever wishes to prepare our **incombustible sulfur** of all the wise should first consider within himself to seek our sulfur in that in which it is incombustible, which cannot happen unless the **salty sea** <note>Likely referring to a salt-based solvent or the "mercurial sea" used to dissolve the matter.</note> has swallowed the body and cast it out from itself again: Then you must exalt it in its grade so that it far surpasses all other stars of heaven in its brightness, and in its essence: let it abound in blood so much that, like a **Pelican** <note>original: "Pelicani." ...and the red blood of the <term>dragon</term> <note>original: "draconis." In alchemy, "Dragon's Blood" usually refers to the deep red color of the Stone at its penultimate stage, though it can also refer to certain resins or minerals.</note>, described by many, and also the purple mantle, highly foliated in our art, with which the **Queen of Health** is covered, and by which all elegant metals can be restored by heat:

Keep this honorable mantle well, together with the **astral salt**, which follows this celestial **sulfur**, lest anything adverse happen to it; and grant to it as much of the bird's volatility as is sufficient. Then the **Cock** <note>original: "Gallus." Usually representing the solar, active, or fixed principle.</note> shall devour the **Fox** <note>original: "vulpes." Usually representing the volatile, acidic, or deceptive principle.</note>, and afterward shall suffocate it in water; and having been resuscitated through fire, it shall be devoured by the fox again, so that like is returned for like.

## IV. THE FOURTH KEY.

<note>The Fourth Key of Basil Valentine, illustrating the alchemical process of putrefaction and resurrection.</note>

**A**ll flesh arisen from the earth must be corrupted and reduced again into earth, as it was earth before; then the **earthly salt** gives a new generation through celestial resuscitation. For where there was no earth before, there resurrection cannot follow in our work: For in the earth is the balsam of nature and the salt of those who have sought the knowledge of all things.

<page-num>401</page-num>
<header>On the Philosophers' Stone.</header>

# On the Philosophers' Stone.

In the final judgment of the world, the world shall be judged by fire, so that what was previously made from nothing by the Master is once again reduced to ash by fire. From this ash, the **Phoenix** <note>A mythical bird that burns to death and is reborn from its own ashes; in alchemy, it represents the final stage of the work and the resurrection of the Stone.</note> shall at last bring forth its young. For in such ash lies hidden the true and genuine **tartar** <note>original: "tartarus." In a chemical sense, it refers to potassium bitartrate or salts; philosophically, it refers to the "hellish" or potent fire-salt trapped within matter.</note>, which must be dissolved, and after its dissolution, the strongest locks of the royal chamber can be opened.

A new heaven and earth shall be formed after the burning, and the new man shall shine far more brilliantly than when he lived in the first world, for he will have been clarified <note>Refined or purified to a state of luminous perfection.</note>.

When ash and sand are well matured and cooked by fire, the glassmaker then fashions glass from them, which thereafter endures in the fire forever. In its transparent color, it resembles a stone and is no longer recognized as ash. To the ignorant, this is a great mystery, but to the expert, it is not so at all, because he understands the method of the workmanship through knowledge and frequent experience.

From stones, the craftsman also prepares **lime** <note>original: "calcem." Quicklime, produced by heating limestone, which acquires a latent heat through fire.</note> through burning, so that it may be useful for his labor. But before it is prepared by fire, it is a stone and cannot be used as lime for work; yet through fire, that stone is matured and acquires a supremely hot degree from the flame. It becomes so potent that, if its fiery spirit of lime is brought to its perfection, scarcely anything can be compared to it.

If any substance is burned into ashes, it yields its own **salt** <note>In alchemy, Salt is the principle of fixity and the physical body.</note> through the art. If, in its "anatomy" <note>The process of separating a substance into its fundamental components.</note>, you can keep the **sulfur** <note>The active, solar principle representing soul and heat.</note> and **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium." The volatile, fluid principle representing spirit.</note> separately and restore them to their salt again according to the requirements of the art, then by the benefit of fire, that which existed before its destruction or "anatomy" can be made from it once more. The "wise" of this world call this folly and consider it nonsense, calling it a "new creation" which God has not granted to a sinner; but they themselves do not understand that the created thing was already there before, and the craftsman merely proves its augmentation and **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium." The finished work or the process of achieving the Great Work.</note> through the seed of nature.

Whichever craftsman lacks ash cannot produce salt for our art, for without salt, our corporeal work cannot be accomplished. For it is salt alone that performs the **coagulation** <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid or "fixing" a volatile substance into a permanent state.</note> of all things.

<summary>Basil Valentine explains the Fourth Key using the metaphor of the Last Judgment, arguing that fire is necessary to reduce matter to ash so that its essential salt can be extracted. He compares the alchemical process to glassmaking and lime-burning, where fire transforms common materials into something enduring and powerful.</summary>

# Brother Basil Valentine's Practice,

Just as salt is the mainstay of all things and preserves them from putrefaction <note>The process of decay or rotting, which alchemists believed was a necessary step before matter could be reborn in a higher form.</note>, so also the salt of our masters protects the metals, lest they be reduced entirely to nothing and corrupted, preventing anything from being made of them again—unless perhaps their **Balsam** <note>original: "Balsamus." In alchemy, this refers to the "radical moisture" or the natural life-force that keeps a body from decaying.</note> should perish, and the spirit incorporated within them should depart from nature. In that case, the body would be altogether dead, and nothing could be fashioned from it with any fruitfulness, because the metallic spirits would have departed, leaving their habitation naked and empty through their natural death, into which no life could be brought back.

Note this well, student of the art: that salt from ashes <note>original: "sal ex cinere." This refers to the potassium-rich salts extracted by leaching the ashes left after combustion.</note> is of great value, and in it many virtues lie hidden. Nevertheless, the salt itself is useless unless its interior is turned out and its exterior is brought in. For it is the spirit alone that gives strength and life; the naked body by itself provides nothing. If you know how to find that spirit, you will truly have the **Salt of the Philosophers** <term>Salt of the Philosophers: One of the three prime principles (with Sulfur and Mercury), representing the fixed, bodily crystalline principle of the Stone.</term> and the **incombustible oil** <note>original: "oleum incombustibile." A legendary substance that can withstand the highest heat without evaporating; a symbol of the perfected and fixed Alchemical Stone.</note>, about which much has been written before me.

> *Have sought me anxiously,*
> *Yet few have considered*
> *My hidden powers.*

<meta>This page continues the alchemical instruction of Basil Valentine, moving from the properties of Salt into a deeper discussion on the "Spirit of the Earth" and the animated nature of all matter, preparing the reader to understand the "First Matter" of the Stone.</meta>

<page-num>403</page-num>
<header>*Concerning the Philosophers' Stone.*</header>

->**T**he<- life-giving power of the earth produces all things that come forth from it, and whoever says that the earth is devoid of life maintains a position contrary to the truth. For that which is dead can supply nothing to another living thing, and growth is absent in the dead because the spirit of life has flown away. Therefore, the spirit is the life and soul of the earth, which dwells within it and works from the celestial and sidereal <note>Sidereal: relating to the stars and distant celestial bodies, which alchemists believed influenced the growth of minerals on Earth.</note> into the terrestrial. For all herbs, trees, and roots, as well as all metals and minerals, receive their powers, growth, and nourishment from the spirit of the earth. Because the spirit is life, which is nourished by the stars, it subsequently grants sustenance to all growing things, and just as a mother hides the fetus in her womb and nourishes it within herself, so also the earth cherishes the minerals submerged in her bosom through her spirit received from above.

For this reason, the earth does not give those powers of its own accord, but rather the life-giving spirit that exists within it. If the earth were deprived of its spirit, it would be dead and would no longer provide nourishment; indeed, its **sulfur** or "fatness" <note>original: "sulphuri aut pinguedini." In alchemy, 'sulfur' represents the principle of combustion and the oily, fertile substance of a body.</note> would lack the spirit that preserves the life-giving force and produces all growing things through nourishment.

Two contrary spirits can dwell together, yet they do not easily agree: for when **gunpowder** <term>Gunpowder: original "pulvis pyrius." Alchemists often used the explosive reaction of gunpowder as a metaphor for the violent release of energy when opposing spiritual forces meet.</term> is ignited, those two spirits from which that powder is composed flee from one another with the greatest crack and force, and fly into the air, so that no one can discern or say where they have fled, unless it was known by experience what kind of spirits they were and in what substance they existed.

From these things you may know, my student of the art, that life is solely the true spirit: and thus everything that the ignorant common folk regard as dead must be brought back again into an imperceptible, visible, and spiritual life, and be preserved within it—if indeed life is to work with life. These spirits feed and nourish themselves on the celestial, and are procreated from celestial, elementary, and terrestrial substance, which is called **unformed matter** <note>original: "materia informis." Also known as the *materia prima*, the raw, chaotic substance before it is shaped into a specific element or metal.</note>.

And just as iron has its own **magnet** <note>original: "magnetem." Alchemists believed in "spiritual magnets"—substances that had a natural, sympathetic attraction to specific celestial or metallic forces.</note>, which attracts it with a wonderful and invisible love, so also our gold has a magnet; this magnet is the **First Matter** of the Great Stone. If you perceive these words of mine, you are rich and blessed before the whole world.
