# The Practice of Brother Basil Valentine

I shall set forth one more explanation for you in this chapter: when a man looks into a mirror, his reflection creates an image; yet, if one tries to touch it with the hands, nothing tangible is found there except the mirror into which the man looked. In the same way, a **visible spirit** must be drawn out from this matter, which is nevertheless intangible. That same spirit, I say, is the root of life for our bodies and the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius Philosophorum." In alchemy, this is not common quicksilver, but a purified, spiritual essence believed to be the "seed" or "soul" of metals.</note>, from which a liquid water is prepared in our art. You must then make this water material again in its composition and, through certain means, lead it from the lowest to the highest degree, reducing it into the **most perfect medicine**.

For our beginning is a locked and tangible body; the middle is a fleeting spirit and a **golden water** without any change <note>original: "aqua aurea." Likely referring to the "aurum potabile" or a stage where the matter takes on a golden, fluid appearance.</note>, from which our masters received their life; but the end is the most fixed medicine for human and metallic bodies alike. Knowledge of this is granted to angels rather than to men, though such men have attained it who seek it from God with prayers proceeding from the heart and are grateful toward Him and toward those in need.

To conclude these matters, I say with total certainty that one labor arises out of another. For our matter, at the start of our work, must be most excellently and highly purified; then it must be dissolved and destroyed, completely corrupted and reduced to dust and ashes. When all that is done, prepare from it a **volatile spirit**, white like snow, and another **volatile spirit**, red like blood. These two spirits contain a third within themselves, and yet they are a single spirit; and these are the three spirits that preserve and increase life. 

Join them together, give them whatever they naturally require in the way of food and drink, and keep them in the <term>chamber of heat</term> <note>original: "thalamo caloris." A poetic term for the alchemical furnace or sealed vessel where the "marriage" of substances takes place under constant warmth.</note> until the perfection of their birth. Then you will see and experience what the Creator and Nature have granted to you. And know this: I have never made such a revelation with my own mouth until now. God has placed more efficacy and wonder in nature than many thousands of men could believe. A seal has been impressed upon me so that others after me may also be able to write of these wonders—things which are natural and granted by the Creator, yet are held to be "unnatural" by the foolish. For the natural takes its first beginning from the **supernatural**, and yet, everything together is found to be nothing but natural.

# THE SIXTH KEY.

**A** male without a female is considered as half a body, and a female without a man likewise occupies the place of half a body <note>This is a foundational alchemical concept: the union of the "male" principle (Sulphur) and the "female" principle (Mercury). Neither can create life alone.</note>: for individuals by themselves can produce no fruit. When too much seed is cast into a field, the field suffers from the excess, so that mature fruit cannot follow; if, however, the seed is too sparse, the fruit is thin and weeds <note>original: "lolium." Often translated as "tares" or "cockle," referring to unwanted plants that choke out a crop.</note> grow in its place, from which no usefulness will follow.

If anyone wishes not to burden his conscience with sin in the selling of merchandise, let him offer a just measure to his neighbor; and let him provide lawful ells <note>original: "ulnas." An "ell" was a historical unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm, used primarily for measuring cloth.</note> and weights, so that he may flee a curse and prepare a sacrifice of praise among the poor.

In great waters one can easily be drowned, and small waters are dried up without difficulty by the heat of the sun, so that they are of no account.

**N**atural heat preserves the life of man: for if natural heat departs, life reaches its end.

Natural fire, if used in a balanced way, defends against the cold, but an excess of it causes destruction. It is not necessary for the sun to physically touch the earth with its own substance; rather, it is enough if it exerts its power from a distance through its rays. These rays become stronger through reflection when they strike the earth. For through these means, the sun has enough efficacy to perform its duty and to ripen all things through concoction <term>concoction (concoctio): the process of "ripening" or refining a substance through steady, gentle heat, similar to digestion or maturation</term>. For because of the distance of the air, the solar rays are brought into a certain temperate state, so that the fire may work by means of the air, just as the air works by means of the fire.

The earth can produce nothing without water, and likewise water can stir nothing into life without the earth. Just as earth and water need each other's help to generate fruit, in no way can fire lack air, nor air lack fire. For fire has no life without air, and air without fire cannot provide its heat and dryness.

The vine, in its final ripening, has more need of the rays and heat of the sun than it does at the beginning of spring. Even if the sun exerts its influence well in the autumn, the vine is accustomed to yield its juice better and more strongly than if the solar rays were lacking due to a deficiency of heat.

In winter, the common folk <note>original: "vulgus"; referring to those uninitiated in the alchemical arts</note> believe all things to be dead because the frost has bound the earth so that nothing can grow from it. However, as soon as spring presents itself and the cold is diminished by the ascent of the sun, all things are recalled to life: the trees and herbs flourish, and the crawling creatures that had fled the icy winter creep forth from the caverns and hollows of the earth. All vegetation spreads a new scent, and their excellent work is signaled by the beautiful, lovely, and various colors of their flowers. Thus summer proceeds in its labor, so that from such blossoms it may bear fruit of every kind, for which you ought rightly to give thanks to the Creator, who fixed a goal for such an arrangement through nature.

So year after year the work proceeds, until the world is again destroyed by its **Architect**, and those who occupy the earth are exalted through the glorification of God; then all terrestrial nature will cease to labor, and the eternal celestial nature will dwell in its place.

When the Sun performs its course far from us in the winter solstice <note>original: "bruma"</note>, it cannot melt the deep snow; but if it draws nearer to us in the summer, the air becomes more fiery and strong, so that the melting snow falls away into water and destroys itself. For the weak is compelled to yield to the stronger, and the stronger dominates the weak.

In this same way, the regulation of the fire must be observed in this <term>magisterio (mastery/Great Work): the entire process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, lest the moist liquor be dried out sooner than is right, and the <term>terra sapientum (earth of the wise): the solid, fixed substance or "salt" that remains at the bottom of the alchemical vessel</term> be melted and dissolved too quickly. Otherwise, you would generate scorpions instead of healthy fish in your waters. <note>In alchemical symbolism, "scorpions" often represent poisonous or corrosive by-products, while "fish" represent the pure, living spirit within the "mercurial water."</note> But if you desire to be a true director of your labor, then take the spiritual water upon which the spirit hovered in the beginning, and shut the door of the fortress against it. For from that time, the Celestial City will be besieged by terrestrial enemies. And your heaven must be strongly guarded by three ramparts and walls, so that there is no entrance except one, and that one must be extremely well defended by guards. Then, when all those things are perfected, light the lamp of wisdom and seek with it the lost Groschen <note>original: "Grossum"; a reference to the Parable of the Lost Coin in Luke 15:8, used here to represent searching for the hidden "light" or "seed" within the matter</note>; give only as much illumination as may suffice. Having previously discussed the glorification of man and the elements, the text now focuses on the necessity of "putrefaction" (the breakdown of matter) as the precursor to all new life and growth, using examples from nature and the domestic sphere.</meta>

<page-num>410</page-num>

<header>*Friar Basilii Valentini*</header>

<meta>catchword: imaginari</meta>

...through putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: In alchemy, this refers to the breakdown or "death" of a substance, which was believed to be necessary to release its life force for a new, higher form of existence.</term>: even the seed of the field and everything belonging to the vegetable kingdom cannot increase unless through putrefaction. Furthermore, many small animals and worms are granted life, so that from mere putrefaction they obtain a living force and action, which deserves to be recognized as a miracle above all others. Truly, nature has granted this very thing, since such living growth and the breathing of life are found most often in the earth, and are stirred up through the other elements by a spiritual seed in that manner.

This is to be demonstrated by examples: the country-woman <note>original: "uxor ruricolæ," literally "the wife of the farmer."</note> knows this best, for she cannot raise any poultry for the household unless it happens through the putrefaction of the egg from which the chick is generated.

If bread should fall into honey, ants are born in it, which is also a singular miracle of nature compared to others. The farmer also observes that small worms arise from putrid flesh in humans, horses, and the bodies of other animals, just as spiders, worms, and the like also arise in nuts, apples, and pears. Who could enumerate the various kinds and species of worms that proceed from putrefaction alone?

The same can be seen in herbs, as diverse kinds of plants, such as nettles and many others of that sort, come forth in places where such a plant never grew, nor did its seed fall. This occurs solely through putrefaction. The cause is that the earth in those places has been "deposited" and, as it were, impregnated for those fruits, which flowed into it from above by a sidereal property <term>Sidereal property: An influence or "influx" coming from the stars (Latin: *sidereus*), which alchemists believed directed the growth and characteristics of things on Earth.</term>: so that it produced a seed within it spiritually. This seed putrefied itself in the earth, and through the action and help of the elements, generated physical matter according to its natural species. Thus the stars, together with the elements, can stir up some new seed which had never existed before, and afterwards it can be increased through the succeeding putrefaction. However, it is not granted to Man to stir up a new seed: for the operation of the elements and the essence of the stars are not within his power to shape. Thus, various kinds of herbs grow solely from putrefaction; but because the farmer regards these as common occurrences, he no longer considers them, nor [understands] the cause of this science for himself...

<summary>Valentine explains the alchemical principle of putrefaction as the source of all generation, citing examples like maggots in meat, chicks from eggs, and plants growing from astral "seeds" in the earth.</summary>

## Practice of the Philosophers' Stone.

...[wherever it] can be imagined, it takes the place of custom among the common people. But you, who ought to know more than an ordinary person, should learn the underlying causes by grasping deeper teachings and ideas. From these foundations, you will see how the quickening of revival and birth arises from this kind of putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: The stage of chemical breakdown or "death" of a substance, seen as essential for its rebirth in a more perfect form.</term>. You must not recognize this merely as a custom, but as a seeker of nature, since in the end, all life originates and is caused through putrefaction.

Every element by itself has its own corruption and, in turn, its own generation. Let the student of this art be made certain of this, and let him know from an overflowing foundation that the other three elements lie hidden within each single element. For air has fire, water, and earth within itself—which might seem incredible, yet it is the very truth. So too, fire contains air, water, and earth within itself; otherwise, it would generate nothing. And water shares in earth, air, and fire; otherwise, no generation could follow, regardless of the fact that each element exists separately, since they are nonetheless mixed together. All of this is discovered through distillation in the separation of the elements.

And so that I may show you this by a legitimate proof, lest you say in your ignorance that my words are mere talk and not at all true, I declare to you—whose duty it is to investigate the separation of nature and the division of the elements—that in the distillation of earth, air passes over first and most easily. After this, in a steady progression, the element of water follows. Fire lies hidden in the air, because both are of a spiritual essence and love each other wonderfully. The earth remains at the bottom, and within it is the salt of preciousness <term>Salt of preciousness: Also called the "precious salt." In alchemy, "Salt" represents the fixed, physical body of a substance that remains after the volatile spirit and soul have been removed.</term>.

In the distillation of water, air and fire proceed first; afterward, the water and the body of the earth remain at the bottom. If the element of fire is reduced to an invisible substance through the extraction of fire, water, and earth, each can be drawn out by itself. Similarly, air dwells in the other three elements, for none of them can exist without air. The earth is nothing, nor can it produce anything without air; fire does not burn, nor has it life without air; water can produce no fruit without air. Furthermore, air can neither consume anything nor dry up moisture [without the others]...

...unless it be done by natural heat. Since, therefore, fervor and heat are found in the air, the element of fire will certainly be in the air. For everything that is hot and dry is assigned to the fiery substance; wherefore one element cannot lack another, but a mixture of the four elements is always found in the generation of all things. He who decides the contrary by no means understands the secrets of nature, nor has he investigated their properties.

For you ought to know, if anything is to be born through putrefaction <note>The alchemical stage where matter "dies" and decays, turning black, which is considered the essential first step toward purification.</note>, it must necessarily happen in this way: Earth, through a hidden and enclosed humidity, is reduced into a certain corruption or destruction, which is the beginning of putrefaction. For without humidity—namely, the element of water—no true putrefaction can occur. If then some generation is to follow from putrefaction, it must be kindled and brought forth through the hot property, acting as the element of fire. For without natural heat, no birth can take place. And if the thing generated is to take on a life-giving breath and motion, this cannot happen without air. For if air did not work together toward this end and perform its duty, then the first compound and substance from which the generation proceeded would be suffocated and perish within itself for lack of air.

Therefore it is clearly found and fundamentally demonstrated that no perfectly generated thing can be destitute of the service of the four elements, and that one element always shows its operation and life within another, and thus manifests through putrefaction. For without that process, nothing is brought into the light, now or in the future. And so that you may know this to be true—namely, that for any living and perfect generation and resuscitation all four elements are necessary—know that when Adam, the first man, was formed from the clod of earth by the supreme Creator, not yet did any perceptible motion of life exert itself, until God himself breathed in the spirit. Then the clod of earth was endowed with life-giving power. In the earth was <term>Salt</term> <note>original: "sal"</note>, that is, the body; the air breathed in was <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, the Spirit; through this breathing-in, the air gave him a genuine and tempered heat, which was <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphur"</note>, that is, fire. Then Adam moved himself and manifested by such motion that a life-giving soul had been infused into him. For fire cannot exist without air, and conversely, no air exists without fire.

Note also this, that it [wine] has a living volatile spirit within it. But as soon as it is reduced into vinegar <note>original: "acetum"</note> through long-lasting heat, its spirit is not as volatile as it was before; for in the distillation of vinegar, the water or aqueousness comes out first, and the spirit comes last. And although the same matter is before your eyes as was previously in the vessel, yet it has far different properties, since it is no longer wine, but has been transmuted through the putrefaction of continuous heat and made into vinegar. ## THE NINTH KEY.

**S**aturn, called the highest of the celestial planets, is of the lowest authority in our <term>Magisterium|The completion of the Great Work or the "mastery" of alchemical transformation</term>; nevertheless, he is the chief key of the whole art. Though placed in the lowest degree and held in the least esteem in our art, and even though through a swift flight he raised himself to the highest summit above all the luminaries, yet by the "clipping of his wings" <note>original: "pennarum ejus resectione"; an alchemical metaphor for 'fixation,' or turning a volatile substance into a solid, stable one</note> he must be brought back to the lowest illumination of all. Through corruption <note>the stage of putrefaction or "death" of the matter</note> he must be advanced toward improvement, so that black is changed into white, and white into red. 

Through the course of the whole "world of colors," the other planets must also pass, until the superabundant proper color of the Triumphant King <note>The final state of the Philosophers' Stone or perfected Gold</note> is reached. And so I say, even if Saturn seems most vile to the whole world, nevertheless he has such power and efficacy within himself that if his precious essence—which is a coldness beyond measure and sensation—enters into and reduces a fiery metallic body, its "running liveliness" <note>original: "currens vivacitas"; a reference to the fluid, mobile nature of Quicksilver or Mercury</note> can be taken away. It can then be reduced to such a workable body as Saturn himself is, but of far greater constancy; which...

It describes the process of 'fixing' volatile elements and the progression through the alchemical color stages (Black, White, and Red) to reach the final goal.</summary>

**T**ransmutation <note>original: "permutatio"; in this context, the alchemical change of one substance into another</note> takes its origin, beginning, and end from **Mercury**, **sulfur**, and **salt**. This will seem difficult for many to understand, as indeed it is; but since the matter itself is common <note>original: "vilis," meaning cheap or lowly. Alchemists often claimed their starting material was something overlooked or discarded by the ignorant</note>, it is necessary that the intellect be sharp and elevated, so that unequal statuses may remain in the world to distinguish masters from servants.

From **Saturn** <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for the metal Lead</note> multiple colors proceed, which are produced through preparation and art: such as black, ash-gray, white, yellow, and red, and besides these, the mixed colors that arise from them. Likewise, the matter of all the wise <note>The "Philosophers," or practicing alchemists</note> shall pass through various colors before that Great Stone is exalted to the certain goal of perfection. For as often as a new gate of entry is opened to the Fire, so often a new form and style of "clothing" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the changing colors of the chemical mixture</note> is granted as a reward, until the destitute one himself acquires riches and no longer needs to borrow from another.

When noble **Venus** <note>Venus represents the metal Copper</note> possesses her kingdom, and according to the custom of the Royal Court distributes offices rightly, she appears in magnificent splendor. **Music** <note>The first of the Seven Liberal Arts mentioned in this allegory</note> carries before her a beautiful banner of red color, upon which is painted **Charity**, most beautiful in green garments. **Saturn** is appointed as the master of her court; when he performs his office, **Astronomy** carries a black banner before him, in which **Faith** is seen depicted in yellow and red clothing.

**Jupiter** <note>Jupiter represents the metal Tin</note> performs the duty of Marshal with his scepter, and **Rhetoric** carries for him a banner of ash-gray color, upon which **Hope**, most highly adorned in splendid colors, is painted.

**Mars** <note>Mars represents the metal Iron</note> is skilled in all matters of war and holds command with a certain fiery heat; **Geometry** holds out before him a blood-red veil, through which **Fortitude**, dressed in red cloth, is seen. **Mercury** <note>Mercury represents Quicksilver</note> holds the office of Chancellor, and **Arithmetic** carries before him a banner of all colors, upon which **Temperance** is painted in marvelous hues.

The **Sun** <note>Sol represents Gold</note> is the Vicar of the kingdom, and **Grammar** carries a yellow banner before him, in which **Justice** is depicted in golden clothing. Although this Vicar has more power in his kingdom, nevertheless Queen **Venus** has blinded and conquered him with her most superabundant splendor.

The **Moon** <note>Luna represents Silver</note> also appears then, and **Dialectic** [carries] for her a silvery and shining...

### Practice of the Philosopher’s Stone

<note>original: "Practica de Lapide Sapient."</note>

[She] <note>The personified metal or virtue mentioned in the preceding text</note> wears a thick veil, upon which **Prudence** was painted in a sky-blue color. And because the **husband of the Moon** <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Gold) is the husband of the Moon (Silver)</note> has died, she has taken his office upon herself, so that she might not allow Queen **Venus** <note>The metal Copper</note> to rule in the future. For the sake of managing the household, she has made an agreement with her, and then the **Chancellor** <note>likely representing a mediating chemical agent or the planet Mercury</note> will come to her aid, a new empire shall be established, and they both shall rule over the Queen. Understand by this that one **Planet** <note>The Seven Planets represented the seven metals: Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead</note> must drive out and remove another from its dominion, office, possession, and power, until the best of them occupy the highest empire. Then, with the best and firmest color belonging to their first mother <note>The original, primordial matter</note>, they obtain victory through their native constancy, love, and kinship. For the old world has passed away, and a new one is acquired in its place; one planet has spiritually consumed another, so that only the strongest remain through the nourishment provided by the others—two or three being overcome by one alone.

For the final conclusion of all these things, understand that you must bring forth the celestial **Scales** <note>Libra</note>, the **Ram** <note>Aries</note>, the **Bull** <note>Taurus</note>, the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note>, the **Scorpion** <note>Scorpio</note>, and the **Goat** <note>Capricorn</note>. On the other side of the scales, place the **Twins** <note>Gemini</note>, the **Archer** <note>Sagittarius</note>, the **Water-bearer** <note>Aquarius</note>, the **Fish** <note>Pisces</note>, and the **Virgin** <note>Virgo</note>. Then, make the **Golden Lion** <note>Leo; often representing purified Gold or the "ferment"</note> leap into the **Virgin’s** lap, and thus that side of the scale will weigh more and prevail over the other side in weight. Then, let the twelve signs of heaven with the **Pleiades** <note>A star cluster in Taurus</note> come forth in opposition; and so, after the completion of all the world’s colors, finally the **conjunction** <note>the chemical union of substances</note> and **union** will occur, so that the greatest coincides with the least, and the least with the greatest.

**I**n our stone—labored upon by me and by many long before me—are contained all the **Elements**, all mineral and metallic forms, and indeed all the qualities and properties of the whole world. For within it must be found the greatest and strongest heat; since by its great internal fire, the cold body of **Saturn** <note>The metal Lead</note> is warmed, and through that burning is changed into the best gold. In it also must be discovered the greatest cold, by whose joining the more fervent degree of **Venus** <note>The metal Copper</note> is tempered, and living **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> is coagulated, and by the same reasoning of its hardening is turned into the best, fixed gold. The reason for this is that all these properties are naturally implanted in the matter of our **Great Stone**; these properties are boiled out and ripened through the degrees of fire until they have reached the highest perfection. This cannot happen until **Mount Etna** in Sicily is extinguished from its burning <note>Symbolizing the taming of raw, volcanic heat</note>, and no more cold is found in the highest **Hyperborean mountains** <note>A mythical land in the far north, symbolizing extreme cold</note>, which place may also be called the **Thicket**.

## Practice, concerning the Stone of the Wise
<note>original: "de Lapide Sapient." The Stone of the Wise is another name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

All fruits of trees, if they are plucked before they reach maturity, are useless and premature, nor can they be used conveniently; just as a potter, unless he sufficiently burns and cooks his works through fire, they are unfit for use, because they have not been sufficiently matured by the fire.

So also regarding our **Elixir** <term>Elixir: from the Arabic 'al-iksir', referring to the potent medicinal or transformative substance derived from the Stone.</term>, it must be observed and diligently considered that the proper time be granted to it, and that nothing be taken away from its goodness before that time, lest it be accused of falsehood and be esteemed as unworthy. For if the flowers are plucked, it is easily known that no fruit can grow from there. Therefore, haste does not suit the **Great Work** <note>original: "magisterio." The mastery or the process of creating the Stone.</note>; for he who hastens too much rarely achieves anything good in this art, but by hastening, more is corrupted than is perfected.

Wherefore the seeker of truth should not allow himself to be seduced by too much desire to take out or pluck anything before the time, lest the apple fall from him, and nothing but the stalk be left in his hand. For in truth, if our stone is not matured enough, it will not be able to produce anything mature.

In the **bath** <note>original: "balneo." Likely referring to the Balneum Mariae or water bath.</note> the matter is dissolved and united through **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the stage of "blackness" or decomposition where the substance breaks down to be reborn.</term>; in the **ash** <note>A higher heat than the water bath, using a container of warm ashes.</note> it produces flowers; through the **sand** <note>An even hotter medium than ash.</note> all superfluous moisture is dried out. But the live **flame** of fire brings forth the exact maturation with **fixity** <term>fixitas: the state where a substance becomes stable under heat and no longer evaporates or changes.</term>. This does not mean that the **Bath of Mary** <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ." A double-boiler or water bath used for gentle heating.</note>, **horse dung** <note>original: "fimo equino." Decomposing manure was used as a natural, steady heat source for long-term digestion.</note>, ash, or sand must be used one after the other in succession, but rather that the degrees and the regulation of the fire should be perfected in that manner. For the stone is made in an empty furnace, of triple fortification, firmly observed, enclosed, and cooked with continuous fire until all clouds and vapors vanish, and the **garment of honors** <note>original: "vestis honorum." A metaphorical reference to the final, brilliant color change of the Stone.</note> appears with the greatest splendor. It remains in one place, of the lowest heaven, and is halted in its course; and when the **arms of the King** <note>The "King" usually represents Gold or the perfected Stone. The "arms" being unable to rise suggests the Stone has become "fixed" and no longer volatile.</note> can no longer be raised upward, the dominion of the world is occupied. For the **King** of eternal fixity is made, and no danger shall harm him hereafter, since he has emerged insuperable.

To this I say in this way: When your earth has been dissolved in its own water, dry out the water entirely by the due fire, and then the air will inspire new life; and when it has been incorporated with this life, you will have the matter, which by right can be called nothing other than the **great stone of the world**, which penetrates human and metallic bodies like a spirit, and is the **universal medicine** without defect. For it expels...
<note>The text continues on the next page, describing how the medicine expels diseases or impurities.</note>

and had married her. But because he had no children by her, he attributed this to his sins, because he had his **sister as a wife** <note>original: "sororem pro conjuge." In alchemy, the union of "brother and sister" refers to the joining of two substances from the same metallic root, typically sophisticated forms of Sulfur and Mercury.</note>, and with constant prayers he contended with the most high God, and persisted in his vows, that grace might be granted to him, and that a place might be given to his prayer.

Then the most powerful offspring is born, nourished by its own flesh, and restored by its own blood of honor. If you do this rightly, you will leave behind a numerous offspring and heirs born of your own body. But know this: the final seed, in the eighth change of time, will complete its course just as your first seed, from which you were made from the beginning. If you do this more often, and always begin anew, you will see the children of your children, so that the **great world** <note>The Macrocosm (the universe).</note> may be fully replenished by the generation of the **lesser** <note>The Microcosm (man or the alchemical work itself).</note>, so that the Creator's heavenly kingdom may be possessed in abundance."

When this was finished, Phoebus flew away again, and that knight, awakened from sleep, rose from his bed. When he followed all these things as they had been commanded, he not only experienced good success in all his purposes, but God also granted many children to him and his spouse, who thereafter possessed a memorable name through their father's testament, and the honor of the knightly dignity continued with riches in that family.

But if now, **son of doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinæ fili." ## THE TWELFTH KEY.

**A** fighter, who does not know how to use his sword, is not useful to himself; for he has not truly learned the practice of its utility. When another, who is more skilled in the use of the sword than he, goes down into battle against him, the one who is unfit is badly punished by the other. But he who has thoroughly perceived the mastery of the **wrestling school** <note>original: "palæstræ magisterium." The "palaestra" was a Greek wrestling school; Valentine uses this as a metaphor for the rigorous training and practical experience required in alchemy.</note> gains the prize.

<note>This final key typically summarizes the practical "Stone of the Wise" and its power to transmute metals. The accompanying image is one of the most famous in alchemy, showing the laboratory as a place where celestial influence (sun and moon) meets terrestrial chemistry (the lion devouring the snake).</note>

<meta>This page provides the practical instructions for the Twelfth and final Key of Basil Valentine's work. Thus, he who has obtained a certain **tincture** <term>tincture: A potent alchemical liquid or powder capable of "staining" or transforming the inner nature of a base metal into a noble one.</term> by the grace of Almighty God, yet knows not how to bring it into use, is in the same position as the fighter we spoke of who has no idea how to use his sword. Since this twelfth and final key is held to be the conclusion of my book, I will not detain you with further parables or figurative speech, but without any omission, I shall open this key of the tincture through the most absolute and true process. Therefore, be attentive to my teaching as follows:

While the **medicine and stone of all the Sages** <term>Lapis Sapientum: The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance sought by alchemists to achieve perfection in both metals and the human soul.</term> is made from the true **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lacte virginis." A common alchemical metaphor for a specific mercurial solvent or starting substance, often described as white and nourishing to the "infant" stone.</note> and is perfectly prepared, take one part of it and three parts of the best and purest gold, melted and purified by **Antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium." In the laboratory, alchemists used antimony to "devour" the impurities in gold, leaving the gold pure and ready for the Great Work.</note>. Reduce this gold into the thinnest plates possible. Put these together into a **crucible** <note>original: "tigillum." A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note> in which metals are usually melted. First, give it a slow fire for twelve hours; then, let it stand in a melted state for three days and nights continuously. Then the purified gold and the stone are made into a pure medicine of the most subtle, spiritual, and penetrating property. For without the **ferment of gold** <term>fermentum auri: Just as yeast or leaven causes bread to rise, this "ferment" allows the Stone to act upon and transform other metals.</term>, the stone cannot work or exercise its power of tinting. It is indeed too subtle and penetrating; but if it be fermented and joined with its own like, then the prepared Tincture receives the power to enter into and act upon other things. 

Next, take one part of the prepared ferment to a thousand parts of molten metal if you wish to tincture it. Then you shall know by the highest truth and faith that it alone will be transmuted into good and **fixed gold** <note>original: "aurum fixum." This refers to gold that is stable and can withstand the "test" of fire and corrosive acids without losing weight or color.</note>. For one body takes hold of another, and even though it is not like itself, it is nevertheless forced to be assimilated to the same through the force and power joined to it, since like takes its origin from like.

Whoever uses this means, all certainty shall be revealed to him; the entrance halls of the palace have their exit at the end, and this subtlety is to be compared to no other creature. For it possesses all things in all, just as can be done in a natural way and origin in this world under the sun.

->O beginning of the first beginning, look to the end,<-
->O end of the last end, look to the beginning.<-

And may the **middle** <note>This refers to the "Way" or the practical process itself, which connects the beginning (raw matter) to the end (the Stone).</note> be faithfully commended to you; then God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit will give you whatever you may require in spirit, soul, and body.

# A BRIEF APPENDIX AND CLEAR RE-
## capitulation or repetition by Brother Basilius Valentinus, of the Benedictine Order,
### *on his book concerning the Great Stone of the Ancients.*
<note>The "Great Stone of the Ancients" refers to the Philosophers' Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and healing all diseases.</note>

**I**, Basilius Valentinus, a Brother of the Benedictine Order, have already written a certain small book before, and in the philosophical manner of the ancients, I have revealed how that most ancient treasure ought to be acquired, by which the truly wise have prolonged their lives into a greater age.

And although—as my conscience must testify before the Most High in the heavens, to whom all hidden secrets are manifest—I have written nothing false, but have set forth the truth itself, so that those who understand would need no further light (for my **Theory** prescribed to them, which was confirmed and approved through the **practice of the twelve keys**, would be more than enough); nevertheless, the restlessness of dreams has driven me through various thoughts to take it upon myself to demonstrate my prescribed book through a **shorter way**, and to refine this light, as if by a middle ground, so that every lover of sought-after wisdom may have all the more splendor and clarity to fulfill their desire. 
<note>Basilius Valentinus is a legendary figure in alchemy. Though traditionally described as a 15th-century monk, his writings likely emerged in the early 1600s. The "Twelve Keys" mentioned here is his most famous work, using twelve allegorical images to describe the stages of the alchemical process.</note>

And although many will think it is revealed too clearly, and that I have therefore taken the burden of many sins upon myself, let everyone know that for those who are stiff-necked, it will be difficult enough to find what they seek; but for the Elect, it will be clear and easy. Therefore, my follower of truth, listen to my discourse, and then you shall find the true way to the art.
<note>The "Elect" refers to those the alchemists believed were divinely chosen to understand these secrets, while the "stiff-necked" (a biblical term for the stubborn) would remain blind to the truth no matter how clearly it was written.</note>

I have written nothing more than what I myself would wish to testify to after my death and the resurrection of my flesh.

Indeed, you shall perceive the **shorter way** faithfully and simply from the following narrative: for my words are founded in simplicity and without the trappings of empty words.

I have made mention and indicated that all things [are] made of three essences

# Practice, concerning the Stone of the Wise.

<note>original: "Practica, de Lapide Sapient."</note>

...be made and composed, namely from <term>Mercury</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, and <term>salt</term>, and that which I have taught is the truth. 
<note>These are the "Tria Prima" or Three Principles of Paracelsian alchemy, representing the spirit, soul, and body of all matter.</note>

Furthermore, you should know that the stone is prepared from five, four, three, two, and one: From **five**, that is, the **quintessence** of its own substance; From **four**, by which are understood the **four Elements**; From **three**, which are the **three principles** of things; From **two**, for there is a **double Mercurial substance**; From **one**: that is, the **First Being** <note>original: "Ens primum"</note> of all things, which was created and flowed forth from the word of the first creation.

Truly, many might be of a wavering mind because of all these words regarding how to obtain a foundation and an understanding for achieving perception; therefore, I will first speak very briefly concerning **Mercury**, second concerning **sulfur**, and third concerning **salt**; for these are the essences of our matter for the stone.

In the beginning, know that no **common quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum vulgi," referring to ordinary liquid mercury found in shops</note> is useful, but our quicksilver is made from the best metal through the <term>spagyric art</term>, pure, subtle, clear, shining like a spring, transparent in the manner of crystal, without any impurity. From this, make a water or a **combustible oil**: for Mercury was in the beginning a water, just as all the Sages agree with this opinion and my teaching.
<note>"Spagyric art" refers to the alchemical process of separating a substance into its components and then recombining them in a purified state.</note>

In this **oil of Mercury**, dissolve its own Mercury, from which the water itself was made, and precipitate that same Mercury with its own oil; then you will have a **double Mercurial substance**. However, you must know that your **gold**—after its purification by the **first key**—must first be dissolved and reduced into a <term>subtle lime</term> in a certain unique water, expressed by my **second key**, just as is held in the **fourth key**. Then, let such a <term>calx</term> be sublimated through the <term>spirit of salt</term> and precipitated again, and by <term>reverberation</term> be reduced into a subtle powder. 
<note>A "calx" is a powder produced by heating a metal; "spirit of salt" is an early name for hydrochloric acid; "reverberation" is a process of heating in a furnace where the flames are reflected back onto the material.</note>

Then its own **sulfur** will be able to enter into its substance more easily and be joined with it: for they love each other marvelously. And thus you have two substances in

->**one, and it is called the Mercury of the Wise, and it is at least a single**<-
->**substance, that is, the first ferment.**<-
<note>In alchemy, a "ferment" acts like yeast in bread, a small amount of substance that triggers a transformation in a much larger mass.</note>

# Brother Basil Valentine
## *Now follows the discourse concerning sulfur.*

Seek your Mercury in a similar metal: Then, when you know how to draw it out from its body through the purification and destruction of the former <term>Iron</term> <note>original symbol: ♂ (Mars); in alchemy, this usually refers to iron or the martial quality of the metal</note> and by <term>reverberation</term> <note>a process of heating a substance in a furnace where the flame is "reverberated" or deflected back onto the material</note>, without any corrosive; these means I have noted silently, and also commemorated in the third key. After this, you shall dissolve that Mercury in its own blood, from which it was made before its fixation, according to its weight indicated in the sixth key; then you have nourished and dissolved the true lion with the blood of the green lion: For the fixed blood of the red lion was made from the non-fixed blood of the green lion, and therefore they are of one nature: and the non-fixed blood makes the fixed volatile again, and the fixed in turn fixes the volatile, just as it had been before its solution: Then cherish them together in a gentle heat, until the <term>Copper</term> <note>original symbol: ♀ (Venus); likely referring to the metallic base or a specific stage of the coloring</note> is totally dissolved, then you have the second ferment, by nourishing the fixed sulfur with the non-fixed, as all Philosophers testify with me: This is afterwards sublimated with spirit of wine until it is red like blood, and it is called **potable gold**, in which no reduction of any body is found.

### *I will also give my opinion.*
## *Concerning the salt of the Philosophers.*

Salt makes things fixed <note>stable and resistant to heat</note> and volatile <note>easily evaporated or transformed into spirit</note>, according to how it is ordered and prepared in its state. For the spirit from the **salt of tartar**, if it is extracted by itself without addition, makes all metals volatile through resolution and <term>putrefaction</term>, and resolves them into true living or running Mercury: as the doctrines of my practice hold.

Salt of tartar by itself fixes most firmly, especially if the heat of **quicklime** <note>original: "calcis vivae"</note> is incorporated into it: For both of these obtain a singular degree of fixing.

So also the **vegetable salt of wine** both fixes and makes volatile according to different preparations, as its use requires, which is certainly a secret of nature, and a miracle of the Philosophical art.

If a man drinks wine for some time, and a clear salt is made from his **urine**, that is volatile, and it makes other fixed things volatile, and carries them with it through [the neck of the vessel].

<summary>Basil Valentine explains how to produce "Potable Gold" using the blood of the Green Lion (sulfur) and details the dual nature of Salt, which can either stabilize or volatilize metals depending on its preparation.</summary>

And although a man has drunk nothing but wine, from whose urine that salt is prepared, it nevertheless has a different property than <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate, typically derived from the sediment in wine barrels</note> or that from the dregs of wine: For a certain transmutation has been performed in the human body, so that from a vegetable—that is, from the spirit of wine—an animal spirit of salt has been made; just as horses, from oats, hay, and the like, undergo a change that corroborates their strength, causes their bodies to grow fat, and produces flesh therefrom. Likewise, the bee creates honey from the most precious flowers and herbs.

The same is to be understood of other things: more clearly, the cause consists solely in <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the process of decomposition, which alchemists believed was essential for the "rebirth" or transformation of matter</note>; from which such separation and transmutation take their origin.

That quite common spirit, which is extracted in the particular way described in my final declaration, makes gold and silver volatile if a small quantity of the <term>spirit of the dragon</term> <note>original: "spiritu draconis"; likely a reference to a strong mineral acid or a corrosive salt derivative</note> is added to it; it dissolves them and carries them up with itself into the alembic, just as the <term>eagle</term> <note>an alchemical symbol for a volatile substance or the process of sublimation</note> does with the spirit of the dragon which dwells in stony places. However, when anything is fused with the salt before the spirit is separated from its body, it fixes it much more than it grants volatility.

Furthermore, I say this: if the spirit of common salt is united with spirit of wine, and distilled together for a third time, it becomes sweet and lays aside its sharpness. This prepared spirit does not dissolve gold physically, but if it is poured onto a prepared <term>calx of gold</term> <note>gold reduced to a fine powder through heat or chemical reaction</note>, it extracts its highest color and redness. If this is done correctly, it brings a white and pure <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "luna"; the alchemical symbol for silver</note> back to such a color as that body possessed from which it was previously taken. The original body can also be gifted again with its own color through the love of alluring <term>Venus</term> <note>the alchemical symbol for copper; here likely referring to the transformative or "loving" affinity between the metals</note>, since it has arisen from its origin, state, and blood, concerning which there is no longer any room for dispute.

Note, however, that the spirit of salt also destroys the Moon and reduces it into a spiritual essence, according to my instruction: from which, afterwards, <term>potable silver</term> <note>original: "luna potabilis"; a liquid form of silver believed to have profound medicinal or alchemical properties</note> can be prepared. The spirit lies hidden in <term>Mercury</term>, you should seek color in <term>Sulfur</term>, and coagulation in <term>Salt</term>; then you have the three things which together can generate something perfect again. That is to say: the spirit in <term>Gold</term> <note>original: "auro"</note> is fermented with its own oil; Sulfur is found abundantly in the property of precious <term>Venus</term> <note>the alchemical name for copper</note>, which ignites the "fixed blood" born from it; the spirit from <term>Philosophical Salt</term> <note>a purified or essential salt used in the Work, often distinct from common table salt</note> gives victory over hardness, although the spirit of <term>tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate</note> and the spirit of urine, along with true vinegar, can accomplish much. For the spirit of vinegar is cold, and the spirit of <term>quicklime</term> <note>calcium oxide, known for its reactive heat</note> is intensely hot, and therefore they are held and found to be of contrary natures. Now, I have not spoken according to the usual philosophical custom; indeed, it will no longer be proper for me to tell anyone how the doors are locked from within.

This I say faithfully as a farewell: Seek your material in the metallic substance. From it, make <term>Mercury</term>, which you ferment with Mercury; then a certain Sulfur, which you ferment with its own Sulfur; and with Salt, bring them back into order. Distill them together, join all according to their weights, and then one single thing will result, which also arose from "One" before. Coagulate and fix that very thing through continuous heat; then increase and ferment it yet a third time according to the teaching of my last two keys. Then you will have and find the end and the limit of your desire. The twelfth key, without any <term>parabola</term> <note>a symbolic or allegorical story</note>, absolutely hands over the use of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>the Philosopher's Stone in its liquid or medicinal form</note> through a certain process.

->*Thanks be to God.*<-

Indeed, as a final appendix, I am compelled to tell you that a spirit can also be extracted from black <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note> and beneficial <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note>, which is afterwards reduced into a truly sweet oil, as its noblest part. This medicine, through its own vitality, will be able to strip common running mercury of its fluidity particularly firmly and improve it, as is also taught in my book.

<page-num>431</page-num>
<header>Practice of the Stone of the Wise <note>original: "Práctica de Lapide Sapient."</note></header>

## Addition.

When you have already obtained the material in this manner, you should care for nothing else afterward but the fire, and how you observe its <term>regimen</term> <note>the systematic regulation of heat over time</note>; for in this the sum of the matter is situated, and the end of the work. For our fire is common fire, and our furnace is a common furnace. And although those who were before me have left it in writing that our fire is not "common," yet in truth I tell you that they have hidden all the secrets according to their custom. Since the material is common <note>original: "vilis," meaning cheap or base</note>, and the work is slight, it is aided and made manifest solely through the regulation of the fire.

The fire of a lamp with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>highly distilled alcohol/ethanol</note> is useless. Furthermore, an incredible expense is spent on it. <term>Horse dung</term> <note>a common method for providing gentle, steady "moist" heat through fermentation</note> is a waste, and the material cannot be completed by such degrees of fire.

Many and various furnaces are not suitable; for in our triple furnace alone are the degrees of fire observed proportionally. Wherefore, let not a talkative <term>Sophist</term> <note>a "false" alchemist who uses tricky language to deceive students</note> seduce you into error with many furnaces; since our furnace is cheap, our fire is cheap, and our material is cheap, and the glass is likened to the "circumference of the earth." You need no further instruction on the fire, its regulation, and the furnace. For he who has the material will find a furnace for himself; he who has flour will also find a furnace for himself; he who has flour can also find a bakery furnace, so that he need not be greatly worried about the baking of the bread.

There is no need to write special books on this matter, as long as you observe the regulation of the heat, by which you know how to distinguish between cold and hot. If you achieve this, you have completed the work and brought the art to its end,

->for which the Creator of all nature be<-
->praised forever and ever, AMEN.<-

<page-num>432</page-num>

-># The Philosophical Furnace and the Stages of the Great Work<-

This illustrative plate depicts the laboratory and symbolic progression of the <term>Great Work</term> <note>the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. It visualizes the hidden "regimen" or regulation of the process through a hierarchy of symbolic creatures and the central laboratory apparatus.

### The Athanor

At the top of the arrangement is the <term>athanor</term> <note>the "ultimate furnace" of the alchemists, designed to provide a steady, slow, and indirect heat over a long period</note>. As mentioned on the previous page, while others claim this furnace is mysterious, it is here shown as the practical heart of the laboratory, the vessel through which all symbolic transformations are made manifest.

### The Three Tiers of Transformation

The "Practice" is divided into stages, each represented by a specific animal or "regimen":

**I. The Principles of Matter**
The highest tier of symbols features the **Crowned Lion**, the **Crowned Eagle**, and the **Crowned Serpent**. 
<note>These represent the mastery over the three principles: the Lion for the "fixed" Sulfur, the Eagle for the "volatile" Mercury, and the Serpent for the Salt or the unified base matter.</note>

**II. The Stages of Decay and Color**
Below these are the **Dragon**, the **Crow**, and the **Peacock**.
*   **The Crow** represents <term>nigredo</term> <note>original Latin: "nigredo," meaning blackness</note>, the first stage where the material must "die" or putrefy in the glass.
*   **The Peacock** represents the <term>peacock's tail</term> <note>original Latin: "cauda pavonis"</note>, a brief and beautiful stage where the matter shifts through all the colors of the rainbow before reaching purity.

**III. The Final Perfection**
At the base of the work are the **Swan** and the **Phoenix**.
*   **The Swan** represents <term>albedo</term> <note>original Latin: "albedo," meaning whiteness</note>, the stage of purification where the matter becomes a white stone capable of transmuting base metals into silver.
*   **The Phoenix** represents the final <term>rubedo</term> <note>original Latin: "rubedo," meaning redness</note>. Rising from the flames, it symbolizes the completion of the work and the creation of the Red Stone, or the Elixir of Life, which has reached total spiritual and physical perfection.

<summary>This page consists of a detailed symbolic engraving illustrating the alchemical "Great Work," showing the stages of transformation from the blackness of the crow to the final perfection of the phoenix. It emphasizes the role of the Athanor furnace in regulating these changes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the Second Preface of Thomas Norton's "Ordinal of Alchemy." It would indeed have been better for them to have kept away in time, for they find nothing but vexation. For certainly, one who is not deeply learned is of too little account to be preoccupied with this work. Believe me, it is a matter of no small importance to know all the secrets relating to this mineral <note>In this context, "mineral" refers to the "Stone" or the primary substance the alchemists sought to transform.</note>; for it is a very profound **Philosophy**, a subtle science, sacred **<term>Alchemy</term>** <note>Alchemy (original: Alchymia): A medieval philosophical and early scientific tradition focused on the transmutation of matter, particularly turning base metals into gold, and achieving spiritual perfection.</note>.

About which I intend to write here, though perhaps not in an overly elaborate style. For he who wishes to teach the common people should, for their sake, use simple and everyday language. And although a plain and humble style must be used, let no honest man think it beneath his notice.

All those who write about this work make their books very obscure to others with poetic fictions, parables, and metaphors. This creates trouble and difficulty for those first entering into the study; for if they attempt to test it in **practice**, they lose all their investment, as is daily evident. 

Hermes, Rhasis, Geber, and Avicenna; Merlin, Hortulanus, Democritus, and Morienus; Bacon and Raymond, along with many others, write hidden under a veil, as does Aristotle <note>This is a "Who's Who" of alchemical authority. It includes legendary figures like Hermes Trismegistus, historical Arabic scholars like Al-Razi (Rhasis) and Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber), and European figures like Roger Bacon and Raymond Lull. Aristotle was widely but falsely believed to have written on alchemy in the Middle Ages.</note>. For whatever they have handed down concerning this matter, they have, by their obscurity, led many astray. They hid the art from the common folk, from the learned, and thus from everyone, lest anyone should discover it through their books—even though they included beautiful explanations. By these, men are led into despair. 

Yet, of all the ancient philosophers I have ever found, Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher who suggested that all things are made of "seeds" containing every quality; alchemists often interpreted this as support for the possibility of transmuting substances.</note> wrote most correctly in his book on natural conversion.

### Chapter One.

**T**he <term>Mastery</term><note>original: *Magisterium*. In alchemy, this refers to the completed "Great Work" or the process of achieving the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> is truly admirable, and the Supreme Mastery
Is the Tincture of holy Alchemy,
A marvelous science of secret Philosophy,
A singular gift and grace of Almighty God,
Which was never discovered by the labor of a man's hands alone,
But only through revelation and the teaching of others.
Never has this been sold or bought for a price
By anyone who has sought it:
Rather, it is given by the grace of God only to a worthy man.
Perfected at great cost, through long labor and time,
It assists a person in their necessities;
It removes vainglory, hope, and fear;
It sets aside ambition, violence, and excess;
It mitigates adversities, so that they do not overwhelm anyone.
Whoever possesses the perfect knowledge of it,
Fleeing extremes, is content with the <term>middle way</term><note>original: *mediocritate*. This refers to the "Golden Mean" or moderation, a key virtue in Renaissance philosophy.</note>.
Some disdain to call this art "holy"
And argue against it in this manner,
Saying that the cursed acquire this science for themselves—
Those to whom God wishes to grant nothing good:

Does not allow them to possess that which is a cause of good.
Furthermore, [they argue] it produces nothing else
Except at most gold or silver for money, cups, or rings,
Which have been judged and found by the wise
To be the least virtuous things of all upon the earth:
Hence, men of that sort conclude—

And they deny that this science, in its effect, is sacred.
To these arguments we respond and protest, as we know,
That this science was never handed down to anyone,
Unless they were most thoroughly proven in every way over a long period of time,
To see whether he be worthy to receive this grace,
By reason of his truth, virtue, and absolute understanding;
If he lacks any of these things, he shall never possess it.
Thus, no one has been able to attain this art,
Unless one were sent by God, by whom he might be instructed:
For the matter is so honorable and rare,
That it must necessarily be handed down to another <term>by word of mouth</term><note>original: *oretenus*. This refers to the tradition of oral transmission (the "Whisper of the Muse"), where the final keys to the work were never committed to paper to ensure they only reached the worthy.</note>.
So it is necessary, even if the most ready will is present,
To receive it under a most sacred and high oath,
That, just as we refuse great honors and fame,
In the same way he himself would wish to refuse the same,
And that he shall never be so bold,
As to presume to impart this secret to his own son;
For closeness of blood or kinship
Is not to be admitted to this dignity,
If blood, insofar as it is blood, does not participate in <insert>virtue</insert>;
But at least virtue possesses this art.
Therefore, inquire secretly and see
All the character and virtues, as well as the suitability
Of the person who may be fit to learn this science,
And for the same reason, bind him with a strict oath,
That no one should leave this art behind them <note>The author warns against leaving written instructions that could be found by the unworthy after the master's death.</note>,
Unless he can find a worthy and proven man.
If age grows heavy upon him, or becomes troublesome,
One indeed he may teach, but not more:
For it is necessary that this science always remain secret.
The reason is this, as you observe:
That if a <term>wicked man</term><note>original: *improbus*. In this context, it refers to someone lacking moral integrity whose possession of the Stone’s power would threaten the social and spiritual order.</note> knew this art,
Much danger would therefrom befall the Christian world.

Hence let everyone enjoy their own fortune,
And send such learned men back to their own ignorance.
Now you, who seek this science,
Learn to distinguish the false from the true;
All true searchers of the art of <term>Alchemy</term> <note>Alchemy: the ancient branch of natural philosophy aiming to transform base metals into gold and discover a universal elixir.</note>

Then Deceit and Greed are perfectly joined.

But above the earth they are not in their proper place,

Just as fish perish out of water,

Since there is no perfect similarity:

Which is not present in just any soil,
But only in certain places and select grounds,
Into which the <term>celestial sphere</term> <note>Celestial sphere: the heavens. Alchemists believed the movements and "rays" of planets and stars directly influenced the growth and type of metals in the earth.</note>

And according to how the matter there is then disposed,
A corresponding metal will be formed:
Few lands are suitable for that generation,
How therefore could their multiplication be above the earth?
Thus all perceive, who are wise,
How congealed water, or ice, behaves

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 449, using an analogy involving ice and water to prove that metals, once formed, do not grow or "multiply" in volume. The author distinguishes between organic growth (plants/animals) and inorganic formation (metals), concluding that while transmutation is possible, the physical quantity of a metal cannot be increased through alchemy.</meta>

<page-num>450</page-num>

# By Thomas Norton of England

Before it has been hardened,
Being more abundant in some places, and less in others,
As water in ditches and torrents
Was a small quantity when it began to freeze;
But waters in lakes have larger <term>veins</term> <note>original: "venas". Here, the author uses "veins" metaphorically to compare masses of ice to the veins of ore found in the earth.</note>
Because of the abundance of the material frozen in them,
Therefore, it would not be quite right to say,
That for this reason the ice itself could be multiplied:
Likewise, although there may be more or fewer veins of metals,
It does not prove that they produce more than they were before,
Thus you must believe without any doubt,
That all ingredients must be reduced to <term>simplicity</term> <note>Simplicity: in alchemical philosophy, this refers to the state of being reduced to primary, unmixed elements or "first matter."</note>,
And the composition must be discerned, as you observe:
For in the multiplication of herbs, nature provided
That each should differ according to its seeds,
Stems and leaves separately, which are virtually within them,
Cannot be brought into actuality so as to be seen by the eyes:
But metals remain in their whole composition,
When they are dissolved by <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: "aquis fortibus". These are mineral acids, like nitric acid, used to dissolve metals for purification or reaction.</note>:
Therefore, since ice is closer to simplicity
Than metals, and yet cannot be increased,
Surely you must believe (as I said before)
That from one ounce of silver, no more can be made.
Furthermore, you will find nothing can be multiplied,
Unless it be of a <term>vegetable or sensitive</term> <note>Vegetable or sensitive: terms from Aristotelian biology referring to the "souls" or life-forces of plants (vegetable) and animals (sensitive). Metals were considered "inanimate" or elemental.</note> kind,
Since metals are at most elemental
And have neither seeds, nor physical sensation:
Therefore we conclude, all <term>multipliers</term> <note>Multipliers: a term for alchemists or frauds who claimed they could physically increase the weight or volume of precious metals through their craft.</note> must cease,
For metal, once generated, never grows:
Nevertheless, we find one metal transmuted
Into another kind of metal
Because of the proximity of the matter which was in them,
As is known between iron and copper,

<summary>Norton uses the analogy of ice formation to argue that the size of a mineral vein is due to the initial amount of material, not subsequent growth. He concludes that because metals lack biological "seeds," their volume cannot be multiplied, though they may be transmuted into other types of metal.</summary>

## Chemical Treatise.

But nothing can make true silver and gold,
Except for the <term>Medicine of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophorum Medicina". In alchemy, this is another name for the Philosopher's Stone, a substance believed to be capable of curing "sick" metals by turning them into gold or silver.</note> alone.
Therefore, works of the kind that <term>multipliers</term> <note>original: "multiplicatores". This refers to charlatans or low-level alchemists who claimed they could "multiply" gold or silver, usually through fraudulent means or simple alloying.</note> employ,
All learned men reject and utterly avoid,
But sacred <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymia". Here, the author distinguishes between high alchemy (sacred chemistry) and the tricks of common forgers.</note> is worthily honored,
Which deals with that precious Medicine
That truly makes pure gold and silver,
Of which a testimony by way of example
Exists in a certain city of Catalonia,
Which the noble <term>Raymund Lull</term> <note>Raymund Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher and polymath. Although many alchemical texts were attributed to him later, he is a legendary figure in the history of the "Great Work."</note>, as it is supposed,
Created in seven statues to demonstrate the truth,
Three were of good silver in the form of matrons,
Four were of gold in masculine dress,
Upon the edges of whose garments letters appeared,
Signifying this message which follows.

<margin>1. Silver from Iron</margin>
"From an old horseshoe," says one who was iron,
"But now I am the purest silver."

<margin>2. Gold from Iron</margin>
"I was," says another, "iron taken from the mine,
But now I am perfect and fine gold,"

<margin>3. Silver from Copper</margin>
"Once I was copper from an old vat,
Now I am entirely silver," says the woman.

<margin>4. Gold from Copper</margin>
The fourth says, "I was copper generated in a lowly place,
But now I am made perfect gold by the will of God,"

<margin>5. Gold from Silver</margin>
The fifth says, "I was pure and fine silver,
But now I am excellent gold, better than before,"

<margin>6. Silver from Lead</margin>
The sixth: "I was a lead pipe for almost two hundred years,
And now I appear to all as the best silver,"

<margin>7. Lead from Gold</margin>
The seventh says, "I am lead made from gold as a monster,
But certainly my sisters are closer than I am." <note>This "monster" refers to a reversal of the natural alchemical process—turning a "perfect" metal like gold back into a "base" metal like lead, which was seen as an unnatural demonstration of power.</note>

This science, as some believe, was named
Long ago after King Alchymus of celebrated fame:
Who was a glorious prince of generous spirit

And excelling in virtue, he hoped to investigate this art;
Having scrutinized nature, that most learned man,
Setting aside all coercion <note>original: "Extorsione omissa". This likely refers to avoiding "violent" chemical processes that force nature, or perhaps avoiding the financial "extortion" practiced by fraudulent alchemists.</note>, he sought and found it.
King **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure portrayed as a great priest, philosopher, and king. He was considered the founder of alchemy (the "Hermetic Art").</note> also did the same,
Who was a man most celebrated for his erudition:
In his fourfold divisions of **Astrology**,
The **Medical Art**, and this **Alchemy**,
As well as **Natural Magic**,
Which he held as the four sciences existing in nature.
And there, he says, he is considered blessed
Who knows things truly, as they are;
And blessed is he who properly proves
That which belongs to science:
For by their own opinions, very many
Are deceived in those things which they have not known.
(It is an old proverb) that in a great heap of imagination
There is not even a small handful of science.
With proper proof and sufficient discretion,
The wise also learn many things daily.
Through science, men know themselves and all things;
For a man is a beast—and worse—without science.
Yet hardly anyone is led by a desire
For a science of which he himself possesses nothing.
And while a lack of erudition makes men bold and wild,
Sufficient science renders them humane.
The nobles now are accustomed to despise
Those who desire to know.
But in ancient times, Kings
Decreed (as many authors relate)
That no one should learn the **Seven Liberal Sciences** <note>The "Septem Scientiae Liberales" were the core curriculum of medieval education: Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note>,
Except for one of noble and liberal character.
And he who was devoted to them might most freely
Lead his life in his studies.

-># A Chemical Treatise<-

Hence the ancients called them the
**Seven Liberal Arts** <note>original: "Septem scientias liberales". These were the foundation of medieval education, consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note>
For whoever wished to learn them perfectly and well
It was necessary for him to enjoy a certain freedom <note>The term "liberal" derives from the Latin *liber* (free). This implies the student must be free from manual labor and worldly distractions to focus on intellectual pursuits.</note>.
He who is to grasp even human laws 
Must abstain from other worldly tasks;
Much more must he renounce the world,
Who wishes to learn many sciences.
And for this reason it seems clear enough
Why learned men are held in contempt <note>The author observes that scholars, because they withdraw from the pursuit of wealth and public life to study, are often looked down upon by those who value material success.</note>.
Yet the memory of that man shall not cease,
Who always increases in the knowledge of things.
The lover of science, justice, and grace
Is rejected in many places.
But he who carries into the court, by whatever means,
A useful thing or a gift, prevails in these times.
Wherefore this science <note>Referring to the "Sacred Science" of alchemy.</note> and many other graces
Are ruined and lost to all.
Furthermore, remember what I say:
Some seek it in their lives,
But **greed** and **science** are of a discordant nature;
He who desires profit will not find this art <note>A fundamental tenet of alchemy was that the "Stone" would never be granted to those motivated by simple avarice or the desire to make common gold for wealth.</note>.
But he who loves science for its own dignity
Can investigate both with a happy genius:
There is no need to hand down more concerning this chapter,
For here it is apparent what sort of people are able to reach it:
That is, only the faithful,
And he who is constant in mind for investigating,
Not ambitious, nor forced to borrow anything from others,
One who is patient, and does not hasten too much,
And who trusts firmly in **God**,
And adheres entirely to science;
And with all these things, one who leads a most upright life.

### *Chapter Two.*

**I**N Normandy there lived recently a certain monk,
Who deceived very many people of every rank.
This man, after he had conceived
In his imagination <note>original: "phantasia". In medieval psychology, the "fantasy" or "imagination" was the faculty that could create false images if not governed by reason.</note> that he knew this art perfectly,
Was filled with such great joy
That he almost began to run mad.
Of whose preposterous joy (although it did not last long)
I will tell this story <note>original: "apologum". A moralizing fable or instructional tale.</note> as an example:
This monk had wandered through France,
Indulging his desires as an apostate <note>A monk who abandons his religious order and his vows without permission.</note>;
And afterwards he came into this kingdom <note>Referring to England, the home of the author Thomas Norton.</note>
Desiring to persuade everyone
That he fully understood the foundation of all <term>Alchemy</term> <note>The ancient art of transmuting metals and seeking the "Philosopher's Stone."</note>,
Which he had found in a certain book of Recipes;
Therefore he completely set his mind
To leave behind certain illustrious deeds and noble acts
By which his name would be made immortal,
And his fame would remain perpetual in this land.
And for this reason he often speculated where he should begin
To spend such great riches as he was about to find;
And he was always thinking: "Behold, I know this,
Where shall I find a certain faithful man
Who would comply with my will
And help bring my purpose into action?
Then I would bring it about, that on the plain..."

In the area of **Salisbury**, there would be gloriously built
Fifteen **Abbeys** <note>Large monasteries or convents under the direction of an Abbot or Abbess.</note> in a short amount of time,
So that each would be distant from the others by a single mile.
For this reason, this **monk** came to me,
With that trust which he said was reported of me;
He opened his mind, already mentioned, to me,
And begged that I would be present to assist him with counsel:
I promised before the image of **Saint James** <note>Likely referring to a statue of St. James the Greater, a popular saint for pilgrims and a witness to oaths.</note>
That I did not wish to reveal his name;
Nevertheless, it is permitted for me to write without fault
Regarding his so vain desire.
When he had revealed his great knowledge to me,
He said that nothing was lacking to him
Except a suitable opportunity
To labor for the **King’s benefit** <note>original: "Regis commodum". The monk intends to offer his alchemical services to the King of England, likely Edward IV, to gain legal protection and status.</note>
And to obtain permission from his council <note>original: "senatu". Referring to the King's advisors or Parliament.</note>
And through the mediation of the Lords,
To buy up fields for the aforementioned Abbeys;
For he himself would satisfy all the expenses.
But he still doubted much
How, from whom, and where the lands were to be bought.
When I had heard of such a great work of his,
I wanted to discover how skilled he was in letters
And how much **scholarly learning** <note>original: "eruditionis scholasticae". The formal university education of the period, involving logic, rhetoric, and philosophy.</note> he possessed,
But in these things, he was found to be at least a fool.
Nevertheless, I endured it and conducted myself in secret,
So that I might know more of his desire.
Then I said the matter was so trivial
That it ought not to be opened to the King;
And if the proof were not suitable,
The King would take it for a foolish tale.
The monk replied that he held in the **fire** <note>original: "igne". A reference to an alchemical process currently underway in a furnace.</note>
The thing which could fulfill his will.

Concerning which [I replied] that I would most certainly learn

For just as the sciences have no beginning <note>original: "scientiæ initium." This likely references the biblical proverb that the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, a common theme in alchemical literature where spiritual piety is a prerequisite for success.</note>,
So without You they do not obtain a good end.
I confess, O Most High <note>original: "Altissime," referring to God.</note>, that no one grasps these things;
Though he may have learned much before, without You he understands nothing.
For so much grace stands always with You, O God,
To perfect a thing just as to begin it, for You are the end and the head.

Although it is contrary to the desire
Of him who delights in this art.

The first care is to acknowledge in the mind

And that no one can acquire this science <term>scientia: In this context, it refers to the specialized "knowledge" or "science" of alchemy.</term>
