Truly learned and of pure intellect is he
Who can apprehend it through the instruction of another;
It is necessary that he knows various diversities,
He who strives to investigate the secret works of nature.
But instruction is not so certain
That it might not happen that someone could err after it;
Just as all those who have now departed from the living
Erred before they found our stone <note>original: "lapidem nostrum." This is the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note>,
Whether at the first or a subsequent time,
All err until the true practice <term>practica: The actual laboratory method and experimental application of alchemical theory.</term> arrives.
But no one wanders further astray in heat and cold
Than the rash and bold craftsman <term>artifex: The alchemist, viewed here as a skilled maker or artist working alongside nature.</term>,
For no one ruins our work faster
Than he who presumes to complete it [too quickly].
But he who is to perfect the matter,
Let him be far-sighted and cautious in his working,
For before all cares this is the most serious:
That if one errs in one thing, he must begin again from the start.
Surely he will have very many cares.

He who desires to attain this art,
Will often change his purpose
Because of the new things he shall have learned;
His plans will often be in vain,
From which misfortune he will never be secure,
And often his mind will waver
With new opinions, afflicted by sorrow,
And so he will continue in fantasies,
That it would be a wonder if he reaches it <note>The "it" refers to the successful completion of the alchemical "Great Work."</note>,
Indeed, you shall undergo the sharpest cares
In this art, whoever you may be.
I shall reveal more to you concerning the troubles
Which will restrain your desire;
It is a great care, as the wise relate,
To know where there is a perfect craftsman <term>artifex: In alchemy, this refers to the skilled practitioner or "adept" who knows the true secrets of the art.</term>:
And although you might happen upon one who may teach you,
Yet you will have various troubles and cares,
For if your mind be dedicated to virtue,
The devil will labor to do you harm;
In three ways he will presume to strike you:
By **haste**, by **despair**, and by **deception**,
On account of the works of virtue which you are to do
If you arrive at this knowledge <term>scientia: Here meaning the sacred "science" or deep knowledge of alchemical transformation.</term>.
The first danger already mentioned is **haste**,
Which destroys and corrupts much;
All authors who write of this art
Say that haste is from the devil.
That little book regarding the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "philosophorum turba." This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, which takes the form of a debate among ancient philosophers.</note>
Says: "All haste is on the part of the devil."
Therefore, he shall ripen the matter
Who proceeds with a slow step;
According to the proverb, you shall know the truth:
That the more one hastens, the slower he will be <note>A variation of the common proverb "More haste, less speed." In alchemy, the chemical reactions (and spiritual growth) cannot be rushed without ruining the entire process.</note>.

But as soon as you wished me to ride to you,
Having received these letters, I soon hastened
To my master, traveling a hundred miles and more,
Where, for forty continuous days,
I learned all the secrets of **alchemy**, <note>While the Latin text uses "alchymia," Norton's original English poem refers to this as "the Holy Alkimy."</note>
Although I had understood philosophy before

Imagine that it can be perfected in forty days;
But you should notice that between a work of forty days
And a teaching of forty days, there is a great difference.
Then obscure doubts appeared clear to me,
Where I found the <term>bonds of nature</term> <gloss>vincula naturæ: The fundamental laws or hidden mechanisms that govern how physical matter transforms.</gloss> unlocked.

If you will meet with your master in such a way,
We conceive no doubt concerning you.
  The third impediment we call **deception**,
Which, among others, was the worst against me:
And this is said regarding the servants who attend
To your work; for some know much of deceit,
And some are negligent, others fall asleep by the fire,
Some are of ill will, who will harm you,
Some are fools, others are far too bold,
Others are disobedient to your teaching,
Some have "retractive fingers" <note>original: "digitos, rerum alienarum retractivos." A poetic way of describing servants with "sticky fingers" who steal the expensive materials or the finished product.</note> for the property of others,
Who handle wicked things, which are very harmful;
Some are drunkards, frivolous, and intent on other matters.
Beware of such as these if you wish to be without loss;
The faithful are foolish, and the wise are false,
One hurts me just as the other hinders me,
For when I had prepared my works well,
Such people stole them and left me with nothing.

"Alas, Dalton," the King then said,

Whether with Buckshorn plantain, Celandine, and Mezereon,

What the substance of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The "Stone" is the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and grant longevity.</note> ought to be."

You would succumb to old age before you could perfect it."
"Do not worry about this, good Master," he replied,
"Enough comfort would come to me
If I could at least know the material
Of that stone, sought by me for so long."
"Tonsilus," I said, "it is no small matter
About which you desire to be made certain,
For many authors write about that doubt,
Yet none of them demonstrate it clearly;
For the authors themselves writing of this art
Prayed to God (according to Democritus)
That He would suddenly take from this world
The souls of those who were about to write books on this matter,

# Chemical Treatise

For many of those authors have feared
Lest they deliver more of this science than is proper,
Each of them taught at least one or two points.
Whereby he might be most certainly recognized by his fellows,
That he was an equal to them;
Since one of them understands another,
They wrote in such a way, not so that they might instruct everyone,
But so that they might manifest themselves through a secret way of speaking.
Therefore, do not be content to read only a single book,
But survey various authors;
"Book opens book," as the learned man Arnold <note>Refers to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist whose works were foundational to the field.</note> asserts,
Just as Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who was often cited by alchemists as an early authority on the nature of matter.</note> testifies concerning the same work.
For he who remains idle in reading various books
Will be judged useless for the practice.

Prudently fashioned, and not without cunning!
However, you have not yet named them except in general terms,

# Thomas Norton of England

Between these there is this difference,
Just as occurs between a mother and her offspring;
You will also observe another diversity between them,

These two kinds will provide you every service

And then it is called our chosen <term>marcasite</term> <note>original: marchasita; usually a metallic sulfide, but alchemists used this term for substances that possessed a metallic "seed" but had not yet become metal.</note>.

It is not sold throughout the Christian world,

That it can be made once, and never again <note>Implying the unique, transformative nature of the process which cannot be simply repeated like a commercial recipe.</note>.
Ancient authors call this thing a matter "of cheap price,"

No one who finds it would care to pick it up

Here I have revealed a wonderful secret,
Which has never been done <note>Meaning, never before revealed so clearly.</note> throughout the whole world.
You must have yet another stone, Tonsilus,
Or otherwise you will lose your principal material;
Which stone is very beautiful and clear,
A stone in commerce, and a stone to the sight.

If it should have an abundance of food and drink,

### *Chapter Five.*

**W**hen Bricius <note>original: "Briseus"; likely a reference to Bryce Shoreditch, a Warden of the Mint during a period of currency reform/debasement in the 15th century.</note> changed the coinage,
It resulted in loss for very many, and joy for many others;
And just as that change appeared to different people
As a new and very rare thing,
So at that time something wondrous happened
Which concerned this science,
When three masters of this art
Lay in one bed near Leadenhall <note>A historic manor and market in the City of London.</note>,
Who possessed the perfect <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "White Elixir" was believed to transmute base metals into silver, while the "Red Elixir" produced gold.</note> white and red.
It is a marvel that such a trio lay in one bed,
And this for the span of ten days,
Since they are scarcely to be found among a million men.
One of them was from the Duchy of Lorraine, as I have heard;
The second was from the middle of England,
From beneath the cross near the border of three Counties;
The third was the youngest in age:
Who, by his <term>birth chart</term> <note>original: "nativitatis figura"; an astrological map of the heavens at the moment of one's birth, used to predict their destiny.</note>, was judged by the learned
To be one who would bring honor to the English land.
One could travel through the whole world
And not find three such masters;
Two of them were to depart, but the younger was to remain
To eventually do much good in this region,
But the sins of princes shall delay
That good which he himself was prepared to provide.
The elder master prophesied <note>original: "vaticinatus est"; to foretell or speak as a prophet.</note> concerning him.

Grace will then be present to that King
When he has reformed ancient customs <note>original: "mores antiquos"; refers to the correction of moral conduct or outdated laws.</note>.
He himself shall investigate in secret
This science through obscure speech;
And among solitaries or monks
He will always be made more certain of that matter.
In this way King Khalid <note>original: "Rex Calid"; Khalid ibn Yazid (died c. 704), an Umayyad prince who, according to legend, was the first major patron to have Greek alchemical texts translated into Arabic.</note> sought it among many,
Until he came upon Morienus <note>A legendary Christian hermit of Jerusalem who reportedly initiated King Khalid into the secrets of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>,
Who brought help to Khalid in his necessity,
For his virtue incited him to this.
But now we shall be silent on this matter,
And we shall hand down the <term>subtle work</term> <note>The "subtle work" (subtile opus) refers to the intricate and delicate chemical procedures required for the final stages of transmutation.</note>.
It is necessary that he be learned
Who wishes to understand the subtle work.

# Of Thomas Norton the Englishman

<meta>catchword: Of</meta>

It is necessary for him to know first philosophy <note>original: "primam philosophiam"; in this context, it refers to natural philosophy or metaphysics—the study of the fundamental nature of reality and existence.</note>,
If he trusts to inquire into Alchemy,
And first, you must understand,
You who are intent upon this work,
When your metals, through preparation,
Have been made fit for generation,
Then they must be separated by division
Into the four Elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>, if you desire to profit;
But if you cannot accomplish this,
Go and learn from the Gardener <note>original: "Hortulano"; likely referring to Hortulanus, a legendary alchemical author who wrote a famous commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes.</note>,
Who made his book on that subject,
How wine is to be divided into four Elements;
And besides, it is fitting that you know
The effects of the four qualities,
Which are called heat, cold, moisture, and dryness,
From which all things are composed;
And because you especially desire in this art
To have a color that persists in the fire,
Know, before you obtain it,
How any color is generated;
For every color that can be named
Will appear here before the whiteness <note>original: "albedo"; the second major stage of the alchemical process, representing purification and the "White Stone" that can transmute base metals into silver.</note> arrives.
In addition to these, you wish to have in the work
An easy liquefaction like wax or gum;
Otherwise, it would not enter nor penetrate
Into the metals, as the authors testify.
Thus, you also desire to have what is fixed and what is flowing,
With an abundance of color, in whatever way possible.
That these three contraries <note>The three opposing goals: being "fixed" (resistant to heat), "fluxible" (melting easily), and "tinging" (capable of coloring other substances).</note> should be joined
In one single subject is a great secret <note>original: "secretum".</note>;
Nevertheless, he who is strong in intellect
Will be able to find it in this chapter.
And first, so that I may give you a brief teaching:

-> # *Chemical Treatise* <-

<sig>Ppp 2</sig>

Concerning the aforementioned four primary qualities,
Heat and cold are active qualities;
Moisture and dryness, however, are passive;
For these latter always undergo the influence of the former,
As when stones become lime and water becomes ice,
From which you will be able to judge very easily,
That nothing is generated, except by heat or cold,
Nevertheless, the passive qualities have some activity,
Just as we see daily in mechanical works,
In the brewing of bread and beer and other crafts
Moisture and dryness do their work.
Aristotle in his *Physics*, and many others
Say that contemplation <note>original: "speculatio"; refers to theoretical inquiry or philosophical reflection.</note> proceeds from actions,
They report that practice is the root and beginning
Of contemplation and of all knowledge.
For the properties of any things
Were perceived through their operations;
Just as by the colors of urine we dare
To pronounce on heat or cold,
Through these four primary qualities
We investigate colors in the course of time;
Concerning which we cannot be certain
Unless in a very pure substance.
Much doctrine you will take from this,
If you know how colors are daily generated,
Color is the boundary <note>original: "extremitas"; following the Aristotelian definition that color is the limit of the transparent in a determinate body.</note> of every clear body,
A clear substance well-bounded is the matter here,
If heat should dominate in dry matter,
The color white <note>original: "albedo"</note> will most certainly be present there,
As it appears to the eye from burnt bones,
And in <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: "calce viva"; calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone or shells, a common substance in early chemistry.</note> made from stones,
Where cold acts on moist and clear matter,
Whiteness will appear in that operation,

<page-num>484</page-num>

-> ### By Thomas Norton the Englishman ### <-

As is evident in ice and things hardened by cold,
The cause of this has already been declared before in philosophy;
But here I do not speak of common philosophy,
But through examples, so that I may hand down the art of <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Alchymia"; the medieval precursor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter.</note>,
One thing can be perceived through another,
Just as offspring is recognized from its mother.
If heat acts in moist and thick matter,
A black color will be generated from it;
If you desire an example of this,
Observe when you have placed green wood upon the fire.
When cold operates in thick and dry matter,
The color will be black, the reason for which is:
Such matter is compact and very thick,
With constricting cold—the enemy of life—
Thickness causes darkness and the deprivation of light;
If color is deprived, <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "nigredo"; the first stage of the alchemical process, representing putrefaction or "the death of the matter."</note> will appear.
Therefore, always be mindful of this:
That clear matter is the matter of <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedo"; the second major alchemical stage, signifying purification and the "white stone."</note>.
The efficient cause can be varied,
For sometimes it is heat, sometimes cold.
But <term>whiteness</term> and <term>blackness</term> (as everyone knows)
Are contrary colors at the extreme ends;
Hence your work will begin with <term>blackness</term>,
If the end must be the perfection of <term>whiteness</term>.
The intermediate color, as the philosophers hand down,
Is <term>red</term> <note>original: "rubeus"; often called the rubedo, the final stage of the work.</note> between black and white;
Nevertheless, believe me firmly:
<term>Red</term> is the ultimate stage in the work of <term>Alchemy</term>.
They also say in their doctrine
That these two colors, <term>reddish-gold</term> <note>original: "rufus"</note> and <term>lemon-yellow</term> <note>original: "citrinus"</note>,
Are intermediate between white and <term>red</term>,
And that <term>green</term> <note>original: "viridis"</note> and <term>lead-grey</term> <note>original: "plumbeus"</note> color
Intervene between <term>red</term> and black.

## *Chemical Treatise.*

A flesh-colored hue comes from very pure matter.
Physicians identify nineteen colors in urine,
[Classified] into white and black, as they themselves teach,
Among which the off-white color is one,
Similar to the color of the <term>Onyx stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis Onichini"; a semi-precious stone often used in alchemical analogies for its translucent or layered appearance.</note>.
In that color, <term>Magnesia</term> <note>original: "Magnesia"; in this context, it refers not to the modern element magnesium, but to the "prime matter" of the alchemists—a mysterious, reflective substance central to the Work.</note> is seen,
But magnesia shines with purity.
In our subtle work of Alchemy,
All colors that are ever known will occur—
A hundred and more, most certainly,
Than have been observed in urine.
Among all those colors, it cannot be
Otherwise than that our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the elusive goal of alchemy believed to transmute base metals and perfect the human body.</note> is contained through every degree,
In every composition of works that are made,
And in every composition conceived by the mind.
However many colors present themselves there,
So many <term>graduations</term> <note>original: "graduationes"; the specific stages of intensity or qualitative shifts required to perfect the alchemical substance.</note> you shall wisely establish.
And if you do not know all these graduations,
Learn them from <term>Raymond</term> <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath whose works on "General Art" were highly influential in later alchemical theory.</note> in his *General Art*.
Gilbert Rymer wrote according to his own discovery
Of seventeen proportions, but those do not suffice
In this science, which he could never find,
Although he was very learned in medicine.
Since the excellence of human nature
Often surpasses the medicines of physicians,
And thus [Nature] not rarely honors her own art
When their medicines are perhaps ineffective;
But it is not so in the <term>medicine of minerals</term> <note>original: "medicina minerarum"; a term for the Philosophers' Stone, highlighting its power to "cure" imperfect metals and transform them into gold.</note>.
For that art exceeds all other types of generation,
And exists solely as the wisdom of man,
As the wise can testify through experience.
And thus the true foundation of alchemy
Lies in composition by means of wise graduation.

# Thomas Norton the Englishman

By knowing heat and cold, or moisture and dryness,
And recognizing that other qualities are generated through them—
Such as hardness and softness, heaviness and lightness,
Roughness and smoothness—through certain weights,
Wisely investigated with number and measure,
In which three things <note>A reference to the biblical verse Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight." Alchemists used this to argue that their work followed God's own laws of creation.</note> everything created by God exists.
For God made all things and surely arranged them
In numbers, weights, and measures.
If you should alter these numbers,
You do an injury to Nature.
Therefore <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>An ancient Greek philosopher; in alchemical texts, he is often cited as an authority on the composition of matter and the "seeds" of things.</note> says: "Take good care,
Lest you proceed to the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The act of joining two substances, often the "Sulfur" and "Mercury" of the philosophers, or the spirit and the body.</note> 
Before you have fully understood the weights
Of all the components which are required here."
<term>Bacon</term> <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English philosopher and friar who was widely (though sometimes apocryphally) credited with great alchemical secrets.</note> says that the ancients concealed nothing
Except only the proportions, which they did not teach.
For there is no author, neither king nor prince,
Writing about this science who agrees with others
In the proportions. If you wish to know these,
<term>Raymond</term> <note>Raymond Lully.</note> along with Bacon and <term>Albert</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prolific scholar and bishop whose name was attached to many alchemical manuals.</note> will teach you;
Along with the elder Anaxagoras. From these four
You will have perfect knowledge, but not all from one alone.
Even if you join the four qualities for one intention,
Then it is necessary to join the individual Elements,
Such as water and earth according to your desire,
Well-composed with air and fire.
Know that in activity, the second and third 
Of any of the degrees are more worthy,
Though the fourth and first cannot be excluded,
For they are useful and most greatly to be employed,
And can best extend their <term>multiplication</term> <note>The stage where the power of the Philosophers' Stone is increased in both quantity and quality.</note>,
In which exists the power of generation;
And this is the earthly <term>Litharge</term> <note>original: "Lithargyrium"; traditionally lead oxide, but in alchemy, it often refers to a specific "dross" or mineral body that must be purified to reach the Stone.</note> of our stone.

<summary>Norton explains that the "Great Work" relies on the precise mathematical proportions of the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) and the four elements. He cites authorities like Bacon and Lully to emphasize that while authors hide their specific ratios, a synthesis of their teachings reveals the truth.</summary>

->Without it there will be no generation,<-
->Nor the fixation of our tincture,<-
->For nothing is fixed except the earth alone,<-
All the other Elements are volatile,
Fire, air, and water, as you see daily,
But fire is the cause of extensibility <note>The quality of being able to be stretched or drawn out, like metal being hammered thin.</note>,
And it makes matter capable of being mixed,
And a clear brilliance in a beautiful color
Arises more from the airy nature,
And air also, if it has been condensed,
Makes things easy to melt,
Such as wax, and butter, and every gum;
A small amount of heat melts them all.
Water cleanses by washing,
And causes "mortified" <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the symbolic death or breakdown of a substance, often characterized by a black color. Water helps bring these "dead" materials back to life in a new state.</note> things to live again.
Nothing seems wondrous about the multiplication of fire,
Which is inferior to the multiplication of the earth,
For the earth generates new herbs every day
Without number; therefore it is true
That earth is as admirable as fire,
Even though a single spark may multiply itself immensely.
If a whole domain were filled with flax <note>A common alchemical metaphor: a small spark can set a whole field of flax ablaze, demonstrating the principle of "multiplication" or the spread of the alchemical transformative power.</note>,
Then a mere spark would grow in it marvelously.
Fire and earth alone multiply themselves,
And those are the causes of the multiplication of our stone.
Regarding this earth, <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>Saint Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a famous philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on minerals and was a major authority for alchemists.</note> mentions
In his book *On Minerals* that <term>litharge</term> <note>Lead oxide (PbO), used here as a technical term for a specific stage or material in the refinement of the "white elixir" or silver-making process.</note> is best
For the white Elixir, and there he reviews it,
Which is also shown in the book of poems:
Now let us approach the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The phase of the work where the separated elements or principles (often called the "soul" and "body") are reunited.</note>;
And let us bring forward some advice regarding it:
**1.** Join your Elements grammatically
Suitably with all their rules,

<page-num>488</page-num>
<header>Thomas Norton, the Englishman</header>

# Thomas Norton, the Englishman

Which rules, for the assistance of the learned,
Are the primary instruments in this work,
For nothing is more contrary to itself
Than being fixed and volatile:
All the Grammarians of England and France
Do not know how to teach you this concord <note>In alchemy, "concord" refers to the harmonious joining of opposing substances, like fire and water.</note>;
This **ORDINAL** <note>original: *ORDINALE*; this refers to Norton's famous poem, the *Ordinal of Alchemy*, which serves as a guidebook or "ordinal" for the chemical process.</note> delivers it, as you will see
In the Physics, in the book concerning the Tree.

2. Join them also in the manner of Rhetoric,
With natures adorned and purified,
Since your tincture <note>The "tincture" is the transformative substance or Elixir that can change the properties of metals.</note> must be pure and beautiful,
Take pure earth, water, fire, and air.

3. In the way of Logic, whenever it is performed,
Mix true categories, not sophistical ones <note>Norton warns against using "sophistical" or false materials/methods that mimic the real ones but lack the true essence required for alchemy.</note>,
The ignorance of which has led many learned men
To lose all their labor and work.

4. Join them together also Arithmetically,
By subtle proportional numbers,
About which little was known until now,
As Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on the "Quadrivium" (arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy) were standard textbooks in the Middle Ages.</note> wrote: "You bind the Elements with numbers."

5. Join your Elements by Music
For two reasons: one for the sake of melody,
Which has its own pleasing harmonies,
When you have found its true effect,
And compose it so, that the Diapason <note>The musical interval of an octave.</note>
With the Diapente <note>The interval of a perfect fifth.</note> and Diatesseron <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note>,
With the *hypate hypaton* <note>The lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system.</note> and the *Lychanos mese* <note>The "index-finger" note of the middle tetrachord in Greek music theory.</note>,
With the rules that are found in Music,
With the proportions that cause harmony,
To which the proportions in Alchemy are very similar;
Namely, regarding the large numbers actually set down,
But for the secret intellectual numbers,
It is necessary that you inquire, as I have said before.

# *Chemical Treatise*

From the doctrine of Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> and Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1219–1292), an English friar and philosopher known as "Doctor Mirabilis" for his emphasis on empiricism.</note>,
Bacon delivers these matters obscurely in his three letters.
And Raymond explains them better in his *General Art*:
Many people believe, when they read these things,
That they understand them, but in truth they are deceived.

6. With **Astrology** <note>In the 15th century, astrology and astronomy were intertwined; here it refers to the influence of celestial bodies on terrestrial matter.</note> join also the **Elements**,
So that whatever their operations may be, they might prosper,
Which things the simple sort—unrefined and inexperienced—
Lead forward prudently until the end is found,
Since in time those things obey
The formed influences of the stars above nature.

7. And the science of **Perspective** <note>original: *perspectiva*; this refers to the medieval study of optics and the behavior of light.</note> provides much evidence
To all those laboring in this noble art,
And so do many other sciences,

8. Especially that regarding the **Full and the Void** <note>original: *pleno & vacuo*; a reference to the physics of the vacuum and the displacement of matter, a major topic in Aristotelian natural philosophy.</note>,
But the one to be held as mistress among all sciences,

9. To serve this art, is **Natural Magic** <note>Natural magic was considered the branch of science that dealt with the hidden or "occult" properties of natural things, such as magnetism or medicinal virtues, rather than demonic sorcery.</note>,
When the four **Elements** have been wisely composed,
And each one ordered in its own degree,
Then from various degrees and digestions
Colors will appear until perfection is reached,
For then the **Natural Heat** <note>term: *Natural Heat* (calor naturalis); the innate, internal energy or "soul" of the matter being worked upon.</note> operates from within,
Which in our substance exists at least intellectually,
Not visible to the sight, nor to be felt by the hands;
Its operation is known to only a rare few,
And when this **Natural Heat** is moved
By the external **Artificial Heat** <note>term: *Artificial Heat* (calor artificialis); the physical fire applied to the alchemical vessel by the chemist.</note>,
Then nature, having been stirred, will not cease to work,
Until it produces the various diversities of the degrees:
Which is one reason, as you may observe from logic,
That so many colors appear in our work;
Therefore, much doubt is caused in this art
By the ignorance of **Intrinsic and Extrinsic Heat**.

## Thomas Norton of England

To know how each of these heats ought to agree,
And which of them should predominate in the work,
The digestions <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow, gentle heating of a substance to bring it to maturity or "ripeness."</note> in this work agree very well
With the digestions of living things,
And above all others (as I can certainly testify)
They are most similar to the concoction <note>original: *coctioni*; the medieval medical term for the transformation of food into bodily nutrients through heat.</note> in man:
Therefore **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> said, our stone in its generation
Is very similar to the creation of man:
In which, says **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), the philosopher mentioned on the previous page.</note>, it is possible to find
All four degrees of the four complexions <note>The "complexions" or temperaments (Sanguine, Choleric, Melancholic, Phlegmatic) resulting from the balance of the four humors.</note>,
And that in actual fact, which you will not be able to find
Among other creatures of any other kind,
Hence, among created things, these two alone
Are called the **Microcosm** <note>original: *Microcosmus*; the "little world" or "miniature universe." Alchemy posits that the laws of the stars and the human body are identical to the laws of the Stone.</note>, **Man** and our stone:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, in order to perfectly understand nutrition,
It is necessary to approach the subject of digestion,
Moisture is solid, consistent with dryness,
Strongly mixed in its degrees,
In the opposite sense, the passive parts properly mixed
Are generated by heat both intrinsic and extrinsic,
Thus our digestion is nothing else
But a perfection created from substantial moisture,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I pray you, oh laypeople <note>original: *laici*; here referring to those not initiated into the secret technical language of alchemy.</note>, that you excuse me,
Even though you are not accustomed to such words,
It is necessary for me to use them, because all authors affirm
That every science has its own proper terms.
Digestion is sometimes increased more
By external cold, as you can see every year,
How in winter men take in more food
Than in summer, when their heat is more intense,
For the cold then forces the heat to flee inward
And joins it more closely, so that it becomes stronger,
Whose virtue and power is greater

## Chemical Treatise.

To perfect digestion, as mentioned before.
But our primary Digestant for this purpose
Is the virtual heat <note>In medieval science, "virtual heat" refers to an inherent power or property within a substance that acts like heat even if it doesn't feel hot to the touch, such as the "heat" in quicklime or strong spirits.</note> of the digesting matter,
Nevertheless, the heat of the thing being digested
Assists the digestion and its operation.
A feverish heat digests nothing,
The sun’s rays can assist, yet also cause destruction.
Digested wine <note>Referring to wine that has been fermented and aged, reaching its "natural" state.</note> possesses more natural heat
Than fresh grape juice, whose heat is merely accidental.
Coagulation is not a substantial form,
But at least a passion <note>In the Aristotelian sense, a "passion" is an attribute or a state of being acted upon—here, the state of becoming solid—rather than a change in the essential nature (substantial form) of the matter.</note> of the material thing.
Furthermore, you ought to know that when colors appear,
They indicate the principal agent in that matter;
For sometimes it is heat, sometimes cold,
And sometimes moisture, sometimes dryness.
To always recognize the principal agent
Requires investigation by subtle reason,
Which is perceived by only a few masters,
For they do not notice how colors arise.
The principal agent of the four qualities
Holds royal power and predominates,
So that it converts the rest into its own kind;
Concerning this conversion, **Anaxagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything." Alchemists used his theories to explain how one element could be transformed into another.</note> teaches
In his book on natural conversion,
The special causes of which **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in alchemical literature often cited for his systematic approach to the "Great Work."</note> provides.
It is no laughing matter or light thing to teach
How your principal agent should be discerned,
Which I shall deliver to you through four signs:
Namely, by color, taste, smell, and liquor <note>In this context, "liquor" refers to the fluidity or the specific consistency of the substance in the vessel.</note>.
And first by color, so that it may serve your purpose
In recognizing the principal agent:
Look into your vessel; whichever color appears most,
Then that which causes it is the principal agent.

It represents the color; for this reason, cease wondering,

God has thus ordained, as King Hermes says,
That wonders may be made from a single thing.
Common philosophers are unable to find from this

A heavy odor is not (as the learned feel)

And yet they wrote in their books
From their own experience (which is not known to me)
That if you mix a sweet and fragrant odor
Equally with a foul one, to test your intention,
The sweet is perceived by the smell, but not the foul.
You will be able to know the cause of that matter:
All sweet things possess more purity,
And are more spiritual than foul things.

Thence a heavy odor arises,
Just as an old fish smells,
Where natural heat putrefies and the odor stinks;
Stench is a vapor and a released smoke
Of things which are of a bad <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine and alchemy, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance.</note>,

And when a bad substance putrefies,
A horrible odor will be generated from it,
Just as the putrid carcasses of dragons and men <note>Alchemical texts frequently used "dragons" as metaphors for certain chemical states, but here the author groups them with human corpses to illustrate the biological danger of decay.</note>

It is not healthy to smell extinguished
Coals, for from that stench even a mare might miscarry.
When the qualities of some thing agree
With your own nature, then a good odor will not be lacking;
But when the substance is contrary to your kind,
Then it will present an unpleasant odor.
Fish love sweet odors, as is well known;
They do not seek putrid bait as they do fresh.
Everything that partakes of a good odor
Has a natural heat suitable to itself;
Although camphor, roses, and other cold things
Have sweet odors, nevertheless authors write
That this [scent] is virtually included in the heat
Along with the purity of the substance, from which they smell so.
Instill this opinion of the ancients into others:
That a good odor is not contrary to another [good odor],
But it is not so with a foul odor,
For the smell of garlic removes the stench of dung.

Which is destined to endure forever in the fire.
A certain man of the common sort, a servant to this art,
Tasted a small particle of the **white stone**, <note>The "white stone" refers to the *albedo* stage of the alchemical process, where the matter has been purified to a white state, capable of transmuting metals into silver, but not yet reaching the final red stage.</note>

Nonetheless, regarding certain separated parts,

By testing before the **conjunction** <note>The "conjunction" is the stage where the "soul" and "body" of the alchemical matter are united; tasting the substance after this point is considered life-threatening.</note> is made,
To see whether the operation was rightly performed or not.
However it may be, the wise man will know enough
To achieve his intention through color and odor;
For many judge a good wine
By its color and odor when it is pure,
But regarding new wine, it is found that generally
Taste is the true judge above all.
For the sense of smell has only one organ,
Discerning nothing except smoky things,
But taste has six organs without doubt,
To perceive qualities both within and without,
Which nature ordained against dangers
For the safety of living things.
The ape judges its food by smell;
Men and parrots trust in taste,
For many things have a good odor
Which nevertheless are not suitable for the taste.

<summary>Norton warns against the extreme toxicity of the Alchemical Stone by recounting how a servant was paralyzed after tasting the 'white stone.' He concludes that while taste is a more precise sense than smell, the chemist should rely on smell and color to avoid death.</summary>

The oily, sharp, salty, bitter, and sweet.

Always generate a watery taste,
As is apparent in the whites of eggs
And the pale faces of young women,
For such persons are cold and moist, <note>In the humoral theory of the Middle Ages, "cold and moist" was the phlegmatic temperament, associated with a pale or "white" complexion and a lack of metabolic "heat."</note>

Therefore they are less desirous of men.
**Isaac** says that the tastes are at least seven, <note>Likely referring to Isaac Israeli the Elder (c. 832–932), a famous Jewish physician whose works on diet and urine were foundational to medieval medicine.</note>
Because the acidic and sub-acid become as one, though unequal
In temperament, being from a single root;
And the insipid [tasteless] would be a privation of taste.
Composite tastes are also found,
Such as a sweet-sourness and many others;
Thus from tastes, men will judge
Different substances, temperaments, and any degrees whatsoever.
And if you hesitate to experiment by tasting,
You should turn to other testimonies,
Just as in medicine one must not trust in urine alone. <note>Uroscopy, or the examination of urine, was the primary diagnostic tool for medieval doctors, but practitioners were often cautioned that it could be deceptive if used without considering other symptoms.</note>

To make the Elixir, the **Permanent Water** <term>Permanent Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua permanens." In alchemy, this is a "water" that does not wet the hands and can endure the fire without evaporating—the ultimate solvent for the Great Work.</note>,

There must be a <term>body</term>, <term>soul</term>, and <term>spirit</term> <note>This triad is the fundamental structure of the "Philosopher's Stone." The Alchemist seeks to unite these three into a permanent, incorruptible whole.</note>.
In our work it is also necessary
That our intermediary [the medium] agrees with every kind
Of either extreme, discovered through wisdom,
Otherwise the whole work would be reduced to nothing.
For wise nature cannot, by its operation,
Complete any thing at a mere whim,
Nor can it leap [directly] between extremes;
But if it first proceeds through all the degrees
Of each intermediary, this is true and legitimate.
Hence nature ordains various mediums.

# Chemical Treatise.

Now after all these things you must know
The seven <term>circulations</term> <note>In alchemy, "circulation" refers to the cyclical process of heating a substance so it evaporates and condenses repeatedly in a closed vessel, mimicking the cycles of nature and the heavens.</note> of each Element;
Which correspond with the number of the seven planets,
Which no one has known, except by celestial grace,
And philosophers of great genius
Say that the circulations ought to be nine.
It is safer to follow them in the work,
Nevertheless seven would suffice for us
Through new discoveries recently found,
By more recent philosophers, whose works are true,
But regarding the circulations of the Elements
Certain learned men think it will be enough for their purpose,
If they descend in order from fire
To air, and that they do not err,
If from here they proceed to water,
And then to earth, when there is need,
And in this way, observing the order
They tend from the highest to the lowest things,
Of which words they consider this the reason,
Because air is found to be the food of fire,
But, believe me, such a circulation
Is at least a certain <term>rectification</term> <note>original: "rectificatio." This is the process of purifying a substance—usually a liquid—through repeated distillation to reach its most "right" or potent state.</note>,
Which serves more for separation
And correction, than for <term>transmutation</term>.
However, it is true that the appetite <note>In this context, "appetite" refers to a natural affinity or the inherent "desire" of one element to act upon or join with another.</note> of fire
Is primarily to work in the earth,
As if in its principal material fuel,
Because fire agrees most of all with earth,
Therefore, because dryness depends on heat;
But air by its nature is more moist,
Although fire does not work without air,
Since the elements are connected among themselves by bonds,
By the hand of God, so that they do not depart from one another.

By any genius or virtue of human art,
Just as you see the example in water pipes <note>The author is likely referring to a siphon or the "horror vacui" (nature's abhorrence of a vacuum), where water appears to defy gravity by following the air.</note>,
Where heavy water ascends after air,

Another circulation beginning with air

From fire toward earth, from here to pure water,
Then to air, and from here through the middle
We proceed to earth, and soon back to fire.
Through these circulations the **Red Work** <note>original: "opus rubeum." Also known as the Rubedo, this is the final stage of the alchemical Great Work, resulting in the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is perfected:
Other circulations are better suited to the <term>Whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedo." The stage of purification preceding the final Red Work.</note>,
Which for that reason are described here.
Each circulation has its own proper time,

For just as one of the planets is heavier <note>In the pre-modern view, "heavier" or "slower" planets like Saturn moved more sluggishly through the zodiac compared to the "lighter" Moon or Mercury.</note>

So certain circulations, which the learned perform,
Require a space of thirty weeks.
Other circulations take less time,
Just as one of the planets is lighter than another;
But the time of one is that in which another ascends,
Extended to 26 weeks by experiment,
After all the coarse preparations made beforehand,
And the circumstances understood,
The ignorance of which has deceived many,
Forcing them to stop where the wise began.
Other common people, who have sought this science,
Thought that this could be completed in forty days <note>The "Philosophical Month" of 40 days was a common trope in alchemical literature; Norton is warning that the true process is much slower and requires more patience.</note>;
They do not know that the things of nature and art
Have their own proper time according to their manner.

Otherwise our stone cannot be nourished.
Authors of the greatest fame

In quantity and quality unto infinity.

The fifth [rule] concerns the harmony and sympathy 
Between your <term>work</term> <note>original: "opus." Beginning from the first, we shall find

Such "flies" <note>Norton uses the metaphor of flies to describe fickle people who flit from one idea to another without depth.</note> will fly wherever they wish, 
And such people should labor to learn the words first, 
Following a most sacred maxim of this kind:

> "Reaching mightily from one end to the other, 
> and ordering all things sweetly." <note>original: "Attingens à fine usque ad finem fortiter / Disponens omnia suaviter." A quotation from the Wisdom of Solomon 8:1. In alchemy, this refers to the need for a process that is both powerful and naturally balanced.</note>

It happens that all who are poorly prudent and changeable of mind

Which strips them of their wealth; 
They are accustomed to agree to every story told to them 
And abandon the ancient teachings. 
But some Lords are constant in mind, 
And they are fit to finish it; 
Whoever such a person may be in this work, 
Whether a layman or a cleric, 
Or a rich man, a knight, an abbot, or a lord, 
He is most suited to this art.

The second concordance with this art is,
When you find skilled assistants <note>original: "ministros." In alchemical literature, these are the laboratory workers who tended the fires and handled the apparatus.</note>,
No servant serves this intention,
Unless he be sober, prudent, and diligent,
Faithful, watchful, and careful,
Guarding his tongue and not physically infirm <note>original: "vitiosus corpore." Literally "vicious in body," meaning free from chronic illness or physical disabilities that would hinder the grueling labor of the laboratory.</note>,
Clean of hand, and meticulous in handling the work,
Not disobedient, nor presumptuous;
Such assistants, intent upon your <term>work</term> <note>original: "operi." The alchemical process or Magnum Opus.</note>
Will preserve it from every injury.
But do not trust that two or three of this kind
Will suffice for you until the end of the work:
If your <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia." The raw chemical substance being transformed into the Stone.</note> is of moderate quantity,
Then eight such servants will be suitable,
But for a small quantity, there will suffice
Four to perform all things:
Half of whom shall work,
While the other half sleeps or is at Church;
For you shall have nothing good from this art,
Unless it is served as well by night as by day:
With continuity, except for the holy Sabbath,
Counting from one evening to the following evening.
And while they work, it is necessary for them to avoid
All wickedness <note>original: "nequitiam." Norton implies that moral impurity or sinful behavior could spiritually corrupt the chemical transformation.</note>; otherwise, this truth will come to pass:
That such great misfortune will intervene,
That they will ruin a part of their work.
Therefore all assistants ought to be male,
Or even let them all be female,
Lest they be employed together in the work;
Although some of them might be from among your kinsfolk,
Nevertheless, it is necessary that they have some comfort
To relieve their great labors,
For nothing shall be more useful,

<header>Of Thomas Norton the Englishman</header>

How this one concordance,
The third rule, is obscure to many:
To organize the instruments necessary for this work.
Just as individual chapters <note>original: "capitula." Here meaning specific stages or processes within the alchemical "Work."</note> have different intentions,
So too do they require different instruments,
In both material and in form,
In harmony, so that no accident occurs.
Just as the works of division and separation
Require small vessels for their operation,
But wide vessels for <term>circulation</term> <note>The process of heating a liquid so that it evaporates, condenses, and flows back into the same vessel repeatedly.</note>,
And long ones for <term>precipitation</term> <note>The process of causing a solid substance to settle out of a solution.</note>,
And both short and long ones serve for <term>sublimation</term> <note>The heating of a solid to turn it into vapor, which then condenses back into a solid on a cooler surface.</note>;
But narrow vessels that are sufficiently tall
Are better suited for correction <note>Refining or adjusting the properties of the matter.</note>.
Some vessels are made of lead,
And some from clay, whether "living" or "dead."
"Dead clay" <note>original: "lutum mortuum." This refers to fired clay that has been ground into powder (known today as grog). It is mixed with raw clay to prevent the vessel from shrinking or cracking under intense heat.</note> is what we call that material
Which has already endured great duration [in the fire].
Such a mixture, with powder and raw clay,
Will tolerate the fire and will not fail in it;
But other kinds of clay will not remain [intact] in the fire,
Which you will not wish to use for your vessels.
Other vessels are made of stones
Able to withstand the fire, but few or none
Are now found among workers
In any region of all England
Which drink in no water <note>original: "nihil aquæ imbibant." Meaning the stone is non-porous and will not absorb the liquid matter.</note>
And yet remain dry in the heat of the fire.
Stone vessels of that kind for our purpose
Would be precious instruments indeed.
All other vessels are made of glass,
Lest the <term>spiritual matter</term> <note>The volatile vapors or gases produced during the chemical reactions, which alchemists believed contained the "spirit" of the substance.</note> escape;
In this region, such glass is made from ash and flint...

# Chemical Treatise

They are made, but elsewhere from small stones;
From our glass, the best kind is found.
The fragments found in the morning usually show
What was only ash the day before
And endured the fire through the night and longer.
A harder species is called <term>freton</term> <note>original: "freton." Derived from "frit," this refers to partially fused ingredients or recycled broken glass (cullet) which, when remelted, produces a more durable and heat-resistant glass.</note>;
It results from the breaking of glass vessels.
The tincture of <term>glassmakers' enamels</term> <note>original: "smaltorum vitriariorum." Smalt was a blue glass colored with cobalt; the author suggests that high-quality glass is so dense it cannot be easily stained or "penetrated" by these pigments.</note>
Will not penetrate it, as they report.
By following this doctrine of selection,
You shall take whatever you wish for your use.
But regarding the shape of the various vessels,
Each person follows their own judgment.
The best form for a vessel, as is evident,
Is that which agrees with the "vessel of nature" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the womb or the egg, suggesting the vessel should facilitate natural-style gestation and growth.</note>,
And a shape that corresponds to the quantity [of the material]
And all other circumstances of the matter.
And **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on the natural sciences and was later legendary in alchemical circles.</note> teaches this best
In his book *On Minerals*.
On this matter, a secret was revealed
By my master, when in this way
> He said: "If God had not given us a vessel,
> He would have given us nothing; and that vessel is glass."
Many instruments are necessary,
Just as suitable furnaces are required.
Ancient authors found for this art
A special furnace for all uses;
Others [invented different ones] according to their own ingenuity,
But many of those are useless.
Some are too wide, others too long;
Many of them do not agree with nature.
Therefore, certain furnaces can be utilized,
But many of them must not be admitted.

### Of Thomas Norton the Englishman

For they were made, at least, by a singular invention
By such as seemed wise, but were not;
A more commendable form of all these
You will find described in this book.

<margin>☞</margin> A certain furnace was recently invented by me,
The likes of which was unknown to the ancients;
Its secret power was sought out by study
And produced at great expense.
In it, sixty operations can be performed
At one and the same time, with almost no cost—
No greater than what is used for a single operation.
From this, certainly, its utility is great.
You will have sixty different degrees <note>Refers to the "degrees of heat" or the intensity of the fire. Precise heat management was considered the most difficult part of the "Great Work."</note>
For as many works, and a different heat for each
In that furnace, to fulfill your desire,
So that all these things are done with a very small fire,
Which measures at least a foot in width;
And yet, each of those 60 spaces is equal to it.
Many purposes can be accomplished there,
Because whatever heat is desired will be present.
Not everyone has knowledge of this instrument,
And therefore it was not added to the illustration.
Another furnace can serve sixty
Glass vessels, and even far more,
Each of which feels an equal heat,
As you will easily perceive from the illustration.
Then another furnace for working
Was invented by me through mental conception,
Which serves best for the <term>separation</term> <note>The process of isolating the various components or "elements" of a substance.</note>
Of things being divided, and for <term>exaltation</term> <note>An alchemical process intended to raise a substance to a higher state of purity, dignity, or power.</note>,
And for the disjunction which is called division,
As well as the correction which is called <term>ablution</term> <note>original: "ablutio." Also known as "washing," this is the purification of a substance by cleansing it with liquid.</note>,
And sometimes it will be suitable for <term>desiccation</term> <note>The process of drying or removing all moisture from a substance.</note>.

And it works best for preparation,
And so it can be useful for six things,
And yet simultaneously and at once for all of them;
This is a new thing, which ought not
To be expressed in a picture, lest everyone see it;
Another furnace can be depicted
More dangerous than all the others,
Made for <term>Magnesia</term> <note>In 15th-century alchemy, Magnesia was not the modern element magnesium, but a "primitive matter" or a specific mineral—often lead or antimony—thought to contain the "seed" of gold.</note>, concerning which the ancients taught
That it cannot be touched by hand, and yet a linen cloth
Placed in its middle is not burned,
Despite the fear of the flame rising from the wood;
When I myself had discovered this subtle furnace,
I perfected many wonderful things in it.
Now it is appropriate to tell at this time
Whose degrees are to be called into doubt,
In which the precious material of Magnesia
Can be kept alive, lest it perish entirely;
To be certain of its graduations,
Consider your <term>registers</term> <note>Sliding plates or dampers used to regulate the flow of air and the intensity of the fire.</note>, and note this:
The more registers there are, the less the heat will be;
Through various registers, you will create various degrees of heat.
He who knows the virtue and the kind of operations
Of each furnace, he will be able to find the truth;
And on the contrary, he who remains ignorant of them,
All his works will proceed by chance.
No one will be certain that he will achieve his intention
Without the proper harmony of art and instruments.
Many other instruments will be required
Than are recounted in this chapter,
Which you will arrange with subtle skill,
And you will test them beforehand, if you are prudent.
The fourth rule is very noteworthy:
Concerning the relationship between this art and a suitable location.

# Chemical Treatise.

Nothing on earth possesses more simplicity,
Than the elements of our <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis". The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance sought by alchemists to transmute base metals and achieve spiritual perfection.</note>,
Therefore, when they are in operation,
They most especially obey the constellation,
Whence a very friendly harmony
Exists in a direct and fixed <term>Ascendant</term> <note>original: "Ascendente". The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the start of the work, believed to "set the soul" of the chemical reaction.</note>,
Which is a common sign for this operation,
On account of the many times it must be repeated.
Make it so that your prevailing Ascendant is fortunate,
And let it be preserved from evil <term>aspects</term> <note>original: "aspectibus". The geometric angles between planets; "evil" aspects like squares or oppositions were thought to hinder the work.</note>;
But if it should be hindered or necessarily afflicted,
Let it be arranged so that it has a good aspect.
For the <term>white work</term> <note>original: "albo opere". The *Albedo*, or whitening stage of the process, which follows the initial blackening (*Nigredo*).</note>, make the Moon fortunate,
So that she may be mistress of the <term>fourth house</term> <note>original: "quartæ domus". In astrology, the fourth house represents the home, foundations, and "hidden treasures."</note>,
For here is the Treasure hidden by the ancients;
Likewise, let her be in the sixth house for the servants of the work.
Keep all of these from great hindrances,
Just as it is shown in the pictures, or for that purpose,
Provided that your own <term>Nativity</term> <note>original: "Nativitas". One's personal birth chart; Norton warns that if the alchemist's own stars are ill-aligned, the work will fail regardless of the laboratory's timing.</note> does not show a corruption
Contrary to this chosen timing.
The power of the mover of the orb is formal,
The power of the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>original: "octavæ sphæræ". The celestial sphere containing the fixed stars, believed to transmit divine influence down to the earth.</note> is instrumental to it,
With its signs and their visible configurations;
The power of a planet is its own and specific,
The power of the Elements here is material,
And the infused power results from all of these.
The first is likened to the operator’s ingenuity,
The second indeed is equal to his hands,
The third is equal to a good instrument,
The rest is like the thing which is being prepared.
Make it so that all these aforementioned things agree with one another,
And you shall deservedly become a great master
In this way of the <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: "Elixir". A potent liquid or powder derived from the Stone, used for transformation.</note> (of which we have made mention).

Things of the <term>second intention</term> <note>original: "secundæ intentionis". In scholastic philosophy, this refers to concepts or mental constructs that depend on the first understanding of physical objects; here, it likely refers to the spiritual or philosophical results of the work.</note> are generated,
Do not trust in <term>Geomancy</term> <note>original: "Geomantiæ". A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note>, a superstitious art,
For God added reason, which is placed elsewhere,

## Chapter Seven.

**R**ecognize him as a perfect master,
Who knows the management of fire, and its degrees;
Nothing will be able to hinder your desire,
Except ignorance of heat and fire.
You find it written by many authors:
☉ The whole work consists in the management of fire, <note>The symbol ☉ represents the Sun or Gold, signifying the ultimate goal of the Alchemical work.</note>
Therefore you shall proceed in all chapters
In such a way that the heat works neither more nor less than required,
In which many of <term>Geber’s cooks</term> <note>original: "Gebri coquis". A derogatory term for "puffers"—unskilled alchemists who followed the recipes of the famous authority Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) by rote without understanding the underlying philosophy.</note>
Have been deceived, though they were learned from books.
1. That kind of heat by which pigs or geese are plucked
Is suitable in this art for <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctione". The process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or mature the mixture.</note>;
For intermediate minerals this heat is fit
To drench <term>litharge</term> <note>original: "lythargyrium". Lead monoxide, a substance often used in the purification of silver and gold.</note> with sweat.
2. Such heat that dries fine linens
Serves our <term>air</term> <note>original: "aeri". In this context, it refers to the volatile or gaseous stage of the matter being transformed.</note> in thirty operations.

He begins defining specific "degrees" of heat, comparing them to everyday temperatures like those used for plucking poultry or drying linen.</summary>

But for division you shall employ this heat,
Which cooks use for the roasting of meat;
3. This same heat along with a **circular fire** <note>original: "circulari igne". A technique where the fire is placed around the vessel rather than directly beneath it to ensure even heating.</note>
Is required for the separation of dividing parts;
4. But for the **circulations of the Elements**,
A glowing fire will be suitable for you,
Which fire must always remain equal
At every minute and at the same time be perpetual;
For it must never fail, nor increase,
Even though this fire never ceases.
You should study wisely and look all around,
So that you may investigate such a fire,
And in that fire there should be no humidity
That the hand might touch or the eye see.
5. There is yet another, a **moist fire**,
And yet it seems a contradiction in terms <note>original: "oppositum in adjecto". A logical fallacy or paradox where the description contradicts the noun, as fire is naturally dry.</note>;
Such a fire separates at a certain time
Materials adhering to the sides of the vessels;
This same heat effects many more things:
It often makes those things which are thick, thin.
The Philosopher prudently asserts concerning this heat
That its highest degree shall be such
As to cause and generate a dryness as equal
As that produced by dry heat in the first degree.
6. Another is the **fire of desiccation** <note>original: "dessicationis". The process of thorough drying or removing all moisture.</note>
For materials which have been soaked in liquids;
7. Another is the **fire of conservation**,
Because all things are dried out by its operation;
8. For <term>Magnesia</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Magnesia" does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but rather to a "mother of metals" or a primary mineral substance used in the Great Work.</note> one uses the **fire of effusion** <note>original: "effusionis". A high-intensity heat used for melting or pouring out substances.</note>,
Which is full of danger and illusion—
Not only the danger that might befall the work,
But it could even harm the master,
Which, if once inhaled <note>original: "receptum". Literally "received," likely referring to toxic fumes or intense heat.</note>, might destroy him.

# Of Thomas Norton the Englishman

Therefore, arrange it so that you may breathe healthily,
Provide for your mouth, ears, eyes, and nostrils,
For it is ten times worse than poison;
Certain men have suffered much harm from this,
Who had not received this warning beforehand.
9.  **Corrosive fire** <note>original: "Ignis corrodens". A fire intense enough to chemically break down or "eat" into substances.</note> serves in this art,
To wisely divide the adjacent Elements;
In one moment of excess, your work has perished,
And in one moment of deficiency, it will not be sufficient;
He who will be certain to find the true degree
Is destined to be a great master in the fire.
It is difficult to know its power,
There is no proof except by sight,
Therefore everyone errs in describing it.
Its heat is learned through expense and experience;
Concerning this heat in particular **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who held that the sun was a red-hot stone; alchemists often cited him regarding the nature of heat and matter.</note> said:
No one is found to be discerning at first glance.
10. Another heat is of **great compulsion** <note>original: "magnæ coactionis". Referring to the forced melting or fusion of recalcitrant materials.</note>
For minerals, which are of hard melting;
This heat cannot be too strong,
Even though it be continued for a very long time.
11. Another is the **heat of calcination** <note>original: "calcinatio". The process of reducing a metal or mineral to a fine powder (calx) by prolonged heating without melting.</note>
For impure metals, and for their preparation,
Which shall not burn them nor melt them,
Otherwise, they would easily be dissipated.
12. The twelfth is the **heat of sublimation** <note>original: "sublimationis". The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then collecting the purified solid as it cools.</note>
Of all the mineral spirits.
13. The last heat is the most excellent of all these,
When your **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note> approaches **projection** <note>original: "projectionem". The final stage where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold.</note>.
Practice makes the craftsman, nothing more is to be said,
Except that he who errs must begin the necessary steps anew.
Now I have taught you everything by its own name,
Just as one man teaches another the way to a certain city.

# *Chemical Treatise.*

Through all villages, waters, bridges and slopes,
So that the wise may well complete their journey,
Thus the learned man will find through this doctrine
That knowledge, if he be of a subtle wit;
All others from this point will recognize themselves as fools.
Let those not interfere who have but a little learning,
For this is the pinnacle of worldly science,
Which neither pope nor king may attain
By their honors, nor by their great councils,
But only by virtue and grace, as the authors pass down.
This <term>precious stone</term> <note>original: "lapis pretiosus". A reference to the Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> can neither be found nor perfected,
Unless it be sought with the highest devotion.
The aforementioned authors, together with this my book,
Demonstrate all true doctrine concerning <term>Alchemy</term>;
If you will fulfill all their instructions
Not by mere opinion, but by this <term>Ordinal</term> <note>original: "Ordinale". This refers to the title of Thomas Norton’s work, the "Ordinal of Alchemy," which was intended to be a definitive "order of operations" for the craft.</note>,
For in this Ordinal I remove every doubt from you;
Nothing is here except what is correctly placed, nor is anything omitted.
On this day, this doctrine thus delivered
Pleased me more than a sum of a thousand pounds;
Three hundred pounds would not please me as much
If this chapter had been left out.
But do not wonder, you Lords or friends,
That such a noble science, as it is here named,
Is here set forth in the <note>original: "Anglicano sermone rudi". Although this specific manuscript is in Latin, Norton originally wrote his "Ordinal" in Middle English verse to make it accessible to his countrymen. This Latin version was translated later for international scholars.</note> crude English tongue;
For this was done so that the multitude
Of unrefined people may be instructed;
Ten thousand laymen are equivalent to ten learned men,
Whence every year great riches in this region
Are easily lost, as the wise understand,
And many others of whatever status...

# THE TESTAMENT OF CREMER,
## ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER, AN ENGLISHMAN, OF THE BENEDICTINE ORDER.
### *THE THIRD TREATISE.*

<note>John Cremer (supposedly active c. 1310–1370) is a semi-legendary figure in alchemical history. He is traditionally described as an Abbot of Westminster who traveled to Italy to seek out the famous philosopher Raymond Lully. Although his name does not appear in the official records of Westminster's abbots, his "Testament" remains a classic of English alchemical literature, focusing on the spiritual and practical preparation required for the "Great Work."</note>

# THE TESTAMENT
## OF CREMER,

->*Abbot of Westminster, Englishman, of the Benedictine Order.*<-
<note>John Cremer is a semi-legendary figure. While he identifies himself as an Abbot of Westminster, historical records do not confirm an abbot by this name during the 14th century. He is often cited in alchemical literature as the man who brought the famous Raymond Lull to the court of King Edward III.</note>

**T**his is the perfection and truth of Alchemy <term>Alchimia</term> <note>Alchemy was the medieval forerunner of chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter, particularly the turning of base metals into gold.</note>, explained with clear reasoning while omitting all those [obscure] technical terms of the art which have been a significant hindrance to all practitioners of this discipline. And I, as a diligent follower of this art and its faculty, was delayed in a marvelous way because the subject was explained to me obscurely in many various books, which I read and practiced according to their instructions for a span of thirty years, at great personal expense and to the detriment of my labor. And the more I read, the more I erred, until by divine providence I traveled to Italy, where it seemed good to God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deo optimo maximo", a common Latin invocation</note>, to bring me into the fellowship of a man endowed with no less dignity than every kind of learning, named Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and philosophy to whom many later alchemical texts were attributed.</note>. I remained in his company for a long time, and I found such favor in the sight of this good man that he revealed some part of this great mystery to me. For this reason, I urged him with many prayers to come with me to this island [England], and he stayed with me for two years. In the course of that time, I completely mastered the whole work <term>opus</term> <note>The "Great Work" refers to the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy.</note>. Afterwards, I brought this eminent man into the presence of the most illustrious King Edward <note>Likely King Edward III (reigned 1327–1377), who according to legend, employed Lull to create gold for coinage.</note>, by whom he was received with due dignity and treated with all kindness; and there, induced by many promises, agreements, and conditions from the King, he was content to make the King wealthy through his art by divine promise.

<summary>John Cremer describes his thirty-year struggle to understand alchemy through books until he met Raymond Lull in Italy, who finally taught him the secret and accompanied him back to England to serve King Edward.</summary>
<keywords>John Cremer, Raymond Lull, King Edward III, Benedictine, Westminster, alchemical history, Great Work, Italy, alchemy</keywords>

### Cremer, Abbot of Westminster

[This gold was provided] under this condition only: that the king in his own person should wage war against the Turks <note>original: "Turcas". I, most blessed Raymond, shall pour out prayers for you to God the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deo optimo maximo"</note>, and likewise my brothers shall do the same.

All wisdom is from God <note>This is a paraphrase of Sirach 1:1, a common opening for medieval scholarly texts.</note>, and it always ends with Him, and it exists before eternity. On this first day of my discourse, I invoke the help of Him who is the source and origin of all good things, so that He might deign through His kindness to increase my knowledge through the truth; so that through the grace of the Holy Spirit He might wish to manifest the light of my teaching (which has lain hidden in darkness), and lead those who are wandering onto the path of truth. ### THE LIVING WATER CALLED THAT WHICH
### *provides life to the whole work of our Art.*

Take three ounces of tartar of good claret wine, strong and pure: and to these five drams <term>ʒ. (dram)</term> of petroleum, two ounces of native sulfur <term>sulphuris vivi (literally "living sulfur," meaning naturally occurring sulfur that has not been melted)</term>, two drams <term>ʒ.</term> of yellow arsenic, three drams <term>ʒ.</term> of Rabusenus <note>original: "Rabuseni." An alchemical term often referring to a red preparation of mercury or a specific vitriol.</note>, and two drams <term>ʒ.</term> of willow charcoal. Mix and distill all these in a Bath of Neptune <note>original: "balneo Neptuni." An alchemical term for a water bath, similar to a double boiler, used for gentle heating.</note>, in a glass vessel, the neck of which must be well-stopped. The receiver shall be one cubit high and well-sealed, lest the spirit or smoke vanish; and when you see it distilling a pale color, then take no more, and remove the upper part of the still until it cools. This process is completed in four days. Avoid its odor; for it is dangerous. This water is to be kept in a strong and thick glass, diligently closed, and it is to be used as is assigned in the following sections.

<note>In alchemical traditions, "unpolluted" (non polluti) refers to sexual purity or virginity. It was believed that the "vital spirit" or life force of the body remained concentrated in the fluids of a chaste person.</note>

## Chapter Two.

Take the water <note>original: "aquam" (meaning urine)</note> of an unpolluted youth after his first sleep for three or four nights or longer, so that three sextaries <term>sextarii (a Roman measure, approximately one pint)</term> are produced, and thus pour it every night into a stone vessel tightly sealed on all sides. Then take the dregs from there, and take one sextary's measure of the purest and thinnest part of the same. Add two urns <term>urnas (a liquid measure)</term> of the strongest wine vinegar; two drams <term>ʒ (drams)</term> of quicklime <term>calcis vivæ</term>; and a half-ounce of the living water, just as we made mention in the first chapter <note>Referring to the solvent prepared on page 538.</note>. Pour these into an earthenware pot, and place upon it an alembic <term>alembicum (a still-head used for distillation)</term> or distilling vessel well-sealed with lute <note>original: "luto." Lute was a specialized alchemical paste or clay used to make apparatus airtight.</note>. Let it stand for one day and one night before you build the fire. Take care that you do not apply too much heat, and thus distill for five or six days and as many nights without intermission. Thus it remains drop by drop in your glass receiver. Diligently seal and re-seal the joint with luting material so that its spirit or smoke does not escape. When the liquid distills or flows down blue or pale, no more is to be drawn from it.

...of the virgin youth, which is described in the second chapter? <note>This refers back to the "Second Water" or urine-based solvent detailed on page 539.</note> Use not all the water, but only as much as may be sufficient. In the middle of that pit, place a chest, the boards or wooden material of which shall contain the measure of two cubits on every side. Closest to the glass, there should be a layer of quicklime <term>calcis vivæ</term> which has not yet been sprinkled with water. Let there be a cover for the chest, which you may occasionally remove from the upper part of the earth, along with the lid itself; but as to whether the lid is "green" <note>original: "viride" - likely referring to the moisture or state of the dung/lime mixture</note> or not, do not look at it at any time except during the full moon. At that time, it will be of various colors until it becomes fixed and hardens. Then it will descend and seek the lower part or the bottom of the glass, and it will be quite black. Let it stand in the pit for twelve weeks; then you may take it up and keep it until the twentieth day of March, and then pound it again, just as is written hereafter.
