## Chapter Five.

Take eight pounds of the purest and softest **lead**, and two pounds of **pure tin**. Melt these in a well-covered clay vessel (as described previously), then place it in a wood fire and blow upon it with a gentle breeze for three hours. Then, remove the scum of the metal dross <note>the *scoria* or impurities that rise to the surface of molten metal</note> until the metal is pure and clear. At that point, cast in a quarter-ounce of the true powder of the **red stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone in its perfected, "red" state, capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note>, finely crushed. Stir it carefully with an iron rod until the metals are glowing red. Then, cover the vessel and let it stand for seventy-two hours. During the final three hours, blow upon it again with a gentle breath. When it is liquid and not **fixed** <note>in this context, "fixed" refers to a state where the metal is no longer volatile or is ready to be shaped</note>, you may cast it into whatever form you desire. Thus, you have the completion of the entire work clearly before your eyes. Therefore, give all glory and honor to God, from whom all good gifts proceed. Amen.

### THE METHOD OF MAKING THE CLAY
### vessel in which metal may be melted so 
### that it can withstand the fire.

## *Chapter Six.*

Take **tascanium** <term>tascanium: a specialized refractory clay or "potter's earth" known for its ability to withstand high heat without cracking</term> or clay that has been worked and tempered in the same way potters prepare their clay. Mix it with a tenth part of horse dung <note>a common additive in historical ceramics to increase porosity and thermal shock resistance</note>. When the vessel has been shaped and is half-dry, add to the clay some fine filings of red copper (or copper from a cauldron) and the powder of red and yellow **arsenic**. When the vessel is completely dried out, take some **saltpeter** <term>Aphronitrum: a mineral salt, often saltpeter or natron, used as a flux or coating</term> that has been dissolved for twelve hours in the "water" described in the first chapter <note>likely the distilled solvent or "mercurial water" mentioned at the start of the treatise</note>. Smear this over the entire lower part of the vessel, using a double jar or container.

## THE METHOD FOR PREPARING THE CLAY.

Make your clay <note>original: *lutum*; a sealing paste or "lute" used to make laboratory vessels airtight</note> so that you may keep your receiver closed and seal your glass vessel, as well as the upper part of it, for the "forty-day works" <note>referring to the *quadragesima*, a traditional forty-day period for the digestion or slow heating of alchemical substances</note>. You shall make it as follows: from bitumen or from quicklime <note>original: *calx viva*</note>, mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, and egg whites, all carefully ground together; make it with a little Armenian bole <note>a reddish medicinal clay used as a binder and heat-resistant seal</note>.

Take diligent care that your petroleum <note>literally "rock oil"; here referring to a mineral oil or naphtha</note> is bright, pure, and yellow; if it is not so, it is imperfect.

Also, ensure that your <term>Rabusenum: an alchemical term for a specific stage of the matter or a particular substance, often associated with the transition between the white and red works</term> is red and white, like the color of Vermilion.

To my dearest brothers in this monastic profession and life, Alexander and Richard, to whom I give command that they observe these rules (in the name of the most blessed Trinity) as described, and guard them with the greatest diligence and care;

First, I command that they reveal this divine work to no one greedy for human things or tainted by the most wicked crime, nor to any other person except for the Abbot and the Prior who shall succeed in this house hereafter. And even then, they shall not reveal it until the keys to our treasury <note>original: *aerarium*</note> are committed to their custody. At that time, you shall take an oath from them upon the most holy Gospels, so that they do not reveal this mystery to any powerful person or most noble man, nor to any of the lower brothers of this house.

Furthermore, I command that none of you perform this work in this house of ours unless it falls into some poverty or ruin—which indeed seems impossible to both you and me, because I have left behind such a great treasure (which is not hidden from you). Therefore, I give you a mandate that you who are placed in the highest rank of dignity in this house—namely the Abbot, the Prior, and the most venerable elders—that one of you renew this work of mine and the practice by rewriting it whenever a period of sixty years has passed. For this will preserve my work so that it can be understood as correctly as possible. And since the style of writing letters and characters varies over time, rewriting it from the beginning is the safest way of preserving our work, so that it may be left whole and inviolate to our successors.

**Magnesia** <note>in this context, not the modern element magnesium, but a general term for a mineral "mother" or crude ore</note> is the dross of iron; when the work appears black, it may be understood by the "black raven" or the "vulture," or as "Virgin's Milk" <note>original: *Lac virginis*; a white, cloudy precipitate</note> or "whale bone" <note>original: *os Ceti*; likely referring to a white mineral substance</note>. For this reason, those who have learned from God rightly drive those who are strangers to Him far away from His secrets.*

# THE TESTAMENT OF ARNALD
# OF VILLANOVA.

**I** *t is said that Arnald of Villanova* <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a Catalan physician and alchemist. His "Testament" is a classic of alchemical literature, summarizing the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, *the pride of our people, once recorded his final thoughts in these verses. That famous Stone of the ancient Sages* <term>Sages</term><note>Latin: "Sophorum." The 'Sages' or 'Philosophers' are the legendary masters of alchemy whose secret knowledge the author seeks to emulate.</note> *arises from the earth, and acquires its perfected powers within the fire. Then, let a clear liquid nourish it for twice six hours* <note>original: "horis bis senis" (twelve hours)</note>, *until its body is swollen and distended on every side; and placed in a dry and moderately warm spot for another twelve hours, it gradually purges itself of excessive and external vapors, and its internal parts begin to harden and solidify. Virgin’s milk* <term>Virgin’s milk</term><note>A common alchemical term (lac virginis) for a white liquid or mercury that appears during the chemical transformation.</note> *pressed from the finest stone is immediately sealed within a glass egg* <note>The "Philosopher's Egg" is the oval glass vessel used in the alchemical furnace to contain the matter during its transformation.</note> *and is wonderfully transformed day by day by the life-giving fire, until the changing colors settle into a permanent, brilliant whiteness. Finally, as the fire’s strength increases, a deep purple hue takes hold—the sure sign of the work’s power and its completion.* <note>The sequence of colors (white to red/purple) represents the final stages of the Great Work, known as the albedo and rubedo.</note>

## FIRST TREATISE
#### Concerning
# NATURE,
### *What it may be, and what sort of people its*
### *Seekers ought to be.*

---

**M**any wise and most learned men from many centuries ago—indeed, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy ("Hermeticism").</note> testifies, even before the Great Flood—wrote extensively about the preparation of the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone</term><note>Latin: "lapide Philosophorum." The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the elixir of life.</note>; and they left us so many writings that if **NATURE** did not perform believable works for us daily, hardly anyone would believe that Nature is real. In earlier ages, there were not so many "inventors" of things; nor did our predecessors consider anything other than Nature itself and the possibilities within Nature. 

And although those men remained only upon the simple path of Nature, they nevertheless discovered things that we, who are now occupied with so many different matters, could hardly have imagined with our own wits. This happens because Nature and the generation of things in the world now seem common and simple to us. Therefore, we direct our minds not toward things already known, but toward such things that can barely be done, or are impossible. 

For this reason, it is actually easier for us to devise "subtle" things—which the Philosophers themselves would not have known how to imagine—than it is to reach the true course of Nature and the intended meaning of those Philosophers. Human nature is so structured that it neglects what it already knows and always seeks after other things; this is even more true of the human intellect, to which Nature is subject. 

For example: you see any craftsman who, once he has reached the very peak of perfection in his craft, either seeks out something else, or misuses his skill, or stops entirely. In the same way, noble Nature always acts, even reaching into the very **Iliadum** <term>Iliadum</term><note>A term used in Paracelsian alchemy (often called "Iliaster") referring to the prime matter, the fundamental chaotic substance from which all things are created.</note>,

-> Aa aa <-
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the First Treatise on Nature, arguing that ancient alchemists succeeded through simplicity while modern seekers fail by over-complicating the natural process. The author emphasizes that the true path of alchemy lies in understanding the fundamental course of Nature rather than seeking "subtle" or impossible inventions.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, Hermes Trismegistus, Philosopher's Stone, alchemy, Iliadum, ancient wisdom vs modern invention</keywords>

Therefore I say **NATURE** is **One**; true, simple, complete in its being, which **GOD** made before the ages, and enclosed a spirit within it: know, moreover, that the Limit of Nature is **GOD**, who is also the beginning of Nature; since no beginning is finished except in that in which it begins. I said it is only one, through which God makes all things: not that God would not know how to operate without it (since He Himself made Nature, and is almighty); but it pleased Him so, and so He did. # SECOND TREATISE,

## *Concerning the Operation of Nature in our purpose and the seed.*

I have already said that NATURE is true, unique, appearing everywhere, and continuous, and that she is known from the things produced, namely wood, herbs, etc. I also said that the searcher of Nature <note>The "searcher" or "scrutator" refers to the practicing alchemist who observes natural processes to replicate them.</note> must be truthful, simple, patient, constant, applying his mind to at least a single thing, etc. Now we must begin with the act of Nature. Just as Nature exists in the will of God, and God created her, or imposed her upon every imagination; so Nature made for herself a seed <term>seed<gloss>original: "sperma". In alchemy, this refers to the concentrated essence or "blueprint" of a substance that dictates what it will become.</gloss></term>, that is, her will in the Elements. She is indeed one, and yet she brings forth diverse things; but she works nothing without seed: whatever the seed wants, Nature performs, for she is like the instrument of some Artisan. Therefore, the seed of each thing is better and more useful to the Artisan than Nature herself: For from Nature without seed you will accomplish as much as a Goldsmith could without fire, gold, or silver, or a farmer without grain and seed. Once the seed is held, Nature will be ready at hand, whether for evil or for good. She works in the seed as GOD works in the free will of man: and this is a great miracle, that Nature obeys the seed, not by compulsion, but of her own accord; just as God grants all things that Man wants, not by compulsion, but from His own will: Therefore He gave man free will, whether for evil or for good. The seed, therefore, is the Elixir of each thing, or the quintessence, or the most perfect decoction and digestion of a thing, or the Balsam of sulfur, which is the same as the radical Moisture <note>The "radical moisture" was believed to be the fundamental life-fluid within metals and living beings that prevented them from becoming brittle or decaying.</note> in Metals. Truly a great discourse could be established here concerning this seed, but we tend only toward our purpose in the Chemical Art. The four elements generate seed, by the will of GOD and the imagination <note>In this context, "imagination" refers to a formative, creative power that gives shape to matter.</note> of Nature: For just as the seed of a man has its center, or the vessel of its female in the kidneys; so the four elements [by their]

By a never-ending motion (each according to its own quality), they project the seed <note>original: "sperma". In this context, it refers to the universal life-force or "blueprint" of matter.</note> into the center of the earth, where it is digested, and then sent outward through motion. But the center of the earth is a certain empty place where nothing can rest; into the "Ex-center" <note>original: "Excentrum". Sendivogius uses this term to describe the area just outside the absolute mathematical center—the margin or inner circumference where the elements meet.</note> (so to speak), or the margin and circumference of the center, the four Elements project their qualities. Just as a man emits his semen into the womb of a woman, in which nothing of the seed remains <note>That is, the seed does not stay in its raw form but is immediately transformed or utilized.</note>, but after the womb has received its due portion, it casts the rest out; similarly, it happens in the center of the earth that the Magnetic force <term>Magnetic force<gloss>original: "vis Magnetica". In early modern science, this refers to a natural power of attraction that specific locations or substances have for their "rightful" components.</gloss></term> of a certain place attracts a thing suited to itself for bringing something forth; the rest is cast out as stones and other waste products. For all things have their origin from that source, nor is anything born in the whole world except through this source.

For example: suppose there is a vessel of water on a flat table, placed in the middle of the table, and various things are placed all around it—different colors, likewise salt, and so on, each separately. If the water is then poured into the middle, you will see that water flow here and there, and while one streamlet touches a red color, it will become red from it; if it reaches the salt, it will borrow the taste of salt, and so on for the rest. *For the water does not change the places, but the diversity of the places changes the water.* <note>original: "Aqua enim loca non mutat, sed locorum diversitas mutat aquam." This is a fundamental alchemical maxim: the universal substance is pure and neutral until it takes on the characteristics of the "matrix" or environment where it settles.</note> In a similar way, from the center of the earth, the seed or sperm projected into the center by the four elements passes to various places, and according to the Nature of the place, the thing is "natured" <note>The Latin "naturatur" implies that the substance is given its specific identity or essential character by the place it inhabits.</note>: if it reaches a place of pure earth and water, it becomes a pure thing. 

The seed and sperm of all things is one, and yet it generates various things, as appears from the following example. The seed of man is a noble seed, and it was created at least for the generation of man; nevertheless, if a man abuses it—which is within his free will—a monstrosity <note>original: "abortus". While this can mean abortion, in alchemical and natural history texts of this period, it often refers to a "failed" or "monstrous" birth that deviates from the intended human form.</note> is born. By such inhuman and detestable mixing of men with beasts, various beasts similar to humans would be produced. For thus it happens: if the seed enters the center, that which was meant to be born from there is born;

# THIRD TREATISE

## *On the True Matter of Metals.*

**T**he first matter of Metals is twofold, but one without the other does not create a metal. The first and principal is the moisture of the air mixed with heat; this the Philosophers named Mercury <term>Mercury<gloss>original: "Mercurium". Not the liquid metal (quicksilver), but the universal alchemical principle of volatility, spirit, and fluidity.</gloss></term>, which is governed by the rays of the Sun and Moon in the philosophical sea <note>A metaphor for the universal solvent or the primordial state of matter in the alchemist's vessel.</note>. The second is the dry heat of the earth, which they called sulfur <term>sulfur<gloss>original: "sulphur". The alchemical principle representing the active, masculine, and combustible force that gives matter its body and color.</gloss></term>. 

But because all true Philosophers have hidden this second matter most of all, we shall explain it a little more clearly—especially the weight, for if the weight is ignored, all things are destroyed. From this it happens that many produce abortions <note>original: "abortus". Used here to mean failed experiments or incomplete chemical reactions.</note> even from good materials. For there are those who take the whole body for the matter, seed, or sperm, while others take only a fragment; all of these stray from the right path. For example: if someone were to take the foot of a man and the hand of a woman, and wished from [them]... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword indicates the sentence continues with "would wish from them to procreate a human."</note>

## FOURTH TREATISE.

### *How metals are generated in the bowels of the earth.*

Metals are produced in this way: after the four Elements have cast their virtues into the center of the earth, the *Archaeus* <term>Archaeus: the invisible governing spirit or vital force that directs natural processes, here acting like an internal alchemist</term>, through distillation, sublimes them by the heat of perpetual motion toward the earth's surface. For the earth is porous, and the wind, trickling through the pores of the earth, is resolved into water, from which all things are born. Therefore, let the sons of learning <note>original: "doctrinæ filii", a common alchemical term for initiates or students of the "Great Work"</note> know that the sperm <note>the seed or vital essence</note> of metals is no different from the sperm of all things: namely, a moist vapor. Thus, artists search in vain for the reduction of metals into the "first matter," <term>Materia Prima: the primordial, undifferentiated substance from which all things originate</term> which is merely vapor.

The Philosophers did not mean such a first matter, but only the "second matter," <term>Materia Secunda: matter that has already begun to take on a specific form or quality, making it the proper starting point for alchemical work</term> as Bernard of Treviso <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist whose writings emphasized the natural growth of metals</note> excellently argues—though not so clearly, because he speaks of the four Elements. Nevertheless, that is what he meant to say, and he spoke only with the "sons" [of the art]. But I, in order to reveal the theory more clearly, wanted to warn everyone here to cease so many solutions, so many circulations, so many calcinations <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash"</term>, and repetitions; for it is sought in vain in a hard thing when it is inherently soft everywhere. Let not the first, but only the second matter be sought—that which, as soon as it is conceived, cannot be changed into another form.

But if you ask how a metal is reduced into such a matter, I follow the intention of the Philosophers in this: I desire this above all else, that the sons of art understand the meaning of the writers and not just their syllables; and where Nature finishes—namely, in the metals which are perfect bodies before our eyes—there the art must begin. But to return to the point (since our intention here is not about the Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy</note> alone), let us now discuss the matter of metals. A little earlier, I said that all things are born from liquid air or vapor,

This fatness, afterwards coming by sublimation to other places which a preceding vapor has already purged, and where the earth is subtle, pure, and moist, fills its pores and is joined to it; and thus it becomes *Gold* <note>original: "Sol"</note>. If, however, that fatness comes to impure, cold places, it becomes *Lead* <note>original: "Saturnus"</note>; but if such earth be pure and mixed with sulfur, it becomes *Copper* <note>original: "Venus"</note>, etc. For the more purified a place is, the more beautiful the metals it renders: for it must be known that this vapor continually goes out from the center to the surface, and by its passage it purges the places. From this it happens that today mines are found in places where a thousand years ago there were none; for by its progress, it always refines the crude and impure, successively drawing the pure along with itself. And this is the repetition and circulation of *Nature*; it is sublimed for so long, producing new things, until the place is perfectly purified; and the more it is purified, the more noble are the things it produces. # FIFTH TREATISE

## *On the generation of stones of every kind.*

**T**he matter of a stone is the same as that of other things; and according to the purity of the locations, they are born in this way. When the four Elements <term>Elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, then believed to be the fundamental components of all matter</term> drip their vapor into the center of the earth, and the *Archaeus of Nature* <term>Archaeus: the internal governing spirit or vital force that directs natural processes</term> ejects and sublimes that same vapor; this, while it passes through the porous places of the earth, draws with it all the impurity of the earth all the way to the surface, which the air afterwards congeals (for what pure air creates, raw air congeals, because air has entry into air and they join each other, for nature rejoices in Nature <note>original: "natura Naturâ lætatur"; a famous alchemical axiom suggesting that like-substances are drawn to and perfected by one another</note>): and thus rocks and stony mountains are made, according to the size of the pores. And the larger the pores of the earth, the better the place is also purified: for while a greater heat and a greater quantity of water pass through such a vent <note>original: "respiraculum"</note>, the more quickly the earth is cleansed; and thus afterwards metals are more easily born in such places. 

Just as experience itself testifies, gold <note>original: "aurum"</note> is not sought or found anywhere except in mountains, which can rarely happen in the plains: for very often such low places are damp, not with vapor, but with Elemental water, which draws that vapor to itself, and they embrace each other so that they are not easily separated; afterwards the Sun of heaven, digesting that mixture, makes the fat clay used by potters. But in places where there is coarse sand, and the vapor has no fatness or sulfur with it, it creates herbs and grass in the meadows. There are also other precious stones, such as the Diamond <note>original: "Adamas"</note>, Ruby, Emerald, and the remaining gems: they are all generated in this way.

<summary>This page explains the geological and alchemical formation of stones, mountains, and gems, attributing their creation to the movement of elemental vapor through the earth's pores. It argues that mountains are the primary sites for gold because their "vents" allow for better purification than the damp plains.</summary>

<header>New Chemical Light</header>

When the vapor of Nature is sublimed by itself, without the addition of the fatness <note>original: "pinguedinis"; in alchemy, this "fatness" or oiliness refers to the combustible principle of Sulfur</note> of sulfur, and reaches a place of pure salt water, Diamonds <note>original: "Adamantes"; refers here to diamonds or the hardest crystalline stones</note> are formed; and this occurs in the coldest places, which that fatness cannot reach, because the fatness would not allow it. For it must be known that the spirit of water is very easily sublimed by a gentle heat; but oil or fatness is not raised except by a great heat, and into warm places: for even if it proceeds from the center, it is congealed by a slight cold and thus stays put. The vapor, however, ascends to the proper places and is congealed in pure water into stones in a granulated manner. As for how colors are produced in gems, it must be known that this happens by reason of sulfur in this way: if the fatness of sulfur is congealed, afterwards, by that perpetual motion, the spirit of water by passing through it digests and purifies it by the power of salt, until it is colored with a digested red or white color. This color, tending toward a better state along with that spirit—because it has been made subtle by so many repeated distillations—is raised up. The spirit afterwards has the power of entering imperfect things, and thus introduces the color, which is then joined to that water (at that time partially congealed), and so it fills its pores and is fixed with an inseparable fixation <term>fixation: the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>. For all water is congealed by heat if it is without spirit, but is congealed by cold if it possesses spirit; but he who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join the spirit with it, will certainly find a thing a thousand times more precious than gold and every other thing. Therefore, let him cause the spirit to be separated from the water, so that it may putrefy <term>putrefy: a stage of alchemical transformation where matter breaks down and blackens, often compared to a seed rotting in the earth before it sprouts</term>, and the grain <note>The "grain" or seed is the concentrated essence that remains after the impurities are removed through putrefaction</note> may appear; afterwards, having rejected the dregs, let him lead the spirit back from on high into the water, and cause them to be joined together: for that union will generate a branch unlike its parents in form.

From the Elements, it receives the matter from which it generates seed: Now indeed, we shall begin a discourse concerning the seed, and the things generated from seed. Every thing having seed is multiplied in it, but this does not happen without the help of Nature: for seed is nothing other than air congealed in some body, or a moist vapor; and unless this is resolved <note>original: "resolvatur"; in this context, it means to be dissolved or melted back into a liquid/vaporous state</note> by a warm vapor likewise, it is of no use. Therefore, let the investigators of the art know what seed is, lest they seek a thing which does not exist: and let them know it is threefold, produced from the four elements. The first is **MINERAL**, of which we speak in this place; the second is **VEGETABLE**; the third is **ANIMAL**. **MINERAL** seed is known by the Philosophers; **VEGETABLE** is common and ordinary, as we see in fruits; **ANIMAL** is known through imagination <note>original: "ex imaginatione"; in alchemical philosophy, "imagination" refers to the formative power of the soul or the internal vital blueprint that shapes living matter</note>. The vegetable shows us how nature creates it from the four Elements. For it must be known that winter is the cause of putrefaction <term>putrefaction: in alchemy, the stage of decay or "blackness" that must precede new growth and regeneration</term>, since it freezes the vital spirits in trees: and when these are resolved by the heat of the Sun (in which is the magnetic force attractive of all humidity), then the heat of nature, stirred up by motion, drives the subtle vapor of water to the circumference, which opens the pores of the tree and makes drops trickle out, always separating the pure from the impure. Sometimes, however, the pure precedes the impure; the pure stays and is congealed into flowers, the impure departs into leaves, and the coarse and thick into the bark. The bark of the tree remains fixed, the leaves fall by cold or heat when its pores are obstructed: the flowers are congealed into such a color as the heat itself is, and they bring forth fruit and seed (like an apple in which there is the sperm, from which the tree is born; but in that sperm is the seed or grain intrinsically, from which the tree is born even without the sperm; for multiplication happens not in the sperm, but in the seed). Thus we see with our own eyes Nature creating seed from the four elements, lest we should occupy ourselves in this in vain; for that which is created does not need a creator <note>meaning: once a seed is created by Nature, it contains its own generative power and does not require a new act of creation to grow</note>. Let it suffice to have warned the reader with this example; but I return to the proposed Mineral. # New Chemical Light

Though the ignorant may doubt this, it is because that which is before their eyes is not perceived by them; much less that which is invisibly hidden. Yet it is most true that **what is above is not otherwise than what is below**, <note>original: "superius non est nisi ut istud quod est inferius"; this is a direct reference to the famous Hermetic maxim from the Emerald Tablet: "As above, so below."</note> and conversely, that which is born above is born from the same source as that which is born below in the bowels of the earth. And what special privilege do vegetables have over metals, that God should implant seed in them, yet undeservedly exclude metals? Are not metals of the same dignity in the eyes of God as trees? 

Let this be established as a certainty: **nothing grows without seed.** For where there is no seed, the thing is dead. It is necessary, therefore, either that the four elements create the seed of metals, or that they produce them without seed. If they are produced without seed, then they cannot be made perfect; for every thing without seed is imperfect by the very nature of its composition. Whoever does not grant this faith to an indubitable truth is not worthy to search out the secrets of nature; for nothing is born in the world that lacks a seed. 

The seed of metals is truly and really implanted within them, and its generation happens in this way: The four elements, in the first operation of nature, distil—by way of the **Archeus of Nature** <term>Archeus: the vitalizing or formative force in nature, often envisioned by alchemists as an internal "chemist" that directs the growth and maturation of matter</term>—a heavy vapor of water into the center of the earth. This vapor is the seed of metals, and it is called **Mercury** because of its fluidity and its ability to join with every thing (not because of its essence alone). It is compared to **Sulfur** because of its internal heat; and after it is congealed <note>original: "congelationem"; in alchemy, this refers to the solidification of a liquid or vapor into a solid state</note>, it becomes the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to be the fundamental moisture of all things, which allows for growth and prevents brittleness</term>.

And although the body of metals is procreated from Mercury—which must be understood as the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers' Mercury" is a refined, theoretical substance, distinct from the common quicksilver found in a pharmacy</note>—one must not listen to those who think that common mercury is the seed of metals. Such people mistake the "body" for the "seed," not considering that even said common mercury has its own seed within itself. 

The errors of all these people will be made clear by the following example: It is manifest that humans have a seed through which they are multiplied. A human body is Mercury <note>meaning the "matter" or "vehicle"</note>; but the seed is hidden in the body, and in proportion to the body, its quantity is very small. Therefore, he who wishes to generate a human being should not take "Mercury" (which is the body), but rather the seed, which is a congealed vapor of water. Thus, common chemists proceed awkwardly in the regeneration of metals: [me]tallic bodies... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "tallica" on the next page.</note>

# SEVENTH TREATISE.

## *On the virtue of the Second matter.*

**B**ut so that you may more easily understand what this **second matter** <term>second matter: material that has already been specialized by Nature into a specific kingdom (like a seed), unlike the universal "prime matter" from which all things first arise.</term> is, I will describe to you the virtues <note>original: "virtutes"; here meaning powers or inherent properties</note> by which you may recognize it. And first, you should know that Nature is divided into three Kingdoms; there are two Kingdoms, each of which can stand by itself even if the other two did not exist: these are the Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal kingdoms. The Mineral can subsist by itself, even if there were no humans in the world, nor trees, nor words. The Vegetable likewise can stand by itself even if there were no metal nor animal: these two were created from one thing through one thing. But the third has life from the aforementioned two, and without them it could not exist; it is nobler and more excellent than the previous two, just as it is also the last among them and dominates them: because virtue is always finalized in the third, and multiplied in the second.

Do you see this in the Vegetable Kingdom? The first matter is the Herb or Tree, which you do not know how to create—Nature alone does this. In this kingdom, the second matter is the **seed** which you see; in this, the Herb or Tree is multiplied. In the Animal Kingdom, the first matter is the Beast or the Man, whom you do not know how to create: but you know the second matter, the **sperm**, in which multiplication occurs. In the Mineral Kingdom, you do not know how to create the metal, and if you boast of it, you are vain and a liar; Nature has done this. And even if you possessed the first matter according to the Philosophers—that **central salt** <note>original: "sal centrale"; a theoretical alchemical substance believed to be the hidden core of matter.</note>—nevertheless, without gold, multiplication would be impossible for you. Moreover, only the **sons of doctrine** <note>Initiates or true students of the alchemical arts.</note> have known the vegetable seed of metals. In vegetables, the seed appears on the outside; the "kidneys" of its digestion is the hot air. In animals, the seed appears inside and outside; the kidneys of its digestion are the kidneys of the male. In minerals, the water is the seed in the center of their heart and their life; the "kidneys" of its digestion is fire.

The earth is the receptacle for the vegetable seed: the female's womb is the receptacle for the animal seed: for water—the mineral seed—the receptacle is the air. And those are the receptacles of the seeds, which are the solidifications <term>congelations: the process by which a fluid substance becomes solid or fixed.</term> of bodies: that digestion is the same as solution; that putrefaction is the same as destruction. ## EIGHTH TRACTATE,

### *How Nature operates in the Seed through Art.*

**E**very seed by itself is of no importance, if it is not placed, either by art or by Nature, into a proper womb <term>matrix: the Latin term for a womb or vessel; in alchemy, it refers to the specific environment—soil, water, or a flask—where a seed can grow</term>. And although the seed in itself is more noble than any creature, yet its womb is the life which makes the sperm or grain rot <term>putrefaction: the essential alchemical stage where a substance breaks down to release its inner life-force</term>, and causes the solidification <term>congelation: the process of a liquid or spirit becoming a solid body</term> of the pure point <note>The "pure point" refers to the essential, indivisible core of the seed that contains its life-force.</note>; moreover, by the heat of its own body, the womb nourishes it and makes it grow: and this happens in all the three aforementioned kingdoms of nature, and it happens naturally, through months, years, and seasons.

Truly, wise art is that which can shorten the process somewhat in the mineral and vegetable kingdoms, but not in the animal kingdom: in the mineral kingdom alone, art perfects that which nature cannot, because crude air has filled the pores of every body by its violence—not in the deep bowels of the earth, but on the surface of the earth, as I have said before in previous chapters. But so that this may be more easily understood, I wished to add further that the Elements, competing among themselves, cast their seed into the center of the earth, as if into the kidneys <note>Alchemists often compared the center of the earth to the kidneys, viewing it as a filtering and processing organ for the world's spiritual and material energy.</note>: the center, truly, through motion, emits it into a womb: the wombs, however, are innumerable; there are as many wombs as there are places, one purer than another, and so on almost to infinity. Know therefore that a pure womb will give a pure offspring after its own kind: For example, in animals there are the wombs of humans, cows, horses, dogs, and so forth. # NINTH TRACTATE,

## ->*On the Commixture of Metals, or on the Extraction of the Metallic Seed.*<-

**W**e have spoken of Nature, of Art, of the body, and of the sperm and seed: let us now descend to practice, namely, how metals ought to be mixed together, and what kind of correspondence exists between them. Know therefore that the woman does not differ from the man; both are born from the same seed and in one womb <term>matrix: the Latin term for the womb or the vessel where development occurs</term>; nothing was lacking except digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of ripening or perfecting a substance through steady, gentle heat.</note>, and that the womb be purer in blood and salt: thus Silver <term>Luna: the Moon</term> is from the same seed as Gold <term>Sol: the Sun</term>, and from the same womb: but the womb had more water than digested blood, according to the time of the celestial Moon. But so that you may more easily imagine how metals come together, so that they may emit and receive seed, look at the heavens and the spheres of the planets: you see that Saturn <term>Saturn: the planet associated with Lead</term> is the highest, followed by Jupiter <term>Jupiter: the planet associated with Tin</term>, then Mars <term>Mars: the planet associated with Iron</term>, then the Sun <term>Sol: the planet associated with Gold</term>, followed by Venus <term>Venus: the planet associated with Copper</term>, then Mercury <term>Mercurius: the planet associated with Quicksilver</term>, and in the last place the Moon <term>Luna: the planet associated with Silver</term> is stationed. Consider now that the virtues of the planets do not ascend, but descend: experience itself has shown this, that Mars is not made from Venus, but Venus is made from Mars, as it is one sphere lower: so also Jupiter is easily transmuted into Mercury, because Jupiter is the second from the Firmament <note>The "Firmament" was considered the outermost sphere of the stars; in this traditional geocentric model, Jupiter is the second planet down from the top, and Mercury is the second planet up from the Earth.</note>, and Mercury is the second from the earth: Saturn is the first from heaven, the Moon the first from the earth: the Sun mixes with all, but is never improved by the lower ones. Furthermore, let it not escape you that there is a great correspondence between Saturn and the Moon, in the midst of which the Sun is positioned: just as between Jupiter and Mercury, in the middle of which the Sun also stands: in exactly the same way between Mars and Venus, which two also have the Sun as an intermediary <note>The author is pointing out a numerical symmetry in the seven traditional planets: if you list them in order, the Sun is the 4th, with pairs (1 & 7, 2 & 6, 3 & 5) balanced on either side of it.</note>. Alchemists <term>Chemistæ</term> have known how to change iron into copper or Venus without the Sun: they also know how to make Mercury out of Jupiter: there are also some who from Saturn make—

# TRACTATE X.

## On the Supernatural Generation of the Son of the Sun.

**W**e have treated of the things which Nature creates, and which God has created, so that the searchers of the art might more easily understand the possibility of nature. But, lest I delay any longer: I now approach the method and art of preparing the Philosophers' Stone. The Philosophers' Stone, or the tincture, is nothing other than Gold <term>Aurum: gold</term> digested <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of ripening or perfecting a substance through steady, gentle heat over time.</note> to the highest degree: for common gold <note>original: "Aurum vulgi," referring to ordinary physical gold as opposed to the "Philosophical Gold" or "Tincture" sought by alchemists.</note> is like a plant without seed; when it ripens, it produces seed; so gold, when it ripens, gives seed or a tincture. But someone will ask why gold or another metal does not produce seed: the reason given is this, because it cannot be mature; due to the rawness <note>original: "cruditatem," meaning an unrefined, cold, or "uncooked" state that prevents growth.</note> of the air, it does not have sufficient heat; and it happens in certain places that pure gold is found...

...what nature wished to perfect, but was hindered by crude air <note>In alchemical theory, "crude air" refers to an environment that is too cold or unrefined to allow the natural "digestion" or ripening of minerals and plants.</note>. For example, we see that Orange trees <term>Pomorum Arantiorum: orange trees; literally "Apples of the Arantians"</term> grow in Poland just like other trees: In Italy and elsewhere, where it is their native soil, they give and bear fruit because they have sufficient heat; but in these colder places, they bear none at all, for where they ought to ripen, they stop because they are overwhelmed by the cold; and thus, their fruit is never obtained from Nature in these places. But if nature is occasionally assisted gently and with ingenuity, then art now perfects what nature could not have achieved alone. The same thing happens clearly with metals: Gold can give fruit and seed, in which it multiplies itself, through the industry of the wise artist who knows how to promote nature; but if he wishes to attempt this without following nature, he will err. For not only in this art, but in every thing, we can do nothing except assist Nature; and this is done by no other means than fire or heat. 

But since this cannot happen—if indeed the spirits do not appear in a frozen metallic body—it is necessary that the body first be dissolved and its pores opened, so that nature can operate. As to what kind that solution ought to be, I would like the reader to be warned here that there is a double solution; although there are many other solutions, they are useless. Only one is the true natural solution; the second is a "violent" solution, under which all other methods are included. The natural solution is of such a kind that the pores of the body are opened in our water <term>Aqua nostra: "Our water," a specialized alchemical solvent or "philosophic mercury" used to break down metals without destroying their essence</term>, so that the digested seed may be emitted and placed into its womb <term>matrix: the vessel or environment where alchemical "conception" occurs</term>. 

Our water, however, is a celestial water, one that does not wet the hands; it is not the water of the common people, but is almost like rainwater. The "Body" is the gold which gives the seed: "Our Moon" <term>Luna nostra: "Our Moon," representing a refined form of silver or mercury that acts as the female principle</term> (not the silver of the common people) is that which receives the seed of the gold. It is governed afterward by our continuous fire for seven months, and sometimes ten, until our water consumes three parts and leaves one; and this is done in double. Afterward, it is nourished by the "milk of the earth" <note>original: "lacte terrae"; a metaphorical nutrient, likely a white, refined alkaline substance or a specific state of the matter</note>, or by its fatness which is born in the breasts of the earth, and it is governed or preserved from putrefaction by the salt of Nature. And thus is generated that infant of the second generation.

## TREATISE XI.

### *On the Practice and preparation of the stone or tincture through art.*

THROUGH so many chapters, the discourse on these matters has been scattered using examples, so that the practice might be more easily understood; it must be performed by imitating nature in the following manner.

Take <note>original: "℞." (Recipe), the standard medical and alchemical command to begin a formula.</note> 11 grains of our earth through 11 degrees, 1 grain of our gold (and not common gold), and 2 grains of our silver <note>original: "Lunæ" (of the Moon)</note> (not common silver). But let you be warned of this: do not take the gold and silver of the common people, for these are dead; take ours, which are alive. Afterward, place them in our fire, and a dry liquor <note>A paradoxical alchemical term for a substance that behaves like a fluid but does not wet the hands.</note> will be made from them. First, the earth will be dissolved into water which is called the Mercury of the Philosophers, and another water will dissolve those bodies of the Sun <note>original: "Solis" (Gold)</note> and the Moon, and it will consume them so that only a tenth part remains with one part, and this will be the metallic radical moisture <term>Humidum radicale: the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist within all metals.</term>. 

Afterward, take the water of saltpeter <note>original: "salis nitri"</note> from our earth, in which there is a stream and a living wave if you dig a pit as deep as a knee; take therefore water from it, but take it clear. Into this place that radical moisture, and place it in the fire of putrefaction and generation—not such a fire as you used in the first operation. Rule everything with great ingenuity until colors appear like a Peacock’s tail <term>Cauda Pavonis: a famous stage in the alchemical process where the material in the flask shifts through many iridescent colors.</term>. Rule it by digesting <note>Heating slowly and steadily, like a stomach digesting food.</note>, and do not let it weary you, until the colors cease and one green color appears throughout, and so on with the others. 

And when you see brown ashes at the bottom and the water almost red, open the vessel, moisten a quill, and smear it on some iron. If it tints <note>If the iron changes color, indicating the "Tincture" is beginning to work.</note> the iron, have ready at hand the water of which mention will be made later, and pour in as much of that water as there entered crude air. Cook it again with the former fire until it tints again. My experience has reached thus far; I can do no more, I have found no more. That water, however, must be the solvent of the world <term>Menstruum mundi: a universal solvent or "menstruum," often associated with the celestial influence of the Moon.</term>, from the sphere of the Moon, rectified so many times that it can calcine <note>To reduce a metal to a powder through heat or chemicals.</note> the Sun. Here I have wished to reveal everything to you,

For know that you can create nothing, for that belongs to God alone; but to make the hidden things lurking in the shadow become visible, and to remove the shadow from them—this is granted to the understanding Philosopher by God through nature. 

I pray you, consider the simple water of a cloud: who would ever believe that it contains within itself everything the world holds—hard stones, salts, air, earth, and fire—when it appears to be only simple water? What shall I say of the earth, which contains water, fire, salts, and air within itself, yet seems to be merely naked earth? Oh, how wonderful is nature! She knows how to produce marvelous fruits from water within the earth, and how to supply life to them from the air. All these things happen, and the eyes of common men do not see them; but the eyes of the intellect and the imagination perceive them with a sight that is most true. For the eyes of the wise see nature differently than common eyes. 

For example, the eyes of the common people see the Sun as being hot; but the eyes of the Philosophers, on the contrary, see the Sun as being rather cold, though its motions are hot <note>This refers to the theory that the Sun is not inherently hot, but generates heat through the friction of its motion against the spheres of the planets.</note>. ...it is [this fire], which by its perpetual motion drives heat or rays upward to the surface of the earth. This internal heat is much more powerful than our common elemental fire, but it is tempered by earthly water, which penetrates the pores of the earth day by day and cools it. In the same way, the air that circles the globe daily tempers the celestial Sun and its heat; and were it not for this, all things would be consumed by such heat, and nothing would be born. For just as that invisible fire or central heat would consume all things if water did not intervene, so the heat of the Sun would destroy all things without the air acting as an intermediary.

But I will explain briefly how these Elements act upon one another. In the center of the earth is the **central Sun**, which by its motion, or that of its firmament, provides a great heat that extends all the way to the earth's surface. That heat generates air in this manner: Water is the womb <gloss>matrix</gloss> of the air, which gives birth to children of its own nature, yet unlike itself and much more subtle; for where entry is denied to water, air enters. Therefore, when that central heat, which is perpetual, acts, it causes the water to distill and grow warm; and thus that water, by the force of heat, is turned into air, and in this way it breaks through to the surface of the earth, because it does not allow itself to be enclosed. There, after it has cooled, it is resolved back into water. Meanwhile, in opposite places, it also happens that not only air, but even water emerges, as is seen when black clouds are raised into the air with violence. Let this domestic example serve for you: Make water boil in a pot; you will see slow vapors and winds with a slow fire; with a more intense fire, thicker clouds will appear.

In exactly the same way, the central heat operates: it raises subtle water into air. That which is thick, made of salt or fatness <gloss>original: pinguedine; an alchemical term for the oily, combustible principle in matter</gloss>, it distributes to the earth, from which various things are born; the remainder becomes rocks and stones. Someone might object that if this were the case, then it should happen continuously, yet often no wind is felt. I reply: if water is not poured violently into a distilling vessel, no wind is produced; for a little water excites only a little wind. # TREATISE XII.

## Concerning the Stone, and its power.

**I**N the preceding [treatises] enough has been said regarding the production of natural things, concerning the Elements, and concerning the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the primordial, unformed substance from which all things are created</note> and the <term>second matter</term> <note>original: *materia secunda*; the specialized substance refined from the first matter that the alchemist actually uses in their work</note>, concerning bodies and seeds, and their use and power: I have also written down the practice of making the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: *lapidem Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and grant longevity</note>: but regarding its power—as much as nature has allowed me, and experience has revealed—I will now disclose. But, so that I may first briefly and in few words summarize the argument of all these treatises, so that the God-fearing reader may grasp my mind and my meaning, the matter stands thus. If anyone doubts the truth of the art, let them read the copious writings of the most ancient Philosophers, verified by reason and Experience; as they are worthy of trust, faith should not be withheld from them in their art. But as for one who does not grant them faith, we know that one must not argue against those who deny principles: for the deaf and the mute cannot speak. For what prerogative would all things in this world have over metals? Why should we undeservedly exclude these alone—by the denial of their seed—from the universal blessing of multiplication of the highest Creator, which the <term>Holy Scriptures</term> <note>original: *sacrae literae*</note> affirm was instilled and imparted to all created things immediately from the foundation of the world? But if they have seed, who is so foolish as not to believe that they can be multiplied in their own seed? In its nature, the art of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Chemiæ*; here referring to the "Higher Chemistry" or Alchemy</note> is true; nature is also true, but a true artist is rare: Nature is one, the art is one, but artists are many. Now, nature creates things from the elements; it generates them through the <term>Will of God</term> <note>original: *velle Dei*</note> from the first matter, which God alone knows: nature creates things and multiplies them from the second matter, which the Philosophers know. Nothing happens in the world without the will of God and of nature. For every element is in its own sphere, but one cannot exist without the other; one lives from the other, and yet when joined they do not agree; but water is the most worthy of all elements, because it is the mother of all things: over this floats the spirit of fire. With fire causing a- <note>This page ends mid-word. The text likely continues with "acting" or "agitating" the water to produce the next stage of creation.</note>

<summary>In this twelfth treatise, Sendivogius defends the reality of alchemy by arguing that metals, like all other created things, possess "seeds" and the divine capacity for multiplication. He distinguishes between "first matter," known only to God, and "second matter," which is the secret of the alchemists.</summary>

...by which the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the fundamental, undifferentiated substance of all things</note> is made, namely through the struggle of fire with water; and thus are generated winds or vapors fit to be congealed with earth, through the crude air which was separated from it from the beginning. And this happens without ceasing, by perpetual motion; because fire or heat is not excited otherwise than by motion: which is easily seen in the case of a blacksmith crushing iron with a file, which grows hot by the more vehement motion just as if it had glowed in the fire. Motion, therefore, causes heat, heat moves the water, and the movement of the water causes the air, which is the life of all living things. 

Things grow, therefore, in this manner, as I said above, namely from water: for out of its subtler vapor come subtle, light things; but out of its oil come heavy and more precious things; and out of its salt, things far more beautiful than the former. However, because Nature is sometimes hindered from producing pure things—since the vapor, the oiliness, and the salt are often stained and mixed with the various places of the earth—therefore experience has taught us to separate the pure from the impure. Thus, if you wish for nature to be improved in its actual state, dissolve the body you wish, and separate that which has been added to nature as <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>original: *heterogeneum*; something of a different kind or foreign to the substance</note>; purge it, and join pure with pure, cooked with cooked, and raw with raw, according to nature’s weight and not the weight of the matter. For know that the central <term>salt of nitre</term> <note>original: *sal nitri centrale*; a vital alchemical salt believed to be the "spirit" of the earth</note> does not take more of the earth than it has need of, whether it be pure or impure. The oiliness of the water, however, behaves differently, for it is never found pure; Art purges it through a double heat, and then rejoins it.

...proportion of nature, he extends his hands to the labors. In this holy and most true science, he who has no sun shining for him dwells in nightly darkness; he who sees no moon at night is in dense shadow. Nature has its own light <note>original: *lumen proprium*; the "Light of Nature" is a central concept in alchemical philosophy, referring to an inner wisdom or intuitive understanding of how the natural world works</note>, which is not accessible to our eyes; the shadow of nature, to our eyes, is the body <note>meaning physical, visible matter</note>. But if the Light of Nature shines upon someone, the mist is immediately removed from his eyes; and without hindrance he can behold the point of our magnet <note>original: *punctum magnetis*; here referring to the center of attraction or the focal point where celestial and terrestrial influences meet</note> corresponding to both centers of radiation—namely, of the sun and of the earth. For the Light of Nature penetrates that far and lays open internal things; let this be an example for you of this matter.

Let a youth of twelve years and a girl of the same age be dressed in uniform clothing; if they are placed next to each other, no one will know who is male and who is female; for our eyes cannot penetrate the clothing, therefore our sight deceives us and accepts the false for the true. But when the clothes are removed and they are stripped bare, so that they appear as nature formed them, each is easily distinguished in their sex. In a clearly similar way, our intellect makes a shadow of nature’s shadow; for the naked body in a human is the shadow of the seeds of nature <note>original: *seminis naturae umbra*; the physical form is merely a "shadow" or covering of the true essence or "seed" within</note>. Just as, therefore, the human body is covered by clothes, so too is human nature covered by the body, which God has reserved for Himself to cover and uncover. I could here discourse at length and philosophically about the dignity of man, his creation, and his generation: but since such things do not belong to this place, they must be passed over in silence; I will deal only with his life in a few words.

Man, created from the earth, lives from the air: for there is in the air a hidden food of life <note>this refers to the alchemical theory of a "vital nitre" or spirit in the air that sustains life</note>, which we call dew by night, and by day rarefied water, whose invisible spirit, once congealed, is better than the whole earth. O holy and admirable Nature, who does not permit the "sons of doctrine" <note>original: *filios doctrinae*; a traditional term for students or initiates of the alchemical arts</note> to go astray, as you demonstrate daily in human life! Furthermore, in these twelve *Treatises* I have brought forward so many natural reasons, so that the desiring and God-fearing reader might more easily understand all those things which, with God's blessing, I have seen with my own eyes and performed with my own hands without any fraud of sophistry: for without the Light and knowledge of nature it is impossible to attain this art, unless it happens to someone by a singular divine revelation.

## New Chemical Light

...or through the secret demonstration of a friend. This matter is both cheap and most precious, and though I have described it several times already, I now repeat it once more. **Take** 10 parts of air; 1 part of living gold or living moon <note>original: *Auri vivi vel lunæ vivæ*; alchemical terms for purified or "philosophical" gold and silver/mercury</note>; place all these into your vessel; cook this air first so that it becomes water, and afterwards something that is not water. If you are ignorant of this, and do not know how to cook air, you will undoubtedly wander in error; for this indeed is the matter of the ancient *Philosophers*. You must accept that which exists, but is not seen until it pleases the artisan; it is the water of our dew, and from this water is extracted the *salt of the stone of the Philosophers* <note>original: *sal petræ Philosophorum*; often interpreted as philosophical saltpeter or the "nitre of the world," a central concept in Sendivogius's work</note>, by which all things grow and are nourished. Its *Matrix* <term>Matrix</term> <note>the "womb" or place of origin where a substance is formed</note> is the center of the sun or moon, whether celestial or terrestrial. To speak more openly: our *Magnet* is that which I called "steel" <note>original: *chalybem*</note> in the preceding sections. Air generates the magnet, and the magnet in turn generates—or makes visible—our air. 

I have holily revealed the truth to you here; pray to God that He may prosper your undertakings. In this passage, you have the truest explanation of *Hermes* <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus and the *Emerald Tablet*</note> when he asserts that *its father is the sun, its mother truly the moon, and that the wind carried it in its belly*. This is surely the *Alkali salt* <term>Alkali salt</term> <note>a basic salt, here used as a symbolic term for a transformative agent</note>, which the *Philosophers* named *Ammoniac and vegetable Salt*, hidden in the belly of *magnesia* <note>original: *magnesiæ*; not modern magnesium, but a term for the "raw" material of the Great Work</note>. Its operation is such: you must dissolve the congealed air, in which you then dissolve a tenth part of gold; seal this and labor with our fire until the air is turned into powders. Once the "salt of the world" is obtained, various colors will appear. 

I would have described the entire process in these Treatises, but because the process—along with the method of multiplication—is sufficiently contained in the books of *Lully* <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century polymath and reputed alchemist</note> and other true *Philosophers*, it was enough for me to treat only the *primary and secondary matter*. This I have done candidly. Do not think that any mortal has presented this more clearly than I have; for I did not write this from a collection of many books, but from the labor of my own hands and my own experience. If, therefore, you do not believe the truth, do not blame my book, but yourself; and believe that God does not wish to reveal this secret to you. Weary Him with prayers, and study this little book through many repeated readings, especially the *Epilogue of these 12 Treatises*. Always consider the possibilities of nature and the actions of the elements—noting what is most important among them, particularly in the thinning <note>original: *rarefactione*</note> of water or air—for in this way the heavens and the whole world were created.

<summary>In this concluding section of the "Twelve Treatises," Sendivogius provides a symbolic recipe for the Philosopher's Stone involving "air" and "living gold," while explaining the Hermetic origins of his theory. He emphasizes that his knowledge comes from practical experience rather than just books, urging the reader to seek divine favor and study the rarefaction of elements.</summary>

I have wanted to signify this to you just as a father to a son. Do not wonder why I have written so many treatises; it was not done for my own sake, as I have no need of books, but to warn many who labor in vain things so that they do not spend their resources for nothing. Everything could indeed have been contained in very few lines—even words—but through reasons and examples I wanted to lead you to the knowledge of nature, so that above all you would know what you ought to seek, whether the first or second matter. You would also have nature laid open, with its light and its shadow. Do not be disturbed that sometimes contradictions, *in the usual custom of the Philosophers* <note>original: *more Philosophorum usitato*</note>, may occur to you; you have need of them if you understand, for a rose is not found without thorns.

Ponder diligently what I have said above: namely, how the four elements drip into the earth's center of <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: *humidum radicale*; in alchemical theory, this is the essential, life-sustaining fluid found in all matter that prevents it from becoming brittle and dying.</note>, and how the central earthly sun, by its own motion, produces and <term>sublimes</term> <note>to refine a substance by heating it into a vapor that then collects as a solid; here it refers to the Earth's internal heat pushing vital vapors upward.</note> that moisture to the surface of the earth. I also said that the celestial sun has a correspondence with the central sun: for the celestial sun and moon have a particular power and virtue of dripping through their rays into the earth; for heat is easily joined to heat, and salt to salt. And just as the central sun has its own sea and perceptible crude water, so the celestial sun also has its sea and subtle, imperceptible water. 

On the surface of the earth, rays are joined to rays, and they produce flowers and all things. Therefore, when rain happens, it receives that power of life from the air and joins it with the <term>salt nitre</term> <note>original: *sal nitri*; Sendivogius is famous for his theory of "the nitre of the world," an invisible life-force in the air that is captured by the earth to make plants grow.</note> of the earth (because the salt nitre of the earth is like calcined <term>Tartar</term> <note>original: *Tartari*; a salt-like crust that forms in wine barrels; when "calcined" or burned, it becomes very thirsty and draws moisture from the air.</note>, drawing the air to itself by its dryness; which air is then resolved within it into water. That salt nitre of the earth has such a power of attracting—which was also air once, and is joined to the "fatness" of the earth). And the more abundantly the solar rays strike at that time, the greater the quantity of salt nitre is produced, and consequently a greater abundance of grain grows; and this happens from day to day.

I only wanted to suggest so much to those who are ignorant concerning the correspondence of things among themselves, and the efficacy of the sun, moon, and stars; for those who already know do not require this instruction. Our subject is turned before the eyes of the whole world and yet is not recognized. O our heaven! O our water! O our Mercury! O our salt nitre dwelling in the sea of the world! O our vegetable! O our fixed and volatile <term>sulfur</term>! # TO THE SONS OF TRUTH.
## PREFACE TO THE ENIGMA
### Philosophical.

**I** have now revealed everything to you, sons of science, from the spring of the universal fountain, so that nothing remains further. For in my preceding Treatises I have sufficiently explained nature through examples: I have manifested the Theory and practice as much as was divinely permitted. But lest anyone should complain of Laconism <note>original: *Laconismo*; refers to the Spartan/Laconian habit of extreme brevity, suggesting the author might have been too concise</note>, as if I had omitted something, I will still describe the whole art to you enigmatically, so that you may see how far I have come under God's guidance. Books treating this art are infinite; yet in hardly any will you find the truth revealed to you to such an extent. I wished to provide this because I have conversed with many who thought they understood the writings of the philosophers well; but I found that they explained those same writings much more subtly than nature—which is simple—required. Indeed, all my true sayings seemed too cheap and incredible to those who always seek deep, complex wisdom. Several times it happened that I suggested the art word for word <note>original: *de verbo ad verbum*</note> to some, but they could in no way grasp it, not believing that there is water in our sea, and yet they wished to be seen as Philosophers. Since, therefore, they could not understand my words spoken by mouth, I do not fear (as other Philosophers have feared) that anyone can so easily conceive of the Work; it is a Gift, I say, of God. I asked: "Can it not be further improved?" He said: "According to the Philosophical scripture, it can be exalted first to ten, then to a hundred, then to a thousand, and ten thousand, and so on." I pressed on: "My Lord, do many know this Water, and does it have a proper name?" He cried out openly, saying: "Few know it, but all have seen it, and see it, and love it; it has names, but many and various; but its proper name is the **Water of our sea**, the **Water of life that does not wet the hands** <note>original: *Aqua vitæ non madefaciens manus*; a classic alchemical paradox describing a dry, mercurial vapor or a solvent that acts on metals without behaving like common water</note>." 
<margin>L</margin> I still asked: "Do others use it for other things?" "Every creature uses it," he said, "but invisibly." "Is anything born in it?" I asked. And he: "From it all things in the world are made, and in it they live; but properly there is nothing in it, but it is a thing that mixes itself with every thing." I asked: "Is it useful without this fruit of the Tree?" To this he said: "In this work, not at all; since it is improved only in this fruit of the **Solar Tree** alone." I began to ask: "Lord, I pray you, name it to me by such a manifest name that I can no longer have any doubt." But he, raising his voice, cried out so as to wake me from sleep; therefore I could no longer ask, nor would he answer me further, nor can I tell you more. Be content with these things, and believe that it is not possible to speak more clearly: For if you do not perceive these things, you will never understand the books of other Philosophers. After the unexpected and sudden departure of **Saturn**, a new sleep came over me, and once again **Neptune** appeared to me in visible form:

# New Chemical Light.

...[The Lord/Master]: congratulates me on my present happiness in the **Gardens of the Hesperides** <note>In mythology, these gardens held golden apples; in alchemy, they represent the place where the "Golden" work is perfected</note>, showing me a mirror in which I saw all **Nature** revealed. After various conversations were exchanged back and forth, I gave thanks to him for the benefits shown; for, under his guidance, I had not only entered this most pleasant Garden, but had even come into that most desired conversation with **Saturn** <note>original: *Saturni*; in alchemy, Saturn represents both the metal Lead and the first stage of the work, known as the "blackness" or *nigredo*</note>. But because some difficulties still remained to be sought and investigated due to Saturn's unforeseen departure, I earnestly asked that he might remove my doubt on this desired occasion. I addressed him with these words: "Lord, I have read the books of the Philosophers asserting that all generation happens through male and female, and yet I saw in my dreams that Saturn placed only the fruit of the **Solar tree** <note>The Solar tree represents Gold</note> upon our **Mercury**; I believe that you, as the Lord of this Sea, know these things well; answer my question, I pray?" 

But he replied: "It is true, son; all generation happens in male and female; but, because of the distinction of the three kingdoms of Nature, a four-footed Animal is born in one way, and a **worm** in another. For although worms have eyes, sight, hearing, and the rest of the senses, they are nonetheless produced through **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactionem*; a key alchemical stage where the matter "dies" and rots to be reborn. At this time, it was believed worms were spontaneously generated from decaying matter</note>, and their place or the earth in which they rot is the female. So in the Philosophical work, the mother of this thing is that **Water** of yours, so often mentioned, and whatever is born from it is born through putrefaction in the manner of worms. 

Therefore the Philosophers created the **Phoenix** and the **Salamander** <note>These mythical creatures represent the Philosopher's Stone: the Phoenix for its ability to be reborn from ashes, and the Salamander for its ability to survive and be perfected in fire</note>. For if it were made from the conception of two bodies, it would be a thing subject to death; but because it only revives itself, once the prior body is destroyed, another incorruptible one shines forth. Indeed, the death of things is nothing other than the separation of one from the other. And in this Phoenix it happens in such a way that life separates itself from the corruptible body by its own power." 

Furthermore I asked: "My Lord, are there different substances or a composition of things in this work?" 

But he said: "It is a **single thing**, with which nothing else is mixed except the **Philosophical Water** manifested to you several times in sleep, which ought to be in a **tenfold** <note>original: *decuplo*; a common alchemical ratio of 10 parts solvent (water/mercury) to 1 part solute (the "fruit" or gold)</note> amount to one part of the body. And you should believe firmly and without doubt, son, that those things which were revealed to you by me and by Saturn through dreams on this island—according to the custom of this region—are in no way dreams, but the purest truth, which a unique experience of things..."

# DIALOGUE

## OF MERCURY, THE ALCHEMIST, AND NATURE.

AT that time the Chemists convened and held a council on how they ought to make and prepare the <term>PHILOSOPHERS' STONE</term> <note>original: *LAPIDEM PHILOSOPHORUM*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and acting as a universal elixir</note>, and so they decided that everyone should express his own opinion by vote. And that gathering took place during the day in a certain meadow, on a certain clear day. And many agreed that Mercury was its first matter, others Sulphur, others other things. But regarding Mercury, the majority held that opinion, especially based on the sayings of the Philosophers, since they hold it as the true <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the primitive, unformed substance from which all things originate</note>, and even as the first matter of Metals: for the Philosophers cry out: <term>OUR MERCURY</term> <note>original: *NOSTER MERCURIUS*; alchemists often distinguished between common quicksilver and "Our Mercury," a refined or philosophical version of the element</note> etc. And while they were thus contending among themselves with various labors (for each of them awaited the conclusion with desire and joy), meanwhile a great storm arose with tempests, clouds, and an unheard-of wind, which dispersed that congregation into various provinces, each one separately and without a conclusion. Each of them, however, impressed upon himself what the end of that dispute ought to have been. Therefore, each began his labors just as before, one in this thing, another in that, seeking the <term>PHILOSOPHERS' STONE</term>, and this continues until now without ceasing. But one of them, mindful of the dispute, that it must necessarily be sought in Mercury—

<summary>The narrator wakes from his alchemical vision in the Garden of the Hesperides, returning to Europe. The text then transitions into a famous allegorical dialogue where a group of alchemists fails to agree on the "first matter" of the Stone before being scattered by a storm.</summary>

[how the] <term>Philosophers’ Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*</note> is to be sought, he said to himself: "Even though no conclusion has been reached, yet I will labor in Mercury, and I myself will make the conclusion once the blessed stone is made"; for he was a man who was always accustomed to speak just as Alchemists are accustomed to do. The wretched Alchemist, ignorant of its nature, beat his wife, saying: "No one could have come here except you; you have taken my Mercury out of the glass for me." The wife, weeping, excused herself, and said quietly to her husband: "May you make dung out of these things." <note>original: *merdam*; the wife's retort is a vulgar play on the alchemist's failure to produce gold from his materials</note> The Alchemist took Mercury again, and again placed it in a vessel, and lest his wife should take it, he guarded it.
