The Alchemist, remembering that the first matter of the philosophers' stone ought to be <term>volatile</term> <note>easily evaporated at normal temperatures; in alchemy, "volatility" was a key spiritual and physical property to be "fixed" or stabilized</note>, rejoiced greatly, persuading himself entirely that he could no longer be deceived now that he possessed this matter. He began now to treat Mercury boldly; he learned afterwards to <term>sublime</term> <note>to heat a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then becomes solid again upon cooling</note> it, and to <term>calcine</term> <note>to reduce a substance to powder or ash by heating</note> it in wondrous ways—now with salts, now with sulfur, now with metals, now with minerals, now with blood, hair, <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: *aquis fortib⁹* (aquae fortes); nitric acid or other powerful mineral acids used to dissolve metals</note>, now with herbs, urine, and vinegar—but he could find nothing to suit his purpose. He left nothing in the world untouched with which he had not treated the good Mercury. And when he could profit nothing at all, he happened upon this saying: *that it is found in the dunghill.* <note>original: *quod in sterquilinio invenitur*; a famous alchemical paradox suggesting that the most precious substance is found in the most common or rejected places</note> He began to treat Mercury with various dungs, both together and separately; and when he had been so fatigued and was full of thoughts, he fell asleep. 

And in his sleep a vision appeared to him: an **Old Man** came to him, who greeted him and said: "Friend, why are you sad?" He replied: "I would gladly make the Philosophers’ Stone." Then the man said: "Friend, from what do you wish to make the Philosophers’ Stone?" 

**Alchemist.** From Mercury, Lord. 

**Old Man.** But from what kind of Mercury? 

**Alchemist.** There is only one Mercury. 

**Old Man.** It is true that there is only one Mercury, but it is varied in various places; one part is purer than the other. 

**Alchemist.** Oh Lord, I know how to purge it best with vinegar and salt, with nitre and vitriol...

The Alchemist, awakened from sleep, pondered what that vision might be, and what that <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>A refined, "living" substance the alchemists sought, as opposed to the common liquid metal (quicksilver)</note> ought to be; but he could think of nothing else except this, his <term>common mercury</term> <note>original: *mercurium vulgi*; the ordinary quicksilver used in trade</note>. And that wretched Alchemist, after so many labors and the consumption of his goods, was now falling into a delirium, always thinking of that old man. But the Alchemist begged him, saying: "Lord, wait!" and the wretch was awakened by his own shouting—yet not without great consolation. Afterward, he took a vessel full of Mercury and began to conjure it in strange ways, just as the dream had taught him. And he remembered the words of the old man, who had said: *Snakes are conjured, and Mercury is depicted with snakes* <note>A reference to the Caduceus, the staff of the god Mercury, which features two entwined serpents</note>. And taking the vessel with the Mercury, he began to say: "*Ux ux, ostas, etc.*" <note>nonsense magic words from the original text</note>. And where the name of the snake should have been in the spell, he placed the name of Mercury, saying: "And you, Mercury, most wicked beast, etc." 

At these words, Mercury began to laugh and spoke to the Alchemist, saying: "What do you want, that you disturb me, my Lord Alchemist?"

**The Alchemist**: "Oho, now you call me 'Lord' when I touch you to the quick! Now I have found a bridle for you; wait a little, soon you will sing my tune!" And he began to speak to him strenuously, as if in anger: "Are you [the one]..."

...to be inconstant; I resolve this for you in this way. I am constant to a constant craftsman, and fixed to one with a fixed mind: but you and those like you are inconstant, wandering from one thing to another, and from one material to another. *Alchemist:* Tell me then, if you are that <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of liquidity, volatility, and the "spirit" of metals.</note> of whom the Philosophers wrote—the one they called the principle of all things along with <term>sulfur</term> and <term>salt</term> <note>These three—Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt—were known as the "Tria Prima," the three fundamental principles of matter according to Paracelsus.</note>—or should another be sought? *Mercury:* Truly, the fruit does not fall far from the tree, but I do not seek my own glory: I am the same as I was, but my years are different. From the beginning I was young as long as I was alone, but now I am older, yet still the same as I was before. *Alchemist:* Now you please me, because you are now older: for I have always sought one who is more mature and more "fixed," <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance that can withstand fire without evaporating, as opposed to "volatile."</note> so that I might more easily come to an agreement with him. *Mercury:* In vain do you visit me as an old man, you who did not know me in my youth. *Alchemist:* Do I not know you? I who will perhaps be mixed with dung again; now I am tortured anew. O miserable me! I beg you, O Master Philosopher, do not mix me with so much pig dung: for otherwise I will perish now, for by this stench I am forced to change my form. And what more do you want me to do? Am I not tortured enough by you? Do I not obey you? Do I not mix myself with the things you wish? Am I not <term>sublimated</term>? <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again.</note> Am I not <term>precipitated</term>? <note>The process of causing a substance to deposit in solid form from a solution.</note> Am I not <term>Turbith</term>? <note>original: *Turbit*. What more do you desire from me now? My body has already been so whipped, so spat upon, that even a stone could pity me: from me you have milk, from me flesh, from me blood, from me butter, from me oil, from me water—and what metal or mineral could ever provide what I alone can? And yet there is no mercy for me. O miserable me! *Alchemist:* Oh ho! It does not hurt you; you are a rogue. Although you may turn yourself inside out in any way, you do not change yourself; you only fashion a "form" for yourself, and you always return again to your original species. *Mercury:* I do as you wish; if you want me to be a body, I am a body: if you want me to be dust, I am dust. I do not know how I should humble myself more than when I become dust and shadow. *Alchemist:* Tell me then, who are you...

...you are in your center? and I will not torture you further. **Mercur.** Now I am forced to speak with you from the foundation <note>meaning: from basic principles or fundamental truth</note>. Tell me if you are the little fountain <note>original Latin: "fontina"</note> of which <term>Bernard, Count of Trevisan</term> <note>An influential 15th-century alchemist; his "fountain" is a famous allegory for the solvent used to dissolve gold.</note> wrote? **Mercur.** I am not a little fountain, but I am water; my little fountain has surrounded me. **Alchem.** Does gold dissolve in you, since you are water? **Mercur.** Whatever is with me I love, like a friend; and whatever is born with me, I give it nourishment; and whatever is naked, I cover with my wings. **Alchem.** I see that there is no talking with you; I seek one thing, you say another: if you do not wish to answer well, I am certainly going to work with you now. **Mercur.** Oh Lord, I beg you, be merciful to me; now I will gladly say what I know. **Alchem.** Tell me then, do you fear fire? **Mercur.** I myself am fire. **Alchem.** And why then do you flee from fire? **Mercur.** My spirit and the spirit of fire love each other, and as much as it can, one accompanies the other. **Alchem.** And where do you usually go when you ascend with fire? **Mercur.** Know that every pilgrim always strives toward his homeland, and when he comes to that place from which he departed, he rests, and he always returns wiser than he left. **Alchemist.** Do you return again sometimes? **Mercur.** I return, but in another form. **Alchem.** I do not understand what this is, nor anything about fire. **Mercur.** If anyone...

...he has known the fire of my heart, he has seen that fire (the required heat <note>original Latin: "calorem debitum"; the specific, balanced temperature needed for alchemical work</note>) is my food: and the longer he eats the fire of the spirit of my heart, the fatter he will be; his death is afterwards the life of all things that are in this kingdom where I am. *Alchem.* Are you great? *Mercur.* You have me as an example: from a thousand droplets I will be one, and from one I give many thousands of drops; and as my body is before your eyes, if you know how to play with me, you can divide me as much as you wish, and again I will be one. What then is my spirit (my heart) internally, which always produces many thousands from the smallest part? *Alchem.* And how, therefore, must one act with you so that you may be so? *Mercur.* I am fire within; fire is my food; but the life of fire is air; without air, fire is extinguished. Fire prevails over air, therefore I do not rest, nor can crude air constrain me. Add air to air so they may both be one and hold weight; join them with hot fire; give them to the times <note>meaning: the passing of seasons or a specific duration of time</note> to be guarded. *Alchem.* What will happen afterwards? *Mercur.* The superfluous will be drawn away; you will burn the residue with fire; you will place it in water and cook it; afterwards, you will give the cooked substance as medicine to the sick. *Alchem.* You tell me nothing in response to my questions. I see that you only wish to elude me with parables. Wife! Bring pig dung! I will treat this Mercury in new ways until he tells me how the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The legendary goal of alchemy, a substance that could transmute metals and heal diseases.</note> is to be made from it. Mercury, having heard these things, begins to lament over the Alchemist and goes to mother Nature; he accuses the ungrateful laborer. Nature believes her son Mercury, who is truthful, and moved by anger she comes to the Alchemist and calls him: "Hey you! Where are you?" *Alchem.* Who is it that calls me? *Natura.* Why, you fool, do you act thus with my son? Why do you do him such injury? Why do you torture him? He who wishes to do all good for you, if only you were willing to understand. *Alchem.* What Devil rebukes me, such a great Man and Philosopher? *Natura.* O fool! Full of pride, you philosophers' dung <note>original: "stercus Philosophorum"; a satirical insult using alchemical terminology, as dung was often used as a heat source</note>! I know the Philosophers and all the Wise Men, whom I love, for they also love me and do everything according to my pleasure; and where I am unable to go, they help me. But you Alchemists—of whose order you are also one—act without my knowledge and consent, indeed...

<summary>In this passage, Mercury describes his transformative, self-multiplying nature through the metaphor of fire and air, but the Alchemist, frustrated by these allegories, threatens to use crude materials like pig dung. This prompts Mother Nature to intervene and rebuke the Alchemist for his arrogance and ignorance of her laws.</summary>

### PREFACE.

*Since I am not permitted, kind Reader, to write more openly than other ancient Philosophers <term>Philosophers: in this context, the term refers to "Natural Philosophers" or alchemists</term> have written, perhaps you will not be satisfied with my writings: Especially since you have so many other books of the Philosophers at hand. But believe me, I have no need to write books for my own sake, because I seek neither profit nor vain ostentation from them; therefore, I do not even wish to reveal who I am. Those things which I have already published for your benefit seemed to me to be more than enough; the rest I had intended to set aside for the *Harmony* <note>The "Harmony" likely refers to a larger, comprehensive work Sendivogius planned on the correspondence between the macrocosm (the universe) and the microcosm (man).</note>, where I have proposed much concerning natural things. Nevertheless, at the urging of friends, I felt compelled to write this treatise on Sulphur <term>Sulphur: for alchemists, "Sulphur" was not just the yellow mineral, but the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle found in all matter</term>; in which I do not know if it is necessary to add anything to my previous works. Indeed, if the writings of so many Philosophers do not satisfy you, neither will this one. And especially if the daily operations of nature are not a sufficient example for you, no other examples will help. For if you would consider with mature judgment how nature works, you would have no need for such volumes of Philosophers, since in my judgment it is better to learn from the master, Nature herself, than from her disciples. Enough was said in the preface of the little book of the Twelve Treatises, and also in the first treatise: there you may find the reason why so many and such great books are found in this art, which now hinder those who search more than they help; and it seems to be so because the writings of the Philo-* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "rum," which would complete the word "Philosophorum" or "of the Philosophers" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page serves as the title and preface for the "Second Treatise on Sulphur" by Michael Sendivogius. The author explains that he writes at the request of friends and encourages the reader to study the operations of Nature directly rather than relying solely on the confusing, often contradictory books of other alchemists.</summary>
<keywords>Sulphur, Michael Sendivogius, Alchemy, Nature as Master, New Chemical Light, Twelve Treatises, Anagram</keywords>

# PREFACE.

*...of the Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophorum," completing the word from the previous page.</note> have grown from such a small scroll of <term>Hermes: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy to whom the "Emerald Tablet" is attributed</term> into such a great and profoundly erroneous labyrinth, and they decline daily toward an eclipse. I believe this has been done by none other than the envious who possess the knowledge; for an ignorant person would not know what ought to be added or taken away, unless perhaps the author's handwriting could not be easily read.*
*If in any science it helps or hinders much if a single word is missing or redundant, it is especially so in this one. For example: it is written in one place:*
*Afterward, you should mix these waters together; another person added the word "not." He added very little, yet he made the entire chapter mean the opposite. Nevertheless, let the diligent student know that the bee gathers honey even from poisonous herbs: for if he directs his reading toward the possibility of nature, he will easily overcome these sophisms <term>sophisms: clever but false arguments intended to deceive</term>. Yet, let him not cease reading, for "one book opens another." But I have understood it thus: that the books of <term>Geber the Philosopher: Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of Islamic alchemy</term>—and who knows if the same is not true for other authors?—are enchanted with the greatest curses, so that they can in no way be understood, nor ought they to be, except upon the thousandth reading, and then only by a clever reader; the foolish are plainly excluded from reading them. Indeed, there are many who interpret him, as well as other authors; but I see that the explanation is often more difficult than the text itself.*
*My advice is that you remain within the text, and whatever you read, apply it all to the possibility of nature; and first of all, investigate what nature is. Everyone writes that the matter is a cheap, easy, and common thing; and it is indeed true, but it should have been added: "to those who know." He who knows recognizes it even among dung, while he who is ignorant does not believe it is present even in gold. And if all those who composed such obscure books did not already know the art, but had to seek the art from books of that kind (which are indeed most true), they would find it with more difficulty than modern seekers do. I do not wish to praise my own writings; he who applies them to the possibility and course of nature shall judge them. And if from my writings, counsels, and examples, he cannot come to know the operation of nature, and its ministers—the <term>vital spirits: the subtle, life-giving forces believed to animate matter</term> that constrict the air—as well as the subject of the <term>first matter: the "prima materia," the original, formless base of all substance</term>, he will hardly understand them from <term>Raymond Lull: a 13th-century polymath and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</term>. For it is difficult to believe that Spirits have such power in the <term>belly of the wind: a famous and cryptic phrase from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes</term>. I was compelled to cross this forest myself, and I have helped to increase it; yet in such a way that my "plants" <note>The author uses "plants" as a metaphor for his instructions or the truths he has planted in his writing.</note> should be signs and as a light and guides for the true sons of the art, and for students of this Sacred Science who wish to cross through this forest; for my plants are like cor[poreal] spirits...*

# PREFACE.

*...temporal <note>original: "porales," completing "temporales" from the previous page</note>. For centuries have already passed when the confidence of friends flourished, and this science was given by word of mouth; now it is acquired only by the inspiration of God the Most High alone. Therefore, let the diligent and God-fearing seeker not despair; if he seeks it, he will find it. For it is obtained more easily from God than from man: for He is a God of immense mercy, who knows not how to desert the one who trusts; with Him, there is no respect of persons; He will not despise a contrite and humbled heart—He who had mercy even on me, the most unworthy of His creatures; whose power, goodness, and inexplicable mercy, which He deigned to show me, I am not sufficient to explain. But if I can give no other thanks, at least with my pen I shall not cease to offer these things to the times. Be of good courage, therefore, honest reader, and He will not deny this grace to you either: if you place your whole hope in Him, if you adore and invoke Him, He will open the door of nature to you; there you will see how nature operates in the simplest way. Know for certain that nature is most simple, nor does she delight in anything but simplicity; and believe me, whatever is more noble in nature is also easier and simpler, because all truth is simple: God the Most High, the creator of things, placed nothing difficult in nature. If, therefore, you wish to be an imitator of nature, I advise you to remain in the simple path of nature, and you will find all good things. But if indeed neither my writings nor my counsel please you, go to other authors: I do not write great volumes so that you do not spend much on them, and you may be able to read through them quickly, so that you have time to turn to other authors. And do not cease to seek, for to the one who knocks, it shall be opened. Now those times also arrive in which many <term>secrets of nature: "arcana naturae," refers to the hidden workings of the physical and spiritual world</term> shall be revealed: Now that <term>Fourth Northern Monarchy: A prophetic concept based on the Book of Daniel, widely discussed in the 17th century, suggesting a final age of wisdom and peace would arise from the North</term> is about to begin. Now the times approach; the <term>mother of sciences: often referring to Alchemy or the "True Philosophy" that underlies all knowledge</term> will come; greater things will be elucidated than happened in these three past Monarchies. Because this Monarchy (as the ancients divined) God will plant through one of the Princes enriched with all virtues, whom perhaps the times have already produced for us. For we have in this northern part a most Wise and warlike Prince, whom none of the Monarchs surpasses in victories, and none excels in humanity and piety. In this Northern Monarchy, God, the creator of all things, will undoubtedly elucidate greater secrets in nature than in those times when the seat was either of Pagans or Tyrant Princes. But these Mo-* <note>original: "Mo-", catchword for "Monarchias" (Monarchies)</note>

...monarchies. Philosophers number them not according to those who are most powerful, but according to the four Quarters <term>Cardines: The four cardinal points or "hinges" of the world (North, South, East, West).</term> of the world: First the Eastern; then the Southern; now indeed they hold the Western; and they expect the final Northern one in this boreal region: regarding which more will be given in the "Harmony" <note>Likely referring to a forthcoming work or section on the "Harmony of the World."</note>. In this Northern, attractive, polar Monarchy (as the Psalmist says): *Mercy and truth shall meet each other; peace and righteousness shall kiss; Truth shall spring from the earth, and Righteousness shall look down from heaven.* <note>A translation of Psalm 85:10-11, often used by alchemists to describe the perfection of the Great Work.</note> *One fold, and one shepherd* (John 10:16). Many sciences without envy: which I also await with desire. You also, honest Reader, invoke God, fear Him, love Him, and read my writings diligently, and surely promise good things to yourself. For if, by God's favor and the operation of nature (which you should imitate), you arrive at the desired harbor of this Monarchy; then you will see and judge that I have told you all things good and true. Farewell.

# ON SULFUR,
## THE SECOND OF THE PRIN-
## CIPLES.

**S**ULFUR <note>original: "SULPHUR"</note> is not the least among the Principles, since it is a part of Metal; indeed, it is the principal part of the Philosophers' Stone <term>Philosophers' Stone: The legendary substance in alchemy capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</term>. Many Wise men have left various and most true accounts concerning Sulfur; indeed, Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 8th-century polymath and the most famous figure in early alchemy.</note> himself in his *Sum of Perfection*, book 1, chapter 28, says: *By the Most High God, it illuminates every body; for it is light from light, and a tincture.* <note>original: "tinctura." In alchemy, a tincture is a substance capable of infusing its properties or color into another body.</note> However, before we treat it, it seemed right to us first to describe the origin of the Principles; especially since Sulfur was anciently held to be the chief of the Principles. Yet, few until now have shown from where the Principles arise; and it is difficult to judge any of the Principles, just as with any other thing whose origin and generation are unknown: for what can a blind man say of color? Therefore, what our predecessors have omitted, we have proposed to fulfill in this Treatise.

There are, however, two principles of things, especially of Metals, according to the ancient Philosophers: Sulfur and Mercury. But according to the Moderns <note>original: "Neotericos", referring to the "New Physicians" or Paracelsians who added a third principle to the traditional Aristotelian/Arabic duo.</note> there are three: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. The origin of these Principles, however, is the four Elements; and it is with their origin that we must primarily begin. Let the Students of this Sacred Science <note>original: "S. Scientiæ", meaning the "Sacred Science" of alchemy.</note> know, therefore, that there are four Elements, and that each of these four has another Element at its center from which it is "elementated" <note>The idea that elements are nested or derived from one another’s core essences.</note>. These are the four Statues of the World, separated from Chaos during the Creation of the World by Divine Wisdom, which hold this mechanism of the World in equality and proportion through their contrary actions, and through the inclination of celestial virtues, they produce all things below and above the earth. These shall be discussed in their proper place; here, for our purpose, we begin first with the closer Element of Earth.

->## ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH.<-

**E**ARTH is an Element of sufficient worth in its quality and dignity. In this Element, the other three—and especially <term>Fire</term>—find their rest. It is a most excellent Element for concealing and manifesting those things which have been entrusted to it. It is dense and porous; heavy in respect to its smallness, but light in respect to its nature. It is also the Center of the World, as well as of the other Elements. The Axis of the World, through both Poles, passes through its Center. It is porous, as we have said, like a sponge which brings forth nothing of itself; but whatever the other three drip and cast into it, it receives all of it—keeping what is to be kept, and manifesting what is to be manifested. That which is heavy is hidden within it, and heat drives that which is light to its surface. It is the nurse and matrix of every seed and mixture; indeed, it can provide nothing else than to protect the seed and the compound until maturity. It is cold and dry, tempered by water;

## ON THE ELEMENT OF WATER.

**W**ATER is the heaviest Element <note>While earth is physically "heavier" in modern terms, alchemy often characterized water's "heaviness" by its ability to permeate and carry dense substances.</note>; full of unctuous phlegm <note>oily or thick moisture</note>; and it is an Element more noble in its quality. It is volatile on the outside, but fixed within; it is cold and moist, and is tempered by air. Whatever the air drips into the water, with fire acting as the cause, the water hands over to the earth. But since His goodness tends toward the better, He will one day exalt His Most Holy Majesty, and will raise higher that purest fire of all which is in the **firmament** for the waters of the heavens, and will give a stronger degree to the **Central fire**, so that all waters may be elevated into the air, and the earth will be <term>calcined</term> <note>calcined: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities and reduce it to a powder</note>: and <unclear>from the pools</unclear>, all impurity being consumed, He will restore the subtle, circulated waters in the air to the purified earth, and thus will effect a much more noble world (if one may otherwise philosophize).

## ON THE ELEMENT OF AIR.

**A**IR is a whole element, most worthy in its quality; externally it is light and invisible, but internally it is heavy, visible, and fixed. It is hot and moist, tempered by fire, and is more worthy than earth and water. It is indeed volatile, but it can be fixed, and when it is fixed, it renders every body penetrable. From its purest substance, the Vital Spirits <term>vital spirits: the refined, airy substance believed to sustain life, breath, and movement in living beings</term> of animals were created; the less pure part was raised into the Air's own Sphere, but the remainder—its coarser part—remained in the water, where it circulates with the water just as fire does with the earth, because they are friends. The pores of the Earth also are preserved by air. In short, the whole structure of the world is preserved by air. Even in animals: a Human is killed if air is taken away, etc. Nothing in the world would grow if there were not the force of penetrating air, altering and attracting with it multiplicative nourishment.

In this Element, the seed <term>semen: the formative principle or "blueprint" of a thing</term> is imagined <note>original: "imaginatum"; here meaning "conceived" or "brought into form" by the creative power of fire</note> by the power of fire, which constricts the *menstruum* of the world <term>menstruum mundi: the universal solvent or life-bearing fluid of nature</term> through that hidden force. In this Element, all things are whole through the imagination of fire; and it is full of divine power. If it is so as it truly is—that the Spirit of the Lord was carried within it—why do you doubt that He left something of His divine power within it? For this Monarch <note>referring to God</note> is accustomed to adorn His dwellings; and He adorned this Element with the vital spirit of every creature. ## ON THE ELEMENT OF FIRE.

**FIRE** is the purest element and the most worthy of all, full of a clinging, oily corrosiveness; it is penetrating, digesting, corroding, and clings most strongly. It is visible on the outside, but truly invisible within; it is most fixed, hot, and dry, and it is tempered by the earth. At the creation, its purest substance and essence was first elevated with the Throne of Divine Majesty when the waters of the heavens were established, as we said in the chapter on the Element of Water. From its less pure substance, the Angels were created. From its even less pure substance, mixed with the purest air, the luminaries and stars were created. A still less pure part was raised into the Sphere to enclose and support the heavens. But the impure and oily part was left and enclosed by the most wise supreme Creator at the center of the earth to continue the operation of motion; this we call <term>Gehenna</term> <note>original: "gehennam"; while often meaning "hell," in this alchemical context it refers to the "central fire" of the earth that provides the heat necessary for the growth of minerals and the movement of the elements</note>. All these fires are indeed divided, but they have a natural sympathy toward one another.

This element is the quietest of all and resembles a chariot; when it is drawn, it runs; when it is not drawn, it stands still. It exists in all things imperceptibly. Within it are the vital principles and the intellect, which are distributed during the first infusion of human life; these are called the **rational soul** <note>original: "anima rationalis"; in medieval and early modern philosophy, this is the highest part of the soul, unique to humans, allowing for reason and connection to the divine</note>, by which alone man differs from other animals and is made like God. This soul is divinely infused into the vital spirit by that most pure elemental fire; because of this, after the creation of all things, man was created as a particular world or **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmum"; the "little world," the idea that a human being mirrors the structure and principles of the entire universe</note>. In this subject, God the Creator of all things has placed His seat and Majesty, as if in the purest and quietest subject, which is governed by His will alone and His immense wisdom.

For this reason, God abhors all impurity; nothing filthy, composite, or stained can approach God. Therefore, no mortal can see God or approach Him by natural means. For that fire which exists in the circumference of the divinity, in which the seat and Majesty of the Most High are carried, is so intense that no eye can penetrate it; for fire does not allow anything **composite** <note>original: "compositum"; in alchemy, anything made of mixed parts rather than a single, pure essence. God is seen as "Simple" or unmixed purity</note> to approach. Indeed, fire is the death and separation of every composite thing. 

We have said that this subject is most quiet (as it truly is); otherwise, it would follow (which is absurd even to think) that God could not be at rest. It is characterized by the quietest silence, more than the human mind can imagine. You have an example in **flint** <note>The author uses the spark hidden in a cold stone to explain how divine "fire" can be present but inactive until "excited" or willed into action</note>, in which there is fire, and yet it is not felt or seen until it is excited by motion and kindled within so that it appears. In the same way, that fire in which the <term>Most Holy Majesty</term> <note>original: "SS. Majestas"; an abbreviation for Sanctissima Majestas</note> of our Creator is located does not move unless it is excited by the own will of the Most High, and thus it is carried to where His <term>Holy Will</term> <note>original: "S. Voluntas"; an abbreviation for Sancta Voluntas</note> intends.

What silence? Even if one of his courtiers moves, the motion is only that of one or another individual, which is not considered. But when the Lord himself moves, there is a noise and a universal motion; then all those in attendance move with him. What then, when that supreme Monarch, the **King of Kings**,

But someone will ask how we know these things, since celestial matters are hidden from human intellect. To them we answer that these things are manifest to all philosophers; indeed, that same incomprehensible wisdom has inspired them with the truth that all things are made according to the example of created nature. They understand that nature derives its hidden retreat <note>original: "retractum"; referring to the internal source or blueprint from which nature operates</note> and its operation from those secrets, and that nothing happens on earth except after the example of the heavenly monarchy, as is seen in the various duties of the angels.

Thus also, nothing is born or generated except by natural means. All human inventions, indeed even the arts and crafts <note>original: "artificia"; this refers to both mechanical inventions and the "Great Art" of alchemy</note> which exist now or will exist in the future, proceed from nothing but the foundations of nature. The Most High Creator wished to manifest all natural things to man; for that reason, He shows us the Heavens themselves, which were made naturally, so that through them His absolute and incomprehensible power and wisdom might be better known. All these things the Philosophers are able to see in the **light of nature** <note>original: "lumine naturae"; a key concept in Hermetic philosophy suggesting that nature itself is a book through which God reveals wisdom to those who study it</note> as if in a mirror.

Therefore, they have greatly valued this science—not out of a greed for gold or silver, but for the knowledge of all natural things and of the power of the Creator Himself. They wished to speak of these things very sparingly and only figuratively, lest the divine mysteries, through which nature is made clear, be revealed to the unworthy.

This you might easily comprehend, if you know how to "know yourself" and are not **stiff-necked** <note>original: "durae cervicis"; a biblical idiom for being stubborn, proud, or resistant to spiritual truth</note>; for you were created according to the likeness of the **greater world** <note>the Macrocosm, or the universe at large</note>, and indeed, in the very image of God. You have the purest blood in the place of fire, in which the seat of the soul is placed (acting as a King) by the vital spirit. You have the heart in the place of earth, where the **central fire** <note>original: "ignis centralis"; the alchemical idea of a sustaining, life-giving heat at the core of all things</note> continually works and holds this machine of the **Microcosm** <note>the human being as a "little world"</note> in its being. 

You have the Arctic pole in your mouth; you have the Antarctic pole in your belly <note>original: "aluum"; referring to the lower torso or bowels, representing the "southern" pole of the human axis</note>, and all your members correspond to the celestial ones. When the soul conceives an idea, the mind knows it all; and all the limbs of the body understand the mind, obeying it and waiting with desire to fulfill its will.

For the body itself knows nothing; whatever strength or movement exists in the body is produced by the mind. The body is merely an instrument for the mind, like the tools of a craftsman. However, the soul—by which man differs from all other animals—operates within the body but has an even greater operation outside of it. It rules absolutely outside the body, and in this way, man differs from animals, which possess only a mind but not the soul of the deity.

In this same way, God the Founder of all things, our Lord and God, works within this world on those things necessary for the world’s existence, and in these He is included within the world; hence it is to be believed that God is everywhere. Yet, through His immense wisdom, He is also set apart outside the "body" of the world, where He works beyond it and imagines things far higher than the body of the world can conceive. These things are beyond nature and are the secrets of God alone.

A clear example of this is found in the soul, which imagines many profound things outside the body; in this, it is made like unto God, who works outside His world beyond the laws of nature. However, these human capacities are still like a single lit candle compared to the light of the midday sun. This is because the soul imagines but cannot execute those thoughts except within the mind; God, however, brings all things into being at the very same moment He imagines them. For instance, the soul might imagine being in **Rome** <note>original: "Romæ"</note> or elsewhere, seeing whatever is happening there in the blink of an eye—but only in the mind. God, being **omnipotent** <note>all-powerful</note>, makes such things real in their very essence. Therefore, God is not enclosed in the world except in the way that the soul is enclosed in the body...

We said above that the **Element of Fire** is most quiet, and that it is awakened by motion—an awakening known to wise men. It is necessary for the Philosopher <note>In this context, "Philosopher" refers to an alchemist or natural scientist</note> to know every kind of generation and the corruption thereof; to him, not only is the **Creation of the heavens** manifest, but also the composition and mixture of all things. In the work of the Philosophers, nature must awaken the fire which was hidden by the Creator within the center of every thing. Such an awakening of fire happens by the will of nature, or sometimes by the will of the wise craftsman <note>the alchemist</note> who arranges nature. For naturally, all impurities and pollutions of things are purged by fire. Every compound is dissolved by fire. Just as water washes and purges all imperfect things that are not **fixed** <term>fixed: a term for substances that remain stable and do not evaporate or change when exposed to heat</term>, so fire purges all fixed things, and they are perfected through fire. Just as water joins everything that is dissolved, so fire separates everything that is joined; it purges and increases that which belongs to its own nature and property—not indeed in quantity, but in **virtue** <note>virtue: here meaning the internal power or medicinal potency of a substance</note>.

This Element acts in wondrous, hidden ways upon the other Elements and upon all things. For just as the soul is from that most pure fire, so the "vegetable" <note>the level of life responsible for growth and nutrition</note> is from the Elemental, which is governed by nature. This Element acts upon the **Center** of every thing in this manner: nature gives motion, motion awakens the air, air awakens the fire, and the fire separates, purges, digests, colors, and causes every seed to ripen.

## On Sulfur.

[Nature or God] inspired the knowledge that the composition of such perfect elements exists in gold. This is because it is impossible for such perfection to occur in animals, since they must sustain their life from corrupted elements; nor is it found in plants, because an inequality of the elements is found within them <note>In alchemical theory, plants and animals are transient and unbalanced, whereas gold represents a perfect, stable balance of elements that does not decay</note>. And since all created things are inclined toward multiplication, the Philosophers <note>The alchemists of old</note> proposed to test this natural possibility within the mineral kingdom. Having discovered this, they saw that innumerable other secrets of nature were contained within it, which they left behind very sparingly, treating them as divine secrets.

Thus, you see how corrupted elements settle in a subject and are separated when one overcomes the other. Because at that point, through the first separation, putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: the alchemical stage where matter is broken down and "dies" so it can be reborn in a purer form</term> occurs; and through putrefaction comes the separation of the pure from the impure. If a new union then takes place by the power of fire, the substance acquires a form much nobler than the first. For in its original state, corruption arose from a coarse mixture that can only be purged and improved through putrefaction. This cannot happen except by the combined forces of the four elements present in every compound. When a compound must fall, it falls through the element of water; and while they lie there in confusion, the fire—which exists potentially in each of the others, such as in earth and air—comes together. Joining forces, they eventually overcome the water, which they digest and "cook," and finally congeal. In this manner, nature assists nature.

For if the hidden central fire <term>Central fire: the internal heat or "vital spark" believed to be hidden within the center of all physical matter</term>, which had been held captive by life, wins out, it acts upon that which is closest and purest to it (just as the fire itself is most pure) and joins with it. Thus it overcomes its opposite, separates the pure from the impure, and a new form is generated. If it is further assisted, it becomes much more excellent than the previous form. Sometimes, through the skill of a clever artisan <note>The alchemist</note>, immortal things are created, especially in the mineral kingdom. Thus, all things are made and brought into being by fire alone, and by the governance of fire <note>original: "regimine ignis"</note>, if you have understood me.

Here, then, the origin of the Elements, their natures, and their operations have been described as briefly as possible, which suffices for our purpose in this place. For otherwise, if each Element were described as it truly is, a great volume would arise, which is not necessary for our goal. All these things, as we have said, we refer to the *Harmony* <note>A reference to a larger, perhaps forthcoming, work by the author titled "Harmony"</note>, where, God willing, if life remains to us, we shall leave a more copious account of natural things.

## ON THE THREE PRINCIPLES
### OF ALL THINGS.

**H**AVING DESCRIBED these four Elements, let us descend to the three principles of things; moreover, receive here how those principles are produced from the four Elements. After Nature received from the Most High Creator of all things the grant of a fief <note>original: *privilegium feudi*; a legal metaphor suggesting Nature governs the world as a vassal under God's authority</note> over this Monarchy of the world, she began to distribute places and provinces to each according to their dignity; and first, she ordained that the four Elements should be the princes of the world. And so that the will of the Most High (in whose will Nature is placed) might be fulfilled, she ordained that one should act incessantly upon the other. Thus, fire began to act upon air and produced <term>Sulfur: in alchemy, the principle of combustibility, soul, and heat</term>; Air also began to act upon water and produced <term>Mercury: the principle of fluidity, spirit, and volatility</term>. Water also began to act upon earth and produced <term>Salt: the principle of solidity, body, and permanence</term>. Earth, however, since it had nothing upon which it could act, produced nothing; instead, that which was produced remained within it. For this reason, only three principles came forth, and Earth was made the nurse and the matrix <note>original: *matrix*; a womb or nurturing source</note> of the others. These three Principles, as we have said, were produced—a fact which the ancient Philosophers did not consider so strictly. They described only two actions of the Elements (or if they remained silent by choice, who shall judge them, since they dedicated their writings only to their own sons? <note>Alchemical authors often claimed to write in riddles to hide secrets from the "unworthy," sharing the truth only with their "sons" or initiates</note>). They named Sulfur and Mercury as the matter of metals, and indeed of the Philosophers' Stone, which for us is also sufficient.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a true seeker of this sacred Science must know the accidents <term>Accidents: the outward, observable properties of a substance (like color or texture) that are not part of its essential nature</term>, and must recognize the accident itself, so that he may learn which subject or Element he proposes to approach. In this way, he may adapt himself to it through intermediate means, if he desires to fulfill the number of four <note>original: *quaternarium numerum*; the "Quaternary," referring to the alchemical goal of bringing the four conflicting elements back into a perfect, unified balance</note>. For just as these three Principles were produced from the four, so it is necessary that by reduction these three should also produce two—the male and the female; then the two shall produce the one incorruptible thing, in which those four elements will be equally pure and refined to the highest degree.

Leave the Elements alone, therefore, for you will make nothing from them, nor will you be able to produce anything except these *three Principles*, since nature produces nothing else from them. If, therefore, you can produce nothing from the Elements other than these three principles, why undertake that vain labor of seeking or wishing to make that which has already been generated by nature?

Is it not better to walk three miles than four? Therefore, let it suffice for you to have **three principles**, from which nature produces all things in and upon the earth; which three you will find whole in every thing. From the proper separation and joining of these, nature produces metals as well as stones in the **mineral kingdom**; in the **vegetable kingdom** trees, herbs, and all things; and in the **animal kingdom**, the body, spirit, and soul; which corresponds most closely to the *Work of the Philosophers* <note>The "Work" or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. 

The **Body** is earth, the **Spirit** is water, and the **Soul** is fire or the <term>sulfur of gold: the active, masculine principle of growth and "fixed" energy in alchemy</term>; the Spirit increases the quantity of the body, but the fire increases its power. But because there is more Spirit by weight than fire, the Spirit is exalted and overcomes the fire, drawing it to itself: and thus each of them grows in power, and the earth, which is the intermediary between them, grows in weight. 

Therefore, let every seeker of the art decide in their mind which of these three they seek, and come to its aid so that it may overcome its opposite; then let them add their own weight to the weight of nature, so that the defect of nature may be fulfilled by art, and thus it will conquer its opposite. We have said regarding the element of Earth that earth is nothing other than the **receptacle** for the others—that is, the subject in which these two, fire and water, struggle with one another, with air acting as a mediator. 

If water predominates, it produces temporal and corruptible things; but if fire wins, it produces perpetual and incorruptible things: consider, therefore, what is necessary for you. Know furthermore that fire and water are in every thing; but neither fire nor water does anything on its own, for they only struggle and fight between themselves for speed and power—and this not by themselves, but through the excitation of **external heat**, which is ignited in the center of the earth by the movement of <term>heavenly powers: the perceived astrological or divine influence of the stars and planets on terrestrial matter</term>. 

Without this heat, these two would never do anything, and each of them would remain fixed in its own limit and weight. But after nature has joined these two in proportion, it then excites them with external heat, and so they begin to fight among themselves, and each of them calls upon its like for help; thus they rise and grow until the earth can no longer rise with them. Meanwhile, those two are refined while being held back by the earth; (for within that subject of earth, fire and water rise unceasingly, and through the reserved pores which the air...

## On Sulfur.

Common mercury does not dissolve gold or silver in such a way that it cannot be separated from them; but **our quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum nostrum"; a term for the purified, philosophical mercury essential to the Great Work.</note> dissolves gold and silver and is never separated from them, just like water mixed with water. Common mercury contains a bad, combustible sulfur which turns things black; our quicksilver contains within itself an incombustible, **fixed** <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating or changing.</note>, good sulfur—both the whitest white and the deepest red. Common mercury is cold and moist; our Mercury is hot and moist. Common mercury blackens and infects bodies; our quicksilver whitens bodies to a crystalline serenity. Common mercury, through precipitation, is turned into a yellow powder (a bad sulfur); our quicksilver, by means of heat, is turned into a most white, good, fixed, and flowable sulfur. The more common mercury is **decocted** <note>original: "decoquitur"; a process of heating or "cooking" a substance over a long period to mature it.</note>, the more liquid it becomes; the more our quicksilver is decocted, the more it thickens. From these circumstances, therefore, you may consider how common mercury differs from the **quicksilver of the Philosophers**. If you still do not understand, do not wait; no mortal will give clearer explanations than those we have spoken here. 

But concerning its virtues: our quicksilver is of such virtue that it is sufficient by itself both for you and for itself; without any addition of an outside thing, it is dissolved and congealed by natural decoction alone. However, for the sake of shortening the work, the Philosophers add to it their own well-digested and mature sulfur, and thus they operate.

We could indeed have cited the writings of the Philosophers to confirm our discourse; but since we have written more clearly than their writings, they require no proof; he who is well-versed in the writings of others will understand. If, therefore, you wish to follow our counsel, we advise that before you approach this art, you first learn to **restrain your tongue** <note>A common alchemical warning to keep the "Secret of the Stone" from the unworthy or the uninitiated.</note> and investigate the nature of minerals and metals, and then of vegetables; for you will find our Mercury in every subject. The Mercury of the Philosophers can be extracted from all things, though it is closer at hand in one subject than in another. Know also for certain that this science is not located in luck or accidental discovery, but in real science.

And there is no other but this unique material in the world through which and from which the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The ultimate goal of alchemy, a substance believed to transform base metals into gold and grant longevity or spiritual perfection.</note> is prepared. It is indeed in all things, but in its extraction life would cease; yet without knowledge of natural things, especially in the mineral kingdom, you will be like a blind man who walks by habit. Conclusively we say that this art is the gift of the Most High God alone, and once it is known, He must be prayed to so that He may deign to give His blessing even to this art; since without the divine blessing it is altogether useless. We ourselves have experienced this, having suffered several very serious dangers because of this knowledge, and we have had more misfortune and trouble from it than benefit: but we believe the time has come in the world when **the Phrygians learn wisdom too late** <note>original: "serò sapiunt Phryges"; a classical proverb meaning to become wise only after suffering disaster, referring to the Trojans who ignored warnings until their city fell.</note>: the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss. Nevertheless, I have admired divine providence in our misfortunes of this kind: for we have always had the protection of our Most High Creator at hand, so that no enemy could oppress us; the Angel of the Lord was always the guardian of this Ark <note>likely referring to the secret vessel of the work or the author's own body/soul as a vessel of the secret.</note>, in which the Most High Creator of things enclosed such a great treasure, which He also protects to the end. ...they were deprived of life: those who indeed invaded our goods lost their own, and some even lost their kingdoms. We have always had such protection from the Creator of all things, who took us under the shadow of his wings straight from our mother’s womb and infused us with the spirit of understanding of natural things—to whom be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages. We have received such great benefits from the Most High God our Creator that it is impossible to comprehend them not only with a pen but even with the mind. We believe this alone: that we have always hoped, do hope, and will hope in Him alone. For we know there is no one among mortals who can help us except this God and Creator alone; because it is vain to trust in Princes, since they are but men, (as the *Psalm* <note>Referring to Psalm 146:3: "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help."</note> says). All these have the Spirit of life from God, which being taken away, all things are dust; but to hope in the Lord God, from whom all good things flow most abundantly as from a fountain of goodness, is safe and secure. 

You, therefore, whoever desires to approach this **Holy Science** <term>S. Scientia</term> <note>Sacra Scientia: the "Sacred Science" of alchemy, viewed here as a spiritual and physical discipline.</note>, place first your entire hope in God your Creator, and weary Him with prayers, and believe firmly that you will not be forsaken by Him. For if God knows your heart to be pure <note>original: candidum, literally "white" or "shining," implying sincerity and lack of malice.</note> and your whole hope placed in Him, He will easily provide the means; through this or another way He will help you to possess your wish. **The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom** <note>original: Initium sapientiæ timor Domini, a common biblical Proverb.</note>. **Pray, but nonetheless also work** <note>original: Ora, sed nihilominus & labora. This is a variation of the famous Benedictine motto "Ora et Labora" (Pray and Work), suggesting that spiritual devotion must be paired with physical laboratory effort.</note>. God indeed gives understanding, but you must know how to use it: for just as a good intellect and a good opportunity are gifts of God, so is it the punishment of sin when a good opportunity is neglected.

If you intend to make metal, let metal be your foundation, because a dog is not generated except from a dog, and metal only from metal. For know for certain, if you do not take the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The *humidum radicale* was considered the essential, life-giving fluid or "soul" of a substance in alchemical theory.</note> from the metal, having separated it perfectly, you will never achieve anything. Without a grain of wheat, you cultivate the earth in vain: there is but one thing, one art, one operation.

If, therefore, you wish to produce metal, you shall ferment with metal; but if you want a tree, let the seed of a tree be your ferment. As we have said, there is only one operation, outside of which there is no other that is true. Therefore, all those err who claim that any **particular** <note>A "particular" (as opposed to a "universal") work refers to a limited alchemical process that achieves a specific, often minor, transmutation rather than the total perfection of the Great Work.</note> work outside this single path and natural matter is true; for a branch is not obtained except from the trunk of a tree. It is impossible and foolish to want to produce the branch before the tree. It is easier to prepare the Stone itself than any "particular" thing, even the simplest, that might be useful and withstand testing alongside a natural substance.

There are many, however, who boast they can make "fixed silver" <note>original: *luna fixa*. "Luna" is the alchemical name for silver; "fixed" means it has been made resistant to the destructive power of fire.</note>, but they would do better to try "fixing" lead or tin; in my judgment, the labor is the same. For lead and tin do not resist the test of fire as long as they remain in their own nature, whereas silver is naturally fixed enough and has no need for a **sophistical fixation** <note>A "sophistical" process refers to a deceptive or artificial trick that mimics a result without achieving true chemical change.</note>. But since there are as many opinions as there are heads, we leave everyone to their own view; let whoever refuses to follow our counsel and imitate nature remain in their error. To be sure, "particulars" can be made once the "tree" is possessed, for its shoots can be grafted onto various trees—just as when one has water, various kinds of meat can be cooked in it, and the broth will take its flavor from the variety of the meats, yet it all comes from the same foundation. We conclude, therefore, that there is but one nature, both in metals and in other things, but its operation is diverse; there is also one universal matter according to...

It was never our proposition that one could multiply wheat without a grain of wheat; but you should know that it is most false to claim that an extracted soul can "tinge" <term>tingere</term> <note>To transform or "color" a base metal into gold or silver.</note> some other metal in a deceptive manner, and all who boast of this are forgers. *Voice:* In all, but not uniformly; in some not so strictly.

*Voice:* Because it would no longer fear those guards once it reached its Royal palace. For then it can be seen; it already looks out freely from the windows, since it is there in its own Kingdom, though not yet as fully as it desires.

*Alchemist:* Lord, and what does it eat?

*Voice:* Its food is wind <note>original: "ventus"; often used in alchemy to represent the air or the "vital spirit" that carries the secret food of life</note>, when it is cooked while free; but in the prisons, it is forced to eat it raw.

*Alchemist:* Lord, could these enmities between it and its guards be reconciled?

*Voice:* Indeed, if anyone were so wise.

*Alchemist:* Why does it not treat for peace with them?

[...wisdom] <note>The beginning of the word is on the previous page</note> where she is accustomed to give audience to Philosophers; but the Philosophers adore it <note>Sulfur</note> swimming in its own sea and playing with Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here representing the alchemical fire or heat</note>, when the Philosophers approach it, unknown, in the most wretched clothing.
*Alchemist:* Lord, why is it not mine in the sea, since it is hidden here more closely?
*Voice:* I told you that its guardians have placed it in the darkest prisons so that you might not be able to see it, for it is in one single subject; but if you have not found it at home, you will hardly find it in the forests. However, lest you despair in seeking it, I tell you most sacredly that it is most perfect in gold and silver, but easiest in quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>.
*Alchemist:* Lord, I would willingly make the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life</note>.
*Voice:* You desire a good thing; the sulfur also would willingly be dissolved.
And thus *Saturn* <note>The planetary spirit associated with lead, often portrayed as a wise or grim figure in alchemy</note> departed. Truly, a heavy sleep overcame the weary Alchemist, and such a vision appeared to him.
He saw in that grove a fountain full of water, around which *Salt* and *Sulfur* were walking, arguing with one another until finally they began to fight; and *Salt* inflicted an incurable wound upon *Sulfur*, from which wound, instead of blood, water like the whitest milk flowed out, and it grew into a great river. Then from that grove came forth *Diana* <note>The Roman goddess of the moon; in alchemy, she often represents silver or the "white" stage of the process</note>, a most beautiful virgin, who began to wash herself in that river. When a certain *Prince*, a most powerful man (and greater than his servants), saw her while passing by, he began to admire her beauty, and because she was of a nature similar to his own, he was captured by love for her. When she saw this, she in turn burned with love for him; wherefore, falling as if into a faint of the soul, she began to sink. Seeing this, the *Prince* commanded his servants to help her; but they all feared to approach the river. To them the *Prince* said: "Why," he said, "do you not help the virgin *Diana*?" To which they replied: "Lord, the river is indeed small, as if dried up, but it is most dangerous. Once before, without your knowledge, we wished to cross this, and we barely escaped the danger of eternal death; we know also that others of our predecessors perished here." Then that *Prince*, having set aside his heavy cloak, jumped into the river just as he was, armed, to bring help to the most beautiful *Diana*, and he reached out his hand to her; she, wishing to save herself, drew the *Prince* himself to her, and both were submerged. And he said to Saturn: "Truly Lord, I see that according to my fantasy..."

# On Sulfur.

"[It] does not want to succeed; I beg you, do it yourself as you know how." 
Then Saturn said, "Look then, and learn." 
And so he took two <term>quicksilvers</term> <note>original: "argenta viva"; liquid mercury</note> of different substance but from a single root, which Saturn washed with his own urine, and he called them the "sulfurs of sulfurs." He mixed the fixed with the volatile and, once the composition was made, he placed it in the proper vessel. So that the sulfur would not flee, he placed a guardian over it, and then placed it in a bath of the slowest fire, as the matter required, and did everything perfectly. 

Thus they made the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>, because from the proper material only the proper work results. The Alchemist, greatly rejoiced, took the stone along with the glass vessel; considering its color, which was like burnt blood <note>A description of the "rubedo" or red stage, the final successful phase of the Great Work</note>, he wondered at it, and out of excessive joy he began to dance. In that dance, the glass slipped from his hands onto the ground and was broken; and thus Saturn vanished. 

The Alchemist also woke up from his dream and found nothing in his hands except those little sulfur candles he had made. The stone indeed flew away, and flies to this day, whence it is called "volatile." And so that wretched Alchemist learned nothing else from that vision than how to make sulfur candles. Later, having abandoned the Stone, he began to be a Physician; by seeking the Philosophers' Stone, he acquired only the stone of the kidneys <note>A play on words in Latin; the Alchemist failed to find the magical Stone but ended up treating kidney stones (calculi) as a doctor</note>. Finally, he led a life as such Alchemists usually do; they mostly become Physicians or <term>soap-makers</term> <note>original: "smegmatistæ"; those who prepare ointments or cleaning agents</note>. This happens to all who approach the art without a foundation, based only on hearsay or recipes found by chance through [mere] logic.

Some afterwards, when it does not succeed for them, say: "We are wise men, we hear the grass grow; if the art were true, we before all others would have possessed it." And so, clothed in shame, lest they be held as unworthy (as they are, indeed, and stiff-necked), they cry out like cuckoos <note>original: "cuculant"; a derogatory term for mocking or babbling</note> against the art. Such people this science hates, and always shows them the beginning at the end. 

We, however, grant that this art is nothing to the unworthy; but to the lovers of virtue, the true seekers, and the sons of doctrine, we highly recommend it, and affirm it to be true, and altogether **most true**. We have occasionally proven this in fact before men worthy of the sight, both of high and low condition. (Yet this <term>Medicine</term> <note>Another name for the Philosophers' Stone or the elixir of life</note> was not made by our own hands, but we received such things from a friend...)

-># On Sulfur.<-

[...yet most true] to the investigation of which we have sufficiently informed the seekers. If our writings do not please them, let them read the lighter works of other authors, though with this caution: that whatever they read, they should always compare it to the possibility of nature, and not attempt anything against nature. Nor should they believe it even if it were written in the books of the Philosophers that fire does not burn, because this is contrary to nature. But if it is written that fire has the power of drying and heating, this is to be believed since it happens naturally. For nature always agrees with sound intellect; in nature nothing is difficult, and every truth is simple. Then they should also learn to recognize which things in nature are most closely related to one another, which we believe can be done more easily through our writings than through others. We think we have written enough until someone else comes along who might describe the whole recipe as clearly as one describes how to make cheese from milk—which is not permitted to us.

But lest we turn everything over to the foolish, we shall also say something to you who have already passed through these hardships. Have you seen that region where the husband led home his wife, whose marriage was celebrated in the house of nature? Have you understood how the common people saw this sulfur along with you? If, therefore, you want the <note>original: "vetulae"; literally "old women," often used in alchemy to refer to simple, common folk or non-adepts who might perform chemical tasks without understanding the theory</note> common folk to practice your Philosophy, show them the whitening of these sulfurs. Say to the common people: "Come and see, for now the water is divided and the sulfur has come out; it will return white, and it will congeal the waters." Therefore, burn sulfur by means of incombustible sulfur, and wash, whiten, and redden it, until the sulfur becomes Mercury, and the Mercury becomes sulfur, which you will afterwards adorn with the soul of gold. For if you do not <term>sublime</term> <note>to heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then becomes solid again, a process of purification</note> sulfur from sulfur, and mercury from mercury, you have not yet found the water which is created and distilled from sulfur and mercury as the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the purest, most refined substance or "soul" of the matter</note>; he who does not descend shall not ascend. Whatever is notable in this art is lost by many during the preparation, for our mercury is sharpened by sulfur, otherwise it would not be useful. A prince without a people is wretched: so is this Alchemist without sulfur and mercury. If you have understood me, I have spoken.

Afterward, the Alchemist, having returned home, lamented the lost stone, and he grieved most especially that he had not asked Saturn what kind of Salt this was, since so many various kinds of salts are found; the rest he told to his wife.

# CONCLUSION.

**E**VERY seeker of this art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy, specifically the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> must first, with mature judgment, examine the creation, operation, and virtues of the four elements, along with their actions. For if he is ignorant of their origin and nature, he will not arrive at the knowledge of the principles, nor will he know the true matter of the stone, much less attain a good end; since every end is determined by its beginning. He who knows well what he begins will know well what he finishes. 

For the origin of the elements is chaos, from which God, the creator of things, created and separated the elements—an act which belongs to God alone. From the elements, however, nature produces the principles of things <note>The "Principles" refer to the *Tria Prima*: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which alchemists believed were the building blocks of all matter.</note>, and this, through the will of God, belongs to nature alone. Afterward, from these principles, nature produces minerals and all things; from which the craftsman, by imitating nature, can perform many wonders. Because nature produces minerals, metals, and all kinds of things from these principles—which are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—and it does not produce metal directly from the elements, but through the principles that serve as the medium between elements and metals. Therefore, if nature herself does not do this, much less can art <note>The human skill of alchemy.</note> achieve it. 

And not only in this example, but in every natural process, the intermediate arrangement must be observed. For this reason, we have here in this treatise described both the elements themselves and their actions and operations, as well as the origin of the principles, quite copiously (something no Philosopher has given more clearly until now), so that the good seeker may more easily consider at what degree the stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> differs from metals, and metals from elements. 

For there is a difference between gold and water, but a smaller one between water and Mercury, and the smallest difference of all between gold and Mercury. For the house <note>In alchemy, "house" often refers to the matrix, container, or natural solvent that holds a substance.</note> of gold is Mercury, and the house of Mercury is water. Sulfur, however, is the coagulant <note>original: "coagulum"; the agent that causes the fluid Mercury to thicken and solidify into metal.</note> of Mercury; which sulfur is indeed prepared with great difficulty, but investigated with even greater difficulty. Because in the sulfur of the Philosophers this whole secret lies hidden, which is also contained in the innermost parts of Mercury. Regarding its preparation, without which it is useless, we shall give instruction at some time in [the book of] the third principle...

The author here clarifies that while the principles of Mercury and Sulfur exist in all things, they do not cross between these distinct realms.</meta>

<header>On Sulfur.</header>

...concerning salt, since here we are discussing the virtue and origin of sulfur, not its practical application.

We have not, however, written this treatise to refute the ancient Philosophers, but rather to confirm their writings and fulfill some things they omitted: for since Philosophers are also men, they cannot do everything so perfectly, nor can one man suffice for all things. Some have even been seduced by miracles away from the linear path of nature, as we read happened to **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and a central figure in medieval science and alchemy.</note>, a most wise man and Philosopher; who wrote that in his time, grains of gold were found between the teeth of a dead man in a tomb. He could not find a certain reason for this miracle, but he attributed it to a mineral power within the human being, and based on this opinion, he fell into agreement with the saying of **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist; the quote "this matter is extracted from you" was often misinterpreted by literalists to mean the Philosopher's Stone came from the human body.</note>, *“and this matter, O King, is extracted from you.”* <note>original: "& hæc materia, Rex, à te extrahitur :"</note> But this is erroneous, for Morienus intended those words to be understood Philosophically.

For the mineral **Virtue** <note>In alchemy, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or active property of a substance.</note> is located in its own kingdom, just as the animal virtue is in its own kingdom, as we have distinguished those kingdoms in the book of the *Twelve Treatises* and divided them into three; because any of these stands and multiplies within itself without outside entry. It is indeed true that in the animal kingdom there is both Mercury as the matter, and sulfur as the virtue, but it is animal, not mineral. If the power of animal sulfur were not in man, it would not congeal the blood (which is animal Mercury) into flesh and bones; likewise, if the power of vegetable sulfur were not in the vegetable kingdom, it would not congeal water (or vegetable Mercury) into herbs and trees. The same must be understood in the mineral kingdom. These three Mercuries do not differ in their power, nor do those three sulfurs, because every sulfur has the natural power to coagulate its own Mercury; and every Mercury has the power to be coagulated by its own sulfur—but not by a foreign one. 

Now, the reason why gold was found or generated between the teeth of the dead man is this: while the deceased was alive, Mercury was introduced into that sick body by some Physician, either by an ointment, or by <term>turbith</term> <note>Turbith (or turpeth) is a root used in older medicine as a purgative, often associated with mercury-based treatments for ailments like syphilis.</note>, or by some other method, as is the custom and use; and the nature of Mercury is to rise to the wall of the bone, and to be evacuated through the sores of the mouth with <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "plegmate". In medieval medicine, phlegm was one of the four humors; here it refers to the salivation caused by mercury poisoning.</note>. If, therefore, during such a cure, the sick man

<meta>catchword: died,</meta>

<summary>The author clarifies that the "Three Kingdoms" of nature (Animal, Vegetable, Mineral) operate independently, explaining that gold found in a corpse's mouth was likely a byproduct of medical mercury treatment rather than a natural alchemical transmutation within the human body.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the story of Albertus Magnus and the gold found in a tomb, using it as a proof that gold is formed from mineral Mercury and Sulfur, rather than from animal or human substances. It serves as the final exhortation and conclusion to the treatise.</meta>

<page-num>645</page-num>
<header>On Sulfur.</header>

...he died, that **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to quicksilver that had been administered as medicine or otherwise introduced to the living man.</note> having no way out, remained in the mouth between the teeth; and that corpse became a natural vessel for the **Mercury**. Thus, shut up for a long time, it was congealed into gold by its own sulfur through the natural heat of **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the process of decay which alchemists believed generated the internal heat necessary for the transformation of metals.</term>, having been purified by the corrosive phlegm of the human body. But if mineral Mercury had not been introduced there, gold would never have been produced. And this is a most true example that nature, in the bowels of the earth, produces gold and silver and other metals from Mercury alone, according to the disposition of the place or the **matrix** <term>matrix: the "womb" or specific geological environment in the earth where minerals grow.</term>. For Mercury has within itself its own sulfur by which it is coagulated into gold, unless it is hindered by some accident, or lacks the required heat, or a sealed-off place. Therefore, it is not the power of *animal* sulfur that congeals Mercury into gold, but into flesh; for if such a power were in man, this would happen in all bodies, which is not the case. Many such miracles and accidents occur which, if not well considered by writers, bring errors to readers. However, a good seeker ought to apply everything to the possibility of nature; if things do not agree with nature, they are to be omitted.

It suffices for the diligent student to have received the origin of the Principles here, since if the beginning is unknown, the end is always doubtful. Concerning these things, we have addressed the seeker in this treatise not enigmatically, but in the clearest speech we could and were permitted. Through this, if God illuminates the mind of anyone, he will know what a successor owes to his predecessors, since this science is always acquired through such intellects. This science, after such a clear demonstration, we place back into the bosom of God the Most High, Creator and our Lord, and we commend ourselves along with our good readers to His grace and immense mercy. To Whom be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages <note>original: "per infinita sæcula sæculorum."</note>.
