### CHAPTER XXII.
### What the Rule of Saturn is, and from where is it named?

**A**s many of the Wise <term>Magi</term> <note>Wise practitioners of the alchemical arts</note> who have written about this labor have spoken of the work and the **Rule of Saturn**, some who understood them poorly have wandered into various errors and deceived themselves by their own opinions. Some, led astray by this name, have worked with physical lead with the greatest hope but the smallest result. But you should know that **our lead** is worthier than any gold. It is the "slime" in which the **Soul of Gold** is joined with **Mercury**, so that they may later produce **Adam** and his wife **Eve** <note>In alchemy, Adam and Eve often symbolize the "fixed" and "volatile" principles, or the masculine and feminine aspects of the matter that must unite</note>. Therefore, since the highest has humbled itself here to become the lowest, one must wait for the redemption of all its brothers in its own blood. The **tomb**, therefore, in which our **King** is buried, is called **Saturn** in our work, and it is the key to the "coins" of the Art. Happy is he who can greet this slow-walking planet. Pray to God, brother, that He deems you worthy of this blessing, because it does not come from the one who runs, nor the one who wills, but this blessing depends on the **Father of Lights** alone.

---

### CHAPTER XXIII.
### Concerning the diverse Rules of this Work.

**T**rust for certain, diligent beginner, that nothing in the whole work of the **stone** has been hidden except the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimen"; the management or "governance" of the fire and the stages of the chemical process</note>, concerning which that saying of the Philosopher is true: *Whoever shall know it scientifically, the Princes and Magnates of the Earth shall honor him.* And I swear to you in good faith that if this alone were proposed openly, fools themselves would laugh at the art. For once it is known, the whole thing is nothing else than **women’s work** and **child's play**, that is: **to boil**. Therefore, with the highest art, the Sages have hidden this secret, and you may firmly believe that we have fundamentally done the same; yet, because I have proposed and promised clarity in this little treatise, it is incumbent upon me to do at least something, lest I fail the hope and labors of ingenious readers. Therefore, know that our **Rule** is one linear path in the whole work, which is **to boil** and **to digest**, and yet this one rule encompasses many others in itself, which the envious have hidden under a diversity of names, and

# Chapter XXIV.
## *Concerning the First Rule of the Work, which is of Mercury.*

**A**nd first, indeed, we shall speak of the **Rule of Mercury**, which is a secret never expressed by any of the Wise. They, for instance, began from the second work, or the **Rule of Saturn**, and revealed no light to the apprentice <term>Tyro</term> <note>A novice or beginner in the alchemical art</note> before the chief sign of the blackness. In this, that good man **Count Bernard of Trevisan** <note>A 15th-century alchemist famous for his allegorical tales of the "King" and the "Fountain"</note> remained silent; in his parable, he teaches that when the **King** comes to the **Fountain**, leaving all strangers behind, he enters the bath alone, dressed in a golden garment, which he takes off and hands to **Saturn**, from whom he receives a black silk robe. But he does not teach in what space of time that golden garment is removed; therefore, he remains silent about one entire rule of perhaps forty or even sometimes fifty days. During this time, without a guide, wretched apprentices apply themselves to uncertain experiments. From the arrival of the blackness until the end of the work, new signs appearing daily sufficiently refresh the craftsman; but here, I confess it is tedious to wander for fifty days without a guide, a sign, or a guarantee. I say, therefore, that from the first firing until the **blackness** <term>nigredo</term> <note>The stage of putrefaction where the matter turns black, symbolizing death before rebirth</note>, the entire interval of time is the **Rule of Mercury**. I mean the **Philosophical Mercury**, because it alone operates through that whole time, while its partner remains dead for the appropriate duration of time; and no one before me has uncovered this. Therefore, once the materials are joined—which are **Gold** <term>Sol</term> and our **Mercury**—do not believe, like the common crowd of Alchemists, that the setting of the "Sun" happens quickly. Not at all. We waited long and much before harmony was made between the water and the fire. The envious ones have hidden this under a short name, calling their matter in the first Work **Rebis**, that is, a thing made from a double thing, according to the Poet:

> The thing is a **Rebis**, two things joined, yet nonetheless one,
> It is dissolved so that at first they are either the Sun, or the seeds of the Moon.
> <note>original: "Res Rebis est bina conjuncta, sed tamen una, / Solvitur ut prima sint aut Sol, aut spermata Lunæ." In alchemy, the "Rebis" represents the hermaphroditic or unified matter composed of two principles.</note>

He critiques earlier masters like Bernard of Trevisan for omitting this period, which involves the slow dissolution of gold into the philosophical mercury.</summary>

Know for certain, therefore, that although our **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to a specialized solvent or "living" metallic principle, not just common quicksilver</note> devours the **Sun** <note>The "Sun" or *Sol* is the alchemical code for Gold</note>, it does not do so in the way that alchemical pretenders <term>Philosophastri</term> <note>A derogatory term for those who practice "puffery" or false alchemy without philosophical understanding</note> believe. For even if you join the Sun with our Mercury, you will recover it from there safe and possessing its original power after a year’s waiting, unless you cook it in a suitable degree of fire; anyone who asserts the contrary is no Philosopher. Those who are on the path of error believe that dissolving bodies is such a light task that they claim gold, once immersed in "Sophic" Mercury, is devoured in the blink of an eye. They poorly understand that passage by **Count Bernard of Trevisan** <note>The 15th-century alchemist mentioned on the previous page</note> regarding his "golden book" immersed irrecoverably into the fountain. Yet, how difficult a task it is to dissolve metallic bodies can be attested by those who have labored over **Dissolution**. I myself, who have been taught these things many times by the testimony of my own eyes, attest that it is a very skillful thing to govern the fire once the matter is prepared, so that it might duly dissolve the bodies without burning the tinctures <note>The "tincture" is the elusive soul or coloring power of the metal being extracted</note>. 

Attend, therefore, to my Teaching: take the body that I have shown you, and place it into the **Water of our Sea** <note>A poetic name for the alchemical solvent or Mercury</note>, and cook it continually with the proper fire, so that the dew and clouds may ascend, and the drops may fall back day and night without interruption. And know that in this circulation, the vapor ascends in its original nature, and the body is left below in its original nature, until—after a long time—the body begins to retain some of the water; and thus each participates in the stages and qualities of the other. 

Because the entirety of the water does not ascend through sublimation <note>The process of a substance turning to vapor and then solidifying again</note>, but a part of it remains below with the body in the bottom of the vessel, the body is therefore boiled and sifted with vigilant diligence in the subsiding water. By this means, the falling drops pierce through the remaining mass, and the water, made more subtle by constant circulation, finally extracts the **Soul of the Sun** <note>The "Soul" represents the internal essence or "Seed" of the gold</note> gently and smoothly. Thus, by the mediation of the soul, the spirit is reconciled with the body, and the **Union** of both takes place in a **black color**. This occurs at the latest by the fiftieth day, and this operation is called the *Rule of Mercury*, because Mercury circulates above, and in it the body of the Sun is boiled below. The body is passive in this work until the appearance of the colors, which appear sparingly around the twentieth day under a good and continuous boiling. These colors subsequently increase, multiply, and vary until the completion in black...

### CHAPTER XXV.

## *Concerning the Second Rule of the Work, which is that of Saturn.*

**O**nce the Rule of Mercury is completed—the work of which is to strip the King of his golden garments, and to agitate and provoke the Lion <note>In alchemy, the "Lion" often represents the fixed metallic substance or "philosophical sulfur" being acted upon</note> with various conflicts until he reaches extreme exhaustion—the Rule of Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical code for Lead and the color black, signifying the stage of decay or "putrefaction"</note> appears next. For God wills that the work begun be brought to its due end, and the law of this stage is that the exit of one is the entrance of another; the end of one is the origin of the other. No sooner does the Rule of Mercury fade away than Saturn enters as his successor, having obtained the Empire by right of succession. When the Lion dies, the crow <note>original: *corvus*; the crow or raven is the classic alchemical symbol for the *Nigredo* or black stage</note> is born. This Rule is quite straightforward regarding color, because there is only one color, and that the blackest; there are no fumes, no winds, nor any symbol of life—at least, sometimes it is seen as a dried substance, and sometimes the compound is seen boiling like liquid pitch. O sad spectacle and image of eternal death! Yet for the craftsman, it is sweet news! For this is not just any blackness, but one seen shining because of its most intense darkness. When you look down and see the matter swelling like dough, rejoice: for you should know that a life-giving spirit is enclosed within, which at the time appointed by the Almighty will restore life to these corpses. Take care, at least, with the fire, which you are bound to rule here with sound judgment; and I swear to you in good faith, that if by forcing the fire in this stage you cause anything to sublimate <term>sublimare</term> <note>To "sublimate" means to cause a solid to turn into vapor and then back to solid; in this context, it refers to the matter rising to the top of the flask prematurely, which would ruin the chemical "death" happening at the bottom</note>, you will lose the entire work beyond recovery. Therefore, be content to be held in prison with the good **Trevisan** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist famous for emphasizing that the matter must remain "at the bottom of the vessel" without being disturbed</note> for forty days and nights, and allow the tender matter to remain in the bottom—which is the nest of conception—trusting for certain that when the period established by the Almighty for this Operation is complete, the spirit will rise glorious and glorify its own body. It will ascend, I say, and circulate gently and without violence; it will ascend from the center to the heavens, and descend again from the heavens to the center, and it will take up the power of the things above and the things below <note>This "ascent and descent" is a direct reference to the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus, describing how the substance gains the virtues of both the spiritual and material worlds</note>.

# *The Open Entrance*

## CHAPTER XXVI.

### *Concerning the Rule of Jupiter.*

**A**fter black Saturn, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>In the alchemical sequence, Jupiter represents a transitional stage between the blackness of Saturn and the whiteness of the Moon. It is often associated with the color blue, gray, or the multicolored "Peacock's Tail."</note> succeeds, who is of a different color. For after the due <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of rotting or breaking down the matter until it turns black.</note> and the conception has taken place at the bottom of the vessel, by God's command, you will again see changing colors and a circulating <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where the substance is vaporized by heat and then condenses again, "circulating" within the sealed glass flask.</note>. This Rule is not lasting, nor does it endure beyond three weeks. During this time, every imaginable color will appear, for which no certain explanation can be given. During these days, the "rains" <note>Liquid condensation dripping back down the sides of the glass.</note> will multiply day by day, and finally, after all these most beautiful sights, a Whiteness shows itself at the sides of the vessel like streaks or hairs. Then rejoice, because you have successfully completed the rule of Jupiter. Let there be the greatest caution in this rule, lest the <term>chicks of the crows</term> <note>original: *corvorum pulli*; a metaphor for the first white specks of purified matter emerging from the black "crow" or *Nigredo* stage.</note>, after they have left their nest, return to the same. Likewise, do not drain the water so immoderately that the earth, settling down, lacks moisture and is left dry and useless at the bottom. Thirdly, do not irrigate your earth so intemperately that you utterly suffocate it. A good management of external heat will remedy all these errors.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

### *Concerning the Rule of the Moon.*

**A**fter the rule of Jupiter is finished, near the end of the fourth month, the sign of the waxing <term>Moon</term> <note>Luna (the Moon) represents the *Albedo* or "Whiteness" stage, the first major goal of the work which produces the "White Stone" capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note> will appear to you; and know that the entire rule of Jupiter was dedicated to washing <term>Latona</term> <note>original: *abluendo Latoni*. In alchemy, Latona is the mother of the Sun and Moon; "washing Latona" is a poetic term for cleansing the dark, base matter to reveal the pure white substance (Diana/Moon) hidden within.</note>. The washing spirit is very white in its nature, but the body to be washed is black, even the blackest of black. In its transition to <term>whiteness</term> <note>The *Albedo* stage.</note>, all intermediate colors appeared; when these are finished, the whole becomes white—yet it does not become perfectly glowing white on the first day, but rather it will rise gradually from white to the most brilliant white. And know, that in this rule the whole becomes like liquid <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti vivi*; mercury.</note> to the sight. This is called "the sealing of the mother in the womb of her infant" whom she has brought forth. In this rule, there will be various beautiful, momentary colors that quickly disappear, but they are closer to whiteness than to blackness, just as the colors in the rule of Jupiter participated more in blackness than in whiteness.

### *CHAPTER XXVIII.*
### *Concerning the Rule of Venus.*

**I**t is wonderful above all things that our stone, now perfected in every way and capable of communicating its perfect tincture, humbles itself again of its own accord and will plan a new <term>volatilitity</term> <note>The ability of the solid "stone" to vaporize and rise again, starting a new cycle of refinement.</note> without any manual intervention. However, if you take it out of its vessel, and that same stone is enclosed again in another vessel after it has cooled, any attempt to lead it further will be in vain. Neither we nor any of the ancient Philosophers are able to give a demonstrative reason for this, except that it is done by the will of **GOD**. At least beware of your fire here, because this is the law of the perfected stone: that it must be <term>fusible</term> <note>Capable of being melted.</note>. Therefore, if you give it more heat than is right, the matter will <term>vitrify</term> <note>Turn into a useless, glass-like substance. This "vitrification" is a common failure where the "living" chemical reactions are permanently stopped.</note>, and once melted it will stick to the sides of the vessel, and you will not be able to advance it any further. And this is that "quickening" of the matter so often warned against by the Philosophers, which is accustomed to happen to the unwary before and after the white work is perfected—namely, from the middle of the Rule of the Moon until the seventh or tenth day of the Rule of Venus. Therefore, let the fire be increased only slightly, so that the composite does not vitrify—that is, melt passively like glass. But by a gentle heat, it will melt and swell of its own accord, and by God's command it will be endowed with a spirit which will fly upward, carrying the stone with it, and will produce new colors, especially the green of Ven... <margin>Venus</margin>

## CHAPTER XXIX.
### Concerning the Rule of Mars.

Once the Rule of Venus is finished—the color of which was mainly greenish and a little reddish with a dark purple, and sometimes leaden, during which time the <term>philosophical tree</term> <note>A crystalline, branch-like structure that forms inside the flask during the cooling and heating cycles.</note> flourished with its multi-colored branches, leaves and all—the <term>Rule of Mars</term> <note>The stage associated with the planet Mars, characterized by yellowing and the "Peacock’s Tail."</note> succeeds it. This stage shows primarily a certain yellowness, diluted as if by a yellowish brownness, and most gloriously displays the transitory colors of the <term>Rainbow and the Peacock</term> <note>Known in Latin as the *Cauda Pavonis*, this is a famous alchemical stage where the matter displays a shimmering array of colors like a peacock's feathers.</note>. Here the state of the compound is drier, in which the matter seems to imitate various masks of forms. A hyacinth color with a very light orange will frequently appear in these days. Here the sealed mother rises in the belly of her infant and is purified, so that because of the great purity in which the compound is placed, the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of "decay" or blackness (*nigredo*) that occurs earlier in the work.</note> may be banished from here. Truly, however, dark colors play as the base throughout this whole regimen, and intermediate colors are formed that are most pleasing to behold. Now you should know that our <term>Virgin Earth</term> <note>The purified, solid matter remaining in the bottom of the flask, ready to be "fertilized" by further heat.</note> is undergoing its final cultivation, so that the <term>fruit of the Sun</term> <note>The final goal of the work: the Red Stone or Alchemical Gold.</note> may be sown and ripened in it. Therefore, continue a good heat, and you will see for certain around the thirtieth day of this regimen that a lemon-yellow color appears, which within two weeks from its first appearance will imbue almost everything with a lemon-yellow hue.

## CHAPTER XXX.

### Concerning the Rule of the Sun.

**N**ow you approach the end of your work, and you have almost completed your business; now everything appears like <term>Pure Gold</term> <note>original: "Auri Obryzi"; refers to gold of the highest purity, refined and tested.</note>, and the <term>Virgin's Milk</term> <note>A common alchemical term for a white, nourishing mercurial liquid used to "feed" the matter.</note> with which you soak this material becomes deeply lemon-yellow. Now give immortal thanks to GOD, the Giver of all good things, who has brought the work this far; pray to Him as a suppliant that He may guide your counsel from here on, lest by perhaps striving to rush the now-perfected work, you lose it entirely. Consider now that you have waited for nearly seven months, and it would not be sane to annihilate the whole thing in a single hour. Therefore, be very cautious, and all the more so because you are closer to perfection. 

If you proceed cautiously, these notable things will occur to you: First, you will observe a certain lemon-colored sweat on the <term>body</term> <note>The solid matter at the bottom of the vessel.</note>, and finally lemon-colored vapors as the body settles, tinged with violet and sometimes with a dark purple. After a wait of twelve or fourteen days in this <term>Rule of the Sun</term> <note>The final stage of the process, also known as the Rubedo or Red Work, associated with the Sun and the perfection of gold.</note>, you will observe the matter to be for the most part moist, and although it is heavy, it is nevertheless "carried entirely in the belly of the wind" <note>A famous phrase from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the volatile state of the substance before it fixes into a solid.</note>. 

Finally, around the twenty-sixth day of this rule, it will begin to dry out, and then it will liquefy and congeal, and liquefy again a hundred times a day, until it begins to granulate. It will appear as if the whole thing has broken apart into grains, and then it will unite again, putting on infinite masks of forms from day to day; and this will last for about two weeks. At last, by the command of GOD, a Light will shine upon your matter such as you can hardly imagine. Then expect the end quickly, which you will see after three days, because the matter will granulate like the atoms of the Sun, and the color will be so intensely red that, due to its surpassing redness, it will look black, like the healthiest clotted blood—though you might not believe that anything of the kind could be produced by art for this <term>Elixir</term>. # CHAPTER XXXI.
## Fermentation of the Stone.

**R**emember that you have now obtained the <term>incombustible red Sulfur</term> <note>A stable, solid state of the alchemical matter that can no longer be changed or destroyed by fire alone.</note>, which cannot be advanced any further by itself through any fire. Be extremely careful about something I forgot to mention in the previous chapter: in the regime of the <term>Yellow Sun</term> <note>original: "Solis citrini"; a stage characterized by a lemon-yellow color before the final red.</note>, before the arrival of the <term>supernatural son</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone itself, viewed as the "offspring" of the chemical marriage.</note>, who is clothed in a true <term>Tyrian color</term> <note>original: "colore verè Tyrio"; a deep, royal purple-red dye highly prized in the ancient world.</note>, do not—I say—turn your material into glass by using improper heat. If you do, it will thereafter be insoluble, and consequently, it will not congeal into those most beautiful, deep red atoms. Therefore, be cautious not to deprive yourself of such a great treasure.

Yet do not believe that you have found the end of your labors here; rather, proceed further, so that from this Sulfur you may obtain the <term>Elixir</term> by a repeated circulation of the <term>wheel</term> <note>The "Wheel" refers to the repeating cycle of vaporization and condensation within the sealed alchemical vessel.</note>. Therefore, take three parts of the most highly purified <term>Gold</term> <note>original: "Solis"; literally "of the Sun," the standard alchemical term for gold.</note>, and one part of this fiery Sulfur (you could take four parts Gold and a fifth part Sulfur, but the aforementioned proportion is better). Melt the Gold in a clean <term>crucible</term>, and once melted, throw in your Sulfur—but do so cautiously, lest it be lost to the smoke of the coals. Make them flow together, then pour it out into a <term>Receiver</term> <note>original: "Excipulum"; a vessel or mold used to catch the molten metal.</note>, and you will have a mass that can be ground into powder, of a most beautiful deep red color, though barely transparent.

Take one part of this finely ground mass and two parts of your <term>Sophic Mercury</term> <note>The alchemist's specialized "living" mercury, distinct from common quicksilver.</note>, mix them perfectly, and seal them in the glass. Govern the heat as before, and within two months you will see all the aforementioned regimes pass by in their proper order. This is the <term>true fermentation</term>, which you may repeat if you wish.

# CHAPTER XXXII.
## Imbibition of the Stone.

**K**now that many authors take "fermentation" in this work to mean an internal, invisible Agent, which they call a <term>ferment</term>. They say that by its power, the fugitive and thin spirits are thickened spontaneously without the "laying on of hands." They call our aforementioned method of fermentation <term>cibation</term> <note>From "cibus" (food); the process of "feeding" the stone to increase its volume or potency.</note> with "bread and milk"; so says <term>Ripley</term> <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a renowned English alchemist whose works were highly influential on Philalethes.</note>. I, however, am not accustomed to citing others, nor to swearing by their words in a matter known as well to me as to them, having my own...

...to observe the specific method. There is, therefore, another Operation by which the Stone is increased more in weight than in power; that is, take your perfected <term>Sulfur</term> <note>The fixed, solid substance produced after previous stages of the work.</note>, whether white or red, and to three parts of Sulfur add a fourth part of <term>Water</term> <note>original: "Aquæ"; refers to the alchemical mercury or solvent used to "feed" the stone.</note>. After a little blackness of six or seven days' cooking, your newly added water will be thickened like your Sulfur. Then add a fourth [part], not in respect to the whole Compound—which has already coagulated one fourth part—but in respect to the Sulfur before the first <term>imbibition</term> <note>The process of the solid material "drinking" or absorbing the liquid solvent.</note>. When this is dried, add more in respect to the three parts of Sulfur originally weighed before the first imbibition; and in this proportion, you should imbibe and congeal three times. Finally, in the seventh imbibition, you should add five parts of water, namely in respect to the Sulfur originally taken. When this is added, seal your vessel, and with a fire similar to the previous one, make it so that the entire compound passes through all the aforementioned <term>regimes</term> <note>The successive stages of color and chemical state: Black (Nigredo), White (Albedo), etc.</note>. This will be completed in one month at most, and then you have the true <term>Stone of the third order</term>, one part of which falls upon ten thousand, and will perfectly <term>tinge</term> <note>The act of transforming base metal into gold or silver by "dyeing" it with the Stone's essence.</note>.

# CHAPTER XXXIII.
## Multiplication of the Stone.

**F**or this, no other labor is required except that the perfected Stone be taken, and one part of it be joined with three, or at most four parts of the <term>Mercury of the first work</term> <note>The purified, "animated" mercury used at the very beginning of the process.</note>, and it should be governed by the proper fire for seven days, the vessel being very tightly closed. All the regimes will pass by with the greatest joy, and you will have the whole enriched with a thousand-fold power compared to the stone before its multiplication. And if you attempt this again, you will run through all the regimes in three days, and the medicine will be exalted yet another thousand-fold in its power of tinging. And if you still wish to repeat it, you will lead the work through all the regimes and colors within a natural day; and the same will be done in a single hour if you attempt it repeatedly, nor will you ever be able to find the [limit of the] power of your Stone. It will be so great that it exceeds the capacity of the mind, provided you persevere in this work. Now remember to give immortal thanks to **GOD**, because you now have the entire treasure of nature in your power.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.
### On the method of projection.

**T**ake of your perfected Stone, as has been said, either the white or the red, and according to the quality of the medicine, take four parts of either <term>luminary</term> <note>original: "luminaris"; refers to the "lights" of the sky—gold (the Sun) or silver (the Moon).</note>. Melt these in a clean crucible, then introduce your Stone according to the type of melted luminary—white or red—and once mixed, pour it into a <term>cone</term> <note>A cone-shaped mold used to separate the metal from slag.</note>. It will become a mass that can be ground into powder. Of this mixture, take one part, and ten parts of well-washed <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver.</note>. Heat the Mercury until it begins to crackle, then cast in your mixture, which will penetrate it in the blink of an eye. Then melt it with an increased fire, and the whole will be a medicine of the lower order. Of this, then take one part and project <note>The act of "throwing" the alchemical powder onto molten metal to trigger transmutation.</note> it upon any metal, melted and purified, as much as your Stone is able to tint; and you will have gold or silver so pure that nature could not provide anything purer. It is better, however, to project it step-by-step until the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The transformative power or "dye" of the Stone.</note> ceases, for in this way it will be more widely extended. This is because when so very little is projected upon so much, unless the projection is done in Mercury, there is a notable loss of the medicine due to the <term>dross</term> <note>original: "scoriae"; the stony waste matter or impurities separated from metals during smelting.</note> that clings to impure metals. Therefore, the better the metals are purified before projection, the better the business succeeds in the fire.

## CHAPTER XXXV.
### On the Manifold Use of this Art.

**H**e who has once perfectly worked out this art, by the blessing of **G O D**, I know not what he could desire in all this world, except that, safe from all evil fraud and deceit, he might continually serve his **G O D**. It would be vain, indeed the vainest of all things, to pant for the common air of worldly pomp; indeed, such things are not in the hearts of those who cultivate this art—rather, they despise and look down on them. He, therefore, who is blessed by **G O D** with this talent, has such a field of pleasure open to him:
First, if he were to live a thousand years, and daily feed a thousand thousand men, he would not lack, because according to his wish he is able to multiply the Stone both in weight and in power. So that all imperfect things, which are...

**W**hen I had already spent the better part of my life in the study of the humanities and the liberal arts, and in conversation with all those more learned men who seemed to possess more wisdom than the common folk, I had reached a point where I seemed to have acquired a firmer judgment—partly through constant reading and partly through the actual experience of things. I began to consider more sharply the various actions of men, which for the most part look toward pomp and the lust for dominating others and being preferred in honors, or toward promoting the gluttony and luxury of the body, or other such enormous vices. I saw that most people, through right or wrong, were preoccupied almost solely with accumulating riches, having cast aside all respect for conscience and all zeal for piety or virtue. Wherefore I hesitated for a long time, doubtful and uncertain, whether I should subscribe to **Democritus’s laughter** or **Heraclitus’s weeping** for the same reason; or whether I should truly pronounce with the Preacher: ***All is vanity of vanities.***

...forgotten, I was gladdened by a singular joy. Regarding the **Phoenix**, many doubt whether it exists anywhere, but far more doubt the aforementioned Medicine: Those who raise doubts for themselves about it, I would wish to refer to *Tacitus*, *Pliny*, and other writers of worldly affairs, who will satisfy them in this place. <note>Tacitus and Pliny the Elder were Roman authors who recorded the legend of the Phoenix as a real, albeit rare, biological phenomenon.</note>

Among these doubters I myself stood for a long time, as I could not bring my mind to believe that a Medicine of this kind was simply possible—although I had heard mention of it made by several most trustworthy men. I thought it to be either a counterfeit or entirely fabulous, just as such things brought from antiquity or distant lands beyond the common order of nature or custom usually tend to appear; I thought this with a preposterous obstinacy of mind. For who, I said, has ever professed a cure for anger, except in words alone, and not by natural remedies? Who does not know how to remove pain with mitigants—<term>narcotics</term>, <term>opiates</term>, and <term>laudanums</term> <note>original: "Narcoticis, Opiatis & Laudanis"; here referring to early pharmaceutical preparations of opium used for sedation and pain relief</note>—unless he is little skilled in Medicine?

Therefore, just as the first (a remedy for anger) is not necessary for a physician, so the second (a remedy for pain) is not unusual, but occurs very frequently in practice itself, so that there is no need to desire or seek a new medicine for either; much less to expend any labor or expense in searching for it. Furthermore, we read in the commentaries of the ancients how a certain Philosopher tried to correct the headlong anger of **Augustus Caesar**—namely, that he should do nothing while hindered by anger until he had silently run through the twenty-four elements of the alphabet in his mind. <note>This refers to the Stoic philosopher Athenodorus Cananites, who advised the Emperor to recite the alphabet to allow time for anger to cool.</note> If these are true aids, they are ready at hand for anyone and do not require expenses or other teachings. Not to add anything regarding the maxims of the moralists, promising remedies for both grief of the soul and for anger, for which it seems as proper to moderate and temper the passions as it is for a Physician to free the body from diseases and to preserve its optimal temperament. But having considered all these arguments, which suggest that no Medicine of this kind worthy of investigation is given, I have conversely brought forward those things which would establish it by affirmation...

...all goodness of the intellect. You have also heard that a certain medicine is called <margin>A certain medicine that brings joy.</margin> "joy-giving" because it gathers all the things that comfort the principal organs, clarify the blood, and generate good blood and <term>spirit<note>In historical medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors produced from the blood that powered movement, sensation, and thought.</term>: according to this, you can also say that a certain medicine <margin>A medicine leading to Paradise</margin> leads to paradise, because it is composed of things that dispose the blood toward mercy, piety, gentleness, and kindness; through these, a good appetite for good works follows. And a certain medicine <margin>A medicine inciting love.</margin> incites love, because it increases blood that is praiseworthy and clear in both quantity and quality, and it strips the blood of <term>melancholy<note>Black bile, associated with sadness and isolation.</note> and <term>phlegm<note>Associated with lethargy and coldness.</note>, which are the causes of worry that prevent sociability, health, and love. Truly, abundant and clear blood does the opposite: it incites a <note>original: "Venereum appetitum"</note> sexual desire, from which men by necessity love and engage in civil conversation, joys, and generosity. From this, it follows that the person loves and is loved and desired by all.

<margin>A medicine making one chaste and religious.</margin> And a certain medicine makes one chaste and religious because it inclines the blood toward coldness and scarcity; when this is done, a man does not desire sexual intercourse, nor women, nor games, nor songs, nor similar things. To speak generally, through medicines you can know the disposition of the blood toward any quality. The entire difference in a man’s character arises from blood that is hot, cold, moist, or dry; and with the aforementioned medicines, you also know how to produce whatever effect you wish in a person. You have also heard from the authors that a <margin>A certain medicine makes one a fool.</margin> certain medicine makes one a fool, and another makes one like a man possessed. If you wish to practice these secrets and be confirmed in them, look at us as familiar examples: not many men are of sound mind or good talent if they have drunk much wine (which is not an "alien" medicine). They are made <margin>From drinking much wine, men become dull.</margin> dull or furious, or possess characters very different from their non-drunken selves. 

And all things that change the blood to an excess of heat or cold transform the character and the intellect away from reason. You have seen that many times a man eats a certain food, and after eating he is rendered <margin>Food and drink sometimes alter the emotions.</margin> cheerful and playful, singing and quite different from how he was before he ate. Sometimes the opposite occurs, because the blood, spirit, and <term>complexion<note>The "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) unique to an individual's constitution.</note> are rectified and improved by the former, but corrupted by the latter. 

<margin>A physician makes a spendthrift out of a miser.</margin> Therefore, a Physician makes a spendthrift out of a miser, a lecher out of the chaste, and a bold man out of the fearful. Generally, just as he changes the complexion of the blood, it is necessary that the subsequent inclinations and temperaments change as well. <margin>The final secrets of medicine...</margin> And these are the ultimate secrets of the art of medicine itself. Sometimes, however, medicine only achieves these things as a distant consequence. Fools, when they read the books of wise and ancient Physicians who knew [these things]...

## A Subtle Allegory

<margin>Innumerable evils from anger.</margin>
...should be considered, at least, what evils have occurred from immoderate anger or wrath, both in princes and in private men. Since these are without number, as evidenced by the monuments of the histories of all times, then a **Medicine** which removes or averts that anger is of immense utility.

Whatever has been said concerning anger ought also to be understood concerning pain. For just as anger appears most evident and enormous among the passions of the soul, <margin>Pain is the sharpest of symptoms.</margin> so among the symptoms of the body, pain is the most sensible and remarkable—so much so that it not infrequently draws the care of the Physician to itself by a certain inevitable necessity, even before the disease is conquered or the cause expelled. <margin>Medicine prevailing over gold.</margin> Therefore, it did not seem ill-advised to embrace such a *Medicine* that ejects pain from the body and anger from the soul at the same time. This, I say, is a Medicine which far prevails over gold, provided that the **Phoenix** <note>In alchemical literature, the Phoenix represents the "Philosopher's Stone" or the perfected medicine, capable of total restoration.</note> from which it is sought can be found. Where shall I look? Where shall I investigate? Whom shall I ask? He who knows will scarcely reveal it; he who knows not will be unable to tell of it. Meanwhile, the die must be cast and the path attempted; since those who idle at home learn scarcely any secret, <margin>Medicine must be sought through travel.</margin> but fortune favors the bold. Hence, it has been established within me by a most certain resolution of mind to leave my fatherland, which is dear to me, and to set out to foreign lands, so that I might either consume my life in pilgrimage or finally bring home with me the longed-for medicine with joy.

<margin>Objection against travel.</margin>
It is heavy, I confess, to change soil and sky—to migrate from the known to the unknown, from fellow-citizens to barbarians, from kinsmen to the <term>Antipodes<note>Literally "those with feet opposite ours"; used here to mean the most distant parts of the earth.</note></term>—on account of a doubtful hope for a medicine preconceived in the mind. Whether such a thing exists in the nature of things is a "dispute still before the judge" <note>original: "sub judice lis est"; a legal phrase meaning the matter is undecided.</note>, as very many will say. But I have nothing to respond to these people, except what <term>Tullius<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note></term> once wrote to his friend <term>Trebatius<note>Caius Trebatius Testa, a lawyer to whom Cicero wrote letters while Trebatius was away in Gaul.</note></term> acting outside of Rome: "Many have managed their own affairs and the public's well while far from their fatherland." Every beginning is difficult, and he who has never been saddened shall not rejoice; he who has never wandered shall not be led back to the true way. For as the <term>Chemists<note>original: "Chymici"; here referring to alchemists.</note></term> <margin>*The Rose Garden of the Philosophers*<note>original: "Rosarium Philosophorum"; a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note></margin> say: there is in Chemistry a certain noble body which is moved from master to master, in the beginning of which there is misery with vinegar, but in the end, joy with gladness. So I have presupposed it will happen to me: that first I would taste, endure, and experience many harsh, bitter, sad, and tedious things, <margin>There is no doubt that the Phoenix exists.</margin> so that finally I might see all things more joyful and easy. Concerning that Medicine, or the Phoenix—whether it exists—I did not doubt; for if I had doubted, how would I have sought it?

<summary>The author argues that a medicine capable of curing both physical pain and the "passion" of anger is more valuable than gold. He announces his decision to go on a pilgrimage to find this secret "Phoenix," acknowledging the hardships of travel but remaining firm in his belief that the goal exists.</summary>

...if I had not sought it, how would I have had the hope of finding it? Let it suffice for me to have seen the shadow of the sun or its rays, even if I have not touched the sun itself with my fingers. Perhaps it would be useless for us—surrounded by these earthly dregs—to be joined to and immediately touch such a noble and bright celestial body. <margin>That which was grand was once narrow. <note>original: "Augustum fuit angustum." A Latin wordplay on "Augustus" (venerable/grand) and "angustus" (narrow/limited).</note></margin> What is grand in human affairs that was not narrow in its beginnings? Is not man himself made from the earth? <note>original: "Annon ipse homo ex humo?" A common Latin etymological pun linking "homo" (man) to "humus" (ground/earth).</note> How then, I ask, would I have perfect knowledge of the **Medicine** which I seek, before I have seen or touched it? How would I turn out to be a master, before I have been a student? I must therefore travel through diverse regions of the world; for "not every land bears all things." <note>A quotation from Virgil’s *Georgics*, implying that specific knowledge or materials are tied to specific locations.</note> Perhaps in one place I will see that which I had not even thought of in a dream in another. <margin>Traveling can harm no one.</margin> Can traveling harm me? I think not at all. For we are all pilgrims in this world, even in our own earthly homeland. From here we shall finally migrate to those brightest ethereal homes, where our Savior, who has gone before, calls and draws us. <margin>Birds teaching us about travel.</margin> Let me look at the swallow, the messenger of spring, the crane, the stork, and many other birds—how they travel annually through the air at fixed times to unknown regions by the instinct and teaching of nature. They provide for man a pattern and example of the travel to be undertaken through the parts of the world, lest he should always grow old in the smoke and dung of his own hearth. <note>original: "lariū" (of the hearth/home). In Roman tradition, the Lares were household gods protecting the home.</note> To the birds the whole <term>sublunary air</term> <note>The region below the moon, which in traditional cosmology was the realm of change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> lies open, and to man the terrestrial globe. <margin>The sun, the great traveler of heaven, delights in motion.</margin> Let me look at heaven itself, and its great traveler, the **Sun**, how it delights in continuous motion and illustrates and illuminates, warms and governs all creatures of the sun and the pole. <margin>The human heart continues life through motion.</margin> Indeed, let me direct my mind into the very depths of my breast, to the heart itself, how it is driven by this perpetual motion as long as life remains; for just as it measures out life by its healthy motion, so it ends life when that motion is removed, injured, or hindered. <margin>It is natural for man to travel. The utility of travel.</margin> It is therefore natural for man to be moved from place to place, from region to region, while he looks within himself, above himself, and around himself. But since all motion is made toward a goal—especially that of sentient and rational beings, driven by an appetite or will directed by the imagination or intellect toward a certain end—hence for the sake of his own profit, the merchant runs through the sea and through lands to the Indies, fleeing poverty; and others are impelled by other causes. <margin>One must travel for the sake of the goods of the soul.</margin> So also we, for the sake of the goods of the soul, the secrets of nature, the gifts of God, and the sciences and arts...

-> Subtilis Allegoria <-

## A Subtle Allegory

...and to seek out and investigate things, why should we not go to more remote places? For he who has grown old in his own home will also bury his wisdom there, and he will not recognize any of those things that are in the world, nor will he be recognized by others; unless he is twice a child. <note>original: "bis puer." A reference to the proverb that "an old man is twice a child," here implying that a man who never travels remains as ignorant as an infant.</note> <margin>The delight of travel</margin> It is also pleasant and wonderful to see so many and such varied nations, descended from the greatest paternal and maternal ancestor of us all, **Adam**, who possess the inheritance left to them by him, subdivided into very unequal parts. <margin>The honor of travel</margin> What is more honorable than to have outpaced the celestial Sun in the course of a single day—that is, by surveying the entire globe of the earth from east to west and then returning to one's homeland having completed the circle—to have anticipated or shown oneself as a companion of its usual journey? <margin>A day is lost or gained by those circumnavigating the globe</margin> For a day is missing for all who circumnavigate the terrestrial globe from east to west, and it is extra for those traveling from west to east; the cause of this was once obscure, but is now well enough known. <note>This is an early description of the "circumnavigation paradox," where traveling around the world results in losing or gaining a calendar day, famously documented by the survivors of Magellan's voyage.</note>

Indeed, the closer something approaches a spiritual essence, having been purged and purified from earthly weight, the faster and more agile it becomes in motion. <margin>The more spiritual, the more mobile</margin> The sluggish earth rests, and rightly so, because it is the immobile center of the world; <note>The author writes from a geocentric perspective, where the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note> But the water moves and the whole Ocean ebbs and flows, and that four times in the space of 24 hours; likewise, the springs and rivers, like the offspring of that great parent, move in a fixed order, and by running, they carry their sweet delights to the Ocean to temper the salt water. <margin>Three elements are moved</margin> With what great force the air is driven is demonstrated by the winds, whirlwinds, and the clouds carried around by them, as well as the massive weights of ships and the mills themselves. Our fire departs in continuous motion, so that it cannot be kept unless it is always generated anew from flammable materials. 

Heaven itself, with its stars—those bodies so vast—how great are the journeys it completes! Indeed, the rush of the stars and of heaven is so great that a man cannot even imagine such speed. <margin>The rush of the heavens is incomprehensible to the imagination</margin> An iron ball from a cannon <note>original: "tormento," a general term for an engine of war, here specifically a cannon.</note> by the force of <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "pulveris Pyrii," literally "fire-powder."</note>, if it were to encircle the entire earth while maintaining the same speed, would perhaps require eight whole days before it finished 5,400 <term>German miles</term> <note>A German mile was roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers; 5,400 of them (approx. 40,500 km) is a very accurate estimate of the Earth's circumference.</note> (that is, the great circle of the earth), returning to the point from which it was launched; but the Sun, at such a great distance from the surface of the earth, covers more distance in one hour than all those miles; indeed, perhaps in a quarter of an hour—a speed which no man can measure in his thoughts.

<summary>The author justifies his travels by observing that motion is a divine and natural law, noting how the four elements and celestial bodies move with increasing speed as they become less "earthly." He highlights the wonder of circumnavigation and the staggering velocity of the heavens compared to man-made objects like cannonballs.</summary>

<margin>Human thoughts are the swiftest things.</margin>
Not to speak of the higher heaven of Saturn or the <term>first moveable sphere</term> <note>original: "primo mobili." In the ancient geocentric model, the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries all others with it.</note>, which are positioned far higher than the sun: what is swifter than human thoughts? There is nothing among human things; yet in these, intellectual substances <note>The author refers here to angels or spiritual beings.</note> are said to be equal in speed, and to be moved in the <margin>Angels are said to move in an instant.</margin> very <term>Now</term> <note>original: "Nunc." A technical term in medieval philosophy for an indivisible moment of time, suggesting instantaneous movement.</note> or moment; since they are indivisible in an indivisible point, not in time. Truly *God*, who is free from all movement, is everywhere, and has no need to move to where He already is. Since it is impossible for a man to be in many <margin>God does not move, because He is everywhere.</margin> places simultaneously and at once (which is the property of God alone), it is closest to divinity to be present in those places at different times, as far as is permitted.

<margin>Why one must travel.</margin>
Therefore, let it not be tedious to me, but by far most pleasant—not dishonorable, but in many ways most honorable—not useless, but joined with the highest utility—to have surveyed many regions of this world; not merely to see stones and forests among foreigners, but to seek out the <term>Phoenician Medicine</term> <note>A poetic alchemical name for the Philosopher’s Stone, which, like the mythical Phoenix, is capable of self-renewal and perfection.</note> in the world by consulting the wisest men and conferring with them about things which the ignorant common folk do not so much respect as despise.

<margin>What the intention and order of the journey is.</margin>
And so I have equipped myself for a long journey, having prepared all things that seem necessary, which are not to be recounted here. First, I have decided to survey the kingdoms and borders of *Europe*; then, if there be need, I have deliberated to cross into *America*, from there into *Asia*, and finally into *Africa*. For I did not doubt that that medicinal bird <note>An alchemical symbol for the volatile spirit or the Stone itself.</note> lies hidden in one of these great parts of the terrestrial globe; and if I could perceive even a faint breeze of its fame, I trusted that in the course of time I would arrive at the knowledge of its perfection. But if, after traveling through all these continents of the Earth, I should hear nothing of so great a Gift of God, I would be deprived of all hope of attaining it.

<margin>Why the order of the journey is such.</margin>
But why I have pre-conceived this order in my mind for undertaking the journey, passing from one part to another, this cause seemed sufficient to me: that I ought to imitate the natural series of the elements, by which they migrate from the thick into the subtle, and from the heavy into the light. For thus *Europe* best represents the image and powers of **earth**, *America* of **water**, *Asia* of **air**, and *Africa* of **fire**.

<margin>The 4 parts of the terrestrial globe are assigned to the elements of the world.</margin>
Furthermore, air is not made from earth except by the mediation of water, and fire is not made from water except by the mediation of air. We shall declare more clearly under each individual section how these parts of the earth are assigned to the said elements. Here let it suffice to have shown some kind of

### EUROPE: EARTH.

<margin>Europe is likened to the element of Earth.</margin>
**H**aving departed my native soil on the very day of the Vernal Equinox <note>The Spring Equinox, usually March 21st, traditionally seen as the beginning of the alchemical year.</note>, when the MOON was positioned with the Sun in the sign of ARIES near the <term>Dragon’s Head</term> <note>original: "caput Draconis." In historical astronomy, this refers to the ascending lunar node, the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic going north; it was considered an auspicious placement.</note>, as the Astronomers call it, I first decided to travel through EUROPE, so that I might learn something certain: whether that bird, the Phoenix, might be there, or if any rumor of its presence might be noticed anywhere. 

<margin>Why Europe is a firm land and the foundation of the world.</margin>
Europe is indeed a firm Land, like the base and foundation of the whole inhabited world, for the following reasons: Earth, as can be seen on a terrestrial globe, is far surpassed by the waters around its surface, although the earth supports the water and is itself supported by no other element except itself or the all-powerful hand of the Divine. 

<margin>Europe surpasses the other parts in many ways.</margin>
Hence *Europe* is far smaller than the other parts of the earth, yet in strength, people, bravery, and spirit it far precedes them. There are those who say this <term>chain of nature</term> <note>original: "cathenam naturæ." A reference to the "Great Chain of Being" or the interconnectedness of the elements.</note> of mutable elements observes this series: 

<margin>The chain of elements and the proportion by which they cohere.</margin>
that one handful of earth gives ten handfuls of water, a hundred of air, and a thousand of fire. If these things are true, they easily indicate the excellence, compaction, weight, and stability of *Earth* over the remaining elements. 

<margin>Europe is strongest in arms.</margin>
In the same way *Europe* (I say this with the peace of the other parts of the world) is the strongest of all, most vigorous in arms, and more ready for resistance. Indeed, since offspring follow their mother in character, hence 

<margin>European warriors.</margin>
*European* warriors have always been the masters and subjugators of other nations, themselves undefeated by others. 

<margin>The 4 great empires of the world.</margin>
As a demonstration from experience, let us look at the four greatest empires of the world, mentioned in the sacred prophecies of the Prophet Daniel <note>The biblical "Four Kingdoms" (Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome) interpreted here as a progression of power toward Europe.</note>: *Asia* held the first monarchy, being fortunate from its first condition, as well as the second, but it barely extended any dominion over *Europe*, except perhaps a tiny bit. 

<margin>Europe's two lights: Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.</margin>
But *Europe*, through that Macedonian youth, *Alexander the Great*, subjected an immense space in the other parts of the world all the way to India. Thus also under *Julius Caesar*, the Roman Emperor, she was the mistress of *Asia and Africa* for the most part.

# On the Super Secrets of Chemistry.

<margin>Europe is a virgin in form, a lion in heart.</margin>
<margin>Why Europe is called a virgin.</margin>
These two lights of Europe have left the strength and power of her soil and people well-attested among the surrounding nations, so that there is no need to bring more evidence into the open. Hence, Europe reflects a **Virgin** in the form of her body, but in the spiritedness of her heart, she truly expresses a **Lion**. Here, therefore, this *Virgin Lion* is the beginning of our survey; in describing her, so that she may be recognized, the first goal of the work to be undertaken is proposed. She is a Virgin, not only in her external face and the lines of her body, but also in her character, her institutions, and her affairs.

<margin>Why Europe is called a lion.</margin>
<margin>The Sun, Europe, and Gold correspond.</margin>
<margin>In England, two Lions were recently born: James and Henry.</margin>
<margin>A venerable land.</margin>
<margin>The Virgin Mother.</margin>
<margin>Germany is the fat belly of Europe.</margin>
For *Europe* has suffered no violence from others, though she has had countless suitors. She is a **Lion** because she rules over many subjects and is subject to none; and as many Kings as she nourishes, she displays just as many Lion-like hearts, just as they appear everywhere upon their shields <note>A reference to heraldry; the lion is one of the most common symbols on European royal coats of arms.</note>. Among the celestial planets, the *Sun* corresponds to Europe, and among metals, *Gold*—that is, the most perfect of each kind. For even if the Sun rarely produces a *Lion* in European lands, nor gold as abundantly as in other more burning regions, nevertheless we know that she lacks neither, though they be brought from elsewhere. We know also that in our age, *Lions* were born in *Albion* <note>original: "Albia." Likely referring to Albion (England), as the marginal note explicitly mentions the English princes James and Henry.</note>, and in countless other places gold has come forth most abundantly, lest Europe be judged less fortunate than the others in these gifts. This is that land which I venerate; this is that mother who is always known as a virgin. This is the most ingenious nurse of peoples, who has supplied many gifts discovered by herself through the most subtle craftsmanship. In her sits the *German Navel* <note>original: "Umbilicus Germanicus." This refers to the central position of Germany within the "Europa Regina" (Queen Europe) maps popular in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>, like an immobile center, upon which the *Axiom of Imperial Dignity* <note>The Holy Roman Empire.</note> depends; likewise, many arts have flowed forth as if from the most fertile *Horn of Amalthea* <note>The Cornucopia or "horn of plenty."</note>. In *Europe* there are various miraculous endowments, which it is not the place to recount here, except as they agree with the element of Earth which we are treating.

<margin>The wonders of Europe.</margin>
<margin>The walls of Madruzzo.</margin>
They write that in certain places of *Pannonia* <note>A Roman province roughly corresponding to modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions.</note>, men live under the waters, because tufa-like stones have hardened and grown out of the waters. In the *Caroline* mountains <note>Likely referring to the region of Karlsbad (Karlovy Vary) in the modern Czech Republic, famous for its mineral springs.</note>, boiling waters similarly turn into stone. Elsewhere, they assert that mortals live within fire—if indeed flint-stones actually contain fire—such as in *Castile*.

<margin>Prussian Amber. Coral is a stone from a shrub.</margin>
Who would not marvel that amber, a transparent and fragrant stone, is birthed from subterranean juices and driven to the shores by the waves of the sea, as in *Sudovia*, the maritime coast of *Prussia*? Not to mention the Corals of Si— <note>The text cuts off mid-word as a catchword for the next page: "Sicily".</note>

<margin>Europe is like Gold.</margin>

Having traveled through many famous places, I could find no one who could make me more certain about the **Phoenix** <note>In alchemy, the Phoenix is a symbol for the Philosopher's Stone or the "Universal Medicine," representing death and perfected rebirth.</note> and its Medicine; truly, I encountered many who mocked me as if I were *wasting work and oil* <note>original: "operam & oleum luserint." <margin>The words and reasons of those who wished to frighten away the seeker of the medicine.</margin>

<margin>What things are neglected while this Medicine is sought.</margin>
Meanwhile, many other useful callings and professions are neglected, expenses are worn away, time passes, and in the end, nothing is found in the seas. To spend certain money and the precious time of life on uncertain things is the mark of an uncertain and vain man." 

"I," another suggested, "would wish to bestow nothing on this medicine unless, while seeking it in passing, I were to handle other more truthful works from which profit might come to me; if you do the same, you will always remain without loss."

...laborious, and strong in talent and the knowledge of things: for if someone should look into this art only in passing, it is the same as if he does nothing at all. <margin>Alchemy requires the whole man.</margin>
The cause is clear: because the matter is most hidden. It is finally noticed only through deep speculation and the use of many things not dissimilar to this, and only after various previous errors regarding the same subject. It is never found by chance by unlearned **Empirics** <term>Empirics: Here used disparagingly to describe "quacks" or practitioners who work by trial and error without understanding the underlying philosophical or natural principles.</term>. And though I do not recognize such and so great gifts in myself, yet I know not by what guidance or nod (I believe, certainly divine) I am swept willy-nilly into these difficulties. I hold a pre-conceived and indubitable hope that I shall finally find the sought-after Medicine by the grace of God. 
<margin>Chemical Medicine is to be preferred above all other goods.</margin>
Just as his Queen seems beautiful to any King, or a bride to her groom, so this **Medicine** smiles upon me above all the goods of the world; by a certain magnetic virtue, it fascinates and binds my mind to itself, such that I would be willing to go without life, friends, and kin, if I must lack it. 

What **Hippocrates** <note>Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> otherwise pronounced regarding Medicine—that *Art is long, life is short, judgment is difficult, and experiment is deceptive*—can be most truly understood regarding this Alchemical Art. To the former [general medicine], very many attain; but to this [alchemy], very few arrive. The reason is that *beautiful things are difficult* <note>original: "pulchra difficilia." A common Latin proverb derived from the Greek "chalepa ta kala," suggesting that anything worthwhile requires great effort.</note>, and sweat is placed before virtue and glory. For one tends toward rest only through the land of labor. 

This was the sum of my response. 
<margin>Journey into Hesperia.</margin>
And now I had traversed a large part of **Europe**, when it occurred to me that mention is very often made among the ancients of **Hesperia** <note>A name used by ancient Greeks to refer to the "Western land," usually Italy or the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal).</note> and **Iberia** when secret matters are dealt with. Wherefore I did not cease to betake myself there. <margin>Geber, Avicenna, and others.</margin>
I did not stop inquiring of the more learned here regarding the three-bodied **Geryon**; and **Hercules**, who drove away Geryon's purple cattle after slaying him; and the **Gardens of the Hesperides** bearing golden apples on trees, which the same Hercules took away. 
<margin>Who is Geryon, son of Chrysaor? Who is Hercules?</margin>
From these learned men I perceived that **Geryon, the son of Chrysaor**, consisting of three bodies, is that which is written of by the Philosophers: *I saw three faces in one parent*; and the cattle are of the same intention. Hercules himself is the laborious craftsman, or the searcher of this medicine, who, being about to go to the cattle, by solar rays...

## A Subtle Allegory

<margin>Hercules was gifted a golden cup by the sun to serve as a ship.</margin>
...being excessively heated by its rays, he glowed white-hot with anger and aimed his bow at the sun itself. On account of this greatness of soul, we read that he was gifted by the sun with a golden cup, which he used in place of a ship to cross the Ocean to the cattle <note>This refers to the tenth labor of Hercules, fetching the cattle of Geryon. In alchemy, Hercules often represents the wandering philosopher or the "agent" that overcomes various chemical transformations.</note>:
<margin>The Cup of Hercules, which contained a medicine for anger and grief.</margin>
In this cup, there was undoubtedly contained a kind of medicine for moderating the anger of Hercules—if not in its outward form, then certainly in its matter <note>The author suggests the "cup" is actually a chemical vessel containing a substance that stabilizes volatile reactions.</note>. Thus, from the Sun, Hercules received the Medicine for Anger and Grief, which he carried away with him. For all wise men have determined that there was a tiny portion of the **Phoenix’s feathers** in that cup.
<margin>The Fortunate Islands, and where they are now located.</margin>
Since many islands are numbered among the Spanish kingdoms, and among the others those called the "Fortunate" or the Canaries, I did not wish to depart from Europe before I had surveyed them as well.
<margin>The seven Canary Islands, and what they are.</margin>
These are seven in number: namely Lanzarote, Fuerteventura <note>original: "Bonaventura"</note>, Gran Canaria, Tenerife, La Gomera, El Hierro <note>original: "Ferro"</note>, and La Palma. Three of these—namely Lanzarote, Gomera, and El Hierro—obey their own individual kings. Regarding this last one, El Hierro, where I landed, they tell of this marvelous property and privilege of nature: that it has water produced within its trees. For since this island is entirely destitute of fresh water, men and animals could not live here unless it were brought from elsewhere. But nature provided for this defect with certain trees having broad leaves, from which, at a certain time, fresh water drips in such abundance that it suffices for the whole island. Since foreigners or pirates arriving on the island are ignorant of this, they are unable to remain there long due to the penury of drinkable water. Anyone will observe from the accounts of history that these things are true.
<margin>Allegory. This Virgin is called by Alphidius <note>Alphidius was a famous, though semi-mythical, Arabic alchemical philosopher often cited in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> a girl with a beautiful face, whose eyes are black and eyebrows joined, pregnant, holding one breast.</margin>
It happened at the same time that the Ruler of Gomera died without a male heir, leaving an only daughter, most beautiful, named **Blanca** <note>The name "Blanca" (White) is a clear reference to the *Albedo*, or the whitening stage of the Alchemical Great Work.</note>. Although she held the legitimate right of succession in her father's kingdom, her subjects nevertheless declared themselves unwilling to submit to a female rule unless she should marry some King. For they said that, besides being against the order of nature for the male sex to be subjected to the female, it introduced a certain "effeminization" of the men, and the domination of women over them—as is established by the experience of those peoples over whom women have ruled for any length of time.
<margin>What the rule of women brings with it.</margin>
For there, women almost represent the men, and men the women; and adulteries are so frequent that married women, in secret brothels, [prostitute] themselves to others, from [the persuasion of] procuresses...

From here, I decided to sail to *America* with a favorable wind, so that there, among the barbarians, if by chance the Phoenix...

# AMERICA, WATER.

<margin>America, water.</margin>
To travel to *America*, called the New World, or the already-known *West Indies*, by ship does not seem a matter of great difficulty, since constant use and habit have found a sort of "Royal Road" through the Ocean by the guidance of the magnet <note>The mariner's compass.</note>. But to have tracked it down for the first time and brought it to the knowledge of others, *this was the work, this the labor.* <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* regarding the difficulty of a great task.</note>
<margin>The Black Eagle on the stern of the ship by which America was sought.</margin>
Leaving the *Fortunate Islands* behind, I boarded a ship, on the stern of which was a **Black Eagle** <note>The "Black Eagle" is a common alchemical symbol, often representing the sublimation of mercury or the "extraction" of the spirit from the material body.</note>. Having crossed the waves of the Ocean, which were horribly black by night, and having endured many dangers inflicted by sea monsters, adverse whirlwinds, and storms, we at last joyfully reached the shores of **Brazil**. 
<margin>What Brazil is.</margin>
Brazil is a great province of *America*, filled with continuous forests. The huts of the settlers are few, towns are very rare, and the men are entirely estranged from the study of the liberal arts. Whom here, I ask, can I consult concerning the most hidden secrets of nature, 
<margin>The Americans were unrefined in letters or writing.</margin>
where the inhabitants, not long ago, regarded the reading of a letter written and sent by Spaniards to one another as a miracle? They thought the paper was "talkative" and a "betrayer of deeds" <note>This refers to a common colonial anecdote where indigenous people, unfamiliar with writing, thought the paper itself was speaking or spying.</note>. Whom should I ask about the **Phoenix**, the rarest of all birds? It is indeed certain that birds of various kinds and colors are found there, such as are not seen in these parts of the earth; but since the Phoenix is of a far different nature and property, there is no reason for us to seek it among common birds. 
<margin>Allegory.</margin>
Here the forests are crowded with fragrant and diversely colored trees. While I was walking among them, occupied in meditation—partly to refresh my eyes with the joyful sight of the trees and flowers, and partly to relax my mind from cares with the natural music of the 
<margin>The discovery of the apple.</margin>
singing birds—by chance I happened upon an **apple** of unusual and miraculous elegance. While I contemplated it from every side, I found an inscription of this kind:

<margin>The Enigma of the Grafted Apple</margin>
> *Within lies what you give to the grandmother; from there arising,* <note>original: *Intus adest aviæ, quod tradas, inde resurgens*. In alchemical symbolism, the "grandmother" usually refers to the Earth, the primary element from which all things spring.</note>
> *The Son can enter into his mother’s embrace.* <note>The "Son" is the refined spirit or seed; the "Mother" is the matter or the tree from which it came.</note>
> *From there, a noble tree will be reborn a little later,*
> *Which will give the farmer gold-haired offspring.* <note>The "gold-haired offspring" refers to the golden apples of the Hesperides, a symbol for the completed Philosopher’s Stone.</note>

<margin>Explanation of the apple enigma</margin>
After considering these things for a long time and with great care, I finally understood that the grain hiding within must be entrusted to the grandmother—that is, the earth—since the tree appeared to be the mother of that apple, and the earth the mother of the tree. Therefore, I took this up as a gift offered by Divine Power, until I might have the opportunity to put it to the test and prove it by experiment, just as the inscription teaches:

<margin>The process of grafting trees</margin>
Indeed, I consider the method of proceeding to be this: that I ought to take the seeds of this apple (perhaps brought there from the **Garden of the Hesperides**) <note>In Greek mythology, a garden producing golden apples; in alchemy, it represents the place where the "gold" of the Great Work is grown.</note> and place them in the earth. Then, in a short time, saplings of that same tree to which the apple belongs will grow up. Afterward, another tree of the same kind must be sought, or one that comes very close to the first, and it must be decapitated or cut down to the trunk. Then the aforementioned cut sapling must be inserted into the trunk as a **graft** <term>surculus: a small shoot or twig used for grafting</term>. When these two have grown together into one tree, that trunk will turn out far more noble than it was before, because of the grafting of the shoot; for it will be entirely converted to the nature of the grafted shoot. And the fruit which arises from it will reflect the nature of the shoot or the apple previously found. No one can deny that this is a natural artifice, which is perfected by the benefit of both nature and art.

<margin>Another allegory: The process of breeding mules from different species of animals</margin>
It is well known that in the same region <note>America/The West Indies.</note>, before the arrival of the Spaniards, there were no horses, and a rider first appeared to those men as a certain miraculous animal. But later, when horses were brought along with donkeys, and the wealthier people used the labor of these beasts of burden, they heard that there was also a third animal produced from both, yet different from either, called a **mule**. Therefore, they applied all their strength to producing this creature. There was, in particular, a certain man of noble birth who took charge of this matter; he had already procured for himself the most noble horses, and he also kept not a few donkeys assigned to the labors of the mills. The method of breeding horses from mares was very well known, as was that of donkeys from their own kind; but it was not so for mules. Hence, this matter had to be tested by experience.

<margin>A dangerous experience</margin>
However, all experience is dangerous or full of errors when it is done without a previously held example of a known thing, or through **reason**...

It highlights the transition from natural growth to "Art," where the alchemist improves upon nature's base products.</summary>

# A Subtle Allegory

...with very true investigation: Fodder was provided for the horse with great care and in abundance, yet from its mounting of the female donkey nothing was generated. This was, without doubt, because there was no proportion between the seeds of both. When this had been tried often in vain, all hope of breeding a mule failed.

<margin>The Philosopher examines the natures of things more sharply than the common people.</margin>
At last, when one of those who examine the nature of things and animals more sharply than those common folk had arrived at that place, and noticed the repeated complaint of the said master regarding that matter, he said: "Even if I am not a doctor for mules or a veterinarian, but a **Philosopher** <note>In this context, a "Philosopher" refers to an Alchemist, a "searcher of nature's secrets."</note>, yet I think I see what is the cause of the frustrated conception of the mule." And when he was begged by the master to declare it, he said, "I will speak as I have received and am able," and thus he began:

->*So that a mule may be brought forth, make the father resemble a little donkey*<-
->*In ears and slow steps; do this:*<-
->*Let each be given their own fodder by the weight of nature,*<-
<margin>Enigma concerning the conception of the mule.</margin>
->*Which, if perchance you wish to ask, how much shall it be?*<-
->*Add half of what belongs to the agent, and double of that one,*<- <note>This refers to alchemical proportions; the "agent" is the active substance (the "father" or horse/donkey) which must be balanced with the "patient" or matter.</note>
->*Then the mare will generate a mule from the donkey.*<-

The master, placing his faith in these words which held little obscurity, and after multiple experiments were finally conducted, obtained a mule—an animal more like the father than the mother, yet different from both. Who does not see that these are the privileges of nature: that from two things a third is generated, which does not agree in species with either, but has a form distinct from them?

<margin>The mule is different from the father and mother.</margin>
If anyone imitates nature in these things, he will without doubt produce many other kinds of animals, vegetables, and metals. It is affirmed for certain that many of the sharpest examiners of nature have already proven this by practice itself.
