# On the Secrets of Chemistry

<margin>*A new technique for softening gold.*</margin>
They say they possess a unique skill above all others: namely, how gold can be softened by a certain water to such an extent that it can be handled with the fingers like wax. Indentations can be pressed into it, and gems can be inserted, with the edges and rims secured on all sides. This technique, which is more commonly used in **Peru**, is a secret of nature and art not to be looked down upon. Indeed, that water does not seem to be made of corrosives; otherwise, it could not be handled with the fingers, or if it were, the gold would have to be shaped with some glass stylus. Whatever the case may be, no one will doubt that it is an invention of **Chemistry** <note>In this 17th-century context, "Chemistry" and "Alchemy" were often interchangeable terms for the study of transforming matter.</note>, since such waters are hardly produced by nature, but by the art of distillation.

<margin>*American Chemical water for softening gold.*</margin>
Having surveyed all these things, since no hope remained here for the medicine I sought, I thought to leave these parts as soon as possible and cross over to **Asia** when the opportunity arose. The most precious thing I saw here in **Brazil** was a wood as black as ebony (to say nothing of that red wood called **Brazilwood**) <note>original: "rubrum illud Brasiliarum dictum"; referring to the pau-brasil tree which gave the country its name.</note>, of great weight and value. I brought back some of it in memory of America, on account of its black color, which I especially admired and held in high esteem.

<margin>*The black color peculiar to America.*</margin>
For this color seems peculiar to America because of the dark-skinned peoples and the earth being imbued with various colors; concerning which the most learned **Monardes** <note>Nicolás Monardes (c. 1493–1588) was a famous Spanish physician who wrote the first comprehensive study of medicinal plants from the New World.</note>, a Physician of Seville, writes thus in his book on medicines brought from the West Indies:

> It is a wonderful thing and worthy of consideration, the variety of colors of the Peruvian earth. For if one observes from a distance, he will see many parts of the soil tinted with different colors, so that they look like cloths of various colors exposed to the sun to be dried. For one part of the earth is green, another blue, another another color, such as yellow, white, black, and red, or yet others, all of which are different minerals of the earth. Regarding the black, a portion of which they sent to me, I can affirm that I made the best ink from it when mixed with water or wine, very suitable for writing; it has a little blue in it, which makes it look better. He says the red earth is a mineral of **quicksilver** <note>original: "mineram argenti vivi"; cinnabar, the primary ore of mercury.</note>, with which those Indians painted themselves.

# ASIA, AIR.

<margin>The origin of the names for the four parts of the earth.</margin>
**T**hey say that **Asia** was named after *Asius, son of Manaus the Lydian*, just as *Europe* was named after *Europa*, the daughter of *Agenor, King of the Phoenicians*, who was abducted by *Jupiter* and car-
<margin>Asia, an airy land.</margin>
ried away to *Crete*. *America*, meanwhile, was named after its discoverer *Amerigo Vespucci*, and *Africa* (which the Greeks called *Libya*) after *Afer*, one of the descendants of *Abraham* by *Keturah*, who is said to have led an army into *Libya* and settled there. Whatever the reasoning for these names, it is of little concern to the matter at hand. However,
*Asia* is the third continent of the world, or an airy land of a more temperate nature than the remaining parts. For just as *Europe* is troubled by cold in certain regions, and *Africa* by heat, *Asia* par-
<margin>Why Asia represents the element of Air.</margin>
takes of neither the most intense cold nor heat. For this reason, it best represents for us the element of Air, which is hot and moist, with its heat tempering the cold and its moisture tempering the dryness. For regions situated on the sea, even if they are quite hot, nevertheless have their heat mitigated by the moisture of the waters; if they are cold, the cold is likewise
<margin>Why islands are less hot and cold.</margin>
softened. For if we carefully consider the nature of hot and moist air and examine its genealogy from its causes, we shall find that
<margin>The genealogy of hot and moist air.</margin>
fiery heat is its father, while watery moisture is its mother. Like a son, Air retains the more active qualities of these parents: namely, heat and moisture together. Hence, it is a mediator between the contrary elements already mentioned, and because it is joined to both by a kind of kinship, it renders them friendly and unites them in every mixture of bodies.
<margin>Air, of whom it is the son.</margin>
In such a way, *Asia*, the most powerful part of the terrestrial *Globe*, binds together *Africa* and *Europe* by a certain intermediate bond, just as the most graceful and subtle element binds fire and earth.
<margin>Why air is a mediator between contraries.</margin>
Otherwise, there would be no coherence between them, nor could one provide its natural virtues in a mixture without the other. Fire indeed willingly clings to earth as if to its fuel and hearth, but take away the air from which it breathes, and it will soon vanish.
<margin>Asia binds Africa with Europe.</margin>
The prerogative of **Asia** is therefore considered to be its position in the middle of the terrestrial world, where the temperament of the air is felt and where it provides us with "airy fruits," such as dates, balsam, spices of all kinds, and gold itself. In Asia, as

<margin>By what means Jason was prepared to seize the Golden Fleece.</margin>

# A Subtle Allegory

I did not doubt that I had received no small gift of nature regarding Medicine: for the *Whiteness* <term>Albedo</term> <note>In alchemy, "Albedo" is the second major stage of the "Great Work," representing purification and the transition from the blackness of decay to a state of spiritual or chemical brilliance.</note> of pearls is especially radiant and beautiful, and without it, all their value perishes. <margin>What the statue of Mercury at the crossroads was like.</margin>
entirely silvered except for the head, which was gilded. With the index finger of its right hand, this statue pointed out a straight line by which one must go to the *Terrestrial Paradise*. # FIERY AFRICA.

<margin>Africa always brings something new.</margin>
<margin>The mountains of Africa abound in serpents and minerals.</margin>
**W**hen I had landed in *Africa*, a full year and more having passed, the *Sun* had already entered *Leo* once again, with the *Moon* holding *Cancer*, the height of her own domicile <note>In astrology, Leo is the "home" of the Sun and Cancer is the "home" of the Moon. This alignment signifies a peak of celestial power for the alchemical work.</note>. This gave me great hope for an excellent omen. *Africa* extends toward the midday Sun opposite *Asia*; for this reason, the seasons of the year are far hotter there than elsewhere, especially the summer, which is felt to be extremely hot. And this is the chief reason why the greatest part of it is uncultivated, scorched, thirsty, sterile, and empty. In this land, as rivers are rarer, animals of various species flock together more frequently to the fresh waters wherever they may be, and there they mix with one another. From this, new offspring and animals of strange appearance are born, and it is not without cause that it is said: *Africa always brings something new.* <note>A famous ancient proverb, "Semper aliquid novi Africam adferre," attributed to Aristotle and Pliny the Elder.</note> There, *Pans, Satyrs, Cynocephali* <note>Dog-headed men, a common feature in medieval and Renaissance travelogues of "monstrous races."</note>, and half-humans are said to dwell, besides innumerable species of beasts. There the *Oryx* is said to detest the heat of the sun with overflowing tears and repeated groans during the greatest heat. There are the *Mountains of the Moon and Atlas*, who supports the heavens on his shoulders; just as they abound in minerals, so do they abound in serpents. In that same place, "dragon's blood" <term>Sanguis Draconis</term> <note>In alchemy, this term often refers to cinnabar (mercury sulfide) or a deep red resin; the story of the elephant and dragon represents the chemical union of opposing forces.</note> is collected, which the dragon sucked from the Elephant; when the Elephant falls dead, the dragon is crushed beneath it and yields back...

Of these, the *Canopic* mouth is the highest, and it is subject to the younger son of the Son of Heaven. <note>The "Son of Heaven" (Caelus/Uranus) refers to Saturn, often associated with the first or "highest" planetary sphere in ancient cosmology.</note> *Canobus*, the pilot of *Menelaus's* ship, is buried here; just as he gave his name to the island and port, so as the highest of the *Planets*, he is like a favorable old overseer. 
<margin>Saturn is the grandfather of Mercury.</margin>
Since he is the grandfather of the *Mercury* you seek, it is no wonder if Mercury sometimes passes to his grandfather’s house. But they reported that *Mercury* was no longer found here, but resided perpetually at another mouth of the same Nile. Astonished by this answer, after much time had passed and errors had been committed, I noticed that I must approach another place more familiar to *Mercury*.

<margin>2. The Bolbitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Therefore, I did not hesitate to go straight to the second, called the *Bolbitic* mouth. But when I asked several people I met there if they had seen *Mercury*, the son of the Nile, whom I needed to meet, and they replied they knew nothing of the *Mercury* of that place, I did not wish to proceed further, lest I waste time and expense in vain.

<margin>3. The Sebennytic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Having been informed about two mouths of the Nile, I ran with a quick step to the third: Near this is the city of *Sebennytos*, from which it is called the *Sebennytic* mouth, inhabited by people who were not very numerous. When I found their customs so barbarian and rigid that I judged them far removed from all civility, I did not wish to stay there any longer, nor inquire any more about the seat of *Mercury*. For how, I said, could *Mercury*—the author of all refined literature and learning—stay among such fierce people? For either they would make him fierce and barbaric like themselves, or he would make them mild and civilized through a longer stay and proximity. And so, after I had left the town, I asked a certain farmer of that place, "Does *Mercury* not have a court here?" He replied, "He does indeed have a very well-fortified court here, but he never lives in it."

<margin>4. The Pelusiac mouth of the Nile.</margin>
I then proceeded to the fourth mouth, called the *Pelusiac*, the most famous of all because of the city of the same name adjacent to it, whose founder, as the story goes, was *Peleus*, the father of *Achilles*. This divides *Asia* and *Arabia* from *Egypt*, and was once very abundant in riches. Regarding this, after...

<summary>The narrator travels through the first four mouths of the Nile (Canopic, Bolbitic, Sebennytic, and Pelusiac), searching for Mercury by seeking correspondences between the river's geography and the planetary spheres.</summary>

Once I had reached it <note>This refers to the fourth mouth of the Nile, Pelusium, mentioned in the transition from the previous page.</note>, and had perceived its gifts and conditions, I did not doubt that I would find the *Mercurial* seat there. For just as they say that *Troy* could not be besieged without *Pelides* (also known as *Achilles*), so *Mercury* cannot be obtained without *Pelusium*. <note>The author uses a play on words between the city "Pelusium" and "Peleus," the father of Achilles. In alchemical terms, this often implies that a specific "strong" substance or "heroic" effort is needed to fix the volatile Mercury.</note> This is the most noble emporium of *Egypt*, which abounds especially in *Arabic* gold. When I arrived there, I asked where *Mercury* might reside. But a certain inhabitant replied that *Mercury* is not always present in this place, although he is a most welcome guest when he is here. Taking it poorly that I had undertaken so many journeys here in vain, I was unwilling to settle my feet until I had visited the remaining gates, not despairing that I would finally meet the longed-for *Mercury* face-to-face in the following places.

<margin>5. The Tanitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
The fifth in order was the *Tanitic* mouth; although its name appeared somewhat obscure, I nevertheless wished to visit it as well, lest I should seem to have provided any reason for avoiding it. But I brought back just as much from there as I did from the previous ones—namely, nothing at all—except for learning that the *Mercury* I was seeking lived there by no means. "Oh, how unhappy I am," I said, "is it really necessary to follow one who is either nowhere, or who flees me as I pursue him, just as that beautiful *Alexis* fled *Corydon*?" <note>original: "ut formosus ille Alexis Corydonem" – A reference to Virgil’s Second Eclogue, depicting a hopeless pursuit.</note> Would it not have been better to progress from the last to the first, imitating the movement of a crab? Does that fleeting and winged young man, <note>original: "petasatus" – Wearing the petasos, the winged hat of Mercury.</note> foreseeing my arrival, feel such disgust that he takes flight before I even approach? But he shall not escape in the end, nor can he be hidden for long, wherever he may be. Two of all the *Nile* mouths remain for me, which I shall also survey, *God* willing, and then I shall bid farewell to all of *Egypt*.

<margin>6. The Phatnitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Therefore, I set out for the sixth mouth of the *Nile*, the *Phatnitic*, which I thought must belong to *Mercury* by the logic of the heavens; I was led by a firm hope in my mind that there would now finally be an end to so many labors. But that confidence also deceived me, as it had so often before. For I received an answer from the inhabitants of that place that *Mercury* had indeed lived here, but had long since changed his seat and migrated elsewhere; many people here had frequently conducted an inquiry for him, but he was never found at home.

<margin>7. The Mendesian mouth of the Nile.</margin>
From here, I undertook the final journey as far as the *Mendesian* mouth. When I had arrived there, I asked about *Mercury*, who was not found here either. Indeed, many replied that they did not even know *Mercury*.

### On the Secrets of Alchemy <note>original: "Super Secreta Chymia." In the 17th century, "Chymia" referred to the inseparable practices of chemistry and alchemy.</note>

<margin>
Where Mercury was found.
Many things learned from Mercury.

The return to Germany.

And so, having surveyed the seven mouths of the *Nile* in order, since I had not found the one I sought, I considered myself deceived by the *Sibyl* <note>The Sibyl acts as a prophetic guide; the narrator fears he has been led into a "labyrinth" of false hope.</note>, who had cast me into these labyrinths only to lead my mind around, nourished by false hope—perhaps out of envy or a preconceived hatred toward strangers. However, when I turned over in my mind every detail that had happened on the journey, I conjectured that I had perhaps been circumvented by the inhabitants of those places with a most deceptive response, for the reason that they loathed and hated all foreigners with a certain innate ferocity. Therefore, I carefully reconsidered what had been answered by them regarding the first, second, and third mouths, and the others; from these reflections, many things occurred to me which increased the doubt I had previously conceived rather than removing it. Consequently, retracing my steps backward, I returned from the last mouth toward the first, and finally, before I reached the first again, I found *Mercury* in one of the mouths where the inhabitants had previously seemed to deny him.

Approaching him, and after many conversations held between us, I was told by him things I had not known. In particular, he pointed out the *Phoenix* and where he ought to be met; he related most clearly that the Phoenix was hiding in a place I had not even thought of before. But when I arrived there, by my misfortune, he had gone out (perhaps having been appointed at that time as the Arbiter between the *Owl* and the other birds pursuing it, a battle which we have described elsewhere <note>This refers to a common alchemical allegory where the "Owl" represents a secret wisdom or a substance that cannot bear the light of common day, often pursued by the "volucres" or volatile spirits.</note>), and he was not to return for several days or a few weeks. 

Truly, since it was not advisable for me to wait so long in foreign lands—especially because the return of the *Phoenix* was very uncertain—I decided to prepare my journey home as soon as possible. I considered it enough for me, for the time being, to have known *Mercury*, where he resided, and also the *Phoenix*, the father and efficient cause of the sought-after *Medicine* <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" is the Philosopher's Stone or the Universal Elixir, capable of curing both metals and human bodies.</note>, to whom I firmly resolved to return at the first offered opportunity. And so, having boarded a ship from the *Pelusiac* mouth, I contended again toward *Europe*, sailing past so many islands and kingdoms all around, until I set foot on *German* soil, from where I had first departed. But lest I should seem ungrateful toward anyone from whom I felt any benefit bestowed upon me on this journey, I shall first pay the honors and praises due to the *Sibyl*, then to *Mercury*, and finally to the *Phoenix* and the *Medicine* itself,

**T** *o you, great Priestess moved by God (and not by a demon),* <note>original: "non dæmone." Early modern writers often specified that the Sibyls were inspired by the true God rather than pagan spirits to justify their inclusion in Christian works.</note>
*Just grace returns from the two Graces:* <note>In mythology, the Graces represent charm and gratitude. The "two Graces" here likely refers to the twin rewards of wisdom and spiritual salvation.</note>

### AN ENCOMIUM FOR THE PHOENIX 
### expressed in an Epigram.

<margin>Praise of the Phoenix.</margin>
**O** *Miracle of the World, Wonder without flaw, unique Phoenix,*
*Who are made the property of the great sages:* <note>The "sages" (sophis) are the master alchemists who have achieved the Philosopher's Stone.</note>
*Clad in purple plumage and a golden neck,*
*You excel among all birds and all riches:*

*Then, gladly at Thebes, you place yourself, worn out, upon the altar,*
*So that Vulcan might give you a new face through his art.* <note>In alchemy, "Vulcan" represents the transformative power of fire. The Phoenix burning on the altar symbolizes the final purification of the alchemical matter.</note>

*And is said to bring relief to human ills.* <note>term: <term>Medicine of Health</term> (Medicina salutis). In alchemical literature, the Phoenix/Philosopher's Stone was believed to be a "Universal Medicine" capable of curing all diseases and extending life.</note>
*The only hope for incurable disease resides in you,*
*And you make old men walk in the manner of youths.*
*Lest I mention your other most divine gifts,*
*The Persian Treasury is scarcely equal to your riches.* <note>original: "Persica Gaza." A classical reference to the legendary wealth of the Persian kings.</note>

# CHAPTER I.

## *Concerning the Right of the Art, its Practitioners, and the True Manner of Seeking the* **Arcanum**. <term>Arcanum<note>A Latin word meaning "secret" or "mystery." In alchemy, it refers to the great hidden secret of nature or the "Philosopher's Stone" that allows for transmutation.</note></term>

**S**ince all men of every rank and fortune propose to themselves some goal for the hours they spend investigating things—so that they may, of course, attain skill in the art in which they are engaged—they exert all their strength to aim at its very summit.

Yet this fortune blesses very few; for although many long for *Architecture*, yet very few *Archimedes* <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was a Greek mathematician and engineer, here used as the archetype for supreme mastery of a technical craft.</note> are found. Many, however much they devote themselves to *Medicine*, yet no more are endowed with the genius of *Paracelsus* <note>A 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine by using chemicals and minerals rather than just herbs.</note>, and few with that of *Helmont* <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician who followed Paracelsus's ideas and is considered a bridge between alchemy and modern chemistry.</note>; indeed, if they can reach even mediocrity in their art, they will not think they have "lost their oil" or their effort <note>original: "oleun, aut operam perdidisse." A classical idiom meaning to waste one's time and labor, referring to the oil burned in a lamp while working late into the night.</note>. Hence it happens that no one thinks he has studied in vain, even though not every *Geometer* is equal to *Archimedes*, or *Poet* to *Homer*, or *Rhetorician* to *Cicero*. For even *Rhetoricians* of a lower rank can be of use to the *Republic* <insert>according to the Talent granted to them</insert> <note>A reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), referring here to one's natural abilities or gifts.</note>. Any men, I say, even if less skilled in the art in which they have practiced, can be considered useful in that *Republic* <insert>where they live</insert>.

However, as many as devote themselves to the *Metamorphosis of Metals* <note>The alchemical process of changing base metals into gold or silver.</note> seem to long for a most useful thing not merely uselessly, but even foolishly. For the very peak of this art is the Workmanship itself; he who has attained it has reached the summit, but he who has not arrived there will carry back nothing of profit. For there is nothing except loss, of both money and time, from a half-learned science of *Alchemy*. Furthermore, and ir- <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page. The catchword "risui" suggests the next page begins with the word "irrisui," meaning "objects of mockery."</note>

<summary>This introductory chapter argues that while mediocrity is acceptable in fields like medicine or rhetoric, alchemy is an "all or nothing" pursuit where partial knowledge leads only to financial and temporal loss.</summary>
<keywords>Arcanum, Archimedes, Paracelsus, Helmont, Alchemy, Metamorphosis of Metals, Transmutation, Republic of Letters</keywords>

--- Page 762 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter I, moving from the comparison of alchemy with other arts to a critique of "false" alchemists and the negative reputation they bring to the discipline.</meta>

...to a poet <note>The previous page ended mid-sentence: "nor every Poet [equal to Virgil or Homer]."</note> he will expose himself to the laughter and reproach of the <term>Alchemy-haters<note>original: "Mysochemicis." From the Greek "misos" (hatred) and "chemeia." It refers to those who mock or dismiss alchemy as a fraud.</note></term>. Yet the object of the Art is so noble that it promises infinite wealth to its possessor, and moreover, the most perfect health. Hence it happens that there is hardly any unlearned person who, after hearing even the slightest bit about the art, does not immediately apply himself to its investigation and instantly takes on the name of Alchemist. Soon, as soon as he has conceived some hope from reading a few recipes, he immediately claims the Title of Philosopher. 

Lest he seem to cultivate a foolish philosophy, each one, according to the luck of his own wit, devises subtleties, and according to his supply of coins, builds furnaces, procures glassware, and approaches the work with wonderful solemnity. Thus he boils everything down until at last "thrift comes too late at the bottom," <note>original: "sera tandem parsimonia sit in Fundo." A reference to a classical proverb from Hesiod and Seneca: "It is too late to spare when the bottom is reached."</note> and very little, if any, household furniture remains. Lest he be accused meanwhile of insane rashness, he knows how to discourse on the *Metallic Prime Matter*, the *rotation of the Elements*, and the *marriage of Gabritius with Bega* <note>Gabritius (or Kybrith) and Bega (or Beja) are alchemical allegories representing the "Chemical Wedding" of the masculine (sulfur/gold) and feminine (mercury/silver) principles.</note>, and that under a language commonly unknown; he will cite the Philosophers and explain them at his pleasure, and console himself not a little with the hope of future fortune. Meanwhile, however, he endures labors in this philosophy even to the consumption of both his strength and his coins, until he has miserably experienced within himself that very *Metamorphosis* which he was seeking in the Metals <note>The author is being witty: instead of the metals changing into gold, the man himself is "changed" into a beggar.</note>.

When the captious alchemy-haters observe this, and see that the same outcome awaits most of them, they immediately laugh at the art as a fable and hold it in derision. But those who have deceived themselves by their own rashness busy themselves with enticing others onto the same path of expense, and stain paper with their fabrications and forged recipes, so that they might seem to have gained at least some skill along with the loss of their money. The world is seen to be so filled with these <term>Sophistries<note>original: "Sophisticationibus." # On the Metamorphosis of Metals

It becomes an inextricable labyrinth for the Chemical Apprentice to distinguish between true and false books; from which deceptive Sophists construct an edifice no less attractive than that of the true Artists; indeed, they generally promise even greater things. Concerning these men, **Bernard of Trevisan** <note>original: "Bernardus Trevicensis." A famous 15th-century alchemist who spent decades—and a fortune—searching for the Stone before allegedly succeeding. He often wrote about the many frauds who deceived him.</note> [a man not inexperienced in this kind of deception] writes thus: *“Unless,”* [he says], *“you avoid them like a plague or an enemy, you will never taste anything good in this art.”* I have therefore written this treatise to more fully instruct those who are blind in this science, lest they wander miserably through pathless ways. And first, I have decided to vindicate the Art from slanders. Then it seemed fit to add the qualifications of those who apply themselves to this; finally, I will describe the method of inquiry. Having set these forth by way of a preface, I will afterwards prepare myself to elucidate the art itself.

For simply because many deceptive Sophists are found practicing Alchemy, it should not therefore be accused of falsehood or absurdity. For the possibility of things must be weighed; if the truth of the art can be disproven by this, let it fall; but if not, to disparage it must be judged not only foolish, but also unworthy of a Philosopher. Consider that the wickedness of men who rashly handle the art does nothing to destroy it. Consider that the Light of Nature is too bright to be obscured by these <term>shufflers<note>original: "Tenebrionibus." Literally "creatures of darkness," a term used here to describe fraudulent alchemists who operate in secrecy or use confusing language to hide their lack of knowledge.</note></term>. I will therefore instruct the <term>Sons of Doctrine<note>original: "Filios Doctrinæ." A traditional alchemical term for dedicated, worthy students who are spiritually and intellectually prepared for the Great Work.</note></term>, lest they be led astray by errors; and it will appear to them more clearly than the Sun that the transmutation of metals is real, possible, and true—from a state of imperfection to perfection—and this through the cooperation of Nature and Art. 

For no material or essential difference is seen between perfect metals <note>Gold and silver.</note> and imperfect metals <note>Base metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron.</note>, but only an accidental one, which consists in a disproportion of maturity. This [alone], in greater or lesser degree, diversifies metals into their species, except for certain added superfluities that appear distinct among the metals. This dross indeed has no correspondence with the Matter, but having been substituted for it in an entirely creeping manner, and not purged due to a defect of <term>digestion<note>original: "digestio." In alchemy, this refers to a process of slow, constant heat that matures, purifies, or "ripens" a substance over time, mimicking the natural heat of the earth.</note></term>, they remained mixed with the undigested pure part. From this comes the distinction of metallic forms. But if ever, through the complete perfection of digestion, these superfluities were rejected, then no longer...

## C H A P T E R I.

...rather than an imperfect metal, a perfect one is seen: hence, miners testify that abundant silver has been found in lead ore that has been left undisturbed for a suitable length of time. Similarly, if this same thing can be achieved outside the veins of the earth through the **Triumphant Art** <note>original: "Triumphantem artem." A term for the "Great Work" of alchemy, suggesting the artist's victory over the stubbornness of matter.</note>, there is no impediment in nature to prevent the same effect from being achieved. The certainty of this is evident from here: [namely, that all Metals arise from the same material] because Mercury <note>The symbol ☿ is used here for Mercury or quicksilver.</note>, which is generated in the veins of the earth, is the universal material progenitor of all those things that take on a metallic appearance. This will not be difficult to prove, because Mercury is adapted to all of these and can be joined to them by art; however, it would be entirely impossible to achieve this unless all things shared in one single matter. For Mercury is a water, yet of such a kind that it mixes with absolutely nothing that is not of the same nature as itself. Since, therefore, it absorbs all metals by "wetting" them <note>The author refers to amalgamation, where mercury dissolves other metals like gold or silver.</note>, it follows that all those metals retain a correspondence of matter with it. I add that through Art serving Nature, Mercury can be successively cooked with all Metals in such a way that one and the same substance—under the same color and form of flow—alternately reflects and exerts the true <term>constitution<note>original: "crasin." From the Greek 'krasis,' meaning a temperament or specific mixture of qualities.</note></term> and true properties of all of them. This would be impossible in Art unless Nature provided the possibility for it through the correspondence of Matter.

Furthermore, other arguments for proving this same thing are not lacking. And first, it is certainly no small matter that all Metals can be reduced into running Mercury, as can the Minerals that consist of Metallic principles. Moreover, these Metallic Mercuries can be so transmuted that a **Saturnine** mercury <note>related to Lead (Saturn)</note> becomes **Martial** <note>related to Iron (Mars)</note> [its own powers being disregarded in the meantime] merely through the decoction of the Martial essence within it by a skillful artifice. Furthermore, that same Martial mercury will become **Venereal** <note>related to Copper (Venus)</note> through the ferment of Venus; and likewise **Lunar** <note>related to Silver (the Moon)</note>, **Jovial** <note>related to Tin (Jupiter)</note>, or even **Solar** <note>related to Gold (the Sun)</note>, through their ferment. In the meantime, no change occurs in either its flow or its color, except that one Mercury becomes purer and more refined than another. From **Antimony** <note>A metallic substance often used by alchemists to "purge" gold or to extract a "philosophical mercury."</note> also, an admirable Mercury is separated, which likewise takes on the nature of Metallic Mercuries, through the subtle [management] of Nature and Art...

...administration. Not only this, but furthermore, the aforementioned "Mercuries" of this kind—derived from both metallic and mineral bodies—will, through their mixing, so transform common Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium vulgarem." In alchemy, "common mercury" is ordinary quicksilver, while "philosophical mercury" is the purified or animated version used in the Great Work.</note> that when it is digested with them, it adopts the same natural qualities as they have. It thus forms one and the same Mercury with them, according to the species of the bodily Mercury joined to it <insert>by a spiritual bond</insert>. 

And this one and the same individual substance can, through successive operations, put on the forms of all things, and choose a new form while setting aside the old, until it has run through all the Kingdoms of the Planets <note>In the alchemical tradition, the "Seven Planets" correspond to the seven metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Iron (Mars), Mercury (Mercury), Tin (Jupiter), Copper (Venus), and Lead (Saturn).</note>. What does this prove, other than that all things claim one single Matter for themselves—the source from which all things come and the end to which they return? It shows that once all things are reduced to this, their Mercurial Matter, they can—depending on the variety of digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature or transform it, mimicking the processes of the earth.</note>—migrate from the power of one species into the virtue of another, and traverse through all of them one after another. 

This argument, as it is most true in itself, so also it remains the firmest and most inviolable foundation of this art. Against these most evident truths, I do not know what could be objected, unless perhaps some people, whose dullness of mind does not reach far enough to grasp these things, complain that they have attempted this many times <insert>and that too according to the instructions of the most famous Authors</insert>, yet the outcome by no means responded to their hope. 

To these people it may be answered that their ignorance does little to disprove so noble an art. For let it not be considered a vice of the art if something <insert>possible in Nature through Art</insert> escapes their understanding. Such an objection would be a sign of no less affected arrogance than of gross ignorance—as if only those things were achievable through the administration of Nature (with the cooperation of art) which fall within the capacity of their own minds without diligent investigation. They exclude everything else by that very fact, as if the measure of their own Intellect were the same as the measure of Nature’s possibility. 

On the contrary, through affirmative experimental science, I would oppose their negative experience. I myself, who write these things, can be a faithful witness of Nature: that all these things said above concerning Metals and Mercuries are true without any falsehood, and certain without disguise; and that I have seen, known, tested, and proved all these things in and around metals through true experience.

### CHAPTER 1.

...one should by no means struggle against eyewitnesses on the basis of bare negations [the foundation of which is ignorance]. I profess myself to be one of these witnesses, and all true Philosophers agree with me with one voice—men such as **Albertus**, **Raymond**, **Ripley**, **Flamel**, **Morienus**, <note>The author lists several "Adept" alchemists: Albertus Magnus, Raymond Lull, George Ripley, Nicolas Flamel, and the legendary hermit Morienus. These were considered the "canon" of reliable alchemical authorities in the 17th century.</note> and many others whose names would be tedious to recite. I admit, at least, that it is no easy task to provide what I have described; on the contrary, I would assert that it is highly concealed by the Philosophers and most deeply hidden in Nature. Accordingly, I make it known that a **"key of the art"** is provided to us by the Philosophers; whoever possesses this key is granted the power to unlock all enclosures, provided he has learned to treat each thing in its proper order and by the true method. For it is not all the same which metal or mineral one should first approach, or by what path or operations one should proceed. In recognizing these things, an ingenious sagacity is required, as well as practical science alongside Theory; otherwise, whether one wishes it or not, one will go astray.

I could here recount various mutations of Metals—for instance, of **Mars** into **Venus** by the acidic drip of Vitriol, <note>In alchemical shorthand, Mars represents Iron and Venus represents Copper. This refers to the "cementation" process where iron placed in vitriol (copper sulfate solution) appears to turn into copper.</note> of **Venus** into **Saturn** <term>Lead</term>, of **Saturn** into **Jupiter** <term>Tin</term>, or of **Jupiter** into the **Moon** <term>Silver</term>. Indeed, many common Chemists [who are far from the pinnacle of the Art] know how to perform these operations. 

I will add something that is known to only a few [and those only the true Philosophers]: that there exists a **middle substance** between Mineral and Metal. It is hidden and noble; one of its ends is mineral, the other is metal. Their joined celestial virtues produce a certain anonymous metal, although it is not truly a metal, but rather **Chaos**—that is, **Spirit**—because it is entirely volatile. From this substance [even though it is entirely fleeting in itself], all Metals can be drawn out without a transmuting Elixir—even gold and silver themselves, as well as **Mercury** <note>The symbol ☿ in the text refers to Mercury or Quicksilver.</note>, whose virtues I cannot easily describe. I have seen, I have performed, and I know its transmutation into all metals, and those who have attained the work <note>original: "adepti." An "Adept" is someone who has successfully discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note> will testify with me that this is true.

I shall say—if you can grasp it—that it is called **Steel** <note>original: "Chalibs." This is a reference to the "Philosophical Steel" mentioned by Michael Sendivogius (the "Author of the New Light"), which acts as a magnet to attract the "astral seed" or life force from the air.</note> by the Author of the New Light; it is the true principle of the work, the true key [provided it is handled correctly] for unlocking the most hidden secrets of the Philosophers. What does it matter, meanwhile, if the Philosophers have hidden all these things and depicted the truth for the sons of Art parabolically under a false mask? Shall this most Divine science be despised on that account? Far from it! For it is certainly clear that...

...in the nature of the imperfect, there is no hindrance to its being transmuted into the perfect, for metals by their own nature retain a propensity for taking on perfection, if only they are acted upon by a <term>Homogeneous Agent</term> <note>original: *Agens Homogeneum*. In alchemy, this refers to a substance of the same "nature" as the metal being transformed—acting like a "starter" or yeast that encourages the base metal to grow into a more perfect form.</note> possessing a powerful digestive force. Now, therefore, it is pleasing to investigate the power of this agent. And first, indeed, we shall establish that through which this must be done. We shall subsequently join together the philosophical reasons. Regarding the former, we profess and shall continue to profess that it is nothing other than <term>Gold</term> <note>original: *Aurum*.</note> digested to the highest degree [to which it can be led by Nature and Art]. This will then be seen not as simple gold, but as something a thousand times more perfect than any common Gold. 

Once exalted in this way, it penetrates metals to their very roots, dyeing and fixing them. Nor should this seem wonderful to anyone; for even while it remains in its bodily existence, it can spread its **tincture** <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is the concentrated essence or power of the Philosopher's Stone that "colors" or transforms the inner nature of a metal.</note> widely, far beyond what is credible to anyone who has not seen it. To such an extent that one single part of gold seems to color nearly six pounds of silver into its own tincture, as if through the smallest particles. 

For example: let a mass of <term>Silver</term> <note>original: *Argenti*.</note> [however large] be gilded; if that mass is afterwards drawn out into a **Wire** [even one rivaling the thinness of a hair], that entire wire will appear to be of the purest Gold. The skill of the craftsman to thin the wire will fail sooner than the power of the gold to color it. Therefore, if this bodily, earthy, and dead metal is able to perform such an ineffable feat, from where—I ask—comes the inconsistency of the tincture? It is only because a body cannot enter another body "alteratively" <note>The author refers to the physics of his day: a solid "body" (gold) can only coat the outside of another "body" (silver). To change the silver's internal essence, the gold must be made into a spirit.</note>. It is not that the tincture lacks the power to transmute, but the "bodiliness" of the dyeing agent stands in the way of transmutation. 

But if this earthy body were to become <term>Spiritual and fiery</term> <note>original: *Spirituale igneum*. This describes the "Quintessence," where the metal is refined from a solid state into a powerful, energetic spirit or vapor.</note>, its genus having been changed, then indeed it would enter to the very roots; and what it had done externally to the sight, it would perform internally by alteration—and much more besides, inasmuch as fire is of a much more subtle property and essence than earth. This being assumed, namely that the earthy Gold of the common people can be so circulated until it is placed upon the **Throne of fiery essence**, it is easily gathered from this that this quintessence is a thousand times more perfect than its previous substance. This is according to the law of disproportion in subtlety between the <term>Four Elements</term> <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. In the alchemical hierarchy, Fire is the most "subtle" and powerful, able to penetrate and change the "heavier" elements like Earth.</note>; therefore it is able to spread its tincture more widely. It has this further advantage: that while it becomes a Spirit, it consequently...

### CHAPTER I.

...at the smallest parts it might be able to be mixed intrinsically: because the body of gold, although it might be spread widely and far, nevertheless could not reach [this state] on account of its own corporality <note>The "corporality" here refers to the solid, physical state of the metal which prevents it from mixing perfectly with other substances until it is broken down.</note>. And if it has entered in this way, it will without doubt transmute: for every physical ingress through the smallest parts is a transmutation of the passive nature, unless there is an identity of nature between the thing entering and the thing entered—just as water is mixed with water. We assert this supposition as true in the place of a preface, and in its proper place we shall describe its method. Here at least we shall bring forward some arguments confirming the possibility. 

Among these, it is of no light weight that the **seed** <note>original: *semen*. In alchemical theory, all things—including minerals—were thought to grow from a spiritual "seed" or life-force.</note> is the perfection of every thing possessing a seed, and that which does not have a seed is imperfect in its whole. Wherefore, as the **Poet** sang: *In Gold are the seeds of gold, though they may recede further hidden away* <note>original: *In Auro semina sunt auri, licet abstrusa recedant longius*. This is a frequent alchemical citation suggesting that the potential for growth and multiplication is hidden deep within the metal.</note>. For this is not only perfect, but most perfect in its metallic species. If, therefore, there is in gold the seed of gold, it follows that this resides in the **water** [which is the dwelling-place of the spirit], for seed is a certain spiritual medium for the preservation of the species. 

From this arises the possibility of the dissolution of Gold, although to find an agent capable of performing this is the work of a most wise Philosopher, blessed by God with no mediocre talent. Furthermore, if Gold is dissolved to draw out its seed, does not Reason persuade us that this must be done only in water of its own homogeneous kind? Once this dissolution has been made, the body has laid aside its form—namely the earthy form of gold—and has put on another, an aqueous golden form. 

Moreover, every movement is from something toward something, and every perfect movement of the generative limit is within the same species; whence movement is a progress, which happens through various homogeneous changes of the thing moved. Therefore, since **gold-ness** <term>Aureitas</term> <note>The essential quality or "soul" of being gold.</note> is the starting point, the same shall be the endpoint, and intermediate progressions will occur in metallic homogeneity by the necessity of Nature's law. When these are observed, the effect is driven to its end by the necessity of the end, provided that the operations have not been interrupted by something contrary. 

Therefore, from dissolved Gold, we place the return of that same dissolved substance to **Gold-ness** beyond controversy, and conclude it is proven. However, this golden form which it will reassume will in no way be the same as that which it laid aside, since a return from **privation to habit** <note>original: *à privatione ad habitum*. A philosophical concept (Aristotelian) stating that once a thing loses its specific form, it cannot simply revert to the exact same individual state, but must transition into a new state or "habit."</note> is impossible. Another, therefore, necessarily remains...

For this, the golden form will be so much more noble and spiritual than the former one, in proportion to how much fire is more subtle and pure than earth. I have written enough and more to guide the **Sons of Doctrine** <note>A traditional term for those initiated into the secrets of alchemy.</note>. Now that this science has been established and vindicated, something must be said about its practitioners. Indeed, as was said above, it is because of the worthlessness of certain **little men** <note>original: *homuncionum*; a diminutive, dismissive term for people of low character or intellect.</note> that this Divine Art, as well as its friends, has suffered no small amount from detractors. For instance, when certain stupid mechanics, led astray by blind presumption, attempt the handling of these matters and lose their money, they immediately curse chemical philosophy in a fit of rage, speak ill of its practitioners, and tear apart the authors writing about it with insults. 

Others, though poorly taught and backward men, blinded by a thirst for gold, gape after the Art and approach the matter without mature deliberation. They err nonetheless, yet they conceive of and believe in the possibility of the Art. They speak well of it, but being ashamed to confess their own ignorance, they pretend to have expertise before those even more unrefined. They perhaps even go on to write about the Art, and, enticed by a secret hope of finally recovering all they have lost, they keep trying until they have multiplied their losses. They console their friends with the hope of future wealth, but while they remain poor and grow poorer every day, they provide an excuse for mockery to the stubborn scoffers of chemistry. 

Indeed, such is their wickedness that, having been deceived themselves, they busy themselves with luring others into the same category of error with their false recipes, lies, and **sophistical** <note>In alchemical literature, "sophistic" refers to fraudulent or "fake" chemistry that uses trickery rather than true natural philosophy.</note> writings. Finally, there are those who, however skilled they may be in the Art, are nevertheless incited by envy to treat the matter in a very rough and deceptive way. Under the promise of true doctrine, they lead <term>Tyrones|A Latin term for recruits or novices; in this context, those just beginning their alchemical studies.</term> astray with wretched impostures. Thus **Geber**, **Arnold**, **Lull**, and almost all the rest; among them, not a single honest writer is found, and if any is found to be delivering the subject, he does so very obscurely. # CHAPTER I.

->**CHAPTER I.**<-

...[formida]ble <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "insuperabilis" (insurmountable) or "horribilis" (dreadful).</note> labyrinth for one about to begin Chemistry <term>Chemiam: In this period, the term referred to the combined study of what we now call alchemy and chemistry</term>, so that it seems to require the very finger of God if anyone desires to enter the right path. Hence also the name of the Art <term>Artis: Refers to the "Great Art" of alchemical transmutation</term> is so hated that it is not easily applied to anyone without the greatest mockery. Therefore, I think it is especially necessary to know what must be cared for in the first place by a future son of science <term>scientiæ filio: A traditional term for a student or initiate of alchemical secrets</term>, so that he might obtain this golden Art and gain possession of this fleece <note>A reference to the Golden Fleece of Greek mythology, a common alchemical metaphor for the successful completion of the Great Work</note>; for indeed, not a few obstacles will be present to push him back, unless there is a firm resolution of the mind. There are many things which might delude hope and expectation, unless he possesses a keen intellect.

First, indeed, so that he may be rendered safe from those who will mock his undertaking with sneers, his path ought to be secret, so that his labor becomes known to no one. Wherefore the Ancient Wise Philosophers <term>Antiqui Philosophi Sapientes: The lineage of historical and legendary alchemical authorities like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</term> commanded that this science be hidden no differently than a word held in the mouth. Nor indeed could it seem useless to give such an exhortation, since the reproaches and quarrels of men—who, abhorring the Art themselves, hold its practitioners in the highest contempt—do no small part in casting despondency into the mind of the novice <term>Tyronis: An apprentice or beginner in a craft</term>. Moreover, if anyone considers the outcome, it will appear that there is a need for the secret concealment of the Art. For if anyone is frustrated in his hope, how can silence be a hindrance? Otherwise, he who is thus frustrated will be held up as an example of a foolish [as it is commonly thought] loss of money and time. If, on the other hand, he has instead gained this Treasure <term>Thesauro: The Philosopher's Stone or the successful result of the alchemical process</term>, it will be found not only useful, but also highly necessary to have remained silent. For suppose a man is set out as prey for tyrants and the wicked if he openly enjoys and uses such a treasure; even some who were slightly too improvident in this matter, having risked the safety of their lives, have at last, wretchedly, performed a late repentance <note>original: *pœnitentiam*; here meaning a regretful realization of their error in being too public</note>. Furthermore, it is fitting for one who would descend into this arena <note>original: *palæstram*; literally a wrestling school, here used to mean a place of rigorous trial or study</note> to be constant of mind: industrious, diligent, learned, a "glutton for books" <note>A voracious reader</note>, of a tranquil mind, not lazy or sluggish, not wanting this one moment and that the next, private, and alone—unless he has some faithful companion, one and no more—and not destitute. For although a small quantity might suffice when the Art <term>Ars: The alchemical process</term> is first attempted, it will nevertheless happen that one errs many times; he has need of money to repair these errors, and moreover to supply the expenses necessary for food and clothing while he devotes himself to this Art, lest...

# CHAPTER I.

Various opinions of Authors are put forth. There are those who affirm that it was Moses <note>original: "Mosen"</note>; at the very least, they agree that he was Egyptian by nation and a most clear-sighted Philosopher. He is called the Father of this Philosophy—that is, the first [among those whose books survive] who treats this Philosophy. Some, however, will have it that this knowledge was derived from Enoch: who, foreseeing the flood, inscribed the seven liberal sciences [among which was Chemistry] on tablets and left them to posterity. Hermes, truly, having entered the valley of Hebron, discovered those which are called the **Emerald Tablets** <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, a foundational Hermetic text said to contain the secrets of the "prima materia" and its transmutation</note> today, and from there he learned his wisdom. Others sharply contend that Noah held this art and carried it *into his ark*. Not a few busy themselves with trying to establish the Art from certain passages of Scripture, and they are eager to write that Solomon possessed it. Some even trace it from Adam himself to Abel, and so on to Seth.

But for my part, as I am about to write on the simplicity of nature, such subtleties do not please me; I think they do not illustrate the Art, but rather cast a shadow over it, so that it appears fanatical <note>In this context, "fanatical" implies something fueled by wild imagination or religious delusion rather than reason</note>. Those who write in such a way provide nothing but an opportunity for mockery to the haters and <term>Misochemists</term> <note>From the Greek *miso* (hate) and *chemeia*; literally "chemistry-haters," referring to critics or skeptics of alchemy</note>. For if this Art has a real foundation in Nature, why should I be anxious about whether this or that man understood it or not? For we have known that its practitioners and experts have hidden themselves with the greatest zeal, just as it is commanded in their other books. None of them, or at least very many of them, became known until after their death; while they were living, they remained hidden with the utmost diligence.

This much, at least, is clear: far from this being a new invention, there has existed a long series of ages of experts who, though different in language and nation, and many living at the same time, have written so concordantly about the art that they are proven [to those who understand correctly] not to have corrupted or handled even a single operation differently. I confess, at least, that a very great difficulty appears to the unskilled man in reading their books; they write so obscurely, metaphorically, allegorically, and figuratively. Some even intermingle many falsehoods to ensnare the unworthy and the careless, so that in this way they may distinguish the Philosophers from the fools. In the end, however, they all strike one mark and lead to the same lodging. Moreover, when they pass down things more obscurely, they do so for no other purpose...

He should not delight himself with mere theory alone, but should know them scientifically—that is, practically. For this, however, there is need for deep, meditative contemplation, so that he may learn and understand the origin of physical things in general, and of mineral bodies in specific. As for what concerns me, being only cursorily intent on the doctrine of metals—insofar as it serves to explain the Art of transmutation—I gladly pass over the origin of natural things in general, content to have said those things which satisfy the aforementioned purpose. Nevertheless, I will briefly touch upon the rest in order.

All the common philosophers have handed down the idea that four elements are given, which originally compose all things; from these, all things come forth, and into these they are eventually resolved, and from their diverse joining, diverse things proceed. To this unfortunate opinion, almost all chemical philosophers have subscribed. I can conjecture no other cause for this than that, without mature deliberation, <insert>having girded themselves for the work itself</insert>, they described these first foundations of things in haste. I do not dare to condemn that opinion of theirs; rather, out of respect and honor for them, I shall treat the matter philosophically according to the truth of the thing. Regarding the elements, which they contend are four, I acknowledge only three, which by their own nature...

## C H A P T E R II.

Experience teaches us that the elements—namely Air, water, and earth—are cold. Indeed, only the lack of heat, caused by the remote distance of the warming Sun, induces cold into all of these; it is more or less intense depending on how great or small the distance of that removal is. I completely reject Elementary Fire <note>In traditional Aristotelian science, Fire was considered one of the four fundamental elements. The author here disputes this, arguing fire is an effect rather than a fundamental building block of nature.</note>; likewise, I deny there is any fire besides our common and ordinary <term>Vulcan</term> <note>original: "Vulcanum"; here used as a personification of the fire used in kitchens and laboratories</note> which burns in kitchens: whose heat is in itself always destructive. Nor do I deny, however, that heat exists in things—flowing surely from light, or from motion, or from life, or from an alterative <term>Blas</term> <note>A term coined by the chemist Van Helmont to describe a "vital pulse" or a transformative force that directs the motion of stars or the growth of living things</note>, and from no other source. The predator <term>Vulcan</term> burns and devastates concrete things by consuming them, and is a most violent motion of corruption, caused by the resistance arising from two opposing active forces. Yet it is not an Element, just as it is not a substance, let alone an accident <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "substance" is a thing that exists by itself, while an "accident" is a property (like color or heat) that only exists within a substance.</note>, as far as actual burning is concerned; rather, it is the expression of the activity of two things acting upon each other in a capable subject. I will not show now which things are required in order for <term>Vulcan</term> to be actually burning, besides the accident of heat and the substance in which this act occurs; at least we assert here that although its heat is an accident, the fire itself is neither substance nor accident, but the expressed operation of the activity of two active forces acting on each other. I could easily demonstrate this activity in every combustible and burning thing, were it not out of place here. And as I completely reject Elemental fire—being content meanwhile with the number of three Elements—and assert that their native primary quality is cold, attributing heat to them only by accident, as has been said; so too I do not admit that these three enter into the composition of natural things by their own mixing. For a disproportion of the things to be mixed removes the possibility of a mixture suitable for <term>Physical generation</term> <note>The process by which nature creates a new, unified substance rather than just a mechanical heap of different parts.</note>. For physical generation occurs through the unified joining of the ingredients. Furthermore, union is the entry of the things to be united through their <term>minima</term> <note>original: "minima"; the smallest possible particles or "atoms" of a substance</note>; but if the minimum of one is ten or a hundred times finer than the minimum of another, these proportional minima cannot come together, since it is necessary for those things we seek to unite at the smallest level to meet at that smallest level. Hence, water mixed with earth is not united with it, just as water is not with wine, or <term>Phlegma</term> <note>The watery, tasteless part of a substance that remains after distillation.</note> with Spirit: indeed, they can be separated because of their inter...

This transformation is necessary, or else the <term>smallest part</term> of one could not meet the <term>smallest part</term> of the other.

And Air is still missing, the <term>smallest part</term> of which is much more fine than that of water, unless all things are held to vanish into air, so that the aforementioned water may have this air as a partner in the process of generating. If that were granted, it would follow that all things consist of air alone. This air—whether it is from its own original nature, or is forged from earth and water transmuted into itself—will still be the same thing, not diversified by the difference of its origin. For unless it were the same, it could not be united; indeed, for water to have the same fineness as air, it is required to have the same primary qualities as air. The same must be judged of earth: that it must be made equal to the rarity of water. 

And if this is the case, then water so thinned will be real air, and earth so thinned will be real water. Where then is the composition of things generated from the Elements, since according to this doctrine all things would necessarily proceed from air—and from something even more fine, like fire—once this Doctrine of the Mixture of the four Elements is admitted? If anyone says it is true that the Elements are converted in this way, I would ask: by what agent are they changed?

Likewise, why mix "new" air with water thinned to the rarity of air? It is as if one and the same Element, having been made convertible into others, could not create a converted thing by itself without the mixing of another element. # CHAPTER I.

...[be] equal to the thinness of water, and yet not be water; just as water is not air. I would then ask whether or not one takes on the <note>Aristotelian physics held that the four elements were defined by pairs of "primary qualities": hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> **primary qualities** of the other. If not, then they will not have any correspondence even in their <note>original: "minimis"; referring to *minima naturalia*, the smallest possible particles of a substance.</note> **smallest parts**, for this would be impossible. If they do, I wish to know whether, if one primary element takes on the primary qualities of another, it does not actually become that element whose qualities it has assumed. To assert the opposite is not **philosophical**.

It is concluded, therefore, that all things take their material origin from one **Element**, which can be neither earth nor air; if I were not aiming for brevity, I could easily demonstrate this. Therefore, only **water** remains, which is the one true material principle of all concrete bodies [which are seen in this world]. **Earth** is the foundation or the floor in which all bodies grow and are preserved. **Air**, into which they grow, is the medium and the carrier of celestial virtues <note>In alchemy, "virtues" are the hidden powers or spiritual influences exerted by the stars and planets upon earthly matter.</note> with which it is filled, and through which they are communicated to all these lower things. 

The **seed** of all things was placed within water by the Creator at the first creation. Some things produce this seed into the air, such as **vegetables** <note>In the 17th century, "vegetables" referred to all plant life.</note>; some keep it within their own loins, such as **animals**; and in some, it is recondite and most deeply hidden, namely in **metals**. This seed is sufficient until the very end of the world for all things that are to be produced from seed, and water [as has been said] is found to be the dwelling place of this seed. 

This seed [which is otherwise dormant] is awakened by its **form**. This form is a certain ineffable particle of light, a celestial power which is ready at hand to imbue and excite to motion those lower things that are aptly disposed [by reason of their location and a suitable agent]. I say, then, that the seed, once awakened by this active power, begins to coagulate the material water by its own "fermentative odor." It changes the water through various fermentations—which are the authors of all transmutations—until it has produced that which the seed was inclined to produce. 

If, therefore, it was a **metallic seed**, there is born from it first a <term>dry, slippery humor that does not wet the hands</term> <note>original: "humor siccus, labilis, malus non madefaciens"; a classic alchemical description of "Philosophical Mercury," which behaves like a liquid but does not dampen surfaces like water does.</note>, which is surely **Mercury** <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note>, the mother of all metals. I could here teach the procreation of every kind of stone, and likewise note many things most worthy of mention regarding the first birth of **Mercury**. However, I deliberately pass over those things as they contribute little to our current purpose. Mercury, that is, the true...

### On the Metamorphosis of Metals

...deserved to be called the material of metals, because before it became **Mercury** <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> or was destined to become a **Metal**, it could happen through some defect that something different from a Metal might result from it. However, once it truly becomes **Mercury**, then indeed nothing else can be born from it except something mineral or metallic. From this arise the different kinds of minerals that are seen, such as **Tin, Lead, Silver, Copper, Iron, and Gold** <note>The original uses planetary symbols: ♃ (Jupiter/Tin), ♄ (Saturn/Lead), ☽ (Moon/Silver), ♀ (Venus/Copper), ♂ (Mars/Iron), and ☉ (Sun/Gold).</note>, all of which have one and the same mother: **Mercury**.

Certain **intermediate minerals** also originate from here, and some are even made from the metals themselves when they are eaten away by an acidic mineral salt. Thus, **Vitriol** <note>A historical term for sulfate minerals, often green or blue.</note> is produced from a vein of **Copper** by an acidic dripping <note>original: "stalagma"</note> that erodes it. It would be irrelevant to teach the generation of that substance here, so I intentionally pass over it.

However, it is not—as some wrongly believe—some intervening **sulfurous oiliness** that is joined to **Mercury**, which Nature might thicken by boiling with its own heat, and the subsequent purification of which constitutes the "perfection" of the metal. We know, for instance, that the **Sulfur** of **Tin** is much more impure than the **Sulfur** of **Lead**, even though the **Mercury** of **Lead** is cruder and more unclean than the **Mercury** of **Tin**; yet even common laborers will testify that **Tin** is a more "perfect" <note>In alchemy, a "perfect" metal is one closer to the stability and purity of gold.</note> metal than **Lead**. 

Therefore, one should not agree with those people regarding metallic digestion occurring through a fatty **"first milk"** <note>original: "colostrum"; used here to mean a hypothetical primary nourishing substance.</note> of that kind. Rather, there is within **Mercury** its own internal digesting agent—namely, the **heat** caused by **celestial influence**, which pours life and motion into this matter of ours. This life and motion equally depend on the proper adaptation of the **womb**—that is, a place suitable for generation. 

For although all things are full of this most abundant virtue of the higher powers <note>The "virtues" or spiritual powers of the stars and planets.</note>, and it is ready at hand for all things to give them form <note>original: "informationem"; the philosophical process of matter receiving a specific shape or identity.</note>, it does not actually act by "forming" (that is, by stimulating toward motion) except insofar as it is assisted by external things that are properly arranged. And thus, this celestial virtue then acts incessantly; though it is uniform and unique throughout the whole world, it varies according to the nature of the **seeds** <note>original: "feminis"; likely a scribal variant for "seminis" (seeds).</note>, just as the **ferments** of things are diversified to produce various transformations. 

Therefore, if this **Mercury** is born and finds for itself a place suitable for generation—even if, outside such a place, it appears cold in itself (as something dead)—nevertheless, within the center of its birth (where generative actions have not yet ceased), this virtue or celestial power, caused both by light and by the rotation of the heavens, and distributed most abundantly to all things through the medium of the air...

## CHAPTER II.

...diffused through all things, this power, I say—**insofar as it reflects light**—will cause a certain heat, and—**insofar as it follows the rotation of the heavens**—will cause motion in this inferior subject. This heat and celestial motion cannot exist without the life of the thing in which they reside—**I mean a formal life, rather than an animal or even a vegetable one**—and from these, ferments are produced by the altering *Blas* <note>original: "Blas alterantem." A term coined by Jean Baptiste van Helmont to describe a vital, transformative force or "astral motion" within matter.</note>. These ferments daily change and transmute matter for as long as the celestial power predominates, inducing a greater or lesser degree of fixity according to the suitability of the location which either aids or retards the **digestion** <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturation or refining through gentle heat.</note>. According to this disproportion of digestion, from one and the same Mother, the aforementioned differing offspring [the various metals] come forth, diversified only by the inequality of their maturity. By reason of this inequality, some crude superfluities—which are not of a metallic nature, but are in **Mercury** <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> and are separable from **Mercury**—are not purged away. Instead, taking on coagulation along with the pure substance, they seem to differentiate <note>original: "specificare," to determine the specific species of a metal</note> the metals. These drossy crudities vary according to the variation of the generating **Mercurial** womb, and are coagulated in different ways according to the differences of the place this **Embryo** <note>The developing metal within the earth.</note> occupies. Therefore, there is but one material for all metals: namely, **Mercury**, which properly strives toward the procreation of **Gold** <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note>. Whether due to a different respect in the degree of perfection, or if any dross was mixed into the **Mercury** during its generation, these things are accidental and do not enter into the essential **Mercurial** substance. Through the diversity of these [impurities] and the difference of the location where the digestion occurs, from the various coagulations of different dross with this one pure substance, the same single thing puts on various masks, and thus produces the imperfect metals according to their species. I would avoid a detailed description of the genealogy of all metals, because I am hastening only toward the renewal and multiplication of **Gold** and **Silver** <note>original: "Solis tantum & Lunæ," literally "of the Sun and Moon."</note>. Therefore, I set myself to the task at hand.

**F**rom the aforementioned source, as has been said, the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol," the alchemical name for Gold</note> was born, along with his sister the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note>: specifically when this matter has been brought to perfection through **digestion** <note>The alchemical process of maturing or refining matter through steady, gentle heat.</note>. Furthermore, perfection is twofold: either begun or complete—that is, partial or total. Complete perfection is the ultimate goal toward which Nature herself aims: namely, that once all **crudity** <note>Raw, unrefined, or "uncooked" matter.</note> has been cooked away and all dross purged, the pure metallic nature triumphs, **coagulated** <note>Solidified from a liquid or vaporous state.</note> without any filth. Here our Sun has its origin, and illuminates the earth with its radiance and splendor.

**Partial perfection**, however—as it were—is not perfection properly so called, and yet, in respect to that which is formally imperfect, it deserves to be called perfection not improperly. For it is to be judged a formal imperfection when the crudity—which was adhering to the pure substance during generation by accident—is not cooked away, nor is the heterogeneous superfluity purged. Rather, it is left mixed with the pure substance during coagulation in such a large quantity that it predominates over it, and finally overcomes it. This happens to all metals <note>such as lead, tin, copper, and iron</note>—**except the Sun and Moon**—which are easily corrupted by all the corrupting Elements and are likewise consumed by fire. 

But when crudity is so defeated, and the drossy superfluity is so purged before coagulation, that the pure substance holds dominion over the impure—being freed from its corruptive tyranny—this is to be considered the first degree of perfection. Indeed, the total purging of dregs and the rejection of the impure is the **crowning achievement** <note>original: "colophon," a finishing stroke or peak</note> or highest perfection of metallic operations. And yet, these crudities and dross were not originally of the same nature or substance as the metallic <term>Mercury <gloss>represented by the symbol ☿</gloss></term>; rather, they were separable. Their separation before coagulation constitutes the perfection of the Metal. 

Truly, if they were not purged before their **congealing** <note>The transition from a fluid state to a solid state in the earth.</note>, this process nevertheless in no way united them into a single substance with the pure part; instead, they remain separable even now. Although they cannot be separated by nature alone without some other assistance, they can be separated through **Art** <note>Alchemy</note> acting as the minister of nature. 

Hence the basis and origin of the Art of Transmutation, and the true foundation of **Alchemy**: namely, that an impure Metal possesses within itself the same pure substance from which **Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> is made. Although some impurity is coagulated along with it, this impurity is by no means of a metallic nature, even though the imperfect Metal...

### C H A P T E R IV.

## *Concerning the Seed of Gold: Also, a determination of the question whether other Metals have Seed.*

**F**or the sake of preserving, propagating, and producing every species, a seed was established for all things by the **Great Creator**. The seed is the perfection of each thing; and that which has no seed must rightfully be judged as imperfect. Therefore, it cannot be doubted that a metallic seed exists. For either all these things that are and have been in the world were created in the first six days, or at the very least, they have grown and increased daily. Reason and experience deny the former <note>The idea that all metal ever to exist was created at once during the biblical creation week.</note>; therefore, if the latter is true, then surely no one can deny that a metallic seed exists. 

And if it is granted that this seed exists, then certainly a Metal does not lose it during **coagulation** <note>The process by which a liquid or "vaporous" metal hardens into a solid mass.</note>. For coagulation is the effect <gloss>m</gloss> [or rather the result of **maturation**, which leads directly to perfection if external conditions have been lawfully arranged]. Furthermore, the sign of perfection is its seed, which is thus matured; it is therefore not probable that the seed is lost through coagulation, but rather that it is rendered more noble. It is clear through this that a metallic seed is present in Metals. It may therefore be asked whether all metals have seed in themselves, and I would respond by positing: They all have one and the same seed, but...
